The defect lowers NADPH.
Low NADPH prevents regeneration of reduced glutathione
Correct: RBCs depend on the PPP for NADPH, so peroxides accumulate.
questions.x: Red cells have no mitochondria, so the pentose phosphate pathway is their only NADPH source. NADPH keeps glutathione reduced, and reduced glutathione detoxifies hydrogen peroxide and other oxidants. With G6PD deficiency, an oxidant stress (certain drugs, fava beans, infection) overwhelms this defense, hemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies, and cells hemolyze.

questions.q: NADPH is required for all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Fatty acid synthesis
Fatty acid synthase uses NADPH for both reduction steps.
Cholesterol synthesis
HMG-CoA reductase uses NADPH.
The neutrophil respiratory burst
NADPH oxidase uses NADPH to make superoxide.
β-oxidation of fatty acids
Correct: β-oxidation produces FADH₂ and NADH and uses no NADPH.
questions.x: NADPH is the cell's reducing currency for anabolism and antioxidant work: fatty acid synthase, HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol synthesis, NADPH oxidase in the neutrophil respiratory burst, and glutathione reductase all consume it. β-Oxidation is catabolic, removing electrons from fatty acids and passing them to FAD and NAD⁺, so it generates FADH₂ and NADH instead.

questions.q: A cell needs large amounts of NADPH but little ribose-5-phosphate. What happens to the excess pentose phosphates?
o: They are excreted as ribose
Cells recycle pentoses.
Transketolase and transaldolase convert them to F6P and G3P
Correct: the non-oxidative phase recycles carbon into glycolytic intermediates.
They are oxidized to CO₂ by 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase
That enzyme acts before the pentoses form.
They are stored as glycogen directly
Pentoses are not added to glycogen.
questions.x: When NADPH demand outstrips the need for ribose, the non-oxidative phase recycles carbon. Transketolase moves two-carbon units and transaldolase moves three-carbon units among sugar phosphates, converting three pentoses into two fructose-6-phosphates and one glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. These can re-enter glycolysis or be recycled to G6P for more NADPH.

questions.q: Which vitamin-derived cofactor does transketolase require?
o: Pyridoxal phosphate
PLP (B₆) is used for transamination.
Biotin
Biotin is a carboxylation cofactor.
Thiamine pyrophosphate
Correct: TPP (vitamin B₁) carries two-carbon units.
Tetrahydrofolate
THF carries one-carbon units.
questions.x: Transketolase transfers two-carbon ketol units between sugar phosphates and uses thiamine pyrophosphate (from vitamin B₁) as its cofactor, like pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Red cell transketolase activity is used clinically to assess thiamine status. Biotin serves carboxylases, PLP serves transaminases, and THF carries one-carbon units.

questions.q: In which tissue is pentose phosphate pathway activity lowest?
o: Liver
The liver needs NADPH for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis.
Adrenal cortex
Steroid synthesis requires much NADPH.
Lactating mammary gland
Milk fat synthesis demands NADPH.
Skeletal muscle
Correct: muscle does little fatty acid or steroid synthesis.
questions.x: Pentose phosphate pathway activity tracks NADPH demand. Liver, adrenal cortex and lactating mammary gland do heavy fatty acid or steroid synthesis, and red cells need NADPH for glutathione, so their PPP flux is high. Skeletal muscle does little reductive biosynthesis and devotes its glucose to ATP production, so its PPP activity is low.

questions.q: A rapidly dividing cell needs lots of ribose-5-phosphate but little NADPH. How can it obtain ribose?
o: By running the oxidative phase in reverse
The oxidative phase is irreversible.
By converting acetyl-CoA to ribose
Acetyl-CoA cannot make sugars in humans.
By reducing ribose from deoxyribose
Deoxyribose is made from ribose, not the reverse.
By running the non-oxidative phase in reverse from F6P and G3P
Correct: transketolase and transaldolase are reversible.
questions.x: Only the oxidative phase of the PPP is irreversible; the non-oxidative transketolase and transaldolase reactions are near equilibrium. A dividing cell needing ribose but not NADPH can run them backward, combining fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate from glycolysis into ribose-5-phosphate. This makes ribose without producing NADPH or losing CO₂.

questions.q: Cells keep the NAD⁺/NADH ratio high, while keeping the NADPH/NADP⁺ ratio high. What does this arrangement allow?
o: NADPH to donate electrons to the ETC
NADPH is not a major ETC substrate.
NAD⁺ drives oxidations while NADPH drives reductive biosynthesis
Correct: separate pools let catabolism and anabolism proceed together.
NAD⁺ to be used in fatty acid synthesis
Fatty acid synthesis uses NADPH.
Both coenzymes to be interchangeable
Enzymes are specific for one or the other.
questions.x: A high NAD⁺/NADH ratio means NAD⁺ is readily available to accept electrons in catabolic oxidations like glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. A high NADPH/NADP⁺ ratio means NADPH is readily available to donate electrons in reductive biosynthesis. Because enzymes distinguish the two by the extra phosphate, oxidation and reduction can proceed at the same time in the same cell.

questions.q: What is the immediate product of glycogen phosphorylase acting on glycogen?
o: Free glucose
Free glucose comes only from debranching at α(1→6) links.
Glucose-1-phosphate
Correct: phosphorolysis uses Pi to cleave α(1→4) bonds.
Glucose-6-phosphate
G6P forms from G1P via phosphoglucomutase.
UDP-glucose
UDP-glucose is the donor for glycogen synthesis.
questions.x: Glycogen phosphorylase cleaves α(1→4) bonds using inorganic phosphate rather than water (phosphorolysis), so it releases glucose-1-phosphate. Phosphoglucomutase then converts G1P to G6P for glycolysis or, in liver, for glucose release. Only the debranching enzyme's hydrolysis of α(1→6) branch points releases free glucose, about one residue in ten.

questions.q: What is the activated glucose donor used by glycogen synthase?
o: Glucose-6-phosphate
G6P is converted to G1P, then activated as UDP-glucose.
ADP-glucose
ADP-glucose is used for starch in plants.
UDP-glucose
Correct: UTP and glucose-1-P form UDP-glucose, whose glucose is added to the chain.
Free glucose
Free glucose lacks the energy needed for the transfer.
questions.x: Glycogen synthesis requires an activated donor. Glucose-1-phosphate reacts with UTP to form UDP-glucose plus pyrophosphate, which is hydrolyzed to make the step irreversible. Glycogen synthase then transfers glucose from UDP-glucose to the nonreducing end of a chain, forming an α(1→4) bond. Plants use ADP-glucose for starch, a common mix-up.

questions.q: What linkage does glycogen branching enzyme create?
o: Correct: it moves a segment of chain to form a branch.
Glycogen synthase makes α(1→4) links.
β(1→4) linkages are found in cellulose.
Glycogen has no β linkages.
questions.x: Glycogen synthase only extends chains with α(1→4) bonds. Branching enzyme (a 4:6 transferase) moves a block of about 6 to 8 residues from the end of a chain and attaches it to an interior residue through an α(1→6) bond. Branches increase solubility and the number of nonreducing ends for rapid synthesis and breakdown; glycogen has no β linkages.

questions.q: When glycogen phosphorylase reaches four residues from a branch point, debranching enzyme acts. What does its α-1,6-glucosidase activity release?
o: Glucose-1-phosphate
That product comes from phosphorylase.
A trisaccharide
The transferase moves three residues to another chain.
UDP-glucose
UDP-glucose is not a breakdown product.
Free glucose
Correct: hydrolysis of the branch point yields one free glucose.
questions.x: Phosphorylase stops four residues from an α(1→6) branch. Debranching enzyme then acts twice: its transferase moves three of those residues onto another chain end, and its α-1,6-glucosidase hydrolyzes the remaining branch residue. Because that bond is cleaved by water rather than phosphate, the product is free glucose, not glucose-1-phosphate.

questions.q: During exercise, epinephrine raises muscle cAMP. What happens to glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase?
o: Phosphorylase is activated; synthase is inactivated
Correct: PKA-driven phosphorylation activates breakdown and blocks synthesis.
Both are activated
Both active would create a futile cycle.
Phosphorylase is inactivated; synthase is activated
That is the pattern after insulin.
Both are inactivated
Exercise requires glycogen breakdown.
questions.x: Epinephrine raises cAMP and activates PKA, which phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase and glycogen synthase. Phosphorylase kinase then phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase, while phosphorylation inactivates glycogen synthase. One phosphorylation signal thus turns breakdown on and synthesis off together, avoiding a futile cycle.

questions.q: After a carbohydrate meal, insulin promotes glycogen synthesis. Which enzyme mediates this by removing phosphates?
o: Protein kinase A
PKA adds phosphates and promotes breakdown.
Phosphorylase kinase
This kinase activates phosphorylase.
Protein phosphatase-1
Correct: PP1 dephosphorylates and activates glycogen synthase and inactivates phosphorylase.
Adenylyl cyclase
Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, which insulin opposes.
questions.x: Insulin reverses the effects of glucagon and epinephrine largely by activating protein phosphatase-1. PP1 removes phosphates from glycogen synthase (activating it), and from glycogen phosphorylase and phosphorylase kinase (inactivating them). The net result is a switch from glycogen breakdown to storage after a carbohydrate meal.

questions.q: During muscle contraction without hormonal input, glycogen breakdown still increases. What activates it?
o: Ca²⁺ binding to phosphorylase kinase and AMP binding to phosphorylase
Correct: contraction signals activate breakdown directly.
Glucagon binding to muscle receptors
Muscle lacks significant glucagon receptors.
A rise in muscle ATP
High ATP inhibits phosphorylase.
Insulin activation of PP1
Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis.
questions.x: Muscle links glycogen breakdown directly to contraction. Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds the calmodulin subunit of phosphorylase kinase and activates it, and rising AMP from ATP use allosterically activates glycogen phosphorylase b even without phosphorylation. Muscle lacks glucagon receptors, and high ATP inhibits phosphorylase.

questions.q: A patient has painful cramps on exercise, and blood lactate fails to rise during an exercise test. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
o: Hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase
That causes fasting hypoglycemia with high lactate.
Lactate dehydrogenase in liver
Hepatic LDH would not stop muscle lactate production.
Muscle carnitine palmitoyltransferase II
CPT II deficiency impairs fat oxidation, but glycolysis is intact, so lactate rises normally.
Muscle glycogen phosphorylase
Correct: muscle cannot break glycogen, so little lactate forms (McArdle disease).
questions.x: During intense exercise, muscle relies on its own glycogen, broken down by muscle glycogen phosphorylase and run through glycolysis to lactate. In McArdle disease that phosphorylase is missing, so exercise causes cramps and fatigue and blood lactate fails to rise. Liver glycogen metabolism is normal, so there is no fasting hypoglycemia, unlike liver enzyme defects.

questions.q: How do the roles of liver glycogen and muscle glycogen differ?
o: Both mainly maintain blood glucose
Muscle cannot export free glucose.
Liver glycogen maintains blood glucose; muscle glycogen fuels the muscle itself
Correct: only the liver has glucose-6-phosphatase to release glucose.
Muscle glycogen maintains blood glucose; liver glycogen fuels the liver
The roles are reversed.
Both serve only as a structural reserve
Glycogen is a fuel store.
questions.x: Liver glycogen is a glucose reserve for the whole body: liver has glucose-6-phosphatase, so G6P from glycogen can be released into blood between meals. Muscle glycogen is a private fuel: muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so G6P stays in the cell and feeds glycolysis during contraction. This difference also explains why their hormonal and allosteric controls differ.

questions.q: Which protein serves as the primer for new glycogen synthesis?
o: Glycogen synthase
Synthase extends chains but needs a primer.
Branching enzyme
Branching enzyme rearranges existing chains.
Phosphoglucomutase
It interconverts G1P and G6P.
Glycogenin
Correct: it attaches glucose to its own tyrosine, starting a chain.
questions.x: Glycogen synthase can only add glucose to an existing chain, so it needs a primer. Glycogenin is a self-glucosylating protein that attaches the first glucose (from UDP-glucose) to one of its own tyrosine residues and extends a short chain. Glycogen synthase and branching enzyme then build the particle, which stays anchored to glycogenin.

questions.q: Glycogen synthase is inactivated by phosphorylation. Which metabolite can still allosterically activate the phosphorylated form?
o: Glucose-6-phosphate
Correct: high G6P signals glucose abundance and stimulates storage.
AMP
AMP activates phosphorylase.
Ca²⁺
Ca²⁺ promotes glycogen breakdown in muscle.
cAMP
cAMP leads to synthase phosphorylation and inactivation.
questions.x: Phosphorylation by PKA or GSK-3 converts glycogen synthase to its less active b form, but high glucose-6-phosphate allosterically activates even the phosphorylated enzyme. This feedforward control lets abundant substrate drive storage regardless of hormone status. AMP and Ca²⁺ are energy-demand signals that promote breakdown, not synthesis.

questions.q: In liver, glycogen phosphorylase a is inhibited when glucose binds it. What is the physiologic significance?
o: It stops glycogen breakdown when blood glucose is already high
Correct: liver phosphorylase acts as a glucose sensor.
It keeps glycogenolysis running after meals
Glucose binding stops breakdown.
It stimulates insulin release
That is a pancreatic β-cell function.
It converts glucose into glycogen directly
Phosphorylase does not synthesize glycogen.
questions.x: Liver phosphorylase a has a binding site for glucose. When blood (and hepatocyte) glucose is high, glucose binds and stabilizes the inactive T state, and it also exposes the enzyme's phosphate to PP1 for removal. This lets the liver shut off glycogen breakdown as soon as glucose is plentiful, acting as a built-in glucose sensor.

questions.q: After about 24 hours without food, which change in hepatic glucose output is expected?
o: Liver glycogen still supplies nearly all glucose
Liver glycogen is mostly gone by then.
Muscle glycogen releases free glucose
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.
Gluconeogenesis supplies most glucose as liver glycogen is largely depleted
Correct: liver glycogen lasts roughly a day.
The liver stops releasing glucose
Blood glucose is maintained by gluconeogenesis.
questions.x: Liver glycogen stores roughly 100 g of glucose, enough to support blood glucose for about 12 to 24 hours of fasting. As it runs out, gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids becomes the main source of hepatic glucose output. Muscle glycogen cannot help directly, because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.

questions.q: Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate into which products?
o: Oxaloacetate, ATP and NADH
Oxaloacetate comes from pyruvate carboxylase.
Acetyl-CoA, CO₂ and NADH
Correct: an oxidative decarboxylation in the mitochondrial matrix.
Lactate and NAD⁺
Those are lactate dehydrogenase products.
Acetaldehyde and CO₂
That is yeast pyruvate decarboxylase.
questions.x: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in the mitochondrial matrix performs an oxidative decarboxylation: pyruvate loses its carboxyl as CO₂, the remaining two-carbon unit is attached to CoA as acetyl-CoA, and the electrons reduce NAD⁺ to NADH. This irreversible step links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle. Carboxylation to oxaloacetate is a separate enzyme, pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.q: Which cofactor is NOT required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
o: Thiamine pyrophosphate
TPP decarboxylates pyruvate in E1.
Biotin
Correct: biotin serves carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase.
Lipoic acid
Lipoamide carries the acetyl group in E2.
FAD
FAD reoxidizes lipoamide in E3.
questions.note: PDH cofactors: TPP, lipoate, CoA, FAD, NAD⁺.
questions.x: PDH uses five cofactors: thiamine pyrophosphate (E1 decarboxylation), lipoic acid and coenzyme A (E2 acetyl transfer), and FAD and NAD⁺ (E3 reoxidation of lipoamide). Biotin is instead the CO₂ carrier for carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Recall the B vitamins behind PDH: B₁, B₂, B₃ and B₅, plus lipoate.

questions.q: A malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use has elevated blood pyruvate and lactate. A deficiency of which vitamin best explains this?
o: Vitamin C
Vitamin C deficiency affects collagen synthesis.
Vitamin K
Vitamin K is needed for clotting factor carboxylation.
Thiamine (B₁)
Correct: TPP is required by PDH, so pyruvate backs up and is converted to lactate.
Cobalamin (B₁₂)
B₁₂ deficiency raises methylmalonic acid, not pyruvate.
questions.x: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase's E1 subunit, as well as α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase. Chronic alcohol use and malnutrition commonly cause thiamine deficiency, so pyruvate cannot enter the citric acid cycle; it accumulates and is diverted to lactate, causing lactic acidosis. B₁₂ deficiency instead raises methylmalonic acid and homocysteine.

questions.q: High mitochondrial ratios of NADH/NAD⁺ and acetyl-CoA/CoA decrease PDH activity mainly by which mechanism?
o: Activating PDH kinase, which phosphorylates and inactivates PDH
Correct: products signal that energy is plentiful.
Activating PDH phosphatase
The phosphatase would activate PDH.
Degrading the PDH complex
Regulation is rapid and reversible.
Increasing pyruvate transport into mitochondria
This would not decrease PDH activity.
questions.x: PDH is controlled mainly by reversible phosphorylation. Its products, NADH and acetyl-CoA, activate PDH kinase, which phosphorylates and inactivates the E1 subunit, so PDH slows when energy and acetyl-CoA are plentiful. PDH phosphatase does the opposite, reactivating the complex, and it is stimulated by Ca²⁺ and insulin.

questions.q: During vigorous contraction, PDH activity in skeletal muscle rises. Which signal most directly causes this?
o: Rising ATP inhibiting PDH phosphatase
High ATP would not activate PDH.
Ca²⁺ activating PDH phosphatase
Correct: contraction-linked Ca²⁺ dephosphorylates and activates PDH.
Glucagon acting on muscle
Muscle has few glucagon receptors.
Acetyl-CoA activating PDH directly
Acetyl-CoA inhibits PDH.
questions.x: Muscle contraction releases Ca²⁺, which activates PDH phosphatase and also several citric acid cycle dehydrogenases. Dephosphorylated PDH is active, so pyruvate oxidation rises to match ATP demand. ADP and pyruvate also inhibit PDH kinase, while ATP, NADH and acetyl-CoA activate the kinase and inactivate PDH.

questions.q: Dichloroacetate inhibits PDH kinase. In a patient with lactic acidosis, what effect is expected?
o: PDH is inactivated, so lactate rises
Inhibiting the kinase prevents inactivation.
PDH stays active, so more pyruvate is oxidized and lactate falls
Correct: blocking the kinase keeps PDH dephosphorylated.
Gluconeogenesis increases, so lactate rises
Dichloroacetate's action shifts pyruvate toward oxidation.
Glycolysis stops completely
Dichloroacetate acts downstream of glycolysis.
questions.x: PDH kinase inactivates PDH by phosphorylation. Dichloroacetate inhibits the kinase, so PDH stays in its dephosphorylated, active form and oxidizes more pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. Less pyruvate is left to be reduced by lactate dehydrogenase, so lactate falls; this is the rationale for using dichloroacetate in some lactic acidosis disorders.

questions.q: Arsenite poisoning inhibits both PDH and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. What do these complexes share that explains this?
o: A biotin prosthetic group
Neither complex uses biotin.
A heme iron center
These complexes contain no heme.
An ATP binding site
They do not use ATP.
A lipoamide cofactor
Correct: arsenite binds the two thiols of reduced lipoamide.
questions.x: PDH and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are homologous multienzyme complexes that both use TPP, lipoamide, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺. During catalysis lipoamide cycles to a reduced form with two adjacent thiol groups, and arsenite binds both thiols tightly, locking the cofactor. Both complexes stall, so pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate oxidation fail and ATP production collapses.

questions.q: Where does the citric acid cycle take place in eukaryotic cells?
o: Mitochondrial matrix
Correct: all cycle enzymes are in the matrix except succinate dehydrogenase, in the inner membrane.
Cytosol
Glycolysis, not the citric acid cycle, is cytosolic.
Intermembrane space
The intermembrane space accumulates pumped H⁺.
Outer mitochondrial membrane
The outer membrane is permeable and houses no cycle enzymes.
questions.x: Pyruvate enters mitochondria and is converted to acetyl-CoA in the matrix, where the citric acid cycle enzymes are dissolved. The one exception is succinate dehydrogenase, which is embedded in the inner membrane because it doubles as Complex II of the electron transport chain. Glycolysis, by contrast, is cytosolic.

questions.q: One turn of the citric acid cycle per acetyl-CoA produces which set of products?
o: 2 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂
Only succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD.
3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 2 GTP, 3 CO₂
One GTP and two CO₂ per turn.
4 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂
Four NADH counts PDH, which is not part of the cycle.
3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂
Correct: three dehydrogenases use NAD⁺, one uses FAD, and one step makes GTP.
questions.x: Per acetyl-CoA, the cycle has three NAD⁺-linked dehydrogenases (isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, malate), one FAD-linked step (succinate dehydrogenase), and one substrate-level phosphorylation (succinyl-CoA synthetase, making GTP or ATP). Two carbons leave as CO₂, matching the two carbons acetyl-CoA brought in. The NADH from pyruvate dehydrogenase comes before the cycle and is not counted.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the first step of the citric acid cycle, joining acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate?
o: Aconitase
Aconitase isomerizes citrate to isocitrate.
Pyruvate carboxylase
It makes oxaloacetate but does not join it to acetyl-CoA.
Malate dehydrogenase
It regenerates oxaloacetate at the end of the cycle.
Citrate synthase
Correct: the condensation forms citrate.
questions.x: Citrate synthase condenses the two-carbon acetyl group of acetyl-CoA with four-carbon oxaloacetate to form six-carbon citrate, releasing CoA. Hydrolysis of the thioester makes this step strongly exergonic, which helps pull the unfavorable malate dehydrogenase step forward. Pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate but is an anaplerotic enzyme, not part of the cycle.

questions.q: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the main control point of the citric acid cycle. Which condition increases its activity?
o: High NADH
NADH is a product and inhibits the enzyme.
High ATP
ATP signals energy surplus and inhibits it.
High succinyl-CoA
Succinyl-CoA inhibits α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase; it does not activate this enzyme.
High ADP and Ca²⁺
Correct: these signal energy demand.
questions.x: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting step of the citric acid cycle and responds to the cell's energy state. ADP signals that ATP is being used, and Ca²⁺ signals muscle contraction, so both activate the enzyme. ATP and NADH signal abundant energy and inhibit it, so cycle flux tracks ATP demand.

questions.q: Which citric acid cycle enzyme is also a component of the electron transport chain?
o: Isocitrate dehydrogenase
It is soluble in the matrix.
Fumarase
Fumarase is a soluble hydratase.
Citrate synthase
Citrate synthase is a soluble matrix enzyme.
Succinate dehydrogenase
Correct: it is Complex II, passing electrons from FADH₂ to ubiquinone.
questions.x: Succinate dehydrogenase oxidizes succinate to fumarate using covalently bound FAD, then passes the electrons through iron–sulfur clusters to ubiquinone. Because it is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, it is also Complex II of the electron transport chain. Unlike Complexes I, III and IV, it pumps no protons.

questions.q: Malonate is a structural analog of succinate. When added to respiring mitochondria, which intermediate accumulates?
o: Fumarate
Fumarate is the product, which would be depleted.
Citrate
Citrate lies upstream; succinate accumulates directly before the block.
Succinate
Correct: malonate competitively inhibits succinate dehydrogenase.
Oxaloacetate
OAA lies downstream and would fall.
questions.x: Malonate resembles succinate, binds the active site of succinate dehydrogenase, and competitively inhibits it. Blocking an enzyme causes its substrate to pile up and its products downstream to be depleted, so succinate accumulates while fumarate, malate and oxaloacetate fall. Competitive inhibition can be overcome by raising succinate concentration.

questions.q: Which citric acid cycle step involves substrate-level phosphorylation?
o: Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate
This step releases CO₂ and NADH.
Fumarate → malate
This is a hydration.
Succinyl-CoA → succinate
Correct: succinyl-CoA synthetase uses the thioester's energy to make GTP or ATP.
Citrate → isocitrate
This is an isomerization.
questions.x: Substrate-level phosphorylation makes a nucleoside triphosphate directly from a high-energy substrate, without the ETC. In the citric acid cycle, succinyl-CoA synthetase uses the energy of succinyl-CoA's thioester bond to phosphorylate GDP (or ADP), releasing succinate and CoA. The other choices are a decarboxylation, a hydration, and an isomerization.

questions.q: Fluoroacetate is converted in cells to fluorocitrate, which inhibits aconitase. Which change is expected?
o: Isocitrate accumulates
Isocitrate is the product, which is depleted.
Succinate accumulates
Succinate lies far downstream of the block.
Citrate accumulates and NADH production falls
Correct: the cycle stalls before the first dehydrogenase.
O₂ consumption rises
Less NADH means less electron flow and less O₂ use.
questions.x: Fluorocitrate blocks aconitase, which converts citrate to isocitrate, so citrate builds up behind the block. Everything downstream, including the NADH-producing isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate and malate dehydrogenase steps, is starved of substrate. Less NADH means less electron flow to O₂, so respiration and ATP production fall, which is why fluoroacetate is a lethal poison.

questions.q: Liver cells exporting citrate for fatty acid synthesis must replace oxaloacetate. Which reaction is the main anaplerotic source?
o: Pyruvate dehydrogenase converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
Acetyl-CoA does not cause net gain of intermediates.
Citrate synthase forming citrate
This consumes oxaloacetate.
Pyruvate carboxylase converting pyruvate to oxaloacetate
Correct: it refills cycle intermediates.
β-oxidation of palmitate
Even-chain fatty acids give only acetyl-CoA.
questions.x: Anaplerotic reactions replace cycle intermediates that are withdrawn for biosynthesis, such as citrate exported for fatty acid synthesis. Pyruvate carboxylase adds CO₂ to pyruvate to make new oxaloacetate, giving a net gain of four-carbon intermediates. Acetyl-CoA from PDH or β-oxidation cannot do this, because its two carbons are matched by the two CO₂ lost each turn.

questions.q: Acetyl-CoA labeled with ¹⁴C in both carbons enters the citric acid cycle. How many labeled carbons are released as CO₂ in the first turn?
o: Correct: both CO₂ in the first turn come from oxaloacetate's carbons.
The label is first lost in later turns.
That counts acetyl-CoA carbons as the ones released immediately.
Only two CO₂ are released per turn.
questions.x: The two CO₂ released in the first turn (at isocitrate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) come from carbons that originated in oxaloacetate, not from the incoming acetyl group. The acetyl carbons end up in succinate, which is symmetric, so the label is scrambled into regenerated oxaloacetate. It begins to be released as CO₂ only in the second and later turns.

questions.q: The citric acid cycle uses no O₂ directly, yet it stops in anoxia. Why?
o: NAD⁺ and FAD are not regenerated without the ETC
Correct: without O₂, NADH and FADH₂ accumulate and the dehydrogenases stall.
O₂ is a cofactor for citrate synthase
Citrate synthase uses no O₂.
Without O₂ acetyl-CoA is converted to glucose
Acetyl-CoA cannot be made into glucose.
Anoxia degrades mitochondrial DNA
That is not why the cycle stops acutely.
questions.x: The citric acid cycle depends on NAD⁺ and FAD for its oxidation steps. These are regenerated only when NADH and FADH₂ pass electrons to the ETC, which needs O₂ as the final acceptor. In anoxia, NADH accumulates, NAD⁺ runs out, and the dehydrogenases stop, so the cycle depends indirectly on O₂ even though no step consumes it.

questions.q: Succinyl-CoA is withdrawn from the citric acid cycle for which biosynthetic pathway?
o: Fatty acid synthesis
Fatty acid synthesis uses exported citrate.
Glutamate synthesis
Glutamate comes from α-ketoglutarate.
Cholesterol synthesis
Cholesterol comes from acetyl-CoA.
Heme synthesis
Correct: succinyl-CoA and glycine form δ-aminolevulinic acid.
questions.x: Citric acid cycle intermediates feed biosynthesis: citrate supplies acetyl-CoA for fatty acids, α-ketoglutarate supplies glutamate, oxaloacetate supplies aspartate and glucose, and succinyl-CoA condenses with glycine in the first step of heme synthesis, catalyzed by ALA synthase. Cholesterol is built from acetyl-CoA, not succinyl-CoA.

questions.q: Fumarase converts fumarate to L-malate. What type of reaction is this?
o: Oxidation
No electrons are removed in this step.
Hydration
Correct: water is added across fumarate's double bond.
Decarboxylation
No CO₂ is released.
Isomerization
A water molecule is added, so it is not a rearrangement.
questions.x: Fumarase adds water across the trans double bond of fumarate, forming L-malate stereospecifically. A hydration adds H and OH without removing electrons or carbon, so it is not an oxidation or a decarboxylation. The next step, malate dehydrogenase, is the oxidation that regenerates oxaloacetate and produces NADH.

questions.q: About how many ATP are made from complete oxidation of one acetyl-CoA via the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation? (2.5 ATP/NADH, 1.5 ATP/FADH₂)
o: Uses older values of 3 ATP/NADH and 2 ATP/FADH₂.
Counts only the three NADH, omitting the FADH₂ and the GTP.
Omits the GTP from succinyl-CoA synthetase.
questions.x: Each acetyl-CoA yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP in the cycle. Using current estimates, 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 ATP from NADH, plus 1.5 from FADH₂, plus 1 from GTP gives 10 ATP. The older value of 12 comes from assuming 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH₂, ratios that overstate how many protons each ATP needs.

questions.q: With 2.5 ATP/NADH, 1.5 ATP/FADH₂ and the malate–aspartate shuttle, about how many ATP come from complete oxidation of one glucose?
o: About 38
That uses older P/O values of 3 and 2.
About 32
Correct: glycolysis 2 + 2 NADH (5) + PDH 2 NADH (5) + 2 cycle turns (20) = 32.
About 30
That fits the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle.
About 20
That counts only the two citric acid cycle turns.
questions.x: Tally per glucose: glycolysis gives 2 ATP and 2 cytosolic NADH (5 ATP via the malate–aspartate shuttle); PDH gives 2 NADH (5 ATP); two cycle turns give 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂ and 2 GTP (15 + 3 + 2 = 20). Total is about 32 ATP. With the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, cytosolic NADH yields only 1.5 ATP each, lowering the total to about 30.

questions.q: Which citric acid cycle intermediate has six carbons?
o: α-Ketoglutarate
α-Ketoglutarate has five carbons.
Succinate
Succinate has four carbons.
Malate
Malate has four carbons.
Citrate
Correct: two carbons from acetyl-CoA plus four from oxaloacetate.
questions.x: Citrate forms when two-carbon acetyl-CoA joins four-carbon oxaloacetate, giving six carbons. Isocitrate is also six carbons, but each of the next two steps releases one CO₂: α-ketoglutarate has five carbons, and succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate, malate and oxaloacetate all have four. Track the carbons to place each intermediate.

questions.q: Where are the electron transport chain complexes located?
o: Outer mitochondrial membrane
The outer membrane is porous and cannot hold a gradient.
Mitochondrial matrix
The matrix contains soluble cycle enzymes.
Cytosol
Prokaryotes use the plasma membrane; eukaryotes the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Inner mitochondrial membrane
Correct: they pump H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
questions.x: In eukaryotes, Complexes I to IV and ATP synthase are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is folded into cristae and is impermeable to protons. As electrons pass along the chain, protons are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building the proton-motive force. The outer membrane is porous and cannot hold a gradient; bacteria use their plasma membrane.

questions.q: What is the final electron acceptor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
o: NAD⁺, reduced to NADH
NADH donates electrons at the start of the chain.
O₂, reduced to H₂O
Correct: Complex IV passes electrons to oxygen.
CO₂, reduced to glucose
That occurs in photosynthesis.
Cytochrome c
Cytochrome c is an intermediate carrier.
questions.x: Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ move through the chain toward carriers of ever higher reduction potential, ending at Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), which transfers them to O₂ to form water. O₂ has the most positive reduction potential, making it the ideal terminal acceptor. Without O₂, electrons back up and the whole chain stops, as happens in cyanide poisoning.

questions.q: Why does FADH₂ from succinate yield fewer ATP than NADH?
o: FADH₂ carries only one electron
FADH₂ carries two electrons.
FADH₂ electrons bypass Complex IV
All electrons reach O₂ via Complex IV.
Its electrons enter at Complex II, which pumps no protons
Correct: bypassing Complex I yields about 1.5 vs 2.5 ATP.
FADH₂ is oxidized in the cytosol
Succinate dehydrogenase is in the inner membrane.
questions.x: NADH donates electrons to Complex I, which pumps protons, and they then pass through Complexes III and IV, which also pump. Succinate's electrons go through FADH₂ at Complex II, which pumps none, and join the chain at coenzyme Q. Fewer protons are pumped per electron pair (about 6 versus 10), so FADH₂ yields about 1.5 ATP versus 2.5.

questions.q: Which electron carrier is a small lipid-soluble molecule that moves within the membrane from Complexes I and II to Complex III?
o: Cytochrome c
Cytochrome c is a water-soluble protein in the intermembrane space.
Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone)
Correct: its hydrophobic tail lets it diffuse within the bilayer.
NADH
NADH is soluble in the matrix.
FAD
FAD is bound tightly to Complex II.
questions.x: Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) has a long hydrophobic isoprenoid tail, letting it diffuse within the lipid bilayer and collect electrons from Complex I, Complex II and other flavoproteins, then deliver them to Complex III. Cytochrome c, by contrast, is a small water-soluble protein in the intermembrane space that shuttles electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.

questions.q: Cytochrome c carries electrons between which components of the ETC?
o: Complex III and Complex IV
Correct: it shuttles one electron at a time in the intermembrane space.
Complex I and Complex III
Coenzyme Q connects Complexes I and III.
Complex II and Complex III
Coenzyme Q links these complexes.
Complex IV and O₂
Complex IV reduces O₂ directly.
questions.x: Cytochrome c is a small, water-soluble heme protein loosely bound to the outer face of the inner membrane. It accepts one electron at a time from Complex III and delivers it to Complex IV, which reduces O₂. Coenzyme Q is the mobile carrier from Complexes I and II to Complex III; release of cytochrome c into the cytosol also triggers apoptosis.

questions.q: Electrons flow spontaneously through the ETC in which direction?
o: From higher to lower reduction potential
That would be uphill and endergonic.
From carriers of lower reduction potential to higher reduction potential
Correct: they move toward O₂, which has the most positive E°′.
From O₂ toward NADH
O₂ is the final acceptor.
Randomly between any two carriers
The sequence is fixed by reduction potentials.
questions.x: Electrons move spontaneously from a donor with lower (more negative) reduction potential to an acceptor with higher (more positive) potential, because positive ΔE°′ means negative ΔG°′. NADH/NAD⁺ is about −0.32 V and O₂/H₂O is about +0.82 V, so electrons flow downhill from NADH through the complexes to O₂, releasing energy used to pump protons.

questions.q: Isolated mitochondria are given malate (an NADH source) plus rotenone, a Complex I inhibitor. O₂ consumption stops. Which addition would restore it?
o: More malate
Malate's NADH still cannot pass Complex I.
Oligomycin
Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase and further reduces respiration.
Antimycin A
Antimycin blocks Complex III, downstream of both entry points.
Succinate
Correct: succinate feeds electrons into Complex II, bypassing the block.
questions.x: Rotenone blocks Complex I, so electrons from NADH-generating substrates like malate cannot reach coenzyme Q. Succinate donates electrons through Complex II, which feeds coenzyme Q directly, bypassing Complex I, so electron flow to Complexes III and IV and O₂ consumption resume. Inhibitors of Complex III or ATP synthase would block flow regardless of substrate.

questions.q: Isolated mitochondria respiring with succinate and ADP are treated with oligomycin, and O₂ uptake drops. Adding 2,4-dinitrophenol then restores O₂ uptake. What does this show?
o: Oligomycin directly inhibits Complex IV
Restoration by an uncoupler shows the ETC itself was intact.
Electron transport is coupled to ATP synthesis through the proton gradient
Correct: dissipating the gradient lets electron flow resume without ATP synthase.
DNP reverses oligomycin binding
DNP acts by carrying protons, not by displacing oligomycin.
ATP synthesis does not depend on O₂
The experiment shows respiration and phosphorylation are linked.
questions.note: Respiratory control: no ADP or a blocked synthase slows the ETC.
questions.x: Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase's proton channel, so the proton gradient builds until pumping is opposed and electron flow and O₂ use slow; this is respiratory control. DNP is an uncoupler that carries protons back across the membrane, dissipating the gradient so electron transport can resume without making ATP. This shows electron transport and ATP synthesis are coupled through the gradient.

questions.q: During active electron transport, how does the mitochondrial matrix compare with the intermembrane space?
o: Lower pH and more positive charge
Those describe the intermembrane space.
Lower pH and more negative charge
The matrix loses protons, so its pH rises.
Higher pH and more negative charge
Correct: protons are pumped out, so the matrix is alkaline and negative.
Equal pH and equal charge
The proton-motive force requires a gradient.
questions.x: Complexes I, III and IV pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. The matrix is therefore left with fewer protons (higher pH, alkaline) and a net negative charge, while the intermembrane space becomes acidic and positive. Both the pH gradient and the membrane potential contribute to the proton-motive force that drives protons back through ATP synthase.

questions.q: Antimycin A blocks Complex III. Which redox states are expected in respiring mitochondria?
o: Coenzyme Q mostly reduced; cytochrome c mostly oxidized
Correct: carriers before the block fill with electrons; those after are drained.
Coenzyme Q mostly oxidized; cytochrome c mostly reduced
This is reversed.
Both mostly reduced
Cytochrome c lies after the block and cannot be reduced.
Both mostly oxidized
Coenzyme Q upstream of the block accumulates electrons.
questions.x: An ETC inhibitor acts like a dam: carriers upstream of the block keep receiving electrons but cannot pass them on, so they become mostly reduced, while carriers downstream keep handing electrons to O₂ and become mostly oxidized. Antimycin A blocks Complex III, so coenzyme Q (upstream) is reduced and cytochrome c (downstream) is oxidized.

questions.q: Newborns use brown adipose tissue to stay warm. How does thermogenin (UCP1) generate heat?
o: It blocks Complex IV so electrons generate heat
Respiration speeds up, not stops.
It hydrolyzes ATP rapidly in the cytosol
UCP1 is a mitochondrial proton channel.
It lets protons flow back into the matrix without making ATP
Correct: gradient energy is released as heat.
It inhibits β-oxidation of fatty acids
Brown fat oxidizes fatty acids rapidly to fuel heat.
questions.x: UCP1 (thermogenin) is a proton channel in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown fat. It lets protons flow back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so the energy of the gradient is released as heat rather than captured as ATP. With the gradient constantly dissipated, the ETC and fatty acid oxidation run rapidly to sustain heat production.

questions.q: How does proton flow through ATP synthase drive ATP formation?
o: Protons directly phosphorylate ADP
Protons supply energy for conformational change.
Protons turn the F₀ c-ring, rotating γ and changing F₁ binding sites
Correct: the binding-change mechanism releases ATP from F₁.
Protons are pumped out of the matrix by ATP hydrolysis
That is ATP synthase in reverse.
Protons reduce O₂ at F₁
O₂ reduction occurs at Complex IV.
questions.x: Protons flowing down their gradient through the F₀ portion turn the c-ring rotor, which spins the central γ stalk inside the F₁ head. Rotation forces F₁'s three β subunits through loose, tight and open conformations (the binding-change mechanism), binding ADP and Pi, forming ATP, and releasing it. Proton energy is converted to mechanical rotation and then to chemical bond energy.

questions.q: Atractyloside inhibits the adenine nucleotide translocase. What is its effect on oxidative phosphorylation in intact mitochondria?
o: It speeds up because ATP is retained
Without ADP entry, synthesis stops.
It is unaffected because the translocase is not needed
The translocase supplies ADP and exports ATP.
It stops because O₂ cannot enter
O₂ diffuses freely across membranes.
It stops because ADP cannot enter the matrix
Correct: ATP synthase needs matrix ADP.
questions.x: ATP synthase makes ATP in the matrix, but the substrate ADP is generated by ATP use in the cytosol. The adenine nucleotide translocase exchanges matrix ATP for cytosolic ADP. When atractyloside blocks it, matrix ADP runs out, ATP synthase stops, protons stop flowing back, and electron transport slows through respiratory control.

questions.q: Cytosolic NADH from glycolysis delivers its electrons via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle in brain and muscle. How many ATP does each NADH yield?
o: About 2.5
That is the malate–aspartate shuttle yield.
About 1.5
Correct: the electrons enter as FADH₂ at coenzyme Q, bypassing Complex I.
About 3
That is an outdated value.
The electrons still enter the ETC.
questions.x: Cytosolic NADH cannot cross the inner membrane, so a shuttle carries its electrons. In the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, DHAP is reduced to glycerol-3-phosphate, which is reoxidized by a mitochondrial FAD-linked enzyme that passes electrons to coenzyme Q, bypassing Complex I. Each cytosolic NADH thus yields about 1.5 ATP, versus 2.5 via the malate–aspartate shuttle.

questions.q: About 4 H⁺ re-enter the matrix for each ATP made and exported (3 through ATP synthase, 1 with Pi). How many H⁺ are pumped per NADH oxidized?
o: That would give only 1.5 ATP per NADH.
That would give 3 ATP per NADH.
Correct: Complex I pumps 4, III pumps 4, IV pumps 2; 10/4 = 2.5 ATP per NADH.
That is the number per ATP, not per NADH.
questions.x: Oxidizing one NADH pumps about 10 protons: 4 at Complex I, 4 at Complex III and 2 at Complex IV. Making and exporting one ATP uses about 4 protons, 3 through ATP synthase and 1 for Pi and ADP transport. Dividing 10 by 4 gives about 2.5 ATP per NADH, the basis of modern P/O ratios; FADH₂ skips Complex I, giving 6/4 = 1.5.

questions.q: Where do most reactive oxygen species arise in normal cells?
o: Electron leak from Complexes I and III to O₂
Correct: partial reduction produces superoxide.
Complete reduction of O₂ at Complex IV
Complex IV fully reduces O₂ to water.
ATP synthase rotation
ATP synthase involves no electron transfer.
Glycolysis in the cytosol
Glycolysis does not reduce O₂.
questions.x: Most reactive oxygen species come from electrons that leak prematurely from the ETC, mainly at Complexes I and III, and reduce O₂ by one electron to superoxide (O₂•⁻). Complex IV, in contrast, holds O₂ until it receives four electrons and fully reduces it to water. Superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase then detoxify these species.

questions.q: Mitochondrial vesicles with no electron transport are equilibrated at pH 8 inside, then placed into pH 4 buffer with ADP and Pi. ATP is briefly synthesized. What does this support?
o: Electron transport directly phosphorylates ADP
Electron transport was absent.
A proton gradient alone can drive ATP synthesis
Correct: it supports the chemiosmotic hypothesis.
ATP synthase requires O₂
No O₂ consumption was needed.
ATP synthesis requires a high-energy intermediate from NADH
No NADH oxidation occurred.
questions.x: The chemiosmotic hypothesis proposes that the ETC's only role in ATP synthesis is to build a proton gradient that ATP synthase uses. Imposing an artificial pH gradient, with no electron transport, NADH or O₂ use, still drove a burst of ATP synthesis that stopped once the gradient was dissipated. This rules out a required high-energy chemical intermediate.

questions.q: A patient in shock has poor tissue O₂ delivery. Why does blood lactate rise?
o: The liver makes more lactate from glucose
The liver normally clears lactate.
Lactate is produced by the ETC
The ETC does not produce lactate.
Cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis and regenerate NAD⁺ via lactate dehydrogenase
Correct: oxidative phosphorylation is limited.
Fatty acid oxidation produces lactate
β-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA.
questions.x: Without enough O₂, the ETC cannot reoxidize NADH, so oxidative phosphorylation and pyruvate oxidation slow. Cells fall back on anaerobic glycolysis, and lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺ for GAPDH. Lactate pours into the blood faster than the liver can clear it, causing lactic acidosis, a marker of tissue hypoperfusion.

questions.q: Coenzyme Q accepts two electrons from Complex I but passes them to cytochrome c, which carries one at a time. What allows this?
o: Cytochrome c accepts two electrons at once
Its single heme iron carries one electron.
CoQ releases one electron as heat
Electrons are not released as heat.
Complex IV transfers electrons back to CoQ
Electron flow is one-way.
CoQ can exist as a stable semiquinone after one electron transfer
Correct: the Q cycle transfers electrons one at a time.
questions.x: Coenzyme Q is a two-electron carrier that can also exist as a stable one-electron semiquinone. In the Q cycle at Complex III, reduced QH₂ gives one electron to cytochrome c (via the iron–sulfur protein and cytochrome c₁) and the other to cytochrome b, which recycles it to another Q. This converts two-electron to one-electron transfer and also pumps extra protons.

questions.q: Where do fatty acid synthesis and β-oxidation occur?
o: Synthesis in the cytosol; β-oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix
Correct: separate compartments keep the opposing pathways apart.
Both in the mitochondrial matrix
Fatty acid synthase is cytosolic.
Synthesis in the mitochondrial matrix; β-oxidation in the cytosol
The locations are reversed.
Both in the cytosol
β-oxidation of most fatty acids is mitochondrial.
questions.x: Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytosol, using NADPH and malonyl-CoA, while β-oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, generating NADH and FADH₂. Compartmentation plus regulation (malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, blocking fatty acid entry into mitochondria) prevents a futile cycle of making and breaking fatty acids at the same time. Very-long-chain fatty acids start oxidation in peroxisomes.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis?
o: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Correct: it carboxylates acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA using biotin.
Fatty acid synthase
It elongates the chain but is not the main control point.
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
CPT-I controls fatty acid entry for β-oxidation.
HMG-CoA reductase
It controls cholesterol synthesis.
questions.x: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses biotin, ATP and bicarbonate to carboxylate acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, the committed step of fatty acid synthesis. It is activated by citrate and insulin-driven dephosphorylation, and inhibited by palmitoyl-CoA and by AMPK or glucagon-driven phosphorylation. Fatty acid synthase then builds the chain but is not the main control point.

questions.q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, malonyl-CoA rises in the liver. How does this prevent newly made fatty acids from being oxidized?
o: Malonyl-CoA activates hormone-sensitive lipase
It does not regulate lipolysis this way.
Malonyl-CoA inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Malonyl-CoA is ACC's product, and the effect is on CPT-I.
Malonyl-CoA inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
Correct: fatty acyl groups cannot enter mitochondria.
Malonyl-CoA degrades acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Regulation is allosteric, not by degradation.
questions.x: Malonyl-CoA, the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, allosterically inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I on the outer mitochondrial membrane. CPT-I is needed to move long-chain fatty acyl groups into mitochondria for β-oxidation, so when synthesis is active, newly made fatty acids cannot enter and be oxidized. This reciprocal control prevents a futile cycle.

questions.q: Acetyl-CoA made in mitochondria is needed in the cytosol for fatty acid synthesis. How is it transported?
o: Directly by an acetyl-CoA transporter
No such transporter exists in the inner membrane.
Bound to carnitine
Carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups into mitochondria.
As citrate, which is cleaved in the cytosol by ATP-citrate lyase
Correct: the citrate shuttle moves acetyl units out.
As malonyl-CoA
Malonyl-CoA is made in the cytosol.
questions.x: Acetyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Instead it condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate, which is exported, and in the cytosol ATP-citrate lyase splits citrate back into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. The oxaloacetate is converted via malate to pyruvate by malic enzyme, which also generates some NADPH for fatty acid synthesis.

questions.q: What is the main end product released by human fatty acid synthase?
o: Stearate (18:0)
Stearate is made by elongation of palmitate.
Oleate (18:1)
Oleate requires elongation and desaturation.
Arachidonate (20:4)
Arachidonate comes from dietary linoleate.
Palmitate (16:0)
Correct: the thioesterase releases the chain at 16 carbons.
questions.x: Fatty acid synthase adds two-carbon units from malonyl-CoA until the chain reaches 16 carbons, when its thioesterase releases palmitate. Longer chains like stearate are made by elongases in the ER, and double bonds are added by desaturases. Humans cannot introduce double bonds beyond Δ9, so linoleate is essential and is the precursor of arachidonate.

questions.q: How many NADPH are required to synthesize one palmitate from acetyl-CoA?
o: Each cycle has two reductions, not one.
Correct: 7 elongation cycles × 2 reductions, each using NADPH.
This counts 8 cycles; the first acetyl-CoA is a primer.
This equals the number of acetyl units.
questions.x: Palmitate (16:0) is built from one acetyl-CoA primer plus seven malonyl-CoA, so there are 7 elongation cycles. Each cycle has two reductions, of the β-keto group and of the enoyl double bond, and each uses one NADPH. That gives 7 × 2 = 14 NADPH per palmitate, much of it supplied by the pentose phosphate pathway.

questions.q: Each round of β-oxidation produces which products?
o: 2 NADH and 1 acetyl-CoA
The first oxidation uses FAD.
1 FADH₂, 1 NADPH and 1 acetyl-CoA
β-oxidation produces NADH, not NADPH.
1 ATP, 1 NADH and 1 acetyl-CoA
No ATP is made directly.
1 FADH₂, 1 NADH and 1 acetyl-CoA
Correct: oxidation, hydration, oxidation and thiolysis.
questions.x: Each round of β-oxidation has four steps: oxidation by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (makes FADH₂), hydration, oxidation of the β-hydroxyl group (makes NADH), and thiolysis by CoA, releasing acetyl-CoA and an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter. No ATP or NADPH is made directly; energy comes later when FADH₂, NADH and acetyl-CoA are oxidized.

questions.q: Stearate (18:0) undergoes complete β-oxidation. How many rounds of β-oxidation occur, and how many acetyl-CoA form?
o: 9 rounds; 9 acetyl-CoA
The final round yields two acetyl-CoA.
8 rounds; 8 acetyl-CoA
18 carbons give 9 two-carbon units.
8 rounds; 9 acetyl-CoA
Correct: the last round splits a four-carbon unit into two acetyl-CoA.
18 rounds; 9 acetyl-CoA
Each round removes two carbons.
questions.note: n carbons → n/2 acetyl-CoA from (n/2 − 1) rounds.
questions.x: An 18-carbon fatty acid contains nine two-carbon units, so it yields 9 acetyl-CoA. Each round of β-oxidation releases one acetyl-CoA, except the final round, where the four-carbon butyryl-CoA is split into two acetyl-CoA. So the number of rounds is one less than the number of acetyl-CoA: 8 rounds, giving 8 FADH₂ and 8 NADH.

questions.q: Fatty acid activation to acyl-CoA uses one ATP. Why is the cost counted as two high-energy bonds?
o: Two ATP molecules are used per fatty acid
One ATP is cleaved.
ATP is converted to ADP twice
ATP goes to AMP.
ATP is cleaved to AMP and PPi, and PPi is then hydrolyzed
Correct: two phosphoanhydride bonds are spent.
The carnitine shuttle consumes one more ATP
The carnitine shuttle uses no ATP.
questions.x: Acyl-CoA synthetase forms fatty acyl-AMP and then acyl-CoA, splitting ATP into AMP and pyrophosphate. Pyrophosphatase then hydrolyzes PPi to 2 Pi, which pulls the activation forward irreversibly. Two phosphoanhydride bonds are spent, equal to converting 2 ATP to 2 ADP, so ATP-yield tallies subtract 2 for activation.

questions.q: Compared with fully saturated stearate, complete β-oxidation of oleate (18:1, cis-Δ9) yields slightly less ATP. Why?
o: Oleate produces fewer acetyl-CoA
Both are 18 carbons and give 9 acetyl-CoA.
Oleate cannot enter mitochondria
Unsaturated fatty acids use the carnitine shuttle.
The cis bond requires ATP to break
The isomerase does not use ATP.
One FAD-linked oxidation is skipped because the double bond already exists
Correct: an isomerase repositions it, so one FADH₂ is lost.
questions.x: Normal β-oxidation begins each round with acyl-CoA dehydrogenase creating a trans-Δ2 double bond and FADH₂. Oleate already has a cis-Δ9 double bond, which after three rounds sits at the Δ3 position; enoyl-CoA isomerase moves it to trans-Δ2, skipping the dehydrogenase. One FADH₂ (about 1.5 ATP) is lost, while acetyl-CoA output is unchanged.

questions.q: In peroxisomal disorders, very-long-chain fatty acids (more than 22 carbons) accumulate. Why?
o: Mitochondria normally oxidize them completely
Mitochondria cannot initiate VLCFA oxidation efficiently.
Peroxisomes initially shorten these fatty acids
Correct: very-long-chain fatty acids are first oxidized in peroxisomes.
They are normally broken down by lysosomal lipases
Lysosomes are not the main route.
They are normally excreted in bile
They must be oxidized.
questions.x: Very-long-chain fatty acids (22 or more carbons) are poor substrates for the mitochondrial carnitine shuttle and enzymes, so peroxisomes first shorten them by β-oxidation, producing H₂O₂ and medium-chain products that mitochondria finish. In peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger syndrome or X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, VLCFAs accumulate, damaging myelin and the adrenals.

questions.q: During fasting, epinephrine and glucagon stimulate lipolysis in adipocytes. Which enzyme is activated by PKA phosphorylation?
o: Lipoprotein lipase
LPL acts in capillaries and is stimulated by insulin.
Pancreatic lipase
It acts in the intestine.
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
PKA phosphorylation inactivates ACC.
Hormone-sensitive lipase
Correct: phosphorylation activates it to release fatty acids.
questions.x: In fasting or stress, glucagon and epinephrine raise adipocyte cAMP and activate PKA, which phosphorylates hormone-sensitive lipase and perilipin on the lipid droplet. This releases fatty acids and glycerol from stored triglycerides for other tissues. Insulin opposes it, and lipoprotein lipase is a different enzyme that hydrolyzes circulating lipoprotein triglycerides.

questions.q: Adipocytes have very little glycerol kinase. What must they use to esterify fatty acids into triacylglycerols?
o: Free glycerol taken from the blood
Without glycerol kinase, adipocytes cannot use glycerol.
Acetyl-CoA
Acetyl-CoA is not the backbone.
Phosphatidylcholine
That is a membrane phospholipid.
Glycerol-3-phosphate made from glycolytic DHAP
Correct: insulin-stimulated glucose uptake provides the backbone.
questions.x: Triacylglycerol synthesis needs glycerol-3-phosphate as the backbone. Liver can make it by phosphorylating free glycerol with glycerol kinase, but adipocytes have little of that enzyme, so they reduce glycolytic DHAP to glycerol-3-phosphate. Fat storage therefore depends on glucose uptake via insulin-stimulated GLUT4, linking fat storage to the fed state.

questions.q: How are free fatty acids released from adipose tissue carried in blood?
o: In chylomicrons
Chylomicrons carry dietary lipid from the intestine.
Dissolved freely in plasma
Long-chain fatty acids are poorly soluble.
Bound to hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is inside red cells and binds O₂.
Bound to albumin
Correct: albumin binds hydrophobic fatty acids.
questions.x: Long-chain fatty acids are hydrophobic and barely soluble in plasma. Once released from adipose tissue by lipolysis, they bind to serum albumin, which has several hydrophobic binding sites and carries them to muscle, heart and liver for oxidation. Chylomicrons and VLDL carry esterified triglycerides, not free fatty acids, and hemoglobin stays inside red cells.

questions.q: What enzyme hydrolyzes chylomicron triacylglycerols so fatty acids can enter tissues?
o: Hormone-sensitive lipase inside adipocytes
That acts on stored triacylglycerol.
Lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium
Correct: it is activated by apoC-II.
Pancreatic lipase in the intestine
It acts in the intestinal lumen.
Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase
LCAT esterifies cholesterol on HDL.
questions.x: Lipoprotein lipase is anchored to the capillary endothelium of adipose tissue, muscle and heart. Activated by apoC-II on chylomicrons and VLDL, it hydrolyzes their triacylglycerols so the released fatty acids can enter nearby cells for storage or oxidation. Hormone-sensitive lipase works inside adipocytes on stored fat, and pancreatic lipase digests dietary fat in the intestinal lumen.

questions.q: Which lipoprotein delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues via receptor-mediated endocytosis?
o: HDL
HDL carries cholesterol from tissues back to the liver.
LDL
Correct: LDL binds the LDL receptor via apoB-100.
Chylomicrons
Chylomicrons mainly deliver dietary triacylglycerol.
VLDL
VLDL mainly carries triacylglycerol from the liver.
questions.x: VLDL from the liver loses triglyceride to lipoprotein lipase and becomes IDL and then LDL, a cholesterol-rich particle with apoB-100. Peripheral cells and liver take up LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis through the LDL receptor, which recognizes apoB-100. HDL runs the opposite direction, collecting excess cholesterol from tissues for return to the liver.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis?
o: HMG-CoA reductase
Correct: it reduces HMG-CoA to mevalonate.
HMG-CoA synthase
Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase is rate-limiting for ketogenesis.
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
This controls fatty acid synthesis.
Squalene synthase
This is a later step.
questions.x: HMG-CoA reductase reduces HMG-CoA to mevalonate using NADPH; this is the committed, rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis and the target of statins. It is regulated by sterol levels via SREBP, by phosphorylation (AMPK inhibits it) and by insulin. HMG-CoA synthase also acts in this pathway, but the mitochondrial isoform controls ketogenesis, not cholesterol synthesis.

questions.q: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase. Which change in liver cells follows?
o: LDL receptor expression decreases
Low cholesterol upregulates the receptor.
LDL receptor expression increases
Correct: low intracellular cholesterol activates SREBP, raising LDL uptake.
Fatty acid synthesis stops
Statins target cholesterol synthesis.
HDL is converted to LDL
Statins do not convert lipoproteins.
questions.x: When statins lower intracellular cholesterol in hepatocytes, the sterol sensor SCAP escorts SREBP-2 to the Golgi, where it is cleaved and enters the nucleus to induce LDL receptor (and HMG-CoA reductase) genes. More LDL receptors at the surface pull more LDL out of the blood, which is the main way statins lower plasma LDL cholesterol.

questions.q: A child with carnitine deficiency has fasting hypoglycemia. Dietary medium-chain triglycerides help. Why?
o: Medium-chain fatty acids are converted directly to glucose
Even-chain fatty acids cannot make net glucose.
Medium-chain triglycerides contain carnitine
They do not.
Medium-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria without carnitine
Correct: they bypass the shuttle and can be oxidized.
Medium-chain fatty acids inhibit gluconeogenesis
That would worsen hypoglycemia.
questions.x: Long-chain fatty acids need carnitine and CPT-I and CPT-II to cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Without carnitine, they cannot be oxidized, so the liver lacks the ATP and acetyl-CoA needed for gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis during fasting. Medium-chain fatty acids cross the membrane directly and are activated inside, bypassing the shuttle and restoring fat oxidation.

questions.q: What is the role of bile salts in fat digestion?
o: They emulsify fats, increasing surface area for lipase
Correct: they also form micelles for absorption.
They hydrolyze triacylglycerols
Lipase hydrolyzes them.
They carry fats through blood
Lipoproteins and albumin do that.
They activate pepsin
Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach.
questions.x: Bile salts are amphipathic derivatives of cholesterol. They emulsify large fat globules into small droplets, increasing the surface area available to pancreatic lipase, and then package the products (fatty acids and monoacylglycerols) into micelles that ferry them to the intestinal surface for absorption. They do not hydrolyze fats themselves.

questions.q: Linoleic acid is essential in the human diet. Why?
o: Humans cannot introduce double bonds beyond carbon 9
Correct: we lack desaturases for the ω-6 and ω-3 positions.
Humans cannot synthesize any fatty acids
Humans make palmitate and others.
Linoleic acid is a saturated fatty acid
It has two double bonds.
It cannot be absorbed from the intestine
It is absorbed well.
questions.x: Human desaturases can insert double bonds only up to carbon 9 counting from the carboxyl end. Linoleic acid (ω-6) and α-linolenic acid (ω-3) have double bonds further toward the methyl end, so they must come from the diet. They are precursors of arachidonate and the eicosanoids, and of omega-3 fatty acids such as EPA and DHA.

questions.q: A toddler becomes lethargic after a prolonged fast with low glucose and low ketones. Which defect best explains this?
o: Glycogen synthase deficiency
It causes fasting hypoglycemia with high ketones, because fat oxidation is intact.
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
Correct: blocked β-oxidation starves ketogenesis and gluconeogenesis.
Excess hormone-sensitive lipase activity
More lipolysis would raise ketones.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency
That causes hemolytic anemia, not fasting hypoketosis.
questions.x: During a prolonged fast, the liver relies on β-oxidation to make ketones and to supply ATP and acetyl-CoA for gluconeogenesis. In MCAD deficiency, fatty acids cannot be fully oxidized, so ketone production fails and gluconeogenesis falters, giving hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Defects in glycogen storage alone cause hypoglycemia with high ketones, because fat oxidation still works.

questions.q: Which lipoprotein carries triacylglycerol made in the liver to peripheral tissues?
o: Chylomicrons
Chylomicrons carry dietary lipid.
HDL
HDL removes cholesterol from tissues.
VLDL
Correct: VLDL exports endogenous triacylglycerol.
LDL
LDL is mainly cholesterol-rich.
questions.x: The liver packages triacylglycerol it synthesizes, together with cholesterol and apoB-100, into VLDL and secretes it into the blood. Lipoprotein lipase then hydrolyzes VLDL triglyceride for uptake by muscle and adipose tissue, converting VLDL to IDL and LDL. Chylomicrons carry dietary (exogenous) triglyceride from the intestine instead.

questions.q: Which compound is NOT a ketone body?
o: Acetoacetate
It is a ketone body.
Acetyl-CoA
Correct: acetyl-CoA is the precursor, not a ketone body.
β-Hydroxybutyrate
It is the main circulating ketone body.
Acetone
It forms from acetoacetate.
questions.x: The three ketone bodies are acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate (its reduced form, and the most abundant in blood) and acetone (formed by spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate and exhaled). They are made in liver mitochondria from acetyl-CoA via HMG-CoA. Acetyl-CoA itself is the precursor; it cannot leave the mitochondrion and is not a ketone body.

questions.q: Where are ketone bodies synthesized?
o: Liver mitochondria
Correct: HMG-CoA synthase in liver mitochondria is rate-limiting.
Brain cytosol
The brain uses ketones.
Skeletal muscle mitochondria
Muscle oxidizes ketones.
Adipose cytosol
Adipose provides fatty acids.
questions.x: Ketogenesis occurs in liver mitochondria, where β-oxidation produces abundant acetyl-CoA during fasting. Two acetyl-CoA form acetoacetyl-CoA, and mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase (the rate-limiting enzyme) adds a third to make HMG-CoA, which is cleaved to acetoacetate. The liver exports ketones to the brain, heart and muscle, which oxidize them.

questions.q: The liver produces ketone bodies but cannot oxidize them. Why?
o: It lacks mitochondria
The liver has many mitochondria.
Ketones cannot enter hepatocytes
The liver makes them.
It lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase)
Correct: it cannot activate acetoacetate.
It lacks β-oxidation enzymes
The liver performs β-oxidation actively.
questions.x: To use acetoacetate as fuel, a tissue must activate it to acetoacetyl-CoA, using succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase), which transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA. The liver lacks this enzyme, so it cannot use the ketones it makes. This design ensures ketones are exported to extrahepatic tissues like brain, heart and muscle.

questions.q: In untreated type 1 diabetes, ketoacids accumulate. Which sequence best explains ketogenesis?
o: Low insulin → lipolysis → acetyl-CoA exceeds oxaloacetate → ketones
Correct: OAA is diverted to gluconeogenesis, so acetyl-CoA goes to ketones.
High insulin → glycogenolysis → acetyl-CoA → ketones
Insulin suppresses ketogenesis.
Low glucagon → glycolysis → lactate → ketones
Glucagon is high, and lactate is not a ketone source.
High insulin → protein synthesis → ketones
Insulin is absent in this case.
questions.x: Without insulin, hormone-sensitive lipase is unchecked, flooding the liver with fatty acids, and β-oxidation generates acetyl-CoA. At the same time high glucagon drives gluconeogenesis, which pulls oxaloacetate away from the citric acid cycle. Acetyl-CoA therefore exceeds the available oxaloacetate and is diverted to ketone bodies, producing ketoacidosis.

questions.q: Which cells cannot use ketone bodies for energy?
o: Neurons
The brain uses ketones in prolonged fasting.
Red blood cells
Correct: ketone oxidation requires mitochondria.
Cardiac muscle cells
Heart readily oxidizes ketones.
Skeletal muscle cells
Muscle oxidizes ketones.
questions.x: Ketone bodies are converted back to acetyl-CoA and oxidized in the mitochondrial citric acid cycle. Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they cannot use ketones or fatty acids and depend entirely on glycolysis. Brain, heart and skeletal muscle all have mitochondria and thiophorase, and the brain shifts substantially to ketones in prolonged fasting.

questions.q: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has fruity-smelling breath. What causes the odor?
o: β-Hydroxybutyrate exhaled
It is not volatile.
Ethanol from fermentation
DKA does not cause ethanol production.
Lactate exhaled
Lactate is not volatile.
Acetone from spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate
Correct: volatile acetone is exhaled.
questions.x: In ketoacidosis, high levels of acetoacetate undergo slow, spontaneous, nonenzymatic decarboxylation to acetone. Acetone is volatile and not efficiently metabolized, so it is exhaled, giving the breath a fruity smell. β-Hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate are nonvolatile acids responsible for the acidosis, not the odor.

questions.q: In severe DKA, a nitroprusside test (which detects acetoacetate) may underestimate ketosis. Why?
o: Acetone interferes with the reagent
Acetone weakly reacts but is not the reason.
Ketones are not filtered by the kidney
They appear in urine.
High NADH shifts most ketones to β-hydroxybutyrate
Correct: the test misses the predominant ketone.
Insulin degrades acetoacetate
Insulin is absent.
questions.x: Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate interconvert via β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase using NADH. In DKA, the high mitochondrial NADH/NAD⁺ ratio pushes this equilibrium toward β-hydroxybutyrate, which can outnumber acetoacetate several-fold. Because nitroprusside detects only acetoacetate (and acetone), it can underestimate total ketones.

questions.q: Which amino acids are purely ketogenic?
o: Alanine and serine
They give pyruvate (glucogenic).
Leucine and lysine
Correct: they give only acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate.
Phenylalanine and tyrosine
They are both glucogenic and ketogenic.
Glutamate and aspartate
They are glucogenic.
questions.x: Glucogenic amino acids give pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates that can be converted to glucose; ketogenic ones give acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate, which cannot. Leucine and lysine are the only purely ketogenic amino acids. Phenylalanine, tyrosine, isoleucine, tryptophan and threonine are both, while alanine, serine, glutamate and aspartate are purely glucogenic.

questions.q: Which cofactor is required for transamination?
o: Thiamine pyrophosphate
TPP is used for decarboxylations.
Biotin
Biotin is used for carboxylations.
Pyridoxal phosphate
Correct: PLP (B₆) carries the amino group.
FAD
FAD is used in redox reactions.
questions.x: Aminotransferases use pyridoxal phosphate, derived from vitamin B₆. PLP forms a Schiff base with the amino acid, accepts its amino group (becoming pyridoxamine phosphate), and then donates it to an α-keto acid such as α-ketoglutarate. PLP also serves amino acid decarboxylases and ALA synthase, whereas biotin serves carboxylases and TPP serves α-keto acid decarboxylations.

questions.q: Alanine aminotransferase transfers alanine's amino group to which acceptor?
o: Pyruvate, forming lactate
Pyruvate is a product.
α-Ketoglutarate, forming glutamate
Correct: the products are pyruvate and glutamate.
Oxaloacetate, forming malate
Malate is not an amination product.
Acetyl-CoA, forming acetoacetate
No amino transfer occurs.
questions.x: Transamination swaps an amino group between an amino acid and an α-keto acid. In the ALT reaction, alanine gives its amino group to α-ketoglutarate, producing pyruvate and glutamate. Most aminotransferases funnel nitrogen into glutamate this way, which the liver can deaminate to release NH₄⁺ for urea synthesis.

questions.q: Which enzyme releases free ammonia from glutamate in the liver?
o: Alanine aminotransferase
It moves an amino group without releasing NH₄⁺.
Glutamine synthetase
It fixes ammonia into glutamine.
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
It uses ammonia.
Glutamate dehydrogenase
Correct: oxidative deamination gives α-ketoglutarate and NH₄⁺.
questions.x: Glutamate dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme in the liver, performs oxidative deamination of glutamate, releasing free NH₄⁺ and regenerating α-ketoglutarate with NAD(P)H. The released ammonia feeds carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and the urea cycle. Aminotransferases only move amino groups between molecules, and glutamine synthetase and CPS I consume ammonia.

questions.q: Where is the urea cycle carried out?
o: Kidney, entirely in cytosol
The kidney excretes urea.
Liver, partly in mitochondria and partly in cytosol
Correct: CPS I and OTC are mitochondrial.
Skeletal muscle mitochondria
Muscle lacks the full pathway.
Liver cytosol only
Two steps are mitochondrial.
questions.x: The urea cycle runs in hepatocytes and spans two compartments. In the mitochondria, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase make carbamoyl phosphate and citrulline. Citrulline moves to the cytosol, where argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase and arginase finish the cycle, releasing urea and regenerating ornithine, which re-enters the mitochondria.

questions.q: Which molecule allosterically activates carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I?
o: N-Acetylglutamate
Correct: it is required for CPS I activity.
Arginine
Arginine stimulates NAG synthesis.
Ornithine
Ornithine is a carrier substrate.
Urea
Urea is the product.
questions.x: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the rate-limiting urea cycle enzyme, is inactive without its obligate allosteric activator N-acetylglutamate. NAG is made from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by NAG synthase, which is stimulated by arginine. After a protein-rich meal, more glutamate and arginine mean more NAG, raising urea cycle flux to match the nitrogen load.

questions.q: The two nitrogens of urea come from which sources?
o: Two molecules of ammonia
One N comes from aspartate.
Glutamine and arginine
These are carriers, not direct sources.
Ammonia (via carbamoyl phosphate) and aspartate
Correct: one N enters each way.
Ornithine and citrulline
They are cycle intermediates.
questions.x: One nitrogen of urea comes from free NH₄⁺, which carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I incorporates into carbamoyl phosphate in mitochondria. The second comes from aspartate, which condenses with citrulline to form argininosuccinate in the cytosol. The carbon comes from bicarbonate. Ornithine and citrulline are carriers that are regenerated each turn.

questions.q: An infant has hyperammonemia and high urinary orotic acid. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
o: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
This deficiency gives no excess carbamoyl phosphate.
Arginase
Arginase deficiency raises arginine with mild hyperammonemia.
Glutamine synthetase
Low glutamine synthetase activity does not cause orotic aciduria.
Ornithine transcarbamylase
Correct: carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis.
questions.x: In OTC deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate cannot combine with ornithine, so it accumulates in mitochondria and leaks into the cytosol. There it enters pyrimidine synthesis, producing excess orotic acid that appears in urine, along with hyperammonemia. CPS I deficiency also causes hyperammonemia, but no carbamoyl phosphate is made, so orotic acid is not elevated.

questions.q: How do peripheral tissues transport ammonia to the liver in a nontoxic form?
o: As glutamine
Correct: glutamine synthetase fixes ammonia.
As free NH₄⁺
It is toxic.
As urea
Only the liver makes urea.
As uric acid
Uric acid is a purine product.
questions.x: Free ammonia is toxic, especially to the brain, so most tissues fix it into glutamine using glutamine synthetase and carry it through the blood to the liver and kidney. There glutaminase releases NH₄⁺ for urea synthesis or urinary excretion. Muscle also exports nitrogen as alanine via the glucose–alanine cycle; only the liver can make urea.

questions.q: Hyperammonemia impairs brain energy production. Which mechanism contributes?
o: Ammonia directly inhibits Complex IV
Hyperammonemia does not act on Complex IV.
α-Ketoglutarate is depleted as ammonia forms glutamate
Correct: the citric acid cycle loses an intermediate.
Ammonia raises brain glucose
Ammonia does not raise brain glucose.
Ammonia blocks glycolysis at PFK-1
Ammonia does not block PFK-1; the key problem is loss of citric acid cycle intermediates.
questions.x: In the brain, excess ammonia is fixed by glutamate dehydrogenase (α-ketoglutarate + NH₄⁺ → glutamate) and glutamine synthetase (glutamate + NH₄⁺ → glutamine). This drains α-ketoglutarate from the citric acid cycle, slowing it and reducing ATP production. Glutamine accumulation in astrocytes also causes swelling, which contributes to the encephalopathy.

questions.q: In untreated phenylketonuria, which amino acid becomes conditionally essential?
o: Tyrosine
Correct: phenylalanine hydroxylase normally makes tyrosine.
Phenylalanine
It accumulates.
Tryptophan
Tryptophan is always essential.
Alanine
It is nonessential.
questions.x: Normally phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, so tyrosine need not come from the diet. In PKU this enzyme (or its BH₄ cofactor) is defective, so tyrosine must be supplied in the diet; it becomes conditionally essential. Phenylalanine builds up and must be restricted, while tryptophan is always essential regardless.

questions.q: Which amino acids are mainly catabolized in skeletal muscle rather than liver?
o: Aromatic amino acids
They are degraded mainly in liver.
Acidic amino acids
They are degraded widely.
Branched-chain amino acids
Correct: muscle has high BCAT activity.
Sulfur-containing amino acids
They are degraded mainly in liver.
questions.x: Leucine, isoleucine and valine are unusual in that their first catabolic step, transamination by branched-chain aminotransferase, occurs mainly in skeletal muscle rather than liver. The resulting branched-chain α-keto acids are then oxidized by the branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex; its deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease. Most other amino acids are degraded mainly in the liver.

questions.q: Which state typically shows a positive nitrogen balance?
o: Growth during childhood
Correct: nitrogen intake exceeds loss.
Prolonged starvation
Protein breakdown causes negative balance.
Severe burns
Catabolism causes negative balance.
Uncontrolled diabetes
Catabolism causes negative balance.
questions.x: Nitrogen balance compares nitrogen intake (mainly dietary protein) with nitrogen loss (mainly urinary urea). It is positive when the body is building net protein, as in growth, pregnancy or recovery from illness. Starvation, severe burns, trauma and uncontrolled diabetes increase protein breakdown and urea excretion, causing negative balance.

questions.q: Which pancreatic cell type secretes insulin in response to rising blood glucose?
o: β cells
