Correct: β cells in the islets release insulin after meals.
α cells
α cells secrete glucagon when glucose is low.
δ cells
δ cells secrete somatostatin, which inhibits both hormones.
Acinar cells
Acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes, not hormones.
questions.x: Pancreatic islet β cells take up glucose through GLUT2 and phosphorylate it with glucokinase, so their ATP production tracks blood glucose. Rising ATP closes K⁺(ATP) channels, depolarizes the cell, opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels and triggers insulin exocytosis. α cells secrete glucagon when glucose is low, and δ cells secrete somatostatin.

questions.q: Glucagon raises blood glucose by acting mainly on which tissue?
o: Liver
Correct: it stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Skeletal muscle
Muscle has few glucagon receptors and cannot export glucose.
Brain
The brain consumes glucose and does not store or release it.
Red blood cells
RBCs neither store glucose nor respond to glucagon.
questions.x: Glucagon's main target is the liver, which has abundant glucagon receptors and glucose-6-phosphatase. Through Gs, cAMP and PKA it stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and inhibits glycolysis and glycogen synthesis, so the liver releases glucose. Skeletal muscle has few glucagon receptors and cannot export glucose; it responds to epinephrine instead.

questions.q: Which effect of insulin most directly increases glucose uptake into skeletal muscle?
o: Inserting GLUT2 transporters into muscle membranes
GLUT2 is the liver and β-cell transporter.
Activating muscle glucose-6-phosphatase
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.
Moving GLUT4 transporters to the plasma membrane
Correct: more transporters at the surface increase facilitated diffusion.
Stimulating glucagon secretion
Insulin suppresses glucagon secretion.
questions.x: Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue express GLUT4, which at rest is stored in intracellular vesicles. Insulin signaling through the PI3K–Akt pathway causes these vesicles to fuse with the plasma membrane, increasing the number of transporters at the surface and therefore glucose uptake by facilitated diffusion. Exercise can also translocate GLUT4 independently of insulin, via AMPK.

questions.q: Which receptor type mediates insulin's effects on target cells?
o: Receptor tyrosine kinase
Correct: insulin binding triggers autophosphorylation and IRS signaling.
G protein-coupled receptor
Glucagon and epinephrine use GPCRs.
Intracellular nuclear receptor
Nuclear receptors bind steroid and thyroid hormones.
Ligand-gated ion channel
These mediate fast neurotransmission.
questions.x: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Insulin binding causes autophosphorylation of the receptor's intracellular tyrosine kinase domains, which then phosphorylate insulin receptor substrate (IRS) proteins, activating PI3K–Akt (GLUT4 translocation, glycogen synthesis) and MAPK pathways. Glucagon and epinephrine instead use G protein-coupled receptors and cAMP.

questions.q: Glucagon binding raises cAMP in hepatocytes. Which enzyme synthesizes the cAMP?
o: Phosphodiesterase
Phosphodiesterase degrades cAMP; insulin activates it.
Protein kinase A
PKA is activated by cAMP but does not make it.
Adenylyl cyclase
Correct: activated Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase to convert ATP to cAMP.
Guanylyl cyclase
Guanylyl cyclase makes cGMP.
questions.x: Glucagon's receptor is coupled to Gs. When glucagon binds, Gs exchanges GDP for GTP and its α subunit activates adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to cAMP. cAMP then activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates metabolic enzymes. Phosphodiesterase ends the signal by hydrolyzing cAMP to AMP, an effect insulin promotes.

questions.q: Hyperthyroidism raises basal metabolic rate. Which mechanism contributes?
o: Decreased numbers of mitochondria
Thyroid hormone increases mitochondrial biogenesis.
Inhibition of fatty acid oxidation
Thyroid hormone increases fuel oxidation.
Reduced oxygen consumption by tissues
Thyroid hormone increases O₂ consumption.
Increased expression of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, raising ATP use
Correct: more pumping consumes more ATP and O₂.
questions.x: Thyroid hormone acts through nuclear receptors to increase transcription of genes such as Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and mitochondrial proteins. More pumping consumes more ATP, and the resulting rise in ADP accelerates oxidative phosphorylation, raising O₂ consumption, heat production and fuel oxidation. This explains heat intolerance and weight loss in hyperthyroidism.

questions.q: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is switched on when cellular ATP falls. Which effect does it produce?
o: It activates fatty acid synthesis
AMPK inhibits ATP-consuming anabolic pathways.
It reduces glucose uptake into muscle
AMPK increases GLUT4 translocation.
It activates HMG-CoA reductase
AMPK phosphorylates and inhibits HMG-CoA reductase.
It inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase, favoring fatty acid oxidation
Correct: lower malonyl-CoA relieves CPT-I inhibition.
questions.x: AMPK is the cell's fuel gauge: when ATP falls and AMP rises, it phosphorylates enzymes to switch off ATP-consuming anabolism and switch on ATP-producing catabolism. It inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase, lowering malonyl-CoA and relieving CPT-I inhibition so fatty acid oxidation rises. It also inhibits HMG-CoA reductase and promotes GLUT4 translocation in muscle.

questions.q: Shortly after a mixed meal, which pair of hepatic processes increases?
o: Gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis
These are fasting processes driven by glucagon.
Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
These raise blood glucose during fasting.
β-oxidation and ketogenesis
These increase when insulin is low.
Glycogen synthesis and fatty acid synthesis
Correct: high insulin promotes fuel storage.
questions.x: After a meal, rising glucose and insulin shift the liver into storage mode. Dephosphorylation activates glycogen synthase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and high fructose-2,6-bisphosphate drives glycolysis, supplying acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis. Malonyl-CoA blocks CPT-I, so β-oxidation and ketogenesis fall, and glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are suppressed.

questions.q: After an overnight fast (about 12 hours), what is the main source of blood glucose?
o: Breakdown of muscle glycogen
Muscle cannot release free glucose.
Breakdown of liver glycogen
Correct: hepatic glycogenolysis dominates early in fasting.
Gluconeogenesis in adipose tissue
Adipose tissue does not perform gluconeogenesis.
Brain glycogen stores
The brain stores very little glycogen.
questions.x: In the first hours after a meal, blood glucose comes from absorbed food. After an overnight fast, the liver maintains blood glucose mainly by breaking down glycogen (glycogenolysis), with gluconeogenesis contributing a growing share. Muscle glycogen cannot be released as glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, and liver glycogen is largely depleted by about 24 hours.

questions.q: Which cells depend on glucose as their only fuel, even in prolonged starvation?
o: Hepatocytes
The liver oxidizes fatty acids during fasting.
Cardiac myocytes
The heart readily uses fatty acids and ketones.
Skeletal muscle fibers
Muscle oxidizes fatty acids and ketones.
Red blood cells
Correct: without mitochondria they cannot oxidize fatty acids or ketones.
questions.x: Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they cannot oxidize fatty acids or ketone bodies and depend entirely on anaerobic glycolysis of glucose, even in starvation. Gluconeogenesis must therefore continue during prolonged fasting partly to supply them. The brain can switch much of its fuel use to ketones after a few days of fasting, so it is not wholly glucose-dependent.

questions.q: After a meal, insulin promotes fat storage in adipose tissue partly by increasing which enzyme?
o: Lipoprotein lipase
Correct: LPL frees fatty acids from chylomicrons and VLDL for uptake.
Hormone-sensitive lipase
Insulin inhibits this lipase to stop lipolysis.
Glucose-6-phosphatase
This hepatic enzyme releases glucose, a fasting function.
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
CPT-I directs fatty acids to oxidation.
questions.x: Insulin increases synthesis and activity of lipoprotein lipase in adipose capillaries. LPL hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL, releasing fatty acids that adipocytes take up and re-esterify into stored fat, using glycerol-3-phosphate from glucose. At the same time, insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, stopping lipolysis of stored fat.

questions.q: Why does the brain rely mainly on glucose rather than fatty acids?
o: Neurons lack mitochondria
Neurons have many mitochondria.
Glucose cannot cross the blood–brain barrier
GLUT1 carries glucose across the barrier.
Fatty acids cross the blood–brain barrier poorly and neurons oxidize them little
Correct: so the brain uses glucose, or ketones in prolonged fasting.
Fatty acids are converted to glucose in the brain
Fatty acids cannot be converted to net glucose.
questions.x: Long-chain fatty acids travel bound to albumin and cross the blood–brain barrier poorly, and neurons have low capacity for β-oxidation. Glucose, in contrast, crosses easily through GLUT1 in the barrier and GLUT3 in neurons. In prolonged fasting, the liver turns fatty acids into water-soluble ketone bodies, which the brain can take up and oxidize.

questions.q: What is the main fuel of the resting adult heart?
o: Glucose from its own glycogen
Cardiac glycogen is a small reserve.
Amino acids
Amino acids are a minor fuel for the heart.
Ethanol
Ethanol is not a normal cardiac fuel.
Fatty acids
Correct: the heart gets most of its ATP from fatty acid oxidation.
questions.x: The heart has a huge, continuous ATP demand and is rich in mitochondria. At rest it obtains most of its ATP (about 60 to 90%) from fatty acid oxidation, supplemented by glucose, lactate and ketones. Its small glycogen store is only a short-term reserve, and it cannot rely on anaerobic metabolism, which is why ischemia quickly damages heart muscle.

questions.q: A patient with hypoglycemia has high serum insulin but low C-peptide. What is the most likely cause?
o: An insulin-secreting tumor
An insulinoma raises insulin and C-peptide together.
Type 1 diabetes without treatment
Untreated type 1 diabetes causes low insulin and hyperglycemia.
Injected insulin
Correct: commercial insulin lacks C-peptide, and it suppresses endogenous release.
Sulfonylurea overdose
Sulfonylureas trigger β-cell release, raising C-peptide.
questions.note: Proinsulin is cleaved into insulin plus C-peptide in equal amounts.
questions.x: β cells cleave proinsulin into insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts, so endogenous insulin secretion raises both. Pharmaceutical insulin contains no C-peptide, and the hypoglycemia it causes suppresses the patient's own β cells, so serum insulin is high while C-peptide is low. Insulinomas and sulfonylureas both stimulate the β cells and raise C-peptide along with insulin.

questions.q: Which hormone, secreted by adipocytes, reduces appetite?
o: Ghrelin
Ghrelin, from the stomach, stimulates hunger.
Leptin
Correct: leptin signals the hypothalamus that fat stores are adequate.
Glucagon
Glucagon raises blood glucose; it is not the main satiety signal.
Cortisol
Cortisol tends to increase appetite.
questions.x: Leptin is secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass and acts on the hypothalamus to reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure. Ghrelin, from the stomach, does the opposite, rising before meals to stimulate hunger. Leptin deficiency or leptin resistance therefore leads to persistent hunger and obesity.

questions.q: A subject fasting for 24 hours has a respiratory quotient (CO₂ produced/O₂ consumed) near 0.7. What fuel is mainly being oxidized?
o: Carbohydrate
Carbohydrate oxidation gives an RQ of 1.0.
Protein
Protein oxidation gives an RQ of about 0.8.
A carbohydrate-rich mix
A mixed fuel high in carbohydrate gives an RQ near 0.9.
Fat
Correct: fatty acid oxidation gives an RQ of about 0.7.
questions.x: The respiratory quotient reflects how much oxygen a fuel needs relative to CO₂ produced. Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) already contains oxygen, so oxidizing it gives RQ = 6 CO₂/6 O₂ = 1.0. Fatty acids are highly reduced, needing more O₂ per CO₂, giving about 0.7, while protein gives about 0.8. An RQ near 0.7 after a 24-hour fast shows fat is the main fuel.

questions.q: Late in a marathon, which fuel supplies an increasing share of muscle ATP?
o: Creatine phosphate
It lasts only seconds.
Fatty acids
Correct: fat oxidation sustains long, moderate exercise as glycogen runs low.
Anaerobic glycolysis alone
It is too inefficient to sustain hours of running.
Muscle protein
Amino acids remain a minor fuel.
questions.x: During prolonged moderate exercise, muscle and liver glycogen become depleted over 1 to 2 hours, so muscle increasingly oxidizes fatty acids released from adipose tissue, aided by high epinephrine and low insulin. Fat oxidation is slower than glycogen use, which is why running pace drops when glycogen runs out ("hitting the wall"). Creatine phosphate lasts only seconds.

questions.q: Insulin leads to dephosphorylation of hepatic PFK-2/FBPase-2. What is the result?
o: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rises and glycolysis is stimulated
Correct: the kinase domain is active when dephosphorylated.
Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls and glycolysis slows
That is the effect of glucagon and PKA.
Gluconeogenesis is stimulated
High F-2,6-BP inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
Glycogen breakdown is stimulated
Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis.
questions.x: PFK-2/FBPase-2 is a single bifunctional enzyme. In the liver, PKA phosphorylation (glucagon) activates its phosphatase domain and lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, while insulin promotes dephosphorylation, activating the kinase domain and raising F-2,6-BP. High F-2,6-BP activates PFK-1 and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, stimulating glycolysis and inhibiting gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: With 2.5 ATP/NADH and 1.5 ATP/FADH₂, about how many net ATP come from complete oxidation of one palmitate (16:0)?
o: This forgets the 2 high-energy bonds spent on activation.
Correct: 7 FADH₂ (10.5) + 7 NADH (17.5) + 8 acetyl-CoA (80) = 108, minus 2 for activation.
That uses the older P/O values of 3 and 2.
This counts only the acetyl-CoA, omitting β-oxidation's NADH and FADH₂.
questions.x: Palmitate (16 carbons) undergoes 7 rounds of β-oxidation, producing 7 FADH₂ (10.5 ATP), 7 NADH (17.5 ATP) and 8 acetyl-CoA, each worth 10 ATP in the citric acid cycle (80 ATP). That totals 108 ATP. Activation to palmitoyl-CoA costs 2 high-energy bonds (ATP → AMP + PPi), giving a net of 106.

questions.q: How many high-energy phosphate bonds are consumed to make one molecule of urea?
o: Correct: 2 ATP at CPS I, plus ATP → AMP + PPi at argininosuccinate synthetase.
This counts ATP molecules, not phosphoanhydride bonds.
This counts only carbamoyl phosphate synthesis.
This counts only argininosuccinate synthetase's single ATP.
questions.x: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I uses 2 ATP (to ADP) to make carbamoyl phosphate from NH₄⁺ and bicarbonate. Argininosuccinate synthetase uses 1 ATP but cleaves it to AMP and PPi, and PPi hydrolysis spends a second phosphoanhydride bond. That is 3 ATP molecules but 4 high-energy bonds per urea, partly recovered when the fumarate released is oxidized to make NADH.

questions.q: Isolated hepatocytes are treated with a cell-permeable cAMP analog. Which result is expected?
o: Higher fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and less glucose release
That is the insulin pattern.
Activated glycogen synthase and pyruvate kinase
PKA phosphorylation inactivates both.
Inhibited glycogen phosphorylase
cAMP activates phosphorylase via phosphorylase kinase.
Lower fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and more glucose release
Correct: PKA activates FBPase-2 and promotes glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
questions.x: A cell-permeable cAMP analog bypasses the receptor and directly activates PKA, mimicking glucagon. PKA phosphorylates PFK-2/FBPase-2 (lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and favoring gluconeogenesis), inhibits liver pyruvate kinase and glycogen synthase, and activates phosphorylase kinase and thus glycogen phosphorylase. The net result is increased hepatic glucose release.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
o: Two continuous protein sheets sandwich a central lipid layer
That is the older Davson–Danielli model, disproved by freeze-fracture images.
Phospholipids flip freely and rapidly between the two leaflets
Flip-flop is slow without flippases; lateral movement is the fast motion.
Proteins are locked in fixed positions by a rigid lipid lattice
The bilayer is fluid; FRAP shows many proteins move laterally.
Lipids and many proteins diffuse laterally within a phospholipid bilayer
Correct: the bilayer is a two-dimensional fluid in which proteins float and move sideways.
questions.note: Fast: lateral diffusion. Slow: flip-flop between leaflets.
questions.x: The fluid mosaic model treats the bilayer as a two-dimensional liquid: lipids and many proteins drift sideways within their own leaflet, while proteins are scattered through it like a mosaic. The tempting idea of free flip-flop fails because moving a polar head group through the hydrophobic core is very costly, so transverse movement is slow unless an enzyme such as a flippase catalyzes it.

questions.q: How does cholesterol affect an animal cell membrane at low temperature?
o: It makes the membrane even more rigid than it would be without it
That describes its effect at high temperature, where it restrains motion.
It greatly raises the bilayer's permeability to ions
Cholesterol actually lowers permeability to small polar solutes and ions.
It catalyzes rapid flip-flop of phospholipids
Cholesterol is not an enzyme; flippases catalyze flip-flop.
It disrupts tight packing of acyl tails, helping keep the membrane fluid
Correct: its rigid ring wedges between tails and prevents them from crystallizing.
questions.note: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer: less fluid when hot, more fluid when cold.
questions.x: Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity. In the cold, its rigid ring system wedges between phospholipid tails and keeps them from packing into a gel, so the membrane stays more fluid than it would be without it. At high temperature the same ring restrains tail motion and reduces fluidity, which is the effect the most tempting distractor wrongly applies to low temperature.

questions.q: A bacterium is shifted from 37 °C to 15 °C. To keep its membrane fluid, it would most likely increase the proportion of:
o: Phospholipids with longer, fully saturated tails
Longer saturated tails pack more tightly and lower fluidity further.
Phospholipids with cis-unsaturated fatty acid tails
Correct: cis double bonds kink tails, preventing tight packing in the cold.
Phospholipids with trans-unsaturated tails
Trans tails are nearly straight and pack like saturated chains.
Phospholipids with fewer double bonds overall
Fewer double bonds means straighter tails and a stiffer membrane.
questions.note: Cold adaptation: shorter and more unsaturated tails.
questions.x: Fluidity depends on how tightly acyl tails pack. Cis double bonds put a rigid kink in the chain, so cis-unsaturated tails cannot line up closely and the membrane stays fluid in the cold. Trans double bonds look like a fix but leave the chain nearly straight, so trans fats pack much like saturated ones and do little to keep the membrane fluid.

questions.q: Why is spontaneous flip-flop of a phospholipid from one leaflet to the other very slow?
o: Its polar head group would have to pass through the hydrophobic core
Correct: dragging a charged head through the nonpolar interior is energetically costly.
Phospholipids are covalently bonded to neighboring membrane proteins
Most phospholipids are not covalently bound to proteins.
Lateral diffusion is equally slow, so all lipid motion is slow
Lateral diffusion is fast, about a micrometer per second.
The cytoskeleton anchors every phospholipid in place
The cytoskeleton anchors some proteins, not individual lipids.
questions.x: Flip-flop requires the hydrated, polar or charged head group to cross the roughly 3 nm nonpolar core of the bilayer, a large energy barrier, so it happens on a scale of hours to days unless flippases catalyze it. Lateral diffusion is the opposite case: the lipid stays within its leaflet with its head group in water, so it is very fast. That is why slow flip-flop cannot be explained by all lipid motion being slow.

questions.q: Phosphatidylserine is normally kept on the cytoplasmic leaflet. Its appearance on the outer leaflet most likely signals that the cell:
o: Is entering mitosis and needs more membrane
Mitosis is not signaled by phosphatidylserine exposure.
Is apoptotic and should be engulfed by phagocytes
Correct: exposed phosphatidylserine is an 'eat me' signal for macrophages.
Has increased insulin receptor signaling
Insulin signaling does not depend on phosphatidylserine flipping out.
Is assembling new tight junctions
Tight junction assembly involves claudins and occludin, not lipid exposure.
questions.note: Membrane leaflets are asymmetric; flippases keep phosphatidylserine inside.
questions.x: Flippases keep the plasma membrane asymmetric, holding phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet. During apoptosis flippases are shut down and scramblases are activated, so phosphatidylserine appears on the outer surface, where macrophage receptors recognize it as an eat-me signal. Mitosis and junction assembly do not use lipid exposure as a signal.

questions.q: Which molecule crosses a protein-free phospholipid bilayer most readily?
o: O₂
Correct: small and nonpolar, it dissolves easily in the hydrophobic core.
Glucose
Large and polar, glucose needs a GLUT carrier.
K⁺
Ions are charged and hydrated; they need channels or carriers.
ATP
ATP is large and highly charged; it cannot cross a bare bilayer.
questions.x: A protein-free bilayer acts like a thin layer of oil: molecules cross by dissolving in the hydrophobic core, so small nonpolar molecules such as O₂, CO₂ and N₂ pass fastest. Glucose is polar and fairly large, and ions such as K⁺ carry a charge and a water shell, so both need transport proteins. ATP is both large and highly charged.

questions.q: Uptake of solute X rises with external [X] but levels off at high [X], is unaffected by blocking ATP synthesis, and never builds [X] inside above outside. X enters by:
o: Simple diffusion through the bilayer
Simple diffusion rises linearly and does not saturate.
Primary active transport
That would depend on ATP and could concentrate X inside.
Secondary active transport
That could concentrate X against its gradient using an ion gradient.
Facilitated diffusion through a carrier
Correct: saturable, needs no energy, and only moves down the gradient.
questions.note: Saturation means a protein is involved; no uphill movement means no energy.
questions.x: Saturation at high [X] means a limited number of protein binding sites, which rules out simple diffusion. Indifference to ATP depletion, together with the fact that X never builds up above its outside concentration, shows movement only down the gradient. That combination defines facilitated diffusion. Secondary active transport also uses a carrier, but it can concentrate X uphill and fails when the ion gradients powered by ATP collapse.

questions.q: Red blood cells (about 300 mOsm inside) are placed in a 300 mM urea solution. Urea crosses the membrane readily. What happens?
o: Nothing, because the solution is isosmotic
Isosmotic is not isotonic when the solute can cross the membrane.
The cells shrink and crenate
Crenation needs an impermeant solute at higher osmolarity outside.
The cells swell and lyse
Correct: urea enters freely, so it adds no lasting osmotic force; water follows it in.
The cells shrink briefly, then stay smaller
Urea does not stay outside, so it cannot hold water out of the cell.
questions.note: Tonicity counts only solutes that cannot cross the membrane.
questions.x: Tonicity depends only on solutes that cannot cross the membrane. Urea enters red cells freely, so its concentration evens out across the membrane and it exerts no lasting osmotic force. The cell's own impermeant solutes then draw water in, and the cell swells and lyses. The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic, so the trap answer of no change fails.

questions.q: Which solution has the highest osmotic pressure at the same temperature?
o: 0.20 M glucose
Glucose does not dissociate: only 0.20 osmol/L.
0.12 M NaCl
i = 2 gives 0.24 osmol/L, less than 0.30.
0.25 M urea
Urea does not dissociate: 0.25 osmol/L.
0.10 M CaCl₂
Correct: i = 3, so 0.30 osmol/L, the largest particle concentration here.
questions.note: Osmotic pressure follows iM, the total particle concentration.
questions.x: Osmotic pressure (π = iMRT) depends on total particle concentration, i × M. Glucose and urea do not dissociate (0.20 and 0.25 osmol/L), NaCl gives 2 × 0.12 = 0.24, and CaCl₂ gives 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 osmol/L. The CaCl₂ solution has the lowest molarity but the most particles, which is why a lower molarity does not mean a lower osmotic pressure.

questions.q: A plant cell placed in a concentrated salt solution will most likely undergo:
o: Lysis, as water floods into the cell
Water leaves, not enters, in a hypertonic solution; the wall also resists lysis.
Increased turgor pressure
Turgor rises in hypotonic solutions, not hypertonic ones.
Breakdown of the cellulose cell wall
Salt does not digest cellulose.
Plasmolysis, as the membrane pulls away from the cell wall
Correct: water leaves the cell and the protoplast shrinks.
questions.x: A concentrated salt solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the vacuole and cytoplasm by osmosis. The protoplast shrinks and the plasma membrane pulls away from the rigid cell wall: plasmolysis. Lysis and higher turgor both need water to flow in, which happens only in hypotonic solutions, and the cell wall resists bursting even then.

questions.q: Why is the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase described as electrogenic?
o: Each cycle moves one more positive charge out than in
Correct: 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in exports a net +1, making the inside more negative.
It opens in response to changes in membrane voltage
That describes voltage-gated channels, not the pump.
It moves Na⁺ and K⁺ in the same direction
Na⁺ goes out while K⁺ comes in; it is an antiporter.
It generates ATP from the ion gradients it creates
It consumes ATP; ATP synthase is the enzyme that makes ATP from a gradient.
questions.note: The pump's direct contribution to resting potential is small; K⁺ leak dominates.
questions.x: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in for each ATP, so each cycle carries one net positive charge out of the cell. Because the pump itself creates a current, it is called electrogenic, and this makes the inside slightly more negative. Electrogenic does not mean voltage-gated: the pump is driven by ATP hydrolysis and does not open in response to voltage.

questions.q: Digoxin partially inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in heart muscle. Why does cytosolic Ca²⁺ rise?
o: Digoxin directly opens L-type Ca²⁺ channels
Its target is the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, not Ca²⁺ channels.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump normally carries Ca²⁺ into the cell
The pump moves only Na⁺ and K⁺.
A smaller Na⁺ gradient slows Ca²⁺ removal by the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger
Correct: the exchanger uses Na⁺ entering down its gradient to push Ca²⁺ out.
Inhibiting the pump raises ATP, which releases Ca²⁺
ATP levels do not trigger Ca²⁺ release this way.
questions.note: One gradient powers another: block the primary pump and secondary transport fails.
questions.x: Digoxin partly blocks the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so Na⁺ builds up inside the cardiac cell and the inward Na⁺ gradient shrinks. The Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger uses that gradient (3 Na⁺ in per Ca²⁺ out), so it removes Ca²⁺ more slowly. More Ca²⁺ stays in the cell and is stored in the SR, which strengthens contraction. Digoxin does not act on Ca²⁺ channels directly.

questions.q: Intestinal cells absorb glucose against its gradient through a Na⁺–glucose symporter. What is the immediate energy source for this step?
o: The Na⁺ electrochemical gradient across the apical membrane
Correct: Na⁺ moving downhill drives glucose uphill (secondary active transport).
ATP hydrolysis by the symporter itself
The symporter has no ATPase activity; that would be primary active transport.
The glucose concentration gradient
Glucose is moving against its own gradient here.
The proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
That gradient drives ATP synthase, not plasma membrane symport.
questions.note: ATP is spent indirectly by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
questions.x: SGLT1 couples glucose entry to Na⁺ entry. Na⁺ moving down its steep electrochemical gradient releases enough free energy to carry glucose up its own gradient. This is secondary active transport: the symporter hydrolyzes no ATP itself, but the gradient it uses is kept up by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. That is why ATP hydrolysis by the symporter is wrong even though ATP is consumed indirectly.

questions.q: A vesicular transporter loads neurotransmitter into synaptic vesicles while H⁺ leaves the vesicle. This transporter is best described as a(n):
o: Symporter performing primary active transport
The substances move in opposite directions, and no ATP is used directly.
Uniporter performing facilitated diffusion
It moves two substances, and transmitter is concentrated uphill.
Antiporter performing secondary active transport
Correct: two substances move in opposite directions, powered by the H⁺ gradient.
ATP-driven pump
The H⁺ gradient, not ATP hydrolysis by this protein, provides the energy.
questions.x: Classify a transporter by two questions: which way do the substances move, and what supplies the energy. Here transmitter enters the vesicle while H⁺ leaves it, so they move in opposite directions: an antiporter. The energy comes from the H⁺ gradient set up earlier by a V-type ATPase, which makes this secondary active transport. It is not a pump, because this protein does not hydrolyze ATP itself.

questions.q: Which is an example of primary active transport?
o: GLUT4 moving glucose into a muscle cell
GLUT4 allows facilitated diffusion down the gradient.
SGLT1 moving glucose into an enterocyte
SGLT1 uses the Na⁺ gradient: secondary active transport.
Aquaporin moving water into a duct cell
Aquaporins are passive water channels.
SERCA pumping Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Correct: SERCA hydrolyzes ATP directly to move Ca²⁺ uphill.
questions.x: Primary active transport uses ATP hydrolysis by the transporter itself to move a solute against its gradient. SERCA is a P-type ATPase that pumps Ca²⁺ from the cytosol into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. SGLT1 is the tempting distractor because it also moves glucose uphill, but it draws on the Na⁺ gradient instead of ATP, so it is secondary active transport.

questions.q: Inserting aquaporins into a cell membrane changes water movement by:
o: Pumping water against its gradient using ATP
Aquaporins are passive; they hydrolyze no ATP.
Raising water permeability while the osmotic gradient still sets direction
Correct: channels speed passive flow but cannot move water uphill.
Letting Na⁺ and water through together
Aquaporins exclude ions, even H⁺.
Changing the osmolarity of the cytosol
They change permeability, not solute content.
questions.note: Trap: channels change rate, not direction.
questions.x: Aquaporins are passive channels. They raise the membrane's water permeability so osmosis is much faster, but the direction of flow is still set by the osmotic gradient. A channel cannot move water against its gradient, because it uses no energy. Aquaporins also exclude ions, including H⁺, so they do not change cytosolic osmolarity directly.

questions.q: A cell has [K⁺] = 140 mM inside and 14 mM outside. At body temperature, what is the K⁺ equilibrium potential?
o: +61 mV
Sign error: K⁺ is higher inside, so the inside must be negative to hold it.
This doubles the answer; z = 1 for K⁺.
This halves the answer as if z were 2.
−61 mV
questions.note: Nernst at 37 °C: E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]) mV.
questions.x: At 37 °C the Nernst equation is E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]) mV. For K⁺, z = +1 and [out]/[in] = 14/140 = 0.1, so log = −1 and E_K = −61 mV. The sign makes sense: K⁺ is more concentrated inside, so it tends to leave, and only a negative interior can hold it in. A positive answer comes from flipping the concentration ratio.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
o: Na⁺
E_Na is about +60 mV; resting permeability to Na⁺ is low.
Ca²⁺
E_Ca is strongly positive and resting Ca²⁺ permeability is tiny.
K⁺
Correct: at rest the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ through leak channels.
H⁺
H⁺ permeability contributes negligibly to resting potential.
questions.x: The resting potential is a permeability-weighted average of the ions' equilibrium potentials (Goldman equation). At rest, K⁺ leak channels make the membrane far more permeable to K⁺ than to other ions, so Vm (about −70 mV) sits close to E_K (about −90 mV). Na⁺ has a large gradient but low resting permeability, so it only pulls Vm a little above E_K.

questions.q: If extracellular [K⁺] rises sharply, the resting potential of a neuron becomes:
o: More negative, because more K⁺ is present
Higher outside K⁺ shrinks the gradient, so the inside is less negative.
Unchanged, because the Na⁺/K⁺ pump compensates
The pump cannot offset the change in E_K; hyperkalemia depolarizes cells.
Positive, overshooting like an action potential
Vm moves toward the new E_K, which is still negative.
Less negative, because E_K becomes less negative
Correct: a smaller K⁺ gradient means less K⁺ efflux to hold the inside negative.
questions.x: Because resting Vm tracks E_K, anything that changes E_K moves Vm. Raising outside [K⁺] brings the [out]/[in] ratio closer to 1, so E_K = 61 log([out]/[in]) becomes less negative and the cell depolarizes. This is why hyperkalemia is dangerous for the heart. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump cannot cancel the shift, because its direct share of the resting potential is small.

questions.q: A toxin makes a resting cell's membrane far more permeable to Na⁺ than to any other ion. The membrane potential will move toward:
o: 0 mV, where no ions move
0 mV is not an equilibrium for Na⁺, given its gradient.
About −90 mV, near E_K
K⁺ is no longer the dominant permeant ion.
−70 mV, because the pump fixes Vm
The pump cannot hold Vm when permeabilities change drastically.
About +60 mV, near E_Na
Correct: Vm approaches the equilibrium potential of the most permeant ion.
questions.note: Goldman logic: Vm is a weighted average set by relative permeability.
questions.x: Vm always moves toward the equilibrium potential of the ion the membrane is most permeable to. If Na⁺ permeability dominates, Vm approaches E_Na, about +60 mV, which is what happens briefly at the peak of an action potential. Staying near E_K would require K⁺ to remain the main permeant ion, and 0 mV is not an equilibrium for any ion with a gradient.

questions.q: Extracellular [Ca²⁺] is 2 mM and cytosolic [Ca²⁺] is 0.0002 mM. What is E_Ca at body temperature?
o: This uses 61 instead of 61/2; z = 2 for Ca²⁺.
Ca²⁺ is higher outside, so the inside must be positive to oppose entry.
+61 mV
This takes the log as 2 instead of 4.
questions.note: Don't forget z = 2 for divalent ions.
questions.x: Use E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]) with z = 2 for Ca²⁺. The ratio is 2/0.0002 = 10⁴, so the log is 4, and E = 30.5 × 4 = +122 mV. The value is positive because Ca²⁺ is far more concentrated outside, and only a positive interior could balance its inward push. Forgetting z = 2 gives +244 mV, the most common slip.

questions.q: During a single action potential in a large neuron, intracellular [Na⁺]:
o: Roughly doubles and must be restored before the next spike
Bulk concentrations change negligibly per spike.
Barely changes, because very few ions must cross to change Vm
Correct: membrane capacitance is small, so a tiny ion flux changes voltage a lot.
Becomes equal to extracellular [Na⁺]
The gradient is essentially preserved; thousands of spikes can occur without the pump.
Falls, because Na⁺ leaves during depolarization
Na⁺ enters, not leaves, during depolarization.
questions.x: Membrane capacitance is small, so only a tiny charge has to cross to change Vm by about 100 mV. During one spike, the Na⁺ that enters changes intracellular [Na⁺] by a negligible fraction in a large neuron. Gradients are therefore essentially unchanged after each spike, and many action potentials can fire even with the pump blocked. The pump restores gradients over the long term rather than after every spike.

questions.q: Receptors for steroid hormones such as cortisol are typically located:
o: On the outer surface of the plasma membrane
That is typical for peptide hormones, which cannot cross the bilayer.
In the membrane of the Golgi apparatus
Steroid receptors are not Golgi proteins.
On the outer mitochondrial membrane
Steroid receptors act as transcription factors, not mitochondrial proteins.
Inside the cell, in the cytoplasm or nucleus
Correct: steroids are lipophilic and diffuse across the plasma membrane.
questions.x: Steroid hormones such as cortisol are lipophilic and derived from cholesterol, so they diffuse across the plasma membrane. Their receptors wait in the cytoplasm or nucleus, and the hormone–receptor complex binds DNA and acts as a transcription factor. Surface receptors are needed for polar peptide hormones, which cannot cross the lipid bilayer.

questions.q: A hydropathy plot of a membrane protein shows seven hydrophobic stretches of about 20 residues each. The protein is most likely a:
o: G protein-coupled receptor
Correct: GPCRs have seven transmembrane α-helices.
Receptor tyrosine kinase
Typical RTKs cross the membrane once.
Peripheral membrane protein
Peripheral proteins have no transmembrane segments.
GPI-anchored surface protein
GPI-anchored proteins are tethered by a lipid, with no transmembrane helices.
questions.x: Each stretch of about 20 hydrophobic residues can form an α-helix long enough to span the bilayer's hydrophobic core. Seven such stretches mean seven transmembrane helices, the signature of G protein-coupled receptors. A receptor tyrosine kinase usually has just one transmembrane helix, so its hydropathy plot shows one peak, not seven.

questions.q: A membrane protein is released into solution by a high-salt wash, with no detergent needed. It is most likely a(n):
o: Multipass transmembrane protein
Transmembrane proteins need detergent to be pulled from the bilayer.
Peripheral protein held by ionic interactions
Correct: high salt disrupts electrostatic attachment to lipids or other proteins.
Protein with a covalent lipid anchor
The lipid anchor stays in the bilayer; detergent is needed.
Single-pass transmembrane receptor
Its hydrophobic helix keeps it in the bilayer despite salt.
questions.note: Salt or pH strips peripheral proteins; integral proteins need detergent.
questions.x: Peripheral proteins attach to the membrane surface through ionic and hydrogen bonds to lipid head groups or to integral proteins. High salt or a change in pH breaks those electrostatic contacts and releases them without disturbing the bilayer. Integral and lipid-anchored proteins have hydrophobic parts buried in the core, so only a detergent that dissolves the bilayer can free them.

questions.q: Which sequence feature best predicts a single-pass transmembrane α-helix?
o: About 20 residues alternating charged and polar
Charged residues are unfavorable in the bilayer core.
About 20 consecutive, mostly hydrophobic residues
Correct: about 20 residues spans the roughly 3 nm hydrophobic core.
About 5 consecutive hydrophobic residues
Five residues are far too short to span the bilayer as a helix.
A long stretch rich in proline and glycine
These residues break α-helices.
questions.x: A transmembrane α-helix must cover the bilayer's hydrophobic core, about 3 nm thick. With an α-helix rising 0.15 nm per residue, that takes about 20 residues, and those residues must be mostly hydrophobic to sit comfortably among lipid tails. A shorter stretch cannot span the membrane, and charged residues are strongly disfavored inside it.

questions.q: Cells take up LDL particles from the blood mainly by:
o: Simple diffusion across the bilayer
LDL particles are far too large to diffuse through the membrane.
Phagocytosis using pseudopodia
Phagocytosis is for large particles like bacteria, mostly by immune cells.
Receptor-mediated, clathrin-dependent endocytosis
Correct: LDL binds receptors clustered in clathrin-coated pits.
Facilitated diffusion through a channel
No channel is large enough for an LDL particle.
questions.x: LDL particles carry cholesterol and are far too large to cross the bilayer. ApoB-100 on the particle binds LDL receptors gathered in clathrin-coated pits, which pinch off as vesicles and deliver LDL to endosomes. Phagocytosis is also a way to take in large material, but it uses actin-driven pseudopodia and is mainly a specialty of immune cells eating microbes and debris.

questions.q: A macrophage extends pseudopodia around a bacterium and encloses it in a vacuole. This process is:
o: Pinocytosis
Pinocytosis takes in extracellular fluid in small vesicles.
Exocytosis
Exocytosis releases material from the cell.
Transcytosis
Transcytosis moves cargo across a cell from one surface to the other.
Phagocytosis
Correct: 'cell eating' of large particles, driven by actin.
questions.x: Phagocytosis means cell eating: actin-driven pseudopodia wrap around a large particle such as a bacterium and close it inside a phagosome, which then fuses with lysosomes. Macrophages and neutrophils are the professional phagocytes. Pinocytosis is the tempting confusion, but it takes in small droplets of extracellular fluid in small vesicles and does not use pseudopodia to engulf particles.

questions.q: Regulated exocytosis of synaptic vesicles is directly triggered by:
o: A rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺
Correct: Ca²⁺ binds synaptotagmin, allowing SNARE-driven fusion.
A fall in cytosolic Na⁺
Na⁺ entry depolarizes the terminal but does not trigger fusion itself.
An increase in cytosolic K⁺
K⁺ helps repolarize; it is not the fusion trigger.
Hydrolysis of cAMP
cAMP can modulate release but is not the direct trigger.
questions.x: When an action potential reaches the terminal, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ flows in. Ca²⁺ binds synaptotagmin, which lets SNARE proteins complete vesicle fusion and release transmitter. Na⁺ entry is upstream of this step, because it depolarizes the terminal, but the direct trigger for fusion is the rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺.

questions.q: A protein domain faces the lumen of a secretory vesicle. After the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, that domain faces the:
o: Cytosol
The cytosolic face of the vesicle becomes the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane.
Extracellular space
Correct: the vesicle lumen becomes continuous with the outside on fusion.
Nucleus
Plasma membrane proteins do not face the nucleus.
Interior of the bilayer
Fusion keeps protein orientation; nothing is buried in the core.
questions.note: Lumen of ER, Golgi and vesicles is topologically equivalent to the outside.
questions.x: The lumen of the ER, Golgi and secretory vesicles is topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell. When a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, its inner surface becomes continuous with the cell exterior, so any domain that faced the lumen now faces the extracellular space. The vesicle's cytosolic face stays cytosolic, so a membrane protein keeps the same orientation.

questions.q: A small fluorescent dye injected into one cardiac muscle cell quickly appears in neighboring cells. Which junction allows this?
o: Tight junctions
Tight junctions seal the space between cells; they do not join cytoplasms.
Desmosomes
Desmosomes give mechanical adhesion, not cytoplasmic continuity.
Hemidesmosomes
Hemidesmosomes attach cells to the basement membrane.
Gap junctions
Correct: connexon channels link cytoplasms and pass ions and small molecules.
questions.x: Gap junctions are built from connexons, connexin channels that line up between neighboring cells and connect their cytoplasms directly. Ions and small molecules up to about 1 kDa pass through them. This is how a small dye spreads from cell to cell and how action potentials spread through heart muscle. Tight junctions also join cells, but they seal the space between them instead of opening a path between cytoplasms.

questions.q: Autoantibodies that attack desmosomal cadherins in the skin would most directly cause:
o: Loss of electrical coupling between skin cells
That would follow damage to gap junctions.
Leakage of fluid between cells without separation
That would reflect tight junction failure alone.
Detachment of the epidermis only at the basement membrane
That involves hemidesmosomes and integrins, not desmosomal cadherins.
Blistering as epidermal cells separate from each other
Correct: desmosomes give cell–cell mechanical strength in epithelia.
questions.x: Desmosomes are spot-weld junctions in which desmosomal cadherins (desmogleins and desmocollins) link neighboring cells and connect inside to keratin filaments. If antibodies destroy those cadherins, epidermal cells lose their grip on each other and separate, forming blisters, as in pemphigus vulgaris. Separation from the basement membrane instead involves hemidesmosomes, which use integrins.

questions.q: Which structure anchors basal epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane?
o: Hemidesmosomes
Correct: integrins in hemidesmosomes bind laminin and link to keratin filaments.
Desmosomes
Desmosomes join one cell to another, not to the basement membrane.
Gap junctions
Gap junctions are channels between neighboring cells.
Tight junctions
Tight junctions seal the apical space between cells.
questions.x: Hemidesmosomes connect the basal surface of epithelial cells to the basal lamina. Integrins in the junction bind laminin outside and link to keratin intermediate filaments inside. Desmosomes look similar under the microscope but join cell to cell with cadherins. A simple rule: desmo- joins cells to cells, while hemi- joins cells to the matrix.

questions.q: Besides sealing the paracellular path, tight junctions help maintain epithelial polarity by:
o: Anchoring microtubules to the basement membrane
Hemidesmosomes and integrins handle basement membrane attachment.
Blocking lateral diffusion of membrane proteins between apical and basolateral domains
Correct: their 'fence' role keeps the two membrane domains distinct.
Passing signaling molecules between adjacent cells
That is a gap junction function.
Pumping Na⁺ toward the basolateral side
Junctions are not pumps; the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase does that.
questions.x: Tight junctions have two jobs. As a gate, they seal the paracellular space. As a fence, they block membrane proteins and outer-leaflet lipids from diffusing between the apical and basolateral surfaces, so each surface keeps its own set of transporters. Passing signals between neighboring cells is a gap junction job and does not explain polarity.

questions.q: Removing extracellular Ca²⁺ with a chelator causes cultured epithelial cells to round up and separate from each other. The best explanation is that:
o: Integrins need Ca²⁺ to bind each other between cells
Integrins bind the matrix, not each other between cells.
Cadherins need Ca²⁺ to keep their adhesive shape
Correct: cadherins are Ca²⁺-dependent adhesion molecules.
Gap junctions close when Ca²⁺ is removed
Gap junctions are not the main adhesion link between cells.
Ca²⁺ loss depolymerizes keratin filaments
Keratin filaments are not directly Ca²⁺-dependent polymers.
questions.note: Cadherin = Ca²⁺-dependent adhesion.
questions.x: Cadherins mediate cell–cell adhesion only when Ca²⁺ is bound: Ca²⁺ ions stiffen their extracellular domains into the shape that binds cadherins on the next cell. A chelator removes Ca²⁺, the domains go floppy, and cells come apart, which is a classic way to dissociate tissues. Integrins also depend on divalent cations, but they bind the matrix rather than linking neighboring cells to each other.

questions.q: Fluorescent membrane proteins in a small patch are bleached by a laser. Within seconds, fluorescence returns to the patch. This shows that:
o: The bleached proteins were rapidly resynthesized
New synthesis and delivery take far longer than seconds.
Membrane proteins diffuse laterally within the bilayer
Correct: unbleached proteins move in from around the patch.
Proteins flip between the inner and outer leaflets
Proteins essentially never flip across the bilayer.
The laser killed the cell
A dead patch would not recover fluorescence.
questions.x: This is FRAP (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching). The laser permanently bleaches the fluorophores in the patch, so fluorescence can return only if unbleached proteins move in from the surrounding membrane. Recovery within seconds shows lateral diffusion in the fluid bilayer. Making and delivering new protein takes far longer than seconds, so resynthesis cannot explain it.

questions.q: In a photobleaching experiment, protein X recovers 90% of its fluorescence but protein Y recovers only 30%. The best explanation is that Y:
o: Is a peripheral protein, not an integral one
Peripheral proteins are often quite mobile.
Is in a more fluid region of the membrane
More fluidity would speed and increase recovery.
Is smaller than X
Smaller size would tend to speed diffusion, not lower recovery.
Is largely anchored to the cytoskeleton
Correct: a tethered, immobile fraction cannot refill the bleached area.
questions.x: In FRAP, the plateau level of recovery measures the mobile fraction, and the speed of recovery reflects the diffusion rate. Only 30% recovery for Y means most Y molecules cannot move, typically because they are tethered to the cytoskeleton or to other fixed structures. A more fluid membrane or a smaller protein would increase mobility and recovery, not reduce them.

questions.q: Which ranking of permeability across a protein-free lipid bilayer is correct?
o: H₂O > O₂ > Na⁺ > glucose
Ions are the least permeant of all, and O₂ beats water.
Glucose > H₂O > O₂ > Na⁺
Large polar glucose barely crosses a bare bilayer.
O₂ > H₂O > glucose > Na⁺
Correct: small nonpolar > small polar > large polar > ions.
Na⁺ > O₂ > H₂O > glucose
Na⁺ is charged and is nearly impermeant.
questions.x: Permeability across a pure lipid bilayer follows size and polarity: small nonpolar gases (O₂) cross fastest, then small uncharged polar molecules (H₂O), then larger polar molecules (glucose), and ions (Na⁺) cross slowest. Charge is the strongest barrier, because an ion must give up its water shell to enter the oily core. That is why Na⁺ ranks below glucose even though it is smaller.

questions.q: Across a series of drugs of similar size, those with higher oil/water partition coefficients crossed cell membranes faster. This supports the idea that:
o: All drugs enter cells through specific carriers
Partition-coefficient dependence points to simple diffusion through lipid.
Polar drugs cross membranes fastest
The data show the opposite.
Membrane permeability depends only on molecular size
Size was held similar; lipid solubility made the difference.
Passive permeability depends on solubility in the lipid core
Correct: more lipophilic solutes dissolve in and cross the bilayer faster.
questions.x: Simple diffusion through a bilayer requires the solute to dissolve in the hydrocarbon core, so permeability rises with lipid solubility, measured by the oil/water partition coefficient (the Meyer–Overton relationship). Because the drugs were similar in size, size could not explain the differences. Carriers would show specificity and saturation, not a smooth trend with lipophilicity.

questions.q: For simple diffusion across a membrane, if membrane thickness doubles and surface area is halved (gradient unchanged), the diffusion rate becomes:
o: Unchanged
The two changes both reduce the rate; they do not cancel.
One-fourth of the original
Correct: rate ∝ area/thickness, so (1/2)/(2) = 1/4.
One-half of the original
This accounts for only one of the two changes.
Four times the original
Thicker membranes and smaller areas both slow diffusion.
questions.note: Fick: rate ∝ A × ΔC / thickness.
questions.x: By Fick's law, the rate of simple diffusion is proportional to area × concentration gradient ÷ membrane thickness. Halving area multiplies the rate by 1/2, and doubling thickness multiplies it by another 1/2, so the new rate is 1/4 of the original. Both changes slow diffusion, so they compound rather than cancel.

questions.q: An uncharged solute moves into a cell from 1 mM outside to 10 mM inside. This process:
o: Has a negative ΔG and occurs spontaneously
Moving from low to high concentration is uphill.
Has a positive ΔG and needs an energy input
Correct: moving up a concentration gradient is nonspontaneous.
Has ΔG = 0 because the solute is uncharged
Uncharged solutes still have a chemical gradient term.
Is driven by the membrane potential
An uncharged solute feels no electrical force.
questions.note: ΔG = RT ln(C_in/C_out) for an uncharged solute moving in.
questions.x: For an uncharged solute moving inward, ΔG = RT ln(C_in/C_out). With C_in = 10 mM and C_out = 1 mM, the ratio is 10, ln 10 is positive, and ΔG > 0, so the move is uphill and needs coupling to an energy source. Being uncharged removes the electrical term from ΔG, but the concentration term still applies.

questions.q: In a resting neuron at −70 mV, the chemical and electrical driving forces on Na⁺ are:
o: Both directed into the cell
Correct: Na⁺ is higher outside and the negative interior attracts cations.
Both directed out of the cell
Neither force pushes Na⁺ outward at rest.
Chemical inward, electrical outward
A negative interior pulls cations in, not out.
Chemical outward, electrical inward
Na⁺ is more concentrated outside, so the chemical force is inward.
questions.x: Each ion feels a chemical force from its concentration gradient and an electrical force from the membrane potential. Na⁺ is about 10 times more concentrated outside, so its chemical force points inward. The inside is negative at −70 mV, which also attracts cations inward. Both forces add up, which is why Na⁺ rushes in when its channels open.

questions.q: A cell rests at −70 mV and E_K is −90 mV. If K⁺ channels open, the net K⁺ movement is:
o: Inward, because the negative interior attracts K⁺
The electrical pull is weaker than the outward chemical push at −70 mV.
Outward, because Vm is less negative than E_K
Correct: driving force Vm − E_K = +20 mV favors K⁺ efflux.
Zero, because K⁺ is at equilibrium
K⁺ is at equilibrium only at −90 mV.
Inward, because K⁺ is more concentrated outside
K⁺ is more concentrated inside.
questions.note: Ion flows to drive Vm toward its own equilibrium potential.
questions.x: The net driving force on an ion is Vm − E_ion. For K⁺ at rest, −70 − (−90) = +20 mV: the membrane is not negative enough to hold K⁺ in, so opening K⁺ channels lets K⁺ flow out and pushes Vm toward −90 mV. The negative interior does attract K⁺, but that pull is smaller than the outward chemical push at any voltage less negative than E_K.

questions.q: Which property distinguishes ion channels from carrier proteins?
o: Channels can move solutes against their gradients
Channels are always passive.
Channels must hydrolyze ATP to open
Most channels gate by voltage, ligands or force, not ATP hydrolysis.
Channels pass ions through an open pore at very high rates
Correct: channels conduct millions of ions per second without a binding cycle for each ion.
Channels undergo a conformational change for each ion moved
That describes carriers, which is why they are slower.
questions.x: Channels form a continuous water-filled pore that, when open, lets ions stream through at millions per second, limited mainly by diffusion. Carriers bind each solute and change shape to release it on the other side, so they move only hundreds to thousands per second and can saturate. Channels are always passive, so they never move solutes uphill; pumps and coupled carriers do that.

questions.q: Inner ear hair cells open ion channels when their stereocilia bend. These channels are:
o: Voltage-gated
They open in response to deflection, not to a voltage change.
Ligand-gated
No chemical messenger binds to open them.
ATP-driven pumps
They are passive channels, not pumps.
Mechanically gated
Correct: physical force on tip links pulls the channels open.
questions.x: Ion channels are grouped by what opens them: voltage, a bound ligand, or mechanical force. In hair cells, bending the stereocilia stretches tip links that pull mechanically gated channels open, so K⁺ flows in and the cell depolarizes. The resulting depolarization later opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, but the first channels respond to force, not voltage or a chemical.

questions.q: K⁺ channels conduct K⁺ about 1000 times better than the smaller Na⁺ ion because:
o: The pore is too narrow for Na⁺ to fit
Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺, so size exclusion cannot explain it.
Na⁺ carries a larger charge than K⁺
Both carry a +1 charge.
Carbonyl oxygens in the filter fit dehydrated K⁺ but are too far apart for Na⁺
Correct: Na⁺ cannot shed its water shell favorably in a filter sized for K⁺.
K⁺ channels use ATP to reject Na⁺
Channels are passive; selectivity is structural.
questions.x: In water, both ions are surrounded by a hydration shell. The K⁺ selectivity filter is lined with backbone carbonyl oxygens spaced to replace that shell exactly for K⁺, so shedding water costs K⁺ almost nothing. Na⁺ is smaller and cannot contact all those oxygens at once, so dehydrating it inside the filter is unfavorable. Selectivity therefore comes from precise energetic fit, not from a pore that is too narrow.

questions.q: In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR reduces Cl⁻ secretion into the airway lumen. Why does the mucus become thick?
o: Less water follows osmotically into the lumen
Correct: reduced ion secretion means less water moves to hydrate mucus.
CFTR normally digests mucus proteins
CFTR is a Cl⁻ channel, not a protease.
Excess Cl⁻ in the lumen dehydrates mucus
Cl⁻ secretion is reduced, not increased.
Cilia beat faster and compact the mucus
Cilia are impaired by dehydrated mucus, not sped up.
questions.x: CFTR is a Cl⁻ channel in airway epithelium. Secreting Cl⁻ into the lumen draws Na⁺ along and creates an osmotic gradient that pulls water out to hydrate the mucus. When CFTR fails, less salt and water reach the airway surface, the mucus dehydrates and thickens, and cilia cannot clear it. The problem is too little Cl⁻ secretion, not too much.

questions.q: After receptor-mediated endocytosis, LDL separates from its receptor in the endosome mainly because:
o: Lysosomal enzymes digest the receptor
The receptor is recycled, not digested, in normal cycling.
The endosome's acidic pH lowers receptor binding affinity
Correct: low pH releases the LDL, and the receptor recycles to the surface.
The clathrin coat pulls the LDL away
The clathrin coat falls off soon after the vesicle forms.
The endosome is more alkaline than the blood
Endosomes are acidic, not alkaline.
questions.x: LDL receptors bind LDL tightly at the neutral pH of blood. After endocytosis, the endosome is acidified by V-type H⁺ pumps, and the low pH changes the receptor's shape so it lets go of its cargo. LDL continues on to lysosomes while the empty receptor returns to the surface for reuse. Digesting the receptor would waste it, which the cell avoids in normal cycling.

questions.q: Clathrin knockdown sharply reduces transferrin uptake but leaves uptake of a fluid-phase dye by macropinocytosis unchanged. This suggests that:
o: Transferrin enters by clathrin-mediated endocytosis
Correct: only the clathrin-dependent pathway was disrupted.
Transferrin enters by simple diffusion
A large protein cannot diffuse across the bilayer, and uptake fell with clathrin loss.
Macropinocytosis requires clathrin
Dye uptake was unaffected, so it does not.
All endocytosis requires clathrin
The fluid-phase pathway continued without clathrin.
questions.x: Knocking down clathrin is a selective test: any pathway that needs clathrin should fail, while others continue. Transferrin uptake fell, so it uses clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Fluid-phase uptake by macropinocytosis was unchanged, so that actin-driven pathway does not need clathrin. The result shows cells have more than one endocytic route, which rules out the idea that all endocytosis depends on clathrin.

questions.q: Binding of acetylcholine to the nicotinic receptor directly opens an ion pore in the receptor itself. This receptor is best classified as a:
o: G protein-coupled receptor
GPCRs act through G proteins and have no pore.
Receptor tyrosine kinase
RTKs phosphorylate proteins rather than conduct ions.
Intracellular nuclear receptor
Acetylcholine is polar and acts at the cell surface.
Ligand-gated ion channel
Correct: the binding site and the pore are part of one protein complex.
questions.x: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is one protein complex that both binds the ligand and forms the ion pore, so binding opens a cation channel within milliseconds. That defines a ligand-gated ion channel (ionotropic receptor). Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are the GPCR version: they act more slowly through G proteins and have no pore of their own.

questions.q: Binding of epidermal growth factor to its receptor tyrosine kinase first causes:
o: Opening of an ion pore in the receptor
RTKs are not channels.
Exchange of GDP for GTP on the receptor
GTP exchange occurs on G proteins, not on RTKs.
Movement of the receptor into the nucleus
RTKs signal from the membrane; they are not transcription factors.
Receptor dimerization and cross-phosphorylation of tyrosines
Correct: paired receptors phosphorylate each other, creating docking sites.
questions.x: Receptor tyrosine kinases are activated when ligand binding brings two receptors together. The paired kinase domains then phosphorylate tyrosines on each other, and these phosphotyrosines serve as docking sites for SH2-domain proteins such as Grb2, which leads to Ras and MAPK signaling. GTP exchange comes later in that pathway, on Ras, not on the receptor itself.

questions.q: Cholera toxin locks the Gsα subunit in its GTP-bound state. The direct result in intestinal cells is:
o: Low cAMP from blocked adenylyl cyclase
Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase; it does not inhibit it.
Rapid breakdown of the GPCR
The receptor is not destroyed; the downstream G protein stays on.
Continuously high cAMP from constant adenylyl cyclase activity
Correct: active Gsα keeps stimulating adenylyl cyclase.
Loss of all G protein signaling
Signaling is stuck on, not lost.
questions.note: GTP-bound α = on; GTP hydrolysis switches it off.
questions.x: Gα subunits act as switches: GTP-bound means on, and their own GTPase activity turns them off. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα so it cannot hydrolyze GTP, which locks it in the on state. Adenylyl cyclase keeps making cAMP, and PKA keeps CFTR open, causing massive Cl⁻ and water loss as diarrhea. The signal is stuck on, not blocked.

questions.q: As a spherical cell's radius doubles, its surface-area-to-volume ratio:
o: Doubles
SA/V falls as cells grow.
Stays the same
Area and volume scale differently with radius.
Halves
Correct: SA ∝ r² and V ∝ r³, so SA/V ∝ 1/r.
Falls to one-eighth
Volume rises 8-fold but area rises 4-fold, so the ratio halves.
questions.note: This limit on exchange is why cells stay small or fold their membranes.
questions.x: For a sphere, surface area is 4πr² and volume is (4/3)πr³, so SA/V = 3/r. Doubling r increases area 4-fold and volume 8-fold, so the ratio halves. A larger cell therefore has less membrane per unit of cytoplasm for exchange, which limits cell size. Dividing 4 by 8 gives one-half, not one-eighth.

questions.q: Inside-out vesicles containing Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase are prepared in a buffer with Na⁺ and K⁺, and ATP is then added to the outside medium. The pump will move:
o: Na⁺ out of the vesicle and K⁺ into it
That would be true for right-side-out vesicles with ATP inside.
Both ions into the vesicle
The pump is an antiporter; the ions move in opposite directions.
Nothing, because ATP cannot reach the pump
ATP binds the cytosolic face, which is exposed to the medium.
Na⁺ into the vesicle and K⁺ out into the medium
Correct: the cytosolic face, with its Na⁺ and ATP sites, now faces the medium.
questions.note: Track which face of the pump touches the ATP.
questions.x: The pump's cytosolic face binds Na⁺ and ATP and releases K⁺; its extracellular face releases Na⁺ and binds K⁺. In inside-out vesicles, the cytosolic face points toward the medium, so only externally added ATP can drive it. Na⁺ is pumped from the medium into the vesicle and K⁺ from the vesicle out to the medium. The rule is to ask which side the ATP-binding face is on.

questions.q: Replacing most extracellular Na⁺ with impermeant choline barely changes a neuron's resting potential. This indicates that:
o: Resting membrane permeability to Na⁺ is low
Correct: if Na⁺ barely contributes to Vm at rest, removing it changes little.
Choline is highly permeant at rest
The stem says choline is impermeant.
Na⁺ is the main determinant of resting potential
Then removing Na⁺ would hyperpolarize the cell noticeably.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump stops at low Na⁺
Pump changes would not explain a stable potential.
questions.x: The Goldman equation weights each ion by its membrane permeability. If removing most extracellular Na⁺ barely changes the resting potential, Na⁺ must contribute little to it, meaning resting Na⁺ permeability is low compared with K⁺. If Na⁺ were the main determinant, removing it would make the cell much more negative. Choline acts only as an impermeant stand-in to keep osmolarity steady.

questions.q: A protein reconstituted into liposomes moves glucose into them only when the outside has more Na⁺ than the inside. The protein is most likely a:
o: GLUT uniporter
A uniporter would move glucose without any Na⁺ gradient.
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
The pump does not carry glucose.
Na⁺–glucose symporter
Correct: glucose transport needs an inward Na⁺ gradient moving the same way.
Glucose-gated ion channel
Ion channels do not carry glucose into the lumen.
questions.x: A reconstitution experiment strips away everything except the protein, so the requirement for an inward Na⁺ gradient must come from the protein itself. Glucose moving in only when Na⁺ can also move in means the two are coupled in the same direction: a Na⁺–glucose symporter such as SGLT. A GLUT uniporter would carry glucose down its own gradient whether Na⁺ were present or not.

questions.q: A 90-kDa cytosolic protein moves into the nucleus after a short stretch of basic residues (PKKKRKV) is added to it. This stretch acts as a:
o: Signal sequence for the ER
ER signal sequences are hydrophobic stretches, usually at the N-terminus.
Nuclear localization signal
Correct: importins recognize basic NLS motifs and carry cargo through nuclear pores.
Mitochondrial targeting sequence
These are amphipathic helices with basic and hydrophobic residues, not a short basic motif.
Nuclear export signal
An export signal would move the protein out of the nucleus.
questions.note: Proteins too large to diffuse through the pore need an NLS.
questions.x: Large proteins (above about 40–60 kDa) cannot diffuse through nuclear pores and need a nuclear localization signal. A classic NLS is a short stretch of basic lysine and arginine residues, as in PKKKRKV from the SV40 large T antigen. Importins recognize it and carry the cargo through the pore, powered by the Ran-GTP gradient. ER signal sequences differ: they are hydrophobic, not basic.

questions.q: The nucleolus is the main site of:
o: mRNA translation
Translation occurs on ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
rRNA synthesis and ribosomal subunit assembly
Correct: rRNA genes cluster there, and subunits are assembled before export.
DNA replication origins only
Replication occurs throughout the nucleus.
Lipid synthesis
Lipids are made in the smooth ER.
questions.x: The nucleolus forms around clusters of rRNA genes. RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNA there, and the rRNA is processed and combined with ribosomal proteins imported from the cytoplasm. The finished small and large subunits are exported through nuclear pores. The nucleolus makes the parts of ribosomes, but translation itself happens in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with the:
o: Golgi apparatus
The Golgi is a separate stack of cisternae.
Plasma membrane
The nuclear envelope does not join the plasma membrane.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: it is studded with ribosomes and joins the ER network.
Inner mitochondrial membrane
Mitochondria are separate organelles.
questions.x: The nuclear envelope is two membranes. The outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER and often carries ribosomes, so the space between the two envelope membranes is continuous with the ER lumen. The inner membrane faces the nucleus and binds the nuclear lamina. The Golgi is a separate set of cisternae reached only by vesicle transport.

questions.q: The folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae) mainly serve to:
o: Store Ca²⁺ for muscle contraction
That is the sarcoplasmic reticulum's role.
House the enzymes of glycolysis
Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol.
Increase surface area for electron transport and ATP synthase
Correct: more membrane holds more respiratory complexes.
Allow free passage of protons
The inner membrane is nearly impermeable to H⁺, which makes the gradient possible.
questions.x: The electron transport chain complexes and ATP synthase are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, so more membrane area means more capacity for oxidative phosphorylation. Cristae fold the inner membrane to increase that area, and very active cells such as heart muscle have densely packed cristae. Glycolysis happens in the cytosol and does not use mitochondrial membranes.

questions.q: Which observation best supports the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria?
o: They contain the enzymes of glycolysis
Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, not mitochondria.
They contain circular DNA and bacteria-like ribosomes
Correct: these features resemble those of free-living bacteria.
All of their proteins are encoded by nuclear genes
Mitochondria keep their own genome, which supports endosymbiosis.
They are surrounded by a single membrane
They have two membranes, consistent with engulfment.
questions.x: The endosymbiotic theory says mitochondria came from engulfed α-proteobacteria. Supporting evidence includes their own circular DNA, 70S-type ribosomes that are sensitive to some antibiotics, two membranes, and division by binary fission. Most mitochondrial proteins are now encoded by nuclear genes, but that reflects gene transfer to the nucleus over time and does not support the theory.

questions.q: A disease caused by a mutation in mitochondrial DNA is typically transmitted:
o: From affected mothers to their children, not from affected fathers
Correct: mitochondria are inherited through the egg cytoplasm.
From affected fathers to all their sons
Sperm mitochondria are normally eliminated after fertilization.
In an autosomal recessive pattern
mtDNA does not follow Mendelian segregation.
In an X-linked pattern
mtDNA is not on the X chromosome.
questions.x: Nearly all mitochondria in a zygote come from the egg, because sperm mitochondria are tagged and destroyed after fertilization. A mitochondrial DNA mutation therefore passes from an affected mother to all her children, while an affected father does not pass it on. Severity can vary because of heteroplasmy, but the pattern is maternal, not Mendelian or X-linked.

questions.q: Compared with the mitochondrial matrix, the intermembrane space during active respiration has:
o: Higher pH and a more negative charge
That describes the matrix.
The same pH, because H⁺ crosses the inner membrane freely
The inner membrane is nearly impermeable to H⁺.
Lower pH and a more positive charge
Correct: the electron transport chain pumps H⁺ out of the matrix into this space.
Lower pH and a more negative charge
Extra H⁺ makes the space positive, not negative.
questions.x: The electron transport chain pumps H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space. That space therefore has a higher [H⁺], meaning a lower pH, and is electrically positive compared with the matrix. Both parts of this proton-motive force drive H⁺ back through ATP synthase. Gaining H⁺ makes a compartment more positive, not more negative.

questions.q: When a lysosome ruptures, its hydrolases do relatively little damage to the cytosol mainly because they:
o: Are immediately exported from the cell
Released enzymes are not exported.
Work poorly at the near-neutral pH of the cytosol
Correct: acid hydrolases are most active near pH 5.
Require ATP, which is absent in the cytosol
The cytosol is rich in ATP, and hydrolases do not need it.
Only digest lipids
Lysosomes digest proteins, lipids, carbohydrates and nucleic acids.
questions.x: Lysosomal hydrolases are acid hydrolases, working best near pH 5, which V-type pumps maintain inside lysosomes. The cytosol is near pH 7.2, where these enzymes have little activity, so a single ruptured lysosome causes little damage. This pH dependence is a built-in safety feature. ATP is not involved, because hydrolases use water to break bonds.

questions.q: Cells unable to add mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes would most likely:
o: Retain the enzymes in the rough ER
The enzymes leave the ER normally; the Golgi sorting step fails.
Send the enzymes into the nucleus
Mannose-6-phosphate is not involved in nuclear import.
Secrete the enzymes, leaving lysosomes full of undigested material
Correct: without the tag, enzymes follow the default secretory path.
Degrade the enzymes in proteasomes immediately
The untagged enzymes are folded and simply mis-sorted.
questions.note: This is I-cell disease: high lysosomal enzyme levels in the blood.
questions.x: In the cis Golgi, lysosomal enzymes receive a mannose-6-phosphate tag. M6P receptors in the trans Golgi then sort them into vesicles bound for lysosomes. Without the tag, the enzymes follow the default secretory route and are released from the cell, so lysosomes fill with undigested material while enzyme levels in the blood rise: I-cell disease. The enzymes still leave the ER normally.

questions.q: An inherited lack of a single lysosomal hydrolase most directly leads to:
o: Failure of protein synthesis on ribosomes
Ribosomes do not depend on lysosomal enzymes.
Loss of the mitochondrial proton gradient
Hydrolases do not maintain the proton gradient.
Buildup of that enzyme's substrate inside lysosomes
Correct: undigested material accumulates, as in lysosomal storage diseases.
Excess synthesis of the substrate in the ER
The defect is in breakdown, not synthesis.
questions.x: Each lysosomal hydrolase breaks down specific substrates. If one is missing, its substrate cannot be broken down and builds up in lysosomes, which swell and impair the cell. Examples include Tay-Sachs (GM2 ganglioside, hexosaminidase A) and Gaucher disease (glucocerebroside). The defect is in breakdown, so synthesis of the substrate does not increase.

questions.q: During starvation, cells break down damaged mitochondria and recycle their parts by:
o: Degrading whole mitochondria in proteasomes
Proteasomes degrade individual proteins, not whole organelles.
Oxidizing them in peroxisomes
Peroxisomes oxidize fatty acids, not organelles.
Exocytosing them from the cell
Recycling requires internal digestion, not export.
Autophagy, as autophagosomes fuse with lysosomes
Correct: whole organelles are enclosed and digested by lysosomal enzymes.
questions.x: Autophagy is the cell's bulk recycling route. A double-membrane autophagosome encloses part of the cytoplasm, even whole organelles such as damaged mitochondria (mitophagy), then fuses with a lysosome whose hydrolases digest the contents for reuse. It increases during starvation. Proteasomes degrade single ubiquitinated proteins and cannot take in whole organelles.

questions.q: Bafilomycin A1 inhibits the V-type H⁺-ATPase. Treated cells would most likely show:
o: Lower lysosomal pH and faster digestion
Blocking the H⁺ pump cannot acidify lysosomes.
Loss of ATP synthesis in mitochondria
Mitochondria use F-type ATP synthase, not V-type pumps.
Higher lysosomal pH and slower breakdown of endocytosed proteins
Correct: without H⁺ pumping, lysosomes cannot stay acidic and hydrolases slow.
Faster mannose-6-phosphate tagging in the Golgi
Tagging does not depend on lysosomal pH.
questions.note: V-type pumps acidify lysosomes and endosomes.
questions.x: V-type H⁺-ATPases use ATP to pump H⁺ into lysosomes and endosomes, keeping them near pH 5. Bafilomycin blocks these pumps, so the lumen becomes more alkaline, acid hydrolases slow down, and receptors cannot release their ligands in endosomes. Mitochondria make ATP with F-type ATP synthase, a related but distinct enzyme, so their ATP production is not the direct target.

questions.q: A secretory protein's N-terminal signal sequence is deleted. The protein will most likely:
o: Be secreted faster than normal
Without the signal, it cannot enter the secretory pathway.
Be sent to the lysosome
Lysosomal targeting also depends on first entering the ER.
Stay in the cytosol, made on free ribosomes
Correct: without a signal for SRP, translation never moves to the ER.
Insert into the plasma membrane
Membrane insertion also requires ER targeting.
questions.x: As the N-terminal signal sequence emerges from the ribosome, SRP binds it and brings the ribosome to the ER, where the protein is threaded into the lumen. Without that signal, translation finishes on a free ribosome and the protein stays in the cytosol. Every route into the secretory pathway, including secretion, lysosomes and the plasma membrane, starts with entry into the ER.

questions.q: Hepatocytes of a person who chronically takes barbiturates show expansion of which organelle?
o: Golgi apparatus
The Golgi sorts and modifies proteins rather than detoxifying drugs.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: its cytochrome P450 enzymes detoxify drugs, and it grows with use.
Nucleolus
The nucleolus makes ribosomes.
Lysosome
Lysosomes digest macromolecules; they do not handle drug oxidation.
questions.x: The smooth ER contains cytochrome P450 enzymes that oxidize lipophilic drugs such as barbiturates, making them more water-soluble so they can be excreted. Repeated drug exposure causes hepatocytes to expand their smooth ER and make more of these enzymes, which also speeds metabolism of other drugs and explains tolerance. The Golgi modifies proteins and does not detoxify drugs.

questions.q: In skeletal muscle, the specialized smooth ER that stores and releases Ca²⁺ is the:
o: Sarcolemma
The sarcolemma is the muscle cell's plasma membrane.
Sarcoplasmic reticulum
Correct: it releases Ca²⁺ to trigger contraction.
T-tubule
T-tubules carry action potentials inward; they do not store Ca²⁺.
Sarcomere
The sarcomere is the contractile unit of actin and myosin.
questions.x: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized smooth ER in muscle that takes up Ca²⁺ using SERCA pumps. When an action potential travels down the T-tubules, the SR releases Ca²⁺ through ryanodine receptors, starting contraction.
