T-tubules are the tempting answer because they sit next to the SR, but they are inward folds of the sarcolemma that carry the signal and do not store Ca²⁺.

questions.q: Proteins arriving from the ER enter the Golgi apparatus at its:
o: Trans face
The trans face is the exit side toward vesicles and the membrane.
Medial cisternae directly
Cargo enters at cis before passing through medial cisternae.
Nuclear pore side
The Golgi has no nuclear pores.
Cis face
Correct: the cis face receives ER cargo, and the trans face ships it out.
questions.x: The Golgi is polarized. ER-derived vesicles arrive and fuse at the cis face (the entry side, facing the ER). Cargo passes through the medial cisternae for further modification, and at the trans face and trans-Golgi network it is sorted into vesicles bound for lysosomes, the plasma membrane or secretion. Cis is in, trans is out.

questions.q: N-linked glycosylation of a secreted protein begins in the:
o: Lumen of the rough ER
Correct: a preformed oligosaccharide is added to asparagine as the protein enters the ER.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi trims N-linked sugars and adds O-linked sugars.
Cytosol
Secreted protein glycosylation happens in the lumen, not the cytosol.
Lysosome
Lysosomes break down sugars; they do not add them.
questions.x: N-linked glycosylation begins in the rough ER lumen. Oligosaccharyltransferase moves a premade 14-sugar oligosaccharide from dolichol onto asparagine in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequences, often while the chain is still being translated. The Golgi then trims and remodels these sugars and adds O-linked sugars. Because the Golgi modifies N-linked sugars, it is a tempting answer, but it does not start them.

questions.q: In a pulse-chase experiment with radioactive leucine in pancreatic acinar cells, the label appears in which sequence?
o: Golgi → rough ER → secretory vesicles
Proteins reach the ER before the Golgi.
Nucleus → rough ER → Golgi
Amino acids are not incorporated into protein in the nucleus first.
Rough ER → Golgi → secretory vesicles
Correct: proteins are made on the RER, processed in the Golgi, then packaged.
Secretory vesicles → Golgi → rough ER
This reverses the secretory pathway.
questions.x: A pulse-chase experiment labels a group of newly made proteins and then tracks them over time. In secretory cells, label appears first in the rough ER, where the proteins are made, then in the Golgi, then in secretory granules, and finally outside the cell. This experiment by Palade defined the secretory pathway. Amino acids are built into proteins on ribosomes, not in the nucleus.

questions.q: An ER-resident chaperone loses its C-terminal KDEL retrieval sequence. It will most likely:
o: Stay in the ER, unaffected
KDEL is needed to retrieve proteins that escape to the Golgi.
Move into the nucleus
KDEL loss does not create a nuclear signal.
Be secreted from the cell
Correct: without KDEL, it is not brought back from the Golgi and follows the default secretory route.
Be degraded in the cytosol right after synthesis
The protein still enters the ER through its signal sequence.
questions.note: Secretion is the default for lumenal proteins with no other signal.
questions.x: Soluble ER residents such as BiP carry a C-terminal KDEL sequence. When they escape to the cis Golgi, KDEL receptors bind them and return them to the ER in COPI vesicles. Without KDEL, the protein is not retrieved and follows the default route for soluble lumenal proteins, secretion. KDEL does not keep proteins in the ER to begin with; it retrieves the ones that leak out.

questions.q: Which organelle contains catalase to break down hydrogen peroxide?
o: Lysosome
Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases, not catalase.
Peroxisome
Correct: peroxisomes make H₂O₂ during oxidation and destroy it with catalase.
Golgi apparatus
The Golgi modifies and sorts proteins.
Rough ER
The rough ER makes secretory and membrane proteins.
questions.x: Peroxisomes carry out oxidation reactions, such as breaking down very-long-chain fatty acids, that make hydrogen peroxide. Catalase in the same organelle converts 2 H₂O₂ to 2 H₂O + O₂, keeping the toxic product contained. Catalase is the marker enzyme for peroxisomes, while acid hydrolases mark lysosomes, the most common confusion between these similar-looking vesicles.

questions.q: Cells with defective peroxisome assembly would most likely build up:
o: Very-long-chain fatty acids
Correct: peroxisomes start the β-oxidation of very long fatty acids.
Glycogen
Glycogen breakdown happens in the cytosol.
Unprocessed rRNA
rRNA processing occurs in the nucleolus.
Misfolded secretory proteins in the ER
That reflects an ER folding problem, not peroxisome failure.
questions.x: Very-long-chain fatty acids (more than 22 carbons) are too long for mitochondrial β-oxidation to start, so peroxisomes shorten them first. If peroxisomes do not assemble, as in Zellweger syndrome, or a VLCFA transporter fails, as in adrenoleukodystrophy, VLCFAs accumulate and damage myelin and other tissues. Glycogen is handled in the cytosol, not by peroxisomes.

questions.q: Which structure is found in both a bacterium and a human liver cell?
o: Ribosomes
Correct: all cells need ribosomes; bacteria have 70S, eukaryotes 80S.
A nuclear envelope
Bacteria have no nucleus.
Mitochondria
Bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles.
A Golgi apparatus
The Golgi is a eukaryotic organelle.
questions.x: Ribosomes are found in all cells, because every cell must translate mRNA. Bacteria have 70S ribosomes (30S + 50S), and eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S (40S + 60S), but both do the same job. Mitochondria, the Golgi and a nuclear envelope are membrane-bound structures found only in eukaryotes, even though bacteria resemble the ancestors of mitochondria.

questions.q: Most proteins inside mitochondria are:
o: Encoded by nuclear genes, made in the cytosol and then imported
Correct: mtDNA encodes only a few proteins; the rest come through TOM/TIM complexes.
Encoded by mitochondrial DNA and made in the matrix
mtDNA encodes only about a dozen proteins in humans.
Made on the rough ER and delivered by vesicles
Mitochondria do not receive proteins by vesicles from the ER.
Taken up from the blood by endocytosis
Mitochondrial proteins are made inside the cell.
questions.x: Human mtDNA encodes only 13 proteins, all parts of the respiratory chain, along with rRNAs and tRNAs. The roughly 1,000 other mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus, made on free cytosolic ribosomes, and imported through the TOM and TIM complexes, often guided by an N-terminal amphipathic targeting sequence. Mitochondria are not part of the vesicle-based secretory pathway.

questions.q: In hepatocytes, the final step that releases free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate occurs in the:
o: Mitochondrial matrix
Gluconeogenesis starts there with pyruvate carboxylase, but not the final step.
Cytosol, by a soluble phosphatase
Glucose-6-phosphate must be moved into the ER to be dephosphorylated.
Lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: glucose-6-phosphatase sits in the ER membrane with its active site in the lumen.
Peroxisome
Peroxisomes do not handle glucose release.
questions.x: Glucose-6-phosphatase is an integral ER membrane enzyme with its active site facing the lumen. G6P is moved into the ER by a transporter, dephosphorylated, and free glucose leaves through the secretory system and GLUT2. This location lets the liver release glucose while keeping G6P in the cytosol for other uses. Mitochondria start gluconeogenesis with pyruvate carboxylase but do not finish it.

questions.q: Insulin is stored in granules and released only when blood glucose rises. This is an example of:
o: Constitutive secretion
Constitutive secretion is continuous and needs no signal.
Regulated secretion
Correct: release waits for a signal, usually through a rise in Ca²⁺.
Receptor-mediated endocytosis
That brings material in, not out.
Transcytosis
Transcytosis moves cargo across a cell, not out from storage.
questions.x: Regulated secretion stores cargo in dense-core granules until a signal arrives. In β-cells, rising glucose raises ATP, closes K-ATP channels and depolarizes the cell, opening Ca²⁺ channels; the Ca²⁺ influx then triggers granule fusion. Constitutive secretion instead releases products such as collagen continuously as they are made, without waiting for any trigger.

questions.q: A drug blocks vesicle transport from the ER to the Golgi. Newly made secretory proteins will accumulate in the:
o: Golgi apparatus
Proteins cannot reach the Golgi if ER export is blocked.
Secretory vesicles
Vesicles form after the Golgi, which cargo never reaches.
Cytosol
Proteins with signal sequences still enter the ER.
Endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: proteins enter the ER but cannot leave it.
questions.x: Secretory proteins move in one direction: rough ER, then Golgi, then vesicles, then the outside. Their signal sequences still bring them into the ER, but if ER-to-Golgi vesicle transport (COPII) is blocked, they cannot leave and build up in the ER. Proteins collect just before the blocked step, so the Golgi and vesicles do not fill.

questions.q: In differential centrifugation of a liver cell homogenate, which component pellets at the lowest speed?
o: Ribosomes
Ribosomes are small and pellet only at very high speeds.
Mitochondria
Mitochondria need higher speeds than nuclei.
Microsomes from the ER
ER fragments pellet only after mitochondria are removed.
Nuclei
Correct: the largest, densest organelles pellet first.
questions.x: Differential centrifugation separates particles by size and density. Larger, denser structures pellet at lower g-forces. Nuclei pellet first at low speed, then mitochondria, lysosomes and peroxisomes at medium speed, then microsomes (ER fragments), and finally ribosomes at the highest speeds. Small size, not low importance, is why ribosomes pellet last.

questions.q: A centrifuge fraction has high acid phosphatase activity. That fraction is enriched in:
o: Peroxisomes
Catalase, not acid phosphatase, marks peroxisomes.
Mitochondria
Succinate dehydrogenase marks mitochondria.
Lysosomes
Correct: acid phosphatase is a classic lysosomal marker enzyme.
Nuclei
Nuclei are marked by DNA, not acid hydrolases.
questions.x: Cell fractions are identified by marker enzymes found mainly in one organelle. Acid phosphatase, an acid hydrolase, marks lysosomes; catalase marks peroxisomes; succinate dehydrogenase marks mitochondria; glucose-6-phosphatase marks the ER. Peroxisomes and lysosomes sediment in similar fractions, which is why marker enzymes are needed to tell them apart.

questions.q: Brown fat produces heat because its mitochondria contain a protein that:
o: Blocks electron transport at complex IV
Blocking electron flow would stop heat and ATP production.
Lets H⁺ flow back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase
Correct: thermogenin uncouples the gradient from ATP synthesis, releasing heat.
Speeds ATP synthase to make extra ATP
Uncoupling lowers ATP output; the energy is released as heat.
Pumps H⁺ out of the intermembrane space using ATP
Heat comes from H⁺ leaking back in, not from pumping.
questions.x: Brown fat mitochondria contain thermogenin (UCP1), a channel that lets H⁺ return to the matrix without going through ATP synthase. The proton gradient then drives no ATP synthesis, and the energy from electron transport is released as heat. Electron transport actually speeds up under uncoupling, because nothing restrains it, so blocking it would stop heat production.

questions.q: Plasmodesmata in plant cells are functionally most similar to which animal structure?
o: Tight junctions
Tight junctions seal gaps between cells rather than linking cytoplasms.
Desmosomes
Desmosomes are for mechanical adhesion.
Hemidesmosomes
Hemidesmosomes attach cells to the basement membrane.
Gap junctions
Correct: both join the cytoplasm of neighboring cells.
questions.x: Plasmodesmata are channels through plant cell walls lined by plasma membrane, so the cytoplasm of neighboring cells is continuous and small molecules can pass between them. Gap junctions do the same job in animals with connexon channels. Tight junctions also connect neighboring cells, but they seal the space between cells instead of joining their cytoplasms.

questions.q: Free ribosomes and ER-bound ribosomes differ in:
o: Only the protein they are making, which decides whether they bind the ER
Correct: the same ribosomes are recruited to the ER when a signal sequence emerges.
Their rRNA sequences
Both kinds use the same rRNA.
Subunit size: bound ribosomes are 70S
Both are 80S in eukaryotes.
The genetic code they read
All cytoplasmic ribosomes read the same code.
questions.x: Free and ER-bound ribosomes are the same. Every ribosome starts translating in the cytosol; if the new chain has an ER signal sequence, SRP binds it and brings the ribosome to the ER. When that protein is finished, the ribosome detaches and can later make a cytosolic protein. The protein being made, not the ribosome itself, decides where the ribosome works.

questions.q: A misfolded cytosolic protein tagged with a polyubiquitin chain is usually degraded by the:
o: Lysosome, by direct fusion with the protein
Lysosomes take in material by endocytosis or autophagy, not single tagged proteins.
Peroxisome
Peroxisomes do not degrade ubiquitinated proteins.
Smooth ER
The smooth ER does not degrade cytosolic proteins.
Proteasome
Correct: polyubiquitin marks cytosolic proteins for proteasomal degradation.
questions.x: Cytosolic proteins marked for destruction receive a chain of ubiquitin molecules from E1, E2 and E3 enzymes. The 26S proteasome recognizes the chain, unfolds the protein, and cuts it into short peptides using ATP. Lysosomes also degrade proteins, but they receive material by endocytosis or autophagy, not by recognizing single ubiquitin-tagged cytosolic proteins.

questions.q: Mature human red blood cells make ATP only through glycolysis because they lack:
o: A plasma membrane
Red cells do have a plasma membrane.
Mitochondria
Correct: without mitochondria there is no oxidative phosphorylation.
Glucose transporters
They take up glucose via GLUT1.
Cytosolic enzymes
Glycolytic enzymes are present in their cytosol.
questions.x: Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus and organelles, including mitochondria, as they mature. Without mitochondria they cannot run the citric acid cycle or oxidative phosphorylation, so they rely on glycolysis and convert pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺. This also means they never use the oxygen they carry. Their cytosol still holds all the glycolytic enzymes.

questions.q: Release of cytochrome c from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol most directly triggers:
o: Caspase activation and apoptosis
Correct: cytosolic cytochrome c helps form the apoptosome.
Increased ATP synthesis
Losing cytochrome c impairs, rather than boosts, electron transport.
Mitochondrial fission for cell growth
Its release is a death signal, not a growth signal.
Enhanced protein import into mitochondria
Cytochrome c release does not drive protein import.
questions.x: In the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis, Bax and Bak make the outer mitochondrial membrane permeable, and cytochrome c escapes into the cytosol. There it binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates caspase-9 and then executioner caspases such as caspase-3. Cytochrome c has two roles: an electron carrier inside mitochondria, and a death signal once released.

questions.q: Cells treated with cytochalasin D during mitosis complete nuclear division but end up with two nuclei in one cell. The best explanation is that the drug:
o: Prevented spindle microtubules from forming
Chromosomes still separated into two nuclei, so the spindle worked.
Stopped DNA replication
Two full nuclei formed, so replication had already occurred.
Prevented the nuclear envelope from reforming
Both nuclei formed normally.
Blocked actin polymerization needed for the contractile ring
Correct: cytokinesis needs an actin–myosin ring; nuclear division does not.
questions.note: Binucleate cells point to failed cytokinesis, which is actin-dependent.
questions.x: Mitosis separates chromosomes using the microtubule spindle, while cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm using a contractile ring of actin and myosin II. Cytochalasin D blocks actin polymerization, so the nuclei divide but the cell cannot pinch in two, leaving one cell with two nuclei. A spindle poison would instead stop chromosomes from separating, so two nuclei would not form.

questions.q: Dividing cells are treated with colchicine, which blocks microtubule polymerization. The cells will accumulate in:
o: G1, unable to commit to division
Colchicine acts on the spindle, which forms in M phase.
S phase, unable to replicate DNA
DNA replication does not need microtubules.
M phase, unable to segregate chromosomes
Correct: without a spindle, cells arrest in mitosis.
G2, unable to condense chromosomes
Condensation does not require microtubules.
questions.x: Colchicine binds tubulin dimers and prevents them from adding to microtubules, so a mitotic spindle cannot form. Without kinetochores attached to the spindle, the spindle assembly checkpoint holds cells in metaphase. This mitotic arrest is used to collect condensed chromosomes for karyotypes. DNA replication in S phase does not use microtubules, so cells pass through S normally.

questions.q: In an axon, vesicles carried from the cell body toward the axon terminal are moved mainly by:
o: Kinesin walking toward microtubule plus ends
Correct: axonal plus ends point toward the terminal, so kinesin carries cargo outward.
Dynein walking toward microtubule minus ends
Dynein carries cargo back toward the cell body.
Myosin walking along intermediate filaments
Intermediate filaments are not motor tracks.
Simple diffusion along the axon
Diffusion is far too slow over axon lengths.
questions.x: Axon microtubules have their plus ends pointing toward the terminal. Kinesin moves toward plus ends, so it carries vesicles and organelles outward (anterograde transport). Dynein moves toward minus ends, carrying material back toward the cell body (retrograde transport). Diffusion is far too slow to supply an axon that can be a meter long.

questions.q: Rabies virus enters at an axon terminal and travels back to the neuron's cell body. Which motor protein most likely carries it?
o: Kinesin
Kinesin carries cargo away from the cell body.
Myosin II
Myosin II drives muscle contraction and cytokinesis on actin.
Tubulin
Tubulin is the track itself, not a motor.
Dynein
Correct: dynein moves toward minus ends, which point toward the cell body.
questions.note: Kinesin: out to the terminal. Dynein: back to the cell body.
questions.x: Retrograde axonal transport carries material from the terminal back to the cell body. Because axonal microtubules have minus ends toward the cell body, this transport uses cytoplasmic dynein, the minus-end-directed motor. Rabies, herpes viruses and tetanus toxin take advantage of this route to reach the CNS. Kinesin moves the opposite way, toward the terminal.

questions.q: The nuclear lamina, which supports the nuclear envelope, is built from:
o: Microtubules
Microtubules radiate through the cytoplasm, not under the envelope.
Intermediate filaments (lamins)
Correct: lamins are a nuclear class of intermediate filament.
Actin microfilaments
Actin forms the cell cortex, not the main nuclear lamina.
Keratin filaments
Keratins are cytoplasmic intermediate filaments of epithelia.
questions.x: The nuclear lamina is a mesh of lamins, a nuclear class of intermediate filaments, lining the inner surface of the nuclear envelope. It holds the nucleus in shape, anchors chromatin, and is phosphorylated and taken apart when the envelope breaks down in mitosis. Keratins are also intermediate filaments, but they are cytoplasmic and found in epithelia.

questions.q: Unlike microtubules and actin filaments, intermediate filaments:
o: Lack polarity and are not used as tracks by motor proteins
Correct: their antiparallel subunits produce a nonpolar rope-like filament.
Are built from globular subunits that bind GTP
That describes tubulin.
Turn over rapidly by dynamic instability
Intermediate filaments are the most stable cytoskeletal fibers.
Drive cell crawling by polymerizing at the leading edge
Actin polymerization drives crawling.
questions.x: Intermediate filament subunits pair into dimers, and the dimers line up antiparallel in tetramers. The two ends of the filament are therefore the same, so there is no plus or minus end for a motor to recognize. They also bind no nucleotide and are very stable, acting like ropes that resist tension. Dynamic instability and GTP binding describe microtubules, and ATP binding describes actin.

questions.q: Which nucleotide bound to β-tubulin is needed for microtubules to grow?
o: ATP
ATP binds actin, not tubulin.
GTP
Correct: GTP-tubulin adds to the plus end; hydrolysis to GDP destabilizes the lattice.
cAMP
cAMP is a second messenger, not a cytoskeletal cofactor.
NADH
NADH is an electron carrier.
questions.x: Tubulin dimers carrying GTP on β-tubulin add to the growing plus end. Soon after, the GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP. A GTP cap at the tip keeps the microtubule growing; if the cap is lost, GDP-tubulin peels away and the microtubule shrinks rapidly (dynamic instability). ATP is the nucleotide for actin, not tubulin.

questions.q: Paclitaxel (Taxol) stabilizes microtubules and prevents them from shrinking. It blocks cell division mainly because:
o: It prevents tubulin from polymerizing at all
That is how colchicine works, not paclitaxel.
It breaks down actin in the contractile ring
Paclitaxel targets tubulin, not actin.
Spindle microtubules must shorten to pull sister chromatids apart
Correct: the spindle depends on dynamic instability; frozen microtubules cannot segregate chromosomes.
It stops DNA replication in S phase
Its block is in mitosis, not S phase.
questions.x: Chromosome segregation requires spindle microtubules that can both grow and shrink. Kinetochore microtubules shorten to pull sister chromatids to the poles in anaphase. Paclitaxel stabilizes microtubules so they cannot depolymerize, and cells stay arrested in mitosis. Colchicine and vinca alkaloids do the opposite, blocking polymerization, but both kinds of drug arrest mitosis.

questions.q: The axoneme of a motile cilium has which microtubule arrangement?
o: Nine outer doublets around a central pair
Correct: the classic 9 + 2 pattern.
Nine triplets with no central pair
That is the 9 + 0 pattern of centrioles and basal bodies.
Thirteen singlets in a ring
Thirteen protofilaments make up one microtubule, not an axoneme.
A single bundle of actin filaments
Actin bundles form microvilli and stereocilia.
questions.x: A motile cilium or flagellum has a 9 + 2 axoneme: nine doublet microtubules around two central single microtubules, with dynein arms linking neighboring doublets. Centrioles and basal bodies instead have nine triplets and no central pair (9 × 3 + 0). Primary, nonmotile cilia lack the central pair (9 + 0). Microvilli and stereocilia have actin cores instead of microtubules.

questions.q: A man has repeated sinus and lung infections and immotile sperm. A mutation in which protein is most likely?
o: Keratin
Keratin defects affect skin strength, not motility.
Axonemal dynein
Correct: dynein arms bend cilia and flagella; without them neither can beat.
Kinesin
Kinesin carries cargo but does not power ciliary bending.
Spectrin
Spectrin supports the red cell membrane.
questions.x: Cilia in the airways and the sperm flagellum share the same 9 + 2 axoneme, which bends when axonemal dynein slides neighboring doublets past each other using ATP. A dynein defect, as in primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome), stops both from beating, causing poor mucus clearance with repeated infections and male infertility. Kinesin is a microtubule motor too, but it carries cargo rather than bending cilia.

questions.q: Basal bodies at the base of cilia are structurally most similar to:
o: Centrioles
Correct: both are cylinders of nine microtubule triplets.
Ribosomes
Ribosomes are RNA–protein machines, not microtubule structures.
Microvilli
Microvilli have an actin core.
Desmosomes
Desmosomes are adhesive junctions.
questions.x: A basal body anchors each cilium and organizes its axoneme. It has the same structure as a centriole, a cylinder of nine microtubule triplets, and centrioles can migrate to the cell surface to become basal bodies. Microvilli are often listed alongside cilia, but they are supported by actin, not microtubules.

questions.q: Microtubules radiate from the centrosome. Which end of each microtubule is anchored there?
o: The plus end, which grows toward the center
Plus ends point away from the centrosome.
Both ends, forming closed loops
Microtubules are linear polymers with two distinct ends.
The minus end, capped by γ-tubulin rings
Correct: nucleation at the centrosome leaves minus ends anchored and plus ends growing out.
Neither end; they attach along their sides
They are nucleated from one end.
questions.x: The centrosome contains γ-tubulin ring complexes that nucleate microtubules. The minus end stays capped and anchored there, while the plus end grows outward toward the cell edge or toward chromosomes. That is why the plus ends are the dynamic ends, and why kinesin carries cargo outward and dynein carries it inward toward the centrosome.

questions.q: Plant cells lack centrioles yet still build working mitotic spindles. This shows that:
o: Plant spindles are made of actin
Plant spindles are made of microtubules too.
Plant cells separate chromosomes without microtubules
Plant mitosis still uses a microtubule spindle.
Centrioles are needed only in prokaryotes
Prokaryotes do not have centrioles.
Centrioles are not required to nucleate spindle microtubules
Correct: other microtubule-organizing centers can nucleate microtubules.
questions.x: Higher plant cells have no centrioles but still assemble microtubule spindles, nucleated by γ-tubulin at other microtubule-organizing centers such as the nuclear surface. This shows that centrioles are not needed to make a spindle. Even in animal cells, spindles can form after centrioles are removed. The spindle is made of microtubules in plants as well as animals.

questions.q: Intestinal microvilli are supported internally by:
o: A bundle of actin filaments
Correct: cross-linked actin bundles hold microvilli up.
A 9 + 2 array of microtubules
That is the axoneme of motile cilia.
Keratin intermediate filaments
Keratin runs across the cell between desmosomes.
A single central microtubule
Microvilli contain no microtubules.
questions.note: Microvilli (actin) absorb; cilia (microtubules) move fluid.
questions.x: Microvilli are finger-like projections that increase the absorptive surface of the intestine. Each has a core of about 20 to 30 parallel actin filaments cross-linked by villin and fimbrin and anchored in the terminal web. They contain no microtubules and do not beat. Motile cilia, by contrast, have a 9 + 2 microtubule axoneme.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts bacterial flagella with sperm flagella?
o: Both are built from tubulin in a 9 + 2 arrangement
Bacterial flagella are made of flagellin, not tubulin.
Sperm flagella rotate; bacterial flagella whip back and forth
This reverses the two mechanisms.
Bacterial flagella rotate using a H⁺ gradient; sperm flagella bend using dynein and ATP
Correct: the bacterial base is a rotary motor; the eukaryotic axoneme bends.
Both are powered directly by ATP hydrolysis at the base
The bacterial motor runs on the proton-motive force.
questions.x: Bacterial and eukaryotic flagella evolved separately. A bacterial flagellum is a rigid helical filament of flagellin turned by a rotary motor at its base, powered by H⁺ (or sometimes Na⁺) flowing into the cell. A sperm flagellum is a 9 + 2 microtubule axoneme that bends in waves as dynein uses ATP to slide neighboring doublets. They share a name, not a structure or mechanism.

questions.q: A neutrophil crawling toward bacteria pushes its leading edge forward mainly by:
o: Dynein beating along cilia
Neutrophils do not crawl using cilia.
Microtubule doublets sliding past each other
That mechanism bends cilia and flagella.
Polymerization of intermediate filaments
Intermediate filaments give strength, not protrusion.
Actin polymerization at the front of the cell
Correct: growing actin networks push out the lamellipodium.
questions.x: Crawling cells push their leading edge forward by polymerizing actin. Branched actin networks nucleated by Arp2/3 grow against the membrane, forming lamellipodia, while myosin-driven contraction at the rear pulls the cell body along and integrins grip the surface. Neutrophils do not crawl by using cilia or by sliding microtubules.

questions.q: Spectrin mutations weaken the cytoskeleton under the red cell membrane. Affected cells tend to:
o: Become sickle-shaped when deoxygenated
Sickling comes from abnormal hemoglobin, not spectrin.
Become spherical and fragile and be destroyed in the spleen
Correct: losing cortical support turns red cells into spheres (spherocytosis).
Gain mitochondria to make more ATP
Mature red cells have no mitochondria.
Divide rapidly in the bloodstream
Mature red cells cannot divide.
questions.x: A mesh of spectrin, attached to the membrane through ankyrin and band 3, supports the red cell membrane and lets it deform and recover its biconcave shape. When spectrin or ankyrin is defective, the cell sheds bits of membrane, becomes a small sphere that cannot squeeze through splenic sinusoids, and is destroyed: hereditary spherocytosis. Sickling is a hemoglobin defect, not a cytoskeleton defect.

questions.q: Mutations in keratins 5 and 14 cause basal skin cells to tear apart with minor friction. This shows that intermediate filaments mainly:
o: Give cells tensile strength against mechanical stress
Correct: keratin networks linked to desmosomes spread out mechanical force.
Move vesicles to the cell surface
Motor proteins on microtubules move vesicles.
Form the contractile ring in cytokinesis
The contractile ring is actin and myosin.
Seal the paracellular space
Tight junction proteins seal the paracellular space.
questions.x: Intermediate filaments are the cell's tension-bearing ropes. In basal keratinocytes, keratins 5 and 14 connect to desmosomes and hemidesmosomes to spread mechanical stress across the epithelium. When they are mutated, as in epidermolysis bullosa simplex, cells break open from minor friction. Moving vesicles is a job for motors on microtubules, not intermediate filaments.

questions.q: Carcinoma cells that lose E-cadherin expression are more likely to metastasize mainly because:
o: They detach more easily from neighboring cells
Correct: E-cadherin anchors adherens junctions that hold epithelial cells together.
They stop dividing
Losing cadherin does not stop proliferation.
They lose all integrins
E-cadherin loss does not remove integrins.
They form more gap junctions
Gap junctions are not what limits cell escape.
questions.x: E-cadherin is the main adhesion molecule of adherens junctions, linking neighboring epithelial cells and connecting to actin inside through catenins. Losing it is a key step in the epithelial–mesenchymal transition: cells loosen from one another, become motile, and can invade and spread. Losing cadherin does not slow growth, and integrins, which bind the matrix, are a separate adhesion system.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines lung alveoli and allows fast gas diffusion?
o: Simple squamous
Correct: one layer of flat cells gives the shortest diffusion distance.
Stratified squamous
Many layers would slow diffusion; this type is for abrasion resistance.
Simple columnar
Tall cells would add distance; they suit absorption and secretion.
Transitional
Transitional epithelium lines the stretchable bladder.
questions.x: Gas exchange depends on a short diffusion distance (Fick's law). Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of very thin, flat cells, so in alveoli it allows a barrier of well under 1 μm between air and blood. Stratified squamous epithelium is also flat at the surface, but its many layers would make the distance far too long.

questions.q: The lining of the esophagus resists abrasion from swallowed food because it is:
o: Stratified squamous epithelium
Correct: many layers can be worn away and replaced from below.
Simple squamous epithelium
A single flat layer would be easily damaged.
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Cuboidal cells suit secretion, as in glands and tubules.
Dense regular connective tissue
Lumens are lined by epithelium, not tendon-like tissue.
questions.x: Surfaces exposed to friction, such as the esophagus, mouth, vagina and skin, are lined by stratified squamous epithelium. Its many layers mean that surface cells can be worn away while basal cells divide to replace them. The esophagus is nonkeratinized, while skin is keratinized. A single layer of any shape would be quickly damaged.

questions.q: In the trachea, every epithelial cell touches the basement membrane, but the nuclei sit at different heights. This epithelium is:
o: Stratified columnar
In a true stratified epithelium, upper cells do not touch the basement membrane.
Pseudostratified columnar
Correct: it only looks layered; all cells rest on the basement membrane.
Simple cuboidal
Simple cuboidal nuclei line up in one row.
Transitional
Transitional epithelium is truly layered and lines urinary organs.
questions.x: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is truly a single layer: every cell rests on the basement membrane, but cells differ in height, so their nuclei sit at different levels and it looks layered. In the airways it carries cilia and goblet cells. In true stratified epithelium, the upper cells do not touch the basement membrane.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder and allows it to stretch?
o: Simple columnar epithelium
Simple columnar lines the intestine.
Simple squamous epithelium
This lines alveoli and vessels; it would tear under stretch.
Transitional epithelium
Correct: its surface cells flatten as the bladder fills.
Pseudostratified epithelium
This lines the airways.
questions.x: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lines the bladder, ureters and part of the urethra. Its large, dome-shaped surface cells flatten and the layers slide as the bladder fills, so it can stretch a lot without tearing, and specialized surface plaques keep it impermeable to urine. Simple squamous epithelium is thin but would tear under this kind of stretch.

questions.q: Epithelial tissues get nutrients mainly by:
o: Capillaries running between epithelial cells
Epithelia lack their own blood vessels.
Absorption through the apical surface only
Most epithelia rely on the connective tissue below.
Diffusion from capillaries in the underlying connective tissue
Correct: epithelia are avascular, so supplies diffuse across the basement membrane.
Gap junctions linking them to blood cells
Blood cells do not form gap junctions with epithelia.
questions.x: Epithelia are avascular: no blood vessels run between epithelial cells. Oxygen and nutrients come from capillaries in the connective tissue beneath and diffuse across the basement membrane, which limits how thick a living epithelium can be. Some epithelia also absorb nutrients through their apical surface, but that is not how they feed themselves in general.

questions.q: The basal lamina beneath an epithelium is rich in:
o: Type IV collagen and laminin
Correct: these form the sheet-like mesh of the basal lamina.
Type I collagen and hydroxyapatite
That combination makes bone.
Keratin and desmoglein
These are intracellular filaments and junction proteins.
Actin and myosin
These are cytoskeletal and contractile proteins.
questions.x: The basal lamina is a thin sheet of extracellular matrix under epithelia. Type IV collagen forms a net-like scaffold, and laminin links that net to cell-surface integrins, with nidogen and perlecan also present. This differs from the thick type I collagen fibers of tendon and dermis and from the mineralized type I collagen of bone.

questions.q: In kidney tubule cells, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is located mainly on which surface?
o: Basolateral membrane
Correct: pumping Na⁺ into the interstitium keeps cell Na⁺ low for apical uptake.
Apical membrane
Pumps on the apical side would push Na⁺ back into the urine.
Tight junctions
Junctions seal the space between cells and hold no pumps.
Nuclear envelope
The pump works at the plasma membrane.
questions.x: In polarized transport epithelia, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase sits on the basolateral membrane. Pumping Na⁺ out into the interstitium keeps cell [Na⁺] low, creating the inward gradient that apical channels and symporters use to bring Na⁺ in from the tubular fluid. The result is net reabsorption from lumen to blood. A pump on the apical side would send Na⁺ back into the urine.

questions.q: Which statement describes an exocrine gland?
o: It releases secretions through ducts onto a surface or into a lumen
Correct: sweat, salivary and pancreatic acinar glands are examples.
It releases hormones directly into the blood
That describes an endocrine gland.
It is formed from connective tissue
Glands are formed from epithelium.
It has no secretory cells
Glands are made of secretory cells.
questions.x: Both exocrine and endocrine glands develop from epithelium. Exocrine glands keep a duct and release their products onto a surface or into a lumen, as with sweat, saliva or pancreatic enzymes. Endocrine glands lose their duct and release hormones into the blood. The pancreas does both: acinar cells are exocrine, while islet cells are endocrine.

questions.q: In an organ such as the liver, the functional cells are called parenchyma. The supporting connective tissue framework is called:
o: Stroma
Correct: stroma is the supporting framework of connective tissue and vessels.
Mesothelium
Mesothelium is the simple squamous lining of body cavities.
Endothelium
Endothelium lines blood vessels.
Glycocalyx
The glycocalyx is a sugar coat on cell surfaces.
questions.x: Organs have two parts: the parenchyma, the functional cells such as hepatocytes, and the stroma, the supporting connective tissue framework with fibers, fibroblasts, vessels and nerves. Endothelium and mesothelium are both simple squamous linings, of vessels and body cavities respectively, not support frameworks.

questions.q: Which cells make most of the collagen and ground substance in loose connective tissue?
o: Mast cells
Mast cells release histamine and heparin.
Fibroblasts
Correct: fibroblasts secrete fibers and ground substance.
Macrophages
Macrophages engulf debris and pathogens.
Adipocytes
Adipocytes store lipid.
questions.x: Fibroblasts are the resident cells of connective tissue proper. They secrete collagen, elastin and reticular fibers as well as the proteoglycan-rich ground substance, and they remodel the matrix during wound healing. Mast cells, macrophages and adipocytes also live in loose connective tissue, but they do not make its matrix.

questions.q: Vitamin C deficiency weakens connective tissue because:
o: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen is impaired
Correct: ascorbate is a cofactor for these hydroxylases, which stabilize the triple helix.
Collagen genes can no longer be transcribed
Vitamin C does not control collagen transcription.
Elastin is digested by lysosomes
Scurvy is a collagen defect, not elastin breakdown.
Fibroblasts lose their mitochondria
Vitamin C deficiency does not remove mitochondria.
questions.x: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate to keep their iron in the active Fe²⁺ form. Hydroxyproline forms hydrogen bonds that stabilize the collagen triple helix, and hydroxylysine allows cross-linking. Without vitamin C, collagen is weak, so scurvy causes bleeding gums, poor wound healing and fragile vessels. Collagen genes are still transcribed normally.

questions.q: Glycine must occupy every third position in a collagen chain because:
o: It forms the disulfide bonds that link the chains
Glycine has no sulfur; cysteine forms disulfides.
It is the residue that vitamin C hydroxylates
Proline and lysine are hydroxylated.
Its tiny side chain fits in the crowded center of the triple helix
Correct: any larger residue there would block tight winding of the three chains.
Its charged side chain binds water
Glycine's side chain is a single uncharged hydrogen.
questions.x: Collagen has a Gly-X-Y repeat, often with proline and hydroxyproline in the X and Y positions. In the triple helix, every third residue faces the crowded central axis where the three chains meet, and only glycine, whose side chain is a single hydrogen, fits there. A point mutation that replaces one of these glycines disrupts the helix and causes osteogenesis imperfecta.

questions.q: Which extracellular matrix protein lets the aorta recoil after it stretches?
o: Type I collagen
Collagen resists stretch but does not recoil elastically.
Laminin
Laminin is a basement membrane adhesion protein.
Keratin
Keratin is an intracellular filament of epithelia.
Elastin
Correct: cross-linked elastin stretches and snaps back like rubber.
questions.x: Elastin is cross-linked by desmosine into a rubbery network that stretches under load and recoils. In large elastic arteries such as the aorta, it lets the wall expand during systole and spring back during diastole, smoothing blood flow. Collagen provides tensile strength and limits stretch, but it does not recoil like elastin.

questions.q: Cartilage resists compression mainly because:
o: It is heavily mineralized with hydroxyapatite
That describes bone.
Negatively charged proteoglycans draw in water and create swelling pressure
Correct: the trapped water pushes back when the tissue is squeezed.
Its chondrocytes are packed tightly with no matrix
Cartilage is mostly matrix, with few cells.
Dense blood vessels keep it pressurized
Cartilage has no blood vessels.
questions.x: Cartilage matrix is full of aggrecan, a proteoglycan whose glycosaminoglycan chains carry many negative charges. These attract cations and therefore water, creating swelling pressure that the type II collagen network holds in place. When a joint is loaded, the trapped water resists being squeezed out, so cartilage absorbs compression. Hydroxyapatite hardens bone, not cartilage.

questions.q: Injuries to articular cartilage heal slowly mainly because cartilage:
o: Contains no living cells
Chondrocytes are alive within lacunae.
Is made entirely of elastin
Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage, rich in type II collagen.
Has no blood supply, so nutrients and repair cells arrive slowly
Correct: chondrocytes depend on diffusion through the matrix.
Is constantly broken down by osteoclasts
Osteoclasts resorb bone, not healthy cartilage.
questions.x: Hyaline cartilage has no blood vessels, nerves or lymphatics. Chondrocytes sit in lacunae and get nutrients only by diffusion through the matrix, which is helped by joint loading. With no blood supply, injury brings no inflammatory cells, stem cells or new matrix, and the few mature chondrocytes divide little, so repair is slow and incomplete. The cells are alive, but there are few of them.

questions.q: Tendons withstand strong pulling in one direction because they are made of:
o: Dense regular connective tissue with parallel collagen bundles
Correct: fibers aligned along the line of force resist tension.
Loose connective tissue with scattered fibers
Loose tissue is weak and flexible.
Dense irregular connective tissue
Irregular fibers resist forces from many directions, as in the dermis.
Elastic cartilage
Elastic cartilage is found in the ear and epiglottis.
questions.x: Tendons connect muscle to bone and are loaded along one axis. Their dense regular connective tissue packs type I collagen bundles parallel to that axis, with rows of fibroblasts between them, giving very high tensile strength in one direction. Dense irregular tissue, as in the dermis, weaves fibers in many directions to resist forces from many angles, but is weaker in any single one.

questions.q: Fibroblasts attach to fibronectin in the extracellular matrix mainly through:
o: Cadherins
Cadherins bind cadherins on neighboring cells.
Integrins
Correct: integrins bind matrix proteins and link to the actin cytoskeleton inside.
Connexins
Connexins form gap junction channels.
Claudins
Claudins seal tight junctions.
questions.note: Cell–matrix: integrins. Cell–cell: cadherins.
questions.x: Integrins are αβ heterodimers that bind matrix proteins such as fibronectin, often at RGD sequences, and link inside to actin through talin and vinculin at focal adhesions. They connect the cell to the matrix and carry signals both ways. Cadherins are the tempting choice because they are also adhesion molecules, but they bind cadherins on neighboring cells.

questions.q: Blood is classified as a connective tissue. Its extracellular matrix is:
o: Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is inside red cells.
The endothelium
Endothelium is the epithelial lining of vessels.
Platelets
Platelets are cell fragments, not matrix.
Plasma
Correct: plasma is the fluid matrix in which blood cells are suspended.
questions.x: A connective tissue has cells scattered in a matrix that they make or that surrounds them. In blood, the cells (red cells, white cells and platelets) are suspended in plasma, a fluid matrix of water, proteins and solutes. Platelets are cell fragments, so they are part of the formed elements rather than the matrix.

questions.q: Bone gets its hardness from hydroxyapatite crystals. Its resistance to bending and pulling comes mainly from:
o: Elastin fibers
Bone contains little elastin.
Keratin filaments
Keratin is an epithelial intracellular filament.
Type I collagen fibers
Correct: collagen adds tensile strength; mineral adds compressive hardness.
Laminin sheets
Laminin is a basement membrane protein.
questions.x: Bone is a composite. Hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate) gives it hardness and resistance to compression, but alone it would be brittle. Type I collagen fibers give tensile strength and some flexibility, so bone can withstand bending and pulling. If collagen is defective, as in osteogenesis imperfecta, the bones become brittle and fracture easily even though they are mineralized.

questions.q: Tumor cells that overexpress matrix metalloproteinases tend to be more invasive because they:
o: Make more collagen to wall themselves off
MMPs break down collagen; they do not make it.
Degrade the basement membrane and surrounding matrix
Correct: breaking down matrix barriers lets cells move into nearby tissue.
Strengthen their own adherens junctions
MMPs act on the matrix, and stronger adhesion would limit invasion.
Speed up DNA repair
MMPs are extracellular proteases, not repair enzymes.
questions.x: Matrix metalloproteinases are zinc-dependent proteases that break down collagen, including type IV collagen in basement membranes, and other matrix proteins. Carcinoma cells must break through the basement membrane to invade, so high MMP activity helps them invade and spread. Stronger adhesion or more matrix would hold tumor cells in place rather than help them escape.

questions.q: Intercalated discs between cardiac muscle cells contain:
o: Tight junctions only
Heart cells must pass current and resist pulling, which tight junctions cannot do.
Hemidesmosomes linking cells to bone
Hemidesmosomes attach epithelia to basement membranes.
Chemical synapses using acetylcholine
Cardiomyocytes are coupled electrically, not by synapses.
Desmosomes for adhesion and gap junctions for electrical coupling
Correct: they hold cells together and let action potentials spread.
questions.x: Cardiac muscle must contract as one unit and withstand repeated strain. Intercalated discs supply both needs: desmosomes and adherens junctions (fascia adherens) hold neighboring cells together under tension, while gap junctions let ions flow directly between cells so action potentials spread as a functional syncytium. Tight junctions seal epithelia and are not their main component.

questions.q: Which structure is present in every prokaryotic cell?
o: A nuclear envelope
Prokaryotes have a nucleoid region with no surrounding membrane.
Mitochondria
Membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria are eukaryotic.
A peptidoglycan cell wall
Most bacteria have one, but Mycoplasma and archaea lack peptidoglycan.
Ribosomes
Correct: all cells, including prokaryotes, need ribosomes to make proteins.
questions.note: Prokaryote = no membrane-bound organelles, but ribosomes are universal.
questions.x: Ribosomes are universal because every cell must translate mRNA into protein. Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles and a nuclear envelope. The tempting wrong answer is the peptidoglycan wall: most bacteria have one, but Mycoplasma has no wall at all and archaea build walls from other materials, so it is not universal.

questions.q: Which describes the ribosomes of a bacterium such as E. coli?
o: 80S, built from 40S and 60S subunits
These are eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes.
80S, built from 30S and 50S subunits
Assumes Svedberg values add; they depend on shape, not just mass.
60S, built from two 30S subunits
Bacterial subunits differ in size; the small is 30S, the large 50S.
70S, built from 30S and 50S subunits
Correct: bacterial ribosomes are 70S with 30S small and 50S large subunits.
questions.note: Svedberg units are not additive: 30S + 50S = 70S.
questions.x: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, made of a 30S small subunit (16S rRNA) and a 50S large subunit. Svedberg units measure sedimentation rate, which depends on mass and shape, so they do not add: 30S plus 50S gives 70S, not 80S. The 80S ribosome with 40S and 60S subunits is the eukaryotic cytosolic type, which is why ribosome-targeting antibiotics can be selective.

questions.q: The glycan backbone of bacterial peptidoglycan is made of alternating units of:
o: Glucose and galactose
These two sugars form lactose, not peptidoglycan.
N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid
Correct: NAG–NAM chains are cross-linked by short peptides.
N-acetylglucosamine alone
A polymer of only NAG is chitin, found in fungal walls.
Lipid A and O-antigen
These are parts of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane.
questions.x: Peptidoglycan is a mesh of glycan strands made of alternating N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), with short peptides on NAM cross-linking neighboring strands. That cross-linked mesh gives the wall its strength. A polymer of NAG alone is chitin, found in fungal walls and arthropod exoskeletons, not bacteria.

questions.q: Septic shock during a Gram-negative bloodstream infection is triggered mainly by which bacterial component?
o: Teichoic acids
Teichoic acids belong to Gram-positive walls.
Secreted protein exotoxins
Endotoxin is a structural membrane component, not a secreted protein.
Lipid A of outer-membrane lipopolysaccharide
Correct: lipid A (endotoxin) strongly activates innate immune signaling, causing fever and shock.
Dipicolinic acid
Dipicolinic acid is found in endospores, not Gram-negative envelopes.
questions.note: Endotoxin = LPS (lipid A), only in Gram-negatives.
questions.x: Endotoxin is lipid A, the membrane anchor of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane. When bacteria in the blood die or shed it, lipid A strongly triggers innate immune signaling (TLR4), driving cytokine release, fever, vasodilation and shock. Exotoxins are secreted proteins with specific actions and are not the defining trigger of Gram-negative septic shock.

questions.q: During Gram staining, why do Gram-positive cells remain purple after the alcohol wash?
o: Their thick peptidoglycan layer traps the crystal violet–iodine complex
Correct: alcohol dehydrates the thick wall, locking the dye complex inside.
Their outer membrane binds the crystal violet tightly
Gram-positives lack an outer membrane; alcohol dissolves Gram-negative outer membranes.
They lack peptidoglycan entirely
Gram-positives have the thickest peptidoglycan of all bacteria.
Safranin binds them more strongly than crystal violet
Safranin is applied after decolorizing and stains cells left colorless.
questions.x: In the Gram stain, crystal violet and iodine form a large complex inside all cells. Alcohol dehydrates and tightens the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positive cells, trapping the complex, while it disrupts the Gram-negative outer membrane and the thin wall lets the dye wash out. Gram-positives have no outer membrane, so the dye retention comes from the thick wall.

questions.q: A technician Gram stains E. coli (Gram-negative) but forgets the alcohol decolorizing step. How will the cells appear?
o: Pink
Pink requires removing crystal violet so safranin shows.
Purple
Correct: without decolorizing, crystal violet is never washed out of the thin wall.
Colorless
Cells keep the primary stain when alcohol is skipped.
Green
No green dye is used in a Gram stain.
questions.note: Skip decolorizer: everything looks Gram-positive.
questions.x: The decolorizing alcohol step is the only step that tells Gram-positive and Gram-negative cells apart. If it is skipped, crystal violet–iodine stays in every cell, and the later safranin is hidden by the dark purple. So Gram-negative E. coli would wrongly look purple, like a Gram-positive.

questions.q: If the safranin counterstain is omitted, how will a smear of Staphylococcus (Gram-positive) mixed with E. coli (Gram-negative) appear?
o: Both purple
That would happen if the alcohol step, not safranin, were skipped.
Staphylococcus purple; E. coli colorless
Correct: E. coli loses crystal violet in alcohol and nothing restains it.
Both pink
Pink comes from safranin, which was left out.
Staphylococcus colorless; E. coli pink
This reverses retention and still assumes safranin was applied.
questions.x: Alcohol still removes crystal violet from the Gram-negative E. coli, while Gram-positive Staphylococcus keeps it and stays purple. Safranin is the step that would turn the decolorized cells pink, so without it E. coli is left colorless. Both purple would be the result of skipping the alcohol step instead.

questions.q: In Gram-negative bacteria, the compartment between the plasma membrane and the outer membrane, which holds a thin peptidoglycan layer, is the:
o: Nucleoid
The nucleoid is the DNA region inside the cytoplasm.
Capsule
The capsule lies outside the outer membrane.
Periplasmic space
Correct: the periplasm lies between the inner and outer membranes.
Cytosol
The cytosol is inside the plasma membrane.
questions.x: The Gram-negative envelope has an inner (plasma) membrane, a thin peptidoglycan layer, and an outer membrane. The space between the two membranes is the periplasm, which holds the peptidoglycan and many binding proteins and enzymes such as β-lactamases. A capsule, if present, lies outside the outer membrane.

questions.q: Mycoplasma species are naturally unaffected by penicillin and cannot be classified by Gram staining. Which feature explains both?
o: They have a thick polysaccharide capsule
A capsule does not remove the penicillin target or block Gram classification.
They have no peptidoglycan cell wall
Correct: no wall means no penicillin target and nothing for the Gram stain to assess.
They have an LPS-containing outer membrane
Such cells stain Gram-negative, so they can be classified.
They form endospores
Mycoplasma do not form spores, and spores would not explain both traits.
questions.x: Mycoplasma has no cell wall, only a plasma membrane stiffened by sterols. Penicillin acts by blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking, so with no wall there is no target. The Gram stain classifies cells by wall structure, so a wall-less cell cannot be meaningfully called Gram-positive or Gram-negative.

questions.q: What directly powers the rotation of a bacterial flagellum?
o: ATP hydrolysis by dynein arms
Dynein drives the whiplike beating of eukaryotic flagella.
GTP hydrolysis by tubulin
Bacterial flagella are made of flagellin, not microtubules.
Proton flow across the plasma membrane
Correct: the flagellar motor is driven by the proton motive force.
Myosin sliding along actin filaments
Actomyosin is a eukaryotic motility system.
questions.note: Bacterial flagellum: flagellin + rotary motor + H⁺ gradient.
questions.x: The bacterial flagellum is a rigid helical filament of flagellin turned by a rotary motor at its base. In E. coli the motor is powered by protons flowing back into the cell down the proton motive force, not by ATP. Eukaryotic flagella are completely different: microtubules that bend because dynein hydrolyzes ATP.

questions.q: As a peritrichous E. coli cell swims up a gradient of an attractant, how does its behavior change?
o: Tumbles become less frequent, so runs last longer
Correct: a biased random walk lengthens runs in favorable directions.
Tumbles become more frequent, so it turns more often
More tumbling occurs when moving toward lower attractant.
Its flagella switch to whiplike beating
Bacterial flagella rotate; they do not beat.
It steers by turning a flagellum like a rudder
E. coli cannot steer; it changes run length instead.
questions.note: Counterclockwise rotation = run; clockwise = tumble.
questions.x: E. coli alternates runs (counterclockwise rotation, flagella bundled) with tumbles (clockwise rotation, random reorientation). It cannot steer, so it senses whether attractant is rising over time and suppresses tumbling when things improve. Runs up the gradient last longer, giving a biased random walk toward the attractant; more frequent tumbling happens when moving the wrong way.

questions.q: Short, numerous hairlike fimbriae on a bacterial surface mainly help the cell:
o: Swim toward nutrients
Swimming uses flagella, not fimbriae.
Adhere to host cells and other surfaces
Correct: fimbriae are attachment structures important for colonization.
Survive boiling temperatures
Heat resistance comes from endospores.
Store extra copies of the genome
Fimbriae are protein appendages, not genetic storage.
questions.x: Fimbriae are many short protein hairs that let bacteria stick to host tissues and surfaces, a key early step in colonization and infection. They do not drive movement; swimming uses flagella. Sex pili are a separate, longer structure used in conjugation.

questions.q: A wild-type bacterial strain with a polysaccharide capsule is lethal to mice, but a capsule-deficient mutant is cleared quickly. The best explanation is that the capsule:
o: Is required for conjugation
Conjugation uses sex pili, not capsules.
Is itself a secreted protein toxin
Capsules are usually polysaccharide coats, not toxins.
Makes the bacterium resistant to every antibiotic
Capsules do not confer broad antibiotic resistance.
Hinders phagocytosis by host immune cells
Correct: capsules make bacteria hard for phagocytes to engulf.
questions.x: A polysaccharide capsule is slippery and hides surface molecules, so phagocytes and complement have trouble grabbing and engulfing the bacterium. That lets encapsulated strains multiply and cause disease, while capsule-less mutants are quickly cleared. The capsule is a virulence factor through immune evasion, not a toxin.

questions.q: Why is boiling for a few minutes often insufficient to sterilize material contaminated with Clostridium?
o: Clostridium cells divide faster than heat kills them
Vegetative cells die quickly at 100 °C.
Its endospores have a dehydrated core that resists heat
Correct: spores with low water and Ca²⁺–dipicolinic acid survive boiling.
Its capsule insulates the cell from heat
Capsules do not provide meaningful heat resistance.
Clostridium grows best at 100 °C
Clostridium species are not hyperthermophiles.
questions.note: Spores, not capsules, explain heat resistance: autoclave at 121 °C.
questions.x: Clostridium and Bacillus form endospores, dormant structures with a dehydrated core, protective coats, and calcium–dipicolinic acid that stabilize DNA and proteins. Spores survive boiling, so sterilization needs autoclaving at 121 °C under pressure. Vegetative cells die quickly at 100 °C, and capsules give no real heat protection.

questions.q: A single vegetative Bacillus cell forms one endospore, which later germinates under good conditions. How many vegetative cells result from that one spore?
o: Correct: sporulation is a survival strategy, not reproduction; one cell becomes one spore becomes one cell.
Confuses sporulation with binary fission.
Confuses sporulation with meiosis producing four products.
Bacterial endospores do not multiply inside the mother cell.
questions.note: Trap: endospores are not reproductive.
questions.x: Endospore formation is a survival response to starvation, not a way to reproduce. One vegetative cell builds one spore inside itself, and when that spore germinates it gives back one vegetative cell. The population grows only afterward, by binary fission.

questions.q: Spherical bacteria arranged in grapelike clusters are described as:
o: Streptococci
Streptococci are cocci in chains.
Staphylococci
Correct: 'staphylo' means cluster; 'coccus' means sphere.
Bacilli
Bacilli are rod-shaped.
Spirochetes
Spirochetes are flexible spiral cells.
questions.x: Bacterial names combine shape and arrangement: cocci are spheres, bacilli rods, spirilla and spirochetes spirals. Staphylococci form grapelike clusters because they divide in multiple planes, while streptococci form chains because they divide in one plane.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes archaeal plasma membranes from bacterial ones?
o: Ester bonds link glycerol to straight fatty acids
That describes bacterial and eukaryotic membranes.
They contain large amounts of cholesterol
Cholesterol is characteristic of animal cell membranes.
Peptidoglycan is embedded within the bilayer
Archaea lack peptidoglycan entirely.
Ether bonds link glycerol to branched isoprenoid chains
Correct: archaeal lipids are ether-linked isoprenoids, which are chemically sturdy.
questions.x: Archaeal membrane lipids attach glycerol to branched isoprenoid chains by ether bonds, while bacteria and eukaryotes use ester bonds to straight fatty acids. Ether bonds resist heat and chemical attack, which helps extremophiles. Some archaea even form monolayers of lipids that span the whole membrane.

questions.q: A newly discovered single-celled organism has no nucleus, wraps its DNA around histones, and starts translation with unmodified methionine. It most likely belongs to:
o: Bacteria
Bacteria initiate with N-formylmethionine and generally lack histones.
Eukarya
Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Archaea
Correct: archaea are prokaryotic yet share histones and Met initiation with eukaryotes.
Viruses
Viruses are not cells and lack their own ribosomes.
questions.x: Archaea are prokaryotes with no nucleus, but in their information-processing machinery they look like eukaryotes. Many package DNA with histones and start translation with plain methionine, while bacteria use N-formylmethionine and generally lack histones. Eukarya is ruled out because those cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.q: In a batch culture, during which phase do new cell divisions roughly balance cell deaths?
o: Lag phase
In lag phase cells adapt and make enzymes; little division or death occurs.
Stationary phase
Correct: nutrient depletion and waste buildup make growth equal death.
Exponential phase
Divisions far outpace deaths during log growth.
Death phase
Deaths exceed divisions in the death phase.
questions.x: In batch culture, stationary phase comes when nutrients run low and wastes build up, so the rate of new divisions roughly equals the rate of cell death and the viable count levels off. In lag phase cells adapt without much division; in log phase divisions far exceed deaths; in death phase deaths win.

questions.q: Cells moved from a rich broth into a minimal glucose–salts medium show a longer lag phase than cells moved into fresh rich broth. Why?
o: They must conjugate before they can divide
Conjugation is not required for growth.
Minimal medium kills most of the transferred cells
Minimal medium supports growth of prototrophs after adaptation.
They must first make enzymes to synthesize amino acids and other building blocks
Correct: lag reflects time to induce biosynthetic pathways before dividing.
Minimal medium causes immediate sporulation
Sporulation is not the reason for a longer lag.
questions.x: Lag phase is the time cells spend adjusting to a new environment before dividing. Cells moved from rich broth to minimal medium must turn on and make enzymes to synthesize amino acids, nucleotides and vitamins that the broth used to supply. Cells moved into the same rich broth need little adjustment, so their lag is short.

questions.q: A bacterium doubles every 20 minutes. If 5 × 10³ cells enter exponential growth, about how many cells are present 2 hours later?
o: Multiplies by 6, the number of generations, instead of by 2⁶.
Uses 5 generations (2⁵ = 32); 120 min ÷ 20 min = 6.
Correct: 6 generations, 2⁶ = 64, and 64 × 5 × 10³ = 3.2 × 10⁵.
Uses 7 generations (2⁷ = 128).
questions.note: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, with n = time ÷ doubling time.
questions.x: Exponential growth follows N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings. In 120 minutes with a 20-minute doubling time, n = 6, so the population rises 2⁶ = 64-fold: 64 × 5 × 10³ = 3.2 × 10⁵ cells. The common error is multiplying by n (6) instead of raising 2 to the n.

questions.q: During exponential growth, a culture rises from 2 × 10⁶ to 1.6 × 10⁷ cells/mL in 90 minutes. What is the doubling time?
o: About 11 min
Divides 90 min by 8, the fold change, rather than by the number of doublings.
30 min
Correct: an 8-fold rise is 3 doublings (2³), so 90 ÷ 3 = 30 min.
45 min
That would give only a 4-fold rise in 90 min.
90 min
That would give only a 2-fold rise.
questions.x: To find doubling time, convert the fold change into a number of doublings. A rise from 2 × 10⁶ to 1.6 × 10⁷ is 8-fold, which is 2³, so three doublings took 90 minutes, or 30 minutes each. Dividing 90 by 8 confuses fold change with the number of doublings.

questions.q: Penicillin kills a culture most effectively during which situation?
o: Exponential phase, when cells are actively building new cell wall
Correct: β-lactams block wall synthesis, which matters most in dividing cells.
Lag phase, when cells are not yet dividing
Little new wall is being assembled before division resumes.
Stationary phase, when nutrients are exhausted
Non-growing cells make little new peptidoglycan, so they tolerate penicillin.
Equally in every phase, since all cells have walls
Penicillin blocks synthesis of new wall, not existing wall.
questions.x: β-lactams such as penicillin block transpeptidases that cross-link new peptidoglycan. Only cells actively growing and dividing are assembling new wall, so exponential-phase cells are weakened and lyse osmotically. Non-growing cells in lag or stationary phase make little new wall and tolerate the drug, even though they still have walls.

questions.q: E. coli grown in a medium containing both glucose and lactose shows two exponential phases separated by a brief plateau. What happens during the plateau?
o: Glucose runs out, cAMP rises, and the lac operon is induced
Correct: cells pause while making lactose-metabolizing enzymes such as β-galactosidase.
Cells conjugate to acquire lactose-utilization genes
E. coli already carries the lac operon on its chromosome.
Lactose becomes toxic and kills part of the population
Lactose is a usable carbon source, not a toxin.
Cells enter the death phase and then recover
The plateau is a metabolic switch, not death.
questions.note: Diauxie: glucose first, then lac induction once glucose is gone.
questions.x: This is diauxic growth. E. coli uses glucose first because glucose keeps cAMP low and blocks lac operon induction. When glucose runs out, cAMP rises, cAMP–CAP plus the lactose inducer switch on the lac operon, and growth pauses until enough β-galactosidase and permease are made to use lactose. The genes are already on the chromosome; no new DNA is needed.

questions.q: In a tube of thioglycolate broth (oxygen high at the top, absent at the bottom), an organism grows only in a band at the very bottom. It is most likely:
o: An obligate aerobe
Obligate aerobes grow only at the oxygen-rich top.
An obligate anaerobe
Correct: it grows only where oxygen is absent.
A facultative anaerobe
Facultative anaerobes grow throughout, densest at the top.
An aerotolerant anaerobe
Aerotolerant organisms grow evenly throughout the tube.
questions.x: Thioglycolate broth sets up an oxygen gradient, so where organisms grow reveals their oxygen needs. Obligate anaerobes are harmed by oxygen and grow only at the oxygen-free bottom. Facultative anaerobes grow throughout but best at the top, and aerotolerant anaerobes grow evenly because they ignore oxygen.

questions.q: In thioglycolate broth, a bacterium grows throughout the tube but most densely near the top. It is best classified as:
o: An aerotolerant anaerobe
Aerotolerant cells do not use O₂, so growth is uniform.
A facultative anaerobe
Correct: it uses O₂ when available (more growth) but can also grow without it.
A microaerophile
Microaerophiles grow in a narrow band just below the surface.
An obligate aerobe
Obligate aerobes cannot grow in the oxygen-free lower region.
questions.x: Facultative anaerobes can respire with oxygen or ferment without it. They grow throughout the tube, but densest at the top because aerobic respiration yields far more ATP. Aerotolerant anaerobes also grow throughout, but evenly, since they never use oxygen.

questions.q: Why does a facultative anaerobe grow faster with oxygen than without it?
o: O₂ is required for glycolysis to proceed
Glycolysis is anaerobic and runs without O₂.
Fermentation generates reactive oxygen species
Fermentation does not need O₂ and does not produce ROS as its main limit.
O₂ is incorporated directly into peptidoglycan
O₂ is not a structural component of the cell wall.
O₂ acts as the final electron acceptor, allowing oxidative phosphorylation and far more ATP per glucose
Correct: aerobic respiration yields much more ATP than fermentation.
questions.x: With oxygen as the final electron acceptor, a facultative anaerobe can run the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation, making many more ATP per glucose than fermentation. Fermentation gives only the 2 ATP of glycolysis. Glycolysis itself does not require oxygen, so that is not the reason for faster growth.

questions.q: Why is oxygen toxic to many obligate anaerobes?
o: O₂ binds and permanently blocks their ribosomes
O₂ is not a ribosome inhibitor.
O₂ dissolves their peptidoglycan
O₂ does not degrade cell walls.
O₂ forces glycolysis to run in reverse
O₂ does not reverse glycolysis.
They lack enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and catalase that detoxify reactive oxygen species
Correct: without these enzymes, superoxide and peroxide damage the cell.
questions.x: Oxygen metabolism produces reactive oxygen species such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. Aerobes and many facultative organisms destroy these with superoxide dismutase and catalase or peroxidase. Many obligate anaerobes lack enough of these enzymes, so oxygen exposure leads to oxidative damage to their proteins, lipids and DNA.

questions.q: Where is the electron transport chain located in an aerobic bacterium?
o: In the inner mitochondrial membrane
Bacteria have no mitochondria.
Free in the cytosol
An ETC must be membrane-bound to build a proton gradient.
In the plasma membrane
Correct: bacteria lack mitochondria, so respiration occurs at the plasma membrane.
In the peptidoglycan cell wall
The porous wall cannot hold a proton gradient.
questions.x: Bacteria have no mitochondria, so they place the electron transport chain and ATP synthase in the plasma membrane and pump protons out to the periplasm or outside. This matches the idea that mitochondria descend from bacteria, whose inner membrane carries the same machinery. A chain floating in the cytosol could not build a proton gradient.

questions.q: A protonophore that makes the bacterial plasma membrane freely permeable to H⁺ is added to motile E. coli. Which outcome is expected?
o: ATP synthesis declines, but motility is unaffected because flagella run on ATP
Bacterial flagella are powered by H⁺ flow, not ATP.
Both ATP synthase activity and flagellar rotation decline
Correct: both depend on the proton motive force that the drug dissipates.
Motility declines, but ATP synthesis rises
ATP synthase also needs the H⁺ gradient, so it falls.
Glycolysis stops completely
Glycolysis makes ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation without a gradient.
questions.x: In bacteria the proton motive force across the plasma membrane powers both ATP synthase and the flagellar motor. A protonophore lets H⁺ leak freely across the membrane, collapsing the gradient, so ATP synthesis and swimming both decline. Glycolysis continues because it makes ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, which does not need a gradient.

questions.q: A soil bacterium gets its carbon from CO₂ and its energy by oxidizing ammonia. It is best classified as a:
o: Photoautotroph
Photoautotrophs get energy from light.
Chemoautotroph
Correct: energy from inorganic chemicals (chemo) and carbon from CO₂ (auto).
Chemoheterotroph
Chemoheterotrophs get carbon from organic compounds.
Photoheterotroph
Photoheterotrophs use light and organic carbon.
questions.x: Nutritional types combine an energy source with a carbon source. Energy from light is photo-, from chemical oxidation is chemo-; carbon from CO₂ is auto-, from organic molecules is hetero-. Oxidizing ammonia for energy and fixing CO₂ for carbon makes this nitrifying bacterium a chemoautotroph.

questions.q: Which statement about bacterial binary fission is correct?
o: Spindle microtubules pull sister chromatids to opposite poles
Bacteria do not form mitotic spindles.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs first
Bacteria are haploid and do not undergo meiotic crossing over.
It begins with breakdown of the nuclear envelope
Bacteria have no nuclear envelope.
Replicated chromosomes separate without a mitotic spindle, giving two identical cells
Correct: chromosomes are partitioned as the cell elongates and divides.
questions.x: Binary fission is a simple asexual division: the circular chromosome is replicated, the copies are moved apart as the cell elongates, and a septum forms between them. There is no nucleus, no mitotic spindle and no crossing over, so the two daughter cells are genetically identical apart from rare mutations.

questions.q: A temperature-sensitive E. coli mutant has an FtsZ protein that cannot form the division ring at 42 °C. What is seen when the mutant grows at 42 °C?
o: Normal division, but daughter cells lack DNA
FtsZ is needed for division itself, not chromosome inheritance.
Immediate lysis of every cell
Loss of FtsZ blocks division; it does not directly lyse cells.
Long filaments that keep replicating DNA but fail to divide
Correct: growth and replication continue, but septum formation fails.
Formation of endospores
E. coli does not form endospores.
questions.x: FtsZ, a tubulin-like protein, forms the Z ring at mid-cell that recruits the division machinery and pinches the cell in two. If FtsZ fails, cells keep growing and copying their DNA but cannot divide, so they form long filaments containing many chromosomes. Lack of FtsZ blocks division; it does not by itself make cells lyse.

questions.q: A typical bacterial chromosome is best described as:
o: Several linear DNA molecules with many origins
This describes eukaryotic chromosomes.
One circular double-stranded DNA molecule with a single origin of replication
Correct: e.g. the E. coli chromosome has one origin, oriC.
A circular single-stranded RNA molecule
Cellular genomes are double-stranded DNA.
A linear double-stranded DNA molecule capped by telomeres
Telomeres solve an end-replication problem that circular DNA lacks.
questions.x: Most bacteria carry a single circular, double-stranded DNA chromosome with one origin of replication (oriC in E. coli), packed in the nucleoid region. Circular DNA has no ends, so bacteria do not need telomeres. Several linear chromosomes with many origins describes eukaryotes.

questions.q: An E. coli chromosome has about 4.6 × 10⁶ bp. If each replication fork moves about 1000 bp/s, roughly how long does it take to replicate the whole chromosome from its single origin?
o: About 4 min
Off by a factor of 10 in the arithmetic.
About 19 min
Assumes four forks; one origin gives only two.
About 38 min
Correct: two forks move bidirectionally, so 4.6 × 10⁶ ÷ 2000 bp/s = 2300 s ≈ 38 min.
About 77 min
Assumes a single fork; replication from oriC is bidirectional.
questions.note: One origin, two forks moving in opposite directions.
questions.x: From one origin, replication proceeds in both directions, so two forks work at once. Two forks at 1000 bp/s copy 2000 bp/s, so 4.6 × 10⁶ ÷ 2000 = 2300 s, about 38 minutes. Forgetting that replication is bidirectional doubles the answer to about 77 minutes.

questions.q: Which statement about bacterial plasmids is correct?
o: They carry genes required for survival under all conditions
Essential genes are on the chromosome; plasmids are usually dispensable.
They replicate independently of the chromosome and often carry nonessential genes such as antibiotic resistance
Correct: plasmids are extrachromosomal DNA that can confer useful traits.
They are made of single-stranded RNA
Plasmids are typically circular double-stranded DNA.
They occur only in eukaryotic cells
Plasmids are most common in bacteria (yeast has a few).
questions.x: Plasmids are small, usually circular double-stranded DNA molecules that replicate independently of the chromosome. They often carry genes useful only in certain conditions, such as antibiotic resistance, toxins or the F factor for conjugation. Genes needed under all conditions are normally on the chromosome, so plasmids are usually dispensable.

questions.q: A plasmid that can either replicate on its own or integrate into the bacterial chromosome is called:
o: An episome
Correct: an episome (e.g. the F factor) can exist free or integrated.
A prophage
A prophage is an integrated phage genome, not a plasmid.
A transposon
Transposons move between sites but do not replicate as independent plasmids.
A provirus
A provirus is integrated retroviral DNA in a eukaryotic genome.
questions.x: An episome is a plasmid that can either replicate on its own in the cytoplasm or integrate into the chromosome. The F factor is the classic case: free it makes an F⁺ cell, integrated it makes an Hfr cell. A prophage is an integrated phage genome, not a plasmid.

questions.q: After conjugation between an F⁺ and an F⁻ E. coli cell, what is the F status of each cell?
o: Both are F⁺
Correct: one strand is transferred while the donor replicates its copy, so both end up with F.
Both are F⁻
The donor keeps a copy of the F plasmid.
The donor becomes F⁻ and the recipient F⁺
Rolling-circle replication means the donor never gives up its F plasmid.
Both become Hfr
Hfr requires the F factor to integrate into the chromosome, which is rare.
questions.x: During F⁺ × F⁻ conjugation, one strand of the F plasmid is nicked and passed into the recipient while the donor rebuilds its copy by rolling-circle replication. The recipient then makes the complementary strand. Both cells end up with a full F plasmid, so both are F⁺; the donor never gives up its copy.
