necrosis through membrane rupture
Fas signaling causes apoptosis, not necrosis.
cell cycle entry through cyclin D
Fas signaling leads to death, not division.
questions.x: Death receptors such as Fas, when bound by their ligand, recruit the adaptor FADD and procaspase-8 into a signaling complex that activates caspase-8, which then activates executioner caspases. This is the extrinsic pathway. The intrinsic pathway begins with internal stress and mitochondrial cytochrome c release, so receptor engagement points to the extrinsic route.

questions.q: If apoptosis fails in the tissue between the developing fingers, the result is:
o: extra fingers
Extra digits come from patterning defects, not failed apoptosis.
webbed fingers (syndactyly)
Correct: programmed cell death normally removes the interdigital tissue.
absent fingers
Too much cell death, not too little, could remove digits.
shortened fingers
Failed apoptosis leaves extra tissue rather than shorter digits.
questions.x: Digits form when apoptosis removes the tissue between them in the developing hand and foot plate. If interdigital cells fail to die, the digits remain joined, giving syndactyly. Extra digits (polydactyly) reflect patterning errors, such as abnormal Sonic hedgehog signaling, rather than failed cell death.

questions.q: Cells are stained with labeled annexin V, which binds phosphatidylserine on the outer leaflet, and propidium iodide (PI), which enters only cells with damaged membranes. Which population represents early apoptosis?
o: Annexin V negative, PI negative
This describes healthy live cells.
Annexin V positive, PI negative
Correct: PS flips outward early, while the membrane is still intact and keeps PI out.
Annexin V positive, PI positive
Both signals indicate late apoptosis or necrosis with a damaged membrane.
Annexin V negative, PI positive
Membrane rupture without PS exposure suggests necrosis or damaged cells.
questions.note: Exposed PS acts as an 'eat me' signal for phagocytes.
questions.x: Healthy cells keep phosphatidylserine on the inner membrane leaflet. Early in apoptosis, PS flips outward and binds annexin V while the membrane is still intact and excludes PI. Late apoptotic or necrotic cells have damaged membranes and are positive for both. Annexin V positive with PI negative is therefore the early apoptotic population.

questions.q: An activating mutation in just one allele of a proto-oncogene can promote cancer because:
o: the resulting oncogene acts as a gain of function, so one altered copy is enough
Correct: oncogenic mutations are dominant at the cellular level.
both alleles must be lost before any effect appears
That two-hit pattern describes tumor suppressor genes.
proto-oncogenes normally stop the cell cycle
Proto-oncogenes normally promote growth; tumor suppressors stop it.
the mutation removes the gene from the genome
Activation alters or overexpresses the gene rather than deleting it.
questions.x: Proto-oncogenes normally promote growth, and activating mutations create oncogenes with gain of function, such as a constantly active protein or overexpression. One mutated allele is enough, so oncogenes act dominantly at the cellular level. Needing both copies lost (two hits) describes tumor suppressor genes, which are recessive at the cellular level.

questions.q: Children who inherit one mutant RB1 allele often develop retinoblastoma in both eyes at an early age. The best explanation is that:
o: RB1 is an oncogene that acts dominantly
RB1 is a tumor suppressor; tumors arise after both copies are lost.
the inherited allele makes Rb hyperactive
Hyperactive Rb would block division, not cause tumors.
retinal cells cannot undergo apoptosis
The key factor is the inherited first hit, not a general apoptosis defect.
every retinal cell already has one hit, so a single somatic mutation inactivates both copies
Correct: the two-hit model needs only one more mutation in an inherited carrier.
questions.note: Inherited tumor suppressor mutations: early, multiple, often bilateral tumors.
questions.x: RB1 is a tumor suppressor, so a cell must lose both copies before control is lost (Knudson two-hit hypothesis). Children who inherit one mutant allele carry the first hit in every retinal cell, so one somatic mutation in any of millions of cells is enough, giving early, often bilateral tumors. Sporadic cases need two somatic hits in the same cell, so they are later and unilateral.

questions.q: Many tumors carry Ras mutations that impair its GTPase activity. These mutations promote cell proliferation because Ras:
o: can no longer bind GTP
That would inactivate Ras and reduce signaling.
becomes a tumor suppressor
Ras is a proto-oncogene product; this mutation makes it an oncogene, not a tumor suppressor.
stays bound to GTP and keeps signaling for growth
Correct: Ras can no longer turn itself off by hydrolyzing GTP.
triggers apoptosis
Constant Ras signaling drives growth, not death.
questions.x: Ras is a small G protein that is active when bound to GTP and switches itself off by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP, helped by GAP proteins. Mutations that impair GTPase activity leave Ras locked in the GTP-bound state, continuously signaling through the MAP kinase pathway to drive proliferation. Losing GTP binding would inactivate Ras, the opposite effect.

questions.q: Loss of E-cadherin expression in carcinoma cells most directly promotes:
o: faster DNA replication
E-cadherin is an adhesion protein, not a replication factor.
increased apoptosis
Loss of E-cadherin is linked to spread, not to more apoptosis.
formation of gap junctions
Gap junctions are formed by connexins.
detachment from neighboring cells, aiding invasion and metastasis
Correct: losing cell–cell adhesion lets tumor cells break away.
questions.x: E-cadherin forms adherens junctions that hold epithelial cells together. Losing it, often during epithelial–mesenchymal transition, lets carcinoma cells detach from their neighbors, invade surrounding tissue and enter vessels to metastasize. It is an adhesion molecule, not a regulator of replication or apoptosis.

questions.q: An antibody that neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) slows tumor growth mainly by:
o: directly killing tumor cells in S phase
Anti-VEGF targets blood vessel growth, not dividing tumor cells.
restoring p53 function
VEGF blockade does not repair p53.
blocking the formation of new blood vessels that supply the tumor
Correct: tumors larger than a few millimeters need angiogenesis for oxygen and nutrients.
reactivating telomerase in tumor cells
Telomerase activity supports, rather than limits, tumor growth.
questions.x: Tumors larger than a few millimeters need new blood vessels for oxygen and nutrients. Tumor cells secrete VEGF to stimulate angiogenesis; a neutralizing antibody (such as bevacizumab) blocks this, starving the tumor of blood supply. It does not directly kill dividing tumor cells, as a cytotoxic chemotherapy drug would.

questions.q: Which feature is the defining difference between a malignant tumor and a benign tumor?
o: A larger size
Benign tumors can be very large.
The ability to invade surrounding tissue and spread to distant sites
Correct: invasion and metastasis define malignancy.
Faster growth in all cases
Growth rate varies and does not define malignancy.
Being made of abnormal cells
Both benign and malignant tumors are made of abnormal cells.
questions.x: Benign tumors stay localized, often encapsulated, and do not invade. Malignant tumors invade surrounding tissue and can metastasize through blood or lymph to distant sites; this capacity defines cancer. Size and growth rate vary in both, and benign tumors can grow very large, so neither distinguishes them.

questions.q: A mutant cell line divides without growth factors, while normal cells arrest. Fusing a mutant cell with a normal cell gives hybrids that arrest without growth factors. The mutation most likely:
o: inactivates a tumor suppressor, and the normal allele restores control
Correct: the normal phenotype is dominant in hybrids, so the mutation is recessive loss of function.
activates an oncogene that dominates the normal genome
A dominant oncogene would make the hybrids divide without growth factors.
causes chromosome loss in the hybrid
The data are explained by the normal gene restoring control.
has no effect on the cell cycle
The mutant cells clearly show altered growth control.
questions.note: Fusion tests dominance: recessive defects are rescued by normal genes.
questions.x: Cell fusion tests whether a phenotype is dominant or recessive. If hybrids regain normal growth control, the normal genome supplies a function the mutant lacks, so the mutation is a recessive loss of function, typical of a tumor suppressor. A dominant oncogene would make the hybrids keep dividing without growth factors.

questions.q: Cultured normal fibroblasts stop dividing when they form a single layer, but transformed cells keep piling up into multilayered foci. This shows that transformed cells have lost:
o: the ability to replicate DNA
Transformed cells replicate DNA continuously.
contact inhibition
Correct: normal cells stop dividing when they touch neighbors on all sides.
dependence on glucose
Glucose use is not what the piling up shows.
their nuclei
Transformed cells still have nuclei.
questions.x: Normal cells in culture stop dividing when they contact neighbors on all sides, forming a monolayer (contact inhibition). Transformed cells lose this control and keep dividing, piling into multilayered foci, a hallmark used to detect transformation. They still replicate DNA, often faster, and still have nuclei.

questions.q: The E7 protein of high-risk human papillomavirus binds and inactivates Rb. In infected cells, this most directly:
o: arrests cells permanently in G1
Losing Rb removes a G1 brake rather than adding one.
activates the spindle checkpoint
Rb acts at G1/S, not during mitosis.
increases expression of p21
E7 removes Rb's control downstream; it does not boost p21.
frees E2F, pushing cells into S phase without normal G1 control
Correct: without Rb, E2F activates S-phase genes regardless of signals.
questions.x: Rb normally binds E2F to hold cells in G1. HPV E7 binds Rb and displaces E2F, which then activates S-phase genes regardless of growth signals, pushing infected cells into S so the virus can use the replication machinery. HPV E6 separately degrades p53. Removing Rb takes away a brake, so G1 arrest is the opposite effect.

questions.q: Most human cancer cells keep dividing well past the normal limit because they:
o: express telomerase, which maintains telomere length
Correct: telomerase lets cancer cells avoid the senescence caused by short telomeres.
lack all DNA repair enzymes
Cells need some repair to survive; this does not explain unlimited division.
have stopped replicating their DNA
Dividing cells must replicate DNA.
have permanently activated caspases
Active caspases would kill the cells.
questions.x: Conventional DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate chromosome ends, so telomeres shorten each division until senescence (the Hayflick limit). About 85–90% of cancers reactivate telomerase, which adds TTAGGG repeats to maintain telomere length and allows unlimited divisions; the rest use alternative lengthening. Losing all repair enzymes would be lethal rather than immortalizing.

questions.q: A researcher finds that a tumor cell line is resistant to DNA-damaging drugs and has lost both copies of a gene whose product halts the cycle and triggers apoptosis after DNA damage. Which statement best describes the gene?
o: It is an oncogene whose loss causes the drug resistance
Oncogenes promote growth when activated; loss of both copies describes a tumor suppressor.
It is a proto-oncogene that needs two hits to activate
Proto-oncogenes are activated by a single gain-of-function mutation.
It is a tumor suppressor gene whose loss lets damaged cells keep dividing
Correct: genes that halt the cycle or trigger apoptosis after damage are tumor suppressors.
It encodes a growth factor that the tumor depends on
A growth factor would not halt the cycle after damage.
questions.x: Genes that halt the cell cycle or trigger apoptosis after DNA damage, such as TP53, are tumor suppressors. Losing both copies removes the checkpoint, so damaged cells keep dividing and resist DNA-damaging drugs that kill through apoptosis. Oncogenes act by gain of function and a single mutation, so losing both copies of a gene points to a tumor suppressor.

questions.q: Normal human fibroblasts in culture stop dividing after a limited number of doublings, mainly because:
o: the cells run out of nutrients in the medium
Fresh medium does not restore division after the limit.
the cells become cancerous
Cancer cells avoid this limit rather than reaching it.
telomeres shorten with each division until a critical length triggers senescence
Correct: the end-replication problem shortens telomeres, setting the Hayflick limit.
the cells switch to meiosis
Somatic fibroblasts do not undergo meiosis.
questions.x: Because DNA polymerase needs a primer and works 5′ to 3′, the lagging strand's very end cannot be completed, so telomeres shorten each division (the end-replication problem). Somatic cells lack enough telomerase, so after about 50 doublings critically short telomeres trigger a DNA damage response and senescence. Fresh nutrients cannot overcome this intrinsic limit.

questions.q: Telomerase can lengthen chromosome ends because it:
o: is a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template
Correct: it uses the RNA template to add repeats to the 3′ overhang.
is a DNA polymerase that needs an RNA primer at the very end
That primer requirement is what creates the end-replication problem.
joins chromosome ends together
End-to-end fusion is harmful and is prevented by telomeres.
removes damaged nucleotides from telomeres
Telomerase adds DNA rather than removing it.
questions.x: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase that carries its own RNA template. It base-pairs that template with the 3′ overhang of the chromosome and adds repeats (TTAGGG in humans); the complementary strand is then filled in by primase and DNA polymerase. Ordinary DNA polymerase's need for a primer is what causes end shortening, not what fixes it.

questions.q: Cellular senescence differs from quiescence (G0) in that senescent cells:
o: are dead and quickly removed by phagocytes
Senescent cells stay alive and metabolically active.
divide more rapidly than normal cells
Senescent cells do not divide.
have lost their nuclei
Senescent cells keep their nuclei.
are essentially permanently arrested even when given growth signals
Correct: senescence is a stable, mostly irreversible arrest; quiescent cells can re-enter the cycle.
questions.x: Quiescent (G0) cells are reversibly arrested and re-enter the cycle when given growth signals, like hepatocytes after injury. Senescent cells are stably and essentially irreversibly arrested, usually by p53–p21 and p16–Rb, even with mitogens. They stay alive and metabolically active, often secreting factors, so they are not dead or anucleate.

questions.q: Senescent cells accumulate in aging tissues and release inflammatory cytokines and proteases. Removing senescent cells from old mice delays some age-related decline. This suggests that senescent cells:
o: are harmless because they no longer divide
If they were harmless, removing them would have no benefit.
actively harm surrounding tissue through what they secrete
Correct: their secretions can drive chronic inflammation and tissue dysfunction.
are the main source of new cells in old tissue
Senescent cells do not divide, so they cannot supply new cells.
prevent all cancers in old animals
The data concern tissue decline, not complete cancer prevention.
questions.note: Senescence blocks tumor growth but its secretions can promote aging.
questions.x: Senescent cells stop dividing but remain metabolically active and release inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and proteases, the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Removing them improves tissue function in old mice, showing their secretions actively harm tissue. Senescence does suppress tumors early by stopping division, but non-dividing does not mean harmless.

questions.q: Which part of a typical neuron is specialized mainly for receiving synaptic input from other cells?
o: Dendrites
Correct: dendrites carry most postsynaptic receptors and collect incoming signals.
Axon terminals
Axon terminals release neurotransmitter; they are the output end.
Axon hillock
The hillock integrates input and initiates the action potential, but it is not the main receiving surface.
Nodes of Ranvier
Nodes are gaps in myelin along the axon where action potentials are regenerated.
questions.x: Neurons are polarized: input arrives on dendrites (and the soma), is integrated at the axon hillock, and leaves through the axon terminals. Dendrites are branched to provide a large surface packed with postsynaptic receptors. The hillock is tempting because it handles integration, but it is the trigger zone, not the main receiving surface.

questions.q: A neuron receives many small excitatory and inhibitory inputs. Where is the decision to fire an action potential normally made?
o: At each dendritic spine independently
Spines generate graded local potentials, not the all-or-none firing decision.
At the axon hillock/initial segment, which has a high density of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Correct: summed potentials reaching threshold here trigger the action potential.
At the axon terminal, where Ca²⁺ channels open
Terminals respond to an action potential that already fired; they do not initiate it.
At the nucleus, which controls membrane voltage
The nucleus controls gene expression, not moment-to-moment electrical integration.
questions.note: Trap: the soma integrates, but the trigger zone is the axon hillock.
questions.x: Graded postsynaptic potentials from dendrites and soma spread passively and sum at the axon initial segment. This region has the lowest threshold because voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are densest there, so it is where an all-or-none spike begins. Individual spines only produce small local potentials; the firing decision depends on the summed signal at the trigger zone.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron (about −70 mV) is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion, and why?
o: Na⁺, because the Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves Na⁺ out
ENa is about +60 mV; resting Na⁺ permeability is low.
Cl⁻, because Cl⁻ is the most abundant extracellular anion
Abundance does not set Vm; relative permeability does.
K⁺, because resting membranes are far more permeable to K⁺ than to other ions
Correct: open K⁺ leak channels dominate resting permeability, pulling Vm toward EK.
Ca²⁺, because Ca²⁺ channels stay open at rest
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels are mostly closed at rest, and ECa is strongly positive.
questions.x: At rest, many K⁺ leak channels are open while few Na⁺ channels are, so the Goldman equation weights K⁺ most heavily and Vm sits near EK (about −90 mV). The small Na⁺ leak pulls Vm slightly positive of EK, to about −70 mV. Ion abundance alone does not set Vm; what matters is which ions can actually cross the membrane.

questions.q: For each cycle of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which ion movement occurs?
o: 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in, using one ATP
The stoichiometry is reversed.
3 Na⁺ in and 2 K⁺ out, using one ATP
This moves both ions down their gradients, which needs no ATP.
1 Na⁺ out and 1 K⁺ in, with no ATP
This is an active pump that requires ATP hydrolysis.
3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, using one ATP
Correct: the unequal exchange makes the pump slightly electrogenic.
questions.x: Each cycle of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase hydrolyzes one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, both against their gradients. Because more positive charge leaves than enters, the pump is slightly electrogenic and adds a few millivolts of negativity. Its main job, though, is to maintain the concentration gradients that leak channels use to set the resting potential.

questions.q: The extracellular K⁺ concentration around a neuron is experimentally raised. What happens to the resting membrane potential?
o: It becomes more negative (hyperpolarizes)
More outside K⁺ reduces K⁺ efflux, which shifts Vm upward, not downward.
It does not change because the pump compensates
The pump cannot offset the change in the K⁺ equilibrium potential.
It becomes less negative (depolarizes)
Correct: a smaller K⁺ gradient makes EK less negative, and Vm follows EK at rest.
It reverses to about +60 mV
That value is ENa; the cell would still be dominated by K⁺ permeability.
questions.note: EK shifts with [K⁺]out, so resting Vm tracks extracellular K⁺.
questions.x: Resting Vm tracks EK because K⁺ dominates resting permeability. Raising extracellular K⁺ shrinks the K⁺ concentration gradient, making EK less negative by the Nernst equation, so the cell depolarizes. This is why hyperkalemia makes excitable tissue such as the heart dangerously unstable. The pump cannot cancel this shift because it does not change the equilibrium potential.

questions.q: Which pair of events together returns the membrane toward rest after the peak of an action potential?
o: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open
Correct: Na⁺ entry stops while K⁺ leaves the cell, making Vm negative again.
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open further and Cl⁻ channels close
More Na⁺ entry would keep the membrane depolarized.
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase rapidly pumps out the Na⁺ that entered
The pump is too slow to repolarize a single spike; it maintains gradients over time.
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ leaves the cell
Ca²⁺ flows into, not out of, neurons through these channels.
questions.note: Trap: the pump does not drive repolarization.
questions.x: Repolarization has two parts: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels inactivate, stopping Na⁺ entry, and delayed voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, letting K⁺ flow out. Together they drive Vm back toward EK. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is a common wrong answer, but it moves ions far too slowly to shape a single spike; it only restores gradients over many spikes.

questions.q: During the absolute refractory period, no second action potential can be fired no matter how strong the stimulus. What is the cause?
o: The neuron has run out of releasable neurotransmitter
Transmitter depletion affects the synapse, not the axon's ability to fire.
The Na⁺ concentration gradient has been abolished
A single spike moves very few ions; the gradient is essentially unchanged.
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are inactivated and closed
K⁺ channels are open during this phase; that drives repolarization.
Most voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen yet
Correct: inactivation gates must reset at negative voltage before Na⁺ channels can open again.
questions.x: After opening, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels enter an inactivated state that cannot be reopened until the membrane repolarizes and the inactivation gate resets. While most channels are inactivated, no stimulus can generate a new spike: the absolute refractory period. The ion gradients are essentially unchanged by one spike, so depletion is not the explanation.

questions.q: A stimulus applied during the relative refractory period can trigger an action potential only if it is larger than normal. Why?
o: All Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so a larger stimulus forces them open
If all were inactivated, no stimulus would work; that describes the absolute period.
The membrane is hyperpolarized and extra K⁺ channels are still open, so more depolarization is needed
Correct: open K⁺ channels oppose depolarization, and some Na⁺ channels are still inactivated.
The threshold voltage rises to about +30 mV
Threshold rises only slightly; it does not approach the peak voltage.
Myelin temporarily blocks current at that site
Myelin does not change during the refractory period.
questions.x: During the relative refractory period, some Na⁺ channels have recovered from inactivation, but many K⁺ channels are still open and the cell is often hyperpolarized. Extra K⁺ conductance opposes depolarization, so a stronger stimulus is needed to reach threshold. If all Na⁺ channels were still inactivated, no stimulus could work; that defines the absolute refractory period.

questions.q: How does a sensory neuron signal that a stimulus has become stronger?
o: By producing action potentials of larger amplitude
Action potentials are all-or-none; amplitude does not grow with stimulus.
By firing action potentials at a higher frequency
Correct: spike amplitude is fixed, so intensity is coded by rate and by number of neurons recruited.
By conducting each action potential more slowly
Velocity depends on axon diameter and myelin, not stimulus strength.
By reversing the direction of propagation
Propagation is always away from the trigger zone.
questions.note: All-or-none: frequency, not size, carries intensity.
questions.x: Action potentials are all-or-none, so each spike from a given neuron has the same amplitude. Stimulus intensity is therefore encoded by firing frequency (rate coding) and by recruiting more neurons (population coding). Conduction velocity is fixed by axon diameter and myelination, so it cannot carry information about stimulus strength.

questions.q: Tetrodotoxin (TTX) blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. What is its most direct effect on an axon exposed to it?
o: Action potentials are generated but cannot repolarize
Repolarization depends on K⁺ channels, which TTX does not block.
The resting potential becomes strongly positive
Resting Vm depends mostly on K⁺ leak, which is unaffected.
Neurotransmitter is released continuously
Without action potentials, terminals are not depolarized, so release falls.
Action potentials cannot be generated or propagated
Correct: without Na⁺ influx, there is no regenerative depolarization.
questions.x: The rising phase of a neuronal action potential depends on regenerative Na⁺ influx through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. TTX plugs these channels, so the axon cannot reach and exceed threshold, and no spikes are generated or conducted. Resting potential is set mainly by K⁺ leak, so it is largely unaffected, and without spikes transmitter release falls rather than rises.

questions.q: Many neurons briefly become more negative than resting potential right after an action potential. What causes this afterhyperpolarization?
o: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels close slowly, so K⁺ permeability stays elevated
Correct: extra K⁺ efflux briefly drives Vm closer to EK than at rest.
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 K⁺ into the cell per cycle
The pump moves 2 K⁺ in and 3 Na⁺ out, and it is not the main cause.
Na⁺ channels open a second time
Na⁺ entry would depolarize, not hyperpolarize.
Cl⁻ is pumped out of the cell
Cl⁻ efflux would depolarize, and it is not the mechanism of afterhyperpolarization.
questions.x: Delayed-rectifier K⁺ channels open late and close slowly, so for a few milliseconds after the spike K⁺ permeability is even higher than at rest. That pulls Vm closer to EK, below the normal resting value, producing the afterhyperpolarization. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is a tempting answer, but its electrogenic effect is small and slow and it moves only 2 K⁺ in per cycle.

questions.q: In a myelinated axon, where are action potentials regenerated as the signal travels?
o: Continuously along every segment under the myelin
That describes conduction in unmyelinated axons.
Only at the axon hillock, with passive spread afterward
Passive spread alone would decay over long axons.
Only at the nodes of Ranvier
Correct: Na⁺ channels cluster at the nodes, so the signal jumps from node to node.
Only at the axon terminal
The terminal is the end point, not the regeneration site.
questions.x: Myelin insulates internodes, so current spreads rapidly and passively under it to the next node of Ranvier. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are clustered at the nodes, where the spike is regenerated, so the impulse appears to jump node to node (saltatory conduction). Passive spread alone, as from the hillock, would decay over a long axon.

questions.q: Two unmyelinated axons differ only in diameter. Why does the wider axon conduct action potentials faster?
o: It has a more negative resting potential
Diameter does not set resting potential.
It has a higher threshold, so it fires less often
Threshold does not determine conduction speed.
It contains more mitochondria to power the spike
ATP does not directly drive the propagating spike; ion gradients do.
Its larger cross-section lowers internal resistance, so current spreads farther along the axon
Correct: lower axial resistance lets depolarization reach more distant membrane quickly.
questions.note: Speed up conduction two ways: wider axon or myelin.
questions.x: Conduction speed depends on how far local current spreads before it decays. Axial (internal) resistance falls with cross-sectional area, so a wider axon passes current farther down its length and depolarizes distant membrane to threshold sooner. Resting potential and threshold are not set by diameter, and the spike is powered by ion gradients rather than ATP directly.

questions.q: In multiple sclerosis, an immune attack destroys myelin within the brain and spinal cord. Which cell type is primarily damaged?
o: Schwann cells
Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves, not CNS tracts.
Astrocytes
Astrocytes support neurons and the blood–brain barrier; they do not make myelin.
Oligodendrocytes
Correct: oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin, each wrapping several axons.
Ependymal cells
Ependymal cells line ventricles and help produce CSF.
questions.note: CNS myelin = oligodendrocytes; PNS myelin = Schwann cells.
questions.x: Multiple sclerosis attacks central myelin, which is made by oligodendrocytes; one oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of many CNS axons. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons and are spared in MS, while being targeted in disorders like Guillain-Barré syndrome. Loss of myelin slows or blocks conduction, producing the varied neurological deficits of MS.

questions.q: Which glial cell forms the myelin sheath around a single segment of a peripheral motor axon?
o: Oligodendrocyte
Oligodendrocytes myelinate in the CNS.
Schwann cell
Correct: in the PNS, each Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one axon.
Microglial cell
Microglia are immune phagocytes of the CNS.
Satellite cell
Satellite cells surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia; they do not form myelin.
questions.x: In the peripheral nervous system, each Schwann cell wraps a single internode of a single axon. Oligodendrocytes do the same job in the CNS but extend processes to many axons. Satellite cells also sit in the PNS, which makes them a tempting choice, but they surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia and do not form myelin.

questions.q: After intense neuronal firing, extracellular K⁺ rises in a brain region. Which glial cell type helps clear this excess K⁺?
o: Astrocytes
Correct: astrocytes take up and redistribute K⁺ and neurotransmitters around synapses.
Microglia
Microglia respond to injury and infection, not routine ion buffering.
Oligodendrocytes
Oligodendrocytes form myelin; ion buffering is mainly an astrocyte job.
Schwann cells
Schwann cells are in the PNS, not brain tissue.
questions.x: Astrocytes regulate the neuronal microenvironment: they take up excess extracellular K⁺ and spread it through gap-junction-coupled networks (spatial buffering), and they clear glutamate from synapses. They also support the blood–brain barrier and supply metabolic substrates. Microglia are immune cells that respond to injury, not routine ion homeostasis.

questions.q: After a small stroke, brain-resident cells engulf dead neurons and debris. Which glial cells perform this role?
o: Ependymal cells
Ependymal cells line the ventricles and move CSF.
Microglia
Correct: microglia are the CNS's resident macrophage-like phagocytes.
Oligodendrocytes
Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons.
Schwann cells
Schwann cells are peripheral myelinating cells.
questions.x: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the CNS, derived from yolk-sac macrophage precursors. When tissue is injured, they become activated, migrate to the site, and phagocytose dead cells and debris. The other glia listed handle myelination (oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells) or CSF movement (ependymal cells), not phagocytosis.

questions.q: Which glial cells line the brain's ventricles and help produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid?
o: Ependymal cells
Correct: ependymal cells (including those of the choroid plexus) produce and move CSF.
Astrocytes
Astrocytes contribute to the blood–brain barrier, not CSF secretion.
Microglia
Microglia are immune cells.
Satellite cells
Satellite cells support neurons in peripheral ganglia.
questions.x: Ependymal cells form the epithelial lining of the ventricles and central canal, and their cilia help circulate CSF. Specialized ependymal cells in the choroid plexus secrete most CSF. Astrocytes are tempting because they help form the blood–brain barrier, but they do not secrete CSF.

questions.q: What event directly triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane?
o: Na⁺ influx through ligand-gated channels on the terminal
Na⁺ entry depolarizes the terminal but Ca²⁺ is the fusion trigger.
K⁺ efflux through leak channels
K⁺ efflux repolarizes; it does not cause exocytosis.
Binding of neurotransmitter to postsynaptic receptors
That happens after release, on the other cell.
Ca²⁺ influx through voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the axon terminal
Correct: Ca²⁺ binding to vesicle proteins triggers SNARE-driven fusion.
questions.x: When an action potential reaches the terminal, depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels. Ca²⁺ rushes in down its steep gradient and binds synaptotagmin, which triggers SNARE proteins to fuse vesicles with the membrane. Depolarization is required, but it is Ca²⁺ entry, not Na⁺ entry itself, that couples the electrical signal to exocytosis.

questions.q: A neuromuscular preparation is bathed in Ca²⁺-free solution, and the motor nerve is stimulated. Nerve action potentials are recorded normally. What happens at the muscle?
o: It contracts more strongly because Ca²⁺ normally inhibits release
Ca²⁺ is required for release, not inhibitory.
It contracts normally because the nerve still fires
Firing alone cannot release transmitter without Ca²⁺ entry.
It fails to contract because acetylcholine is not released
Correct: transmitter release requires extracellular Ca²⁺ entering the terminal.
It contracts continuously because acetylcholinesterase is inactive
Acetylcholinesterase does not require extracellular Ca²⁺.
questions.note: The nerve fires, but the synapse fails without Ca²⁺.
questions.x: Nerve conduction uses Na⁺ and K⁺ channels, so the motor axon still fires in Ca²⁺-free solution. However, release of acetylcholine requires Ca²⁺ influx through voltage-gated channels at the terminal. With no extracellular Ca²⁺, no transmitter is released and the muscle never gets depolarized, showing that synaptic transmission, not axonal conduction, is Ca²⁺-dependent.

questions.q: Activation of GABA-A receptors opens Cl⁻ channels in a mature neuron where ECl ≈ −75 mV and resting Vm ≈ −65 mV. What is the effect?
o: An excitatory postsynaptic potential that moves Vm toward threshold
Cl⁻ flows in here, adding negative charge.
An action potential carried by Cl⁻
Cl⁻ channels do not generate action potentials.
No effect, because Cl⁻ is already at equilibrium
Vm (−65) differs from ECl (−75), so there is a driving force.
An inhibitory postsynaptic potential that moves Vm toward −75 mV
Correct: Cl⁻ entry hyperpolarizes the cell, moving it away from threshold.
questions.note: Current flows to move Vm toward the ion's equilibrium potential.
questions.x: Ions flow so as to push Vm toward their equilibrium potential. Here ECl (−75 mV) is more negative than Vm (−65 mV), so Cl⁻ enters, adding negative charge and hyperpolarizing the cell: an IPSP. If ECl were close to Vm, opening Cl⁻ channels would still inhibit by shunting excitatory current, but here there is a real driving force, so Vm moves toward −75 mV.

questions.q: A single presynaptic neuron fires three times in rapid succession, and each small EPSP builds on the last until threshold is reached. This is an example of:
o: Spatial summation
Spatial summation combines inputs from different synapses at the same time.
Temporal summation
Correct: repeated input from one source arrives before earlier potentials decay.
Saltatory conduction
Saltatory conduction is node-to-node propagation in myelinated axons.
Long-term depression
LTD is a lasting decrease in synaptic strength, not a rapid summation.
questions.note: Temporal = same synapse over time; spatial = many synapses at once.
questions.x: Temporal summation occurs when one presynaptic input fires repeatedly before earlier postsynaptic potentials have decayed, so each adds to the residual depolarization. Spatial summation instead combines simultaneous inputs from different synapses. The key clue is a single presynaptic neuron firing in rapid succession.

questions.q: Several different presynaptic neurons fire at the same moment, and their EPSPs add together at the postsynaptic cell. This is called:
o: Temporal summation
Temporal summation is repeated input from the same synapse.
Convergent inhibition
Inhibition would lower, not raise, the summed potential.
Spatial summation
Correct: simultaneous inputs at different locations combine.
Facilitated diffusion
Facilitated diffusion is a membrane transport mechanism.
questions.x: Spatial summation is the adding together of postsynaptic potentials that arrive at the same time from different synapses on the same neuron. Temporal summation instead relies on repeated firing of one input. Both allow subthreshold EPSPs to combine and reach threshold at the axon hillock; the clue here is several different neurons firing at once.

questions.q: A drug inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction. What is its expected effect?
o: Acetylcholine stays in the cleft longer, prolonging stimulation of the muscle
Correct: less breakdown means more receptor binding over time.
Acetylcholine release from the motor neuron is blocked
Release depends on Ca²⁺ entry, not on acetylcholinesterase.
Nicotinic receptors are permanently blocked
The drug acts on the enzyme, not the receptor.
Acetylcholine is broken down faster, weakening contraction
Inhibiting the enzyme slows breakdown.
questions.x: Acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft rapidly hydrolyzes ACh into acetate and choline, which ends its action. Inhibiting the enzyme leaves ACh in the cleft longer, so nicotinic receptors are stimulated repeatedly and contraction is enhanced; this is how drugs treat myasthenia gravis. ACh release depends on Ca²⁺ entry, not on the enzyme, so release is unchanged.

questions.q: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are used to treat depression. What do they do at serotonergic synapses?
o: Inhibit monoamine oxidase in the cleft
MAO is intracellular; MAO inhibitors are a different drug class.
Block postsynaptic serotonin receptors
That would reduce, not enhance, serotonin signaling.
Block the transporter that returns serotonin to the presynaptic neuron, raising synaptic serotonin
Correct: less reuptake leaves more serotonin in the cleft.
Increase serotonin synthesis from tyrosine
Serotonin is made from tryptophan, and SSRIs do not affect synthesis.
questions.x: Serotonin signaling is ended mainly by the serotonin transporter (SERT) pumping it back into the presynaptic terminal. SSRIs block SERT, so serotonin lingers in the cleft and keeps acting on receptors. MAO inhibitors raise monoamines through a different mechanism, by blocking intracellular breakdown, and serotonin is synthesized from tryptophan, not tyrosine.

questions.q: Why do ionotropic receptors usually produce faster postsynaptic responses than metabotropic receptors?
o: Ionotropic receptors bind neurotransmitter with higher affinity
Speed comes from the mechanism, not binding affinity.
Metabotropic receptors are located only on axons
Metabotropic receptors are found on dendrites and somata too.
Ionotropic receptors act through cAMP, which diffuses quickly
cAMP is a metabotropic second messenger.
The receptor is itself an ion channel, so binding opens it directly
Correct: no G-protein or second-messenger steps are needed.
questions.x: Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels: transmitter binding opens the pore directly, producing a response within about a millisecond. Metabotropic receptors are G-protein-coupled and act through G proteins and often second messengers such as cAMP, which adds steps and delay but allows amplification and longer effects. Speed reflects mechanism, not binding affinity.

questions.q: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor on skeletal muscle is best described as:
o: A ligand-gated cation channel
Correct: ACh binding opens a pore that passes Na⁺ (and K⁺), depolarizing the end plate.
A G-protein-coupled receptor
That describes muscarinic receptors.
A receptor tyrosine kinase
Receptor tyrosine kinases bind growth factors and insulin.
A voltage-gated Na⁺ channel
Voltage-gated channels respond to voltage, not ACh.
questions.x: The muscle nicotinic receptor is a pentameric ligand-gated channel. Binding two ACh molecules opens a nonselective cation pore; Na⁺ influx exceeds K⁺ efflux, so the end plate depolarizes and triggers a muscle action potential. Muscarinic receptors, by contrast, are G-protein-coupled and act more slowly.

questions.q: Acetylcholine slows the heart by binding receptors on pacemaker cells. Which receptor type mediates this?
o: Nicotinic receptors, which are ligand-gated channels
Nicotinic receptors are at the NMJ and autonomic ganglia, not on the SA node.
M2 muscarinic receptors, which are G-protein coupled
Correct: Gi signaling opens K⁺ channels and slows pacemaker depolarization.
β1-adrenergic receptors
β1 receptors bind norepinephrine and speed the heart.
α1-adrenergic receptors
α1 receptors mediate vasoconstriction, not vagal slowing.
questions.x: Vagal ACh acts on M2 muscarinic receptors on SA-node cells. These Gi-coupled receptors open K⁺ channels (via βγ subunits) and lower cAMP, which hyperpolarizes the cells and slows pacemaker depolarization, so heart rate falls. Nicotinic receptors are tempting because they also bind ACh, but they sit at the NMJ and autonomic ganglia, not on pacemaker cells.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin causes flaccid paralysis. What is its mechanism?
o: It cleaves SNARE proteins, preventing acetylcholine release
Correct: vesicles cannot fuse, so motor neurons cannot signal muscle.
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase
That would cause excessive stimulation, not flaccid paralysis.
It blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in the axon
That is how tetrodotoxin acts.
It activates nicotinic receptors permanently
Persistent activation would produce spasm before block, and is not botulinum's mechanism.
questions.x: Botulinum toxin is a protease that cleaves SNARE proteins such as SNAP-25 and synaptobrevin in cholinergic terminals. Without functional SNAREs, vesicles cannot fuse, ACh is not released, and muscles become flaccid. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition does the opposite, causing excess ACh and overstimulation.

questions.q: Curare-like drugs cause paralysis during surgery. Which action explains this effect?
o: Blockade of muscarinic receptors in skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle uses nicotinic, not muscarinic, receptors.
Increased acetylcholine release from the motor neuron
More ACh would promote contraction.
Competitive antagonism of nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate
Correct: ACh cannot depolarize the end plate, so muscle fibers do not fire.
Inhibition of Ca²⁺ release inside the muscle fiber
That is a different drug class acting on the ryanodine receptor.
questions.x: Curare and similar neuromuscular blockers compete with ACh for nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate. With receptors occupied, ACh cannot depolarize the end plate to threshold, so muscle fibers do not fire and paralysis results. The block can be overcome by raising ACh with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Skeletal muscle uses nicotinic, not muscarinic, receptors at the NMJ.

questions.q: What is the major excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain?
o: GABA
GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain.
Glutamate
Correct: glutamate acts on AMPA and NMDA receptors at most excitatory synapses.
Glycine
Glycine is mainly inhibitory, especially in the spinal cord.
Acetylcholine
ACh is important but not the predominant excitatory transmitter in the brain.
questions.x: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter of the brain, acting on ionotropic AMPA, NMDA and kainate receptors and on metabotropic receptors. GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain, and glycine is a major inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem. ACh excites at the NMJ and in some brain circuits but is not the predominant brain transmitter.

questions.q: Strychnine blocks glycine receptors and causes severe muscle spasms. What does this suggest about glycine's normal role in the spinal cord?
o: It is an excitatory transmitter at the neuromuscular junction
The NMJ uses ACh; blocking an excitatory input would cause weakness.
It is a hormone that raises blood glucose
Glycine is not a glucose-regulating hormone.
It forms myelin in spinal cord tracts
Glycine is an amino acid transmitter, not a myelin component.
It is an inhibitory transmitter that restrains motor neuron firing
Correct: removing inhibition lets motor neurons fire excessively.
questions.note: Blocking an inhibitor looks like overexcitation.
questions.x: Glycine opens Cl⁻ channels on spinal motor neurons, producing IPSPs that restrain their firing. Strychnine blocks these receptors, so inhibition is lost and motor neurons fire excessively, causing spasms. The logic generalizes: blocking an inhibitory transmitter produces signs of overexcitation, while blocking an excitatory one causes weakness.

questions.q: Parkinson disease involves loss of dopamine-producing neurons. Where are these neurons located?
o: Substantia nigra
Correct: nigral dopamine neurons project to the basal ganglia to support movement.
Cerebellar cortex
Cerebellar Purkinje cells are GABAergic.
Hippocampus
The hippocampus is mainly linked to memory formation.
Medulla oblongata
The medulla controls autonomic functions, not this dopaminergic pathway.
questions.x: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta project to the striatum (the nigrostriatal pathway), where dopamine helps initiate and smooth movement. Their degeneration in Parkinson disease causes tremor, rigidity and slowed movement. The cerebellum also coordinates movement, which makes it tempting, but its Purkinje cells are GABAergic, not dopaminergic.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter do most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release onto their target organs?
o: Acetylcholine
Preganglionic fibers release ACh; most sympathetic postganglionic fibers do not.
Norepinephrine
Correct: most sympathetic postganglionic fibers are adrenergic.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine is released mainly by the adrenal medulla as a hormone.
Dopamine
Dopamine is a precursor of norepinephrine, not the main released transmitter.
questions.note: Exception: sympathetic fibers to sweat glands release ACh.
questions.x: In the sympathetic division, preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors in ganglia, and most postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors. Epinephrine is tempting, but it is secreted as a hormone mainly by the adrenal medulla, which acts like a modified sympathetic ganglion. Sympathetic fibers to sweat glands are the cholinergic exception.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes electrical synapses from chemical synapses?
o: They require Ca²⁺-dependent vesicle release
That is a feature of chemical synapses.
They can produce only inhibitory responses
Electrical synapses can transmit depolarization.
Ions pass directly between cells through gap junctions with almost no delay
Correct: connexin channels couple the cytoplasm of the two cells.
They always transmit in one direction only
Many electrical synapses are bidirectional.
questions.x: Electrical synapses link cells through gap junctions made of connexins, so ions and small molecules pass directly from one cytoplasm to the next. Transmission is nearly instantaneous and often bidirectional, which helps synchronize groups of cells. Chemical synapses instead rely on Ca²⁺-triggered vesicle release, which introduces a synaptic delay.

questions.q: Acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle but inhibits cardiac pacemaker cells. What best explains these opposite effects?
o: Acetylcholine is converted to norepinephrine in the heart
ACh is hydrolyzed to choline and acetate, not converted to norepinephrine.
The heart releases more acetylcholinesterase
Breakdown rate would change duration, not reverse the sign of the response.
Skeletal muscle has a more negative resting potential
Resting Vm does not explain excitation versus inhibition here.
The two tissues express different receptor types linked to different responses
Correct: the receptor, not the transmitter, determines the effect.
questions.x: A transmitter has no inherent excitatory or inhibitory effect; the response depends on the receptor and its signaling pathway. Skeletal muscle has nicotinic receptors, ligand-gated cation channels that depolarize the cell, while pacemaker cells have M2 muscarinic receptors that open K⁺ channels via Gi and slow firing. Changing ACh breakdown would alter duration, not reverse the sign.

questions.q: Ouabain irreversibly blocks the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Over the next several hours, what happens to an isolated neuron's resting potential?
o: It immediately becomes strongly positive
The pump's direct electrogenic contribution is only a few millivolts.
It hyperpolarizes as Na⁺ accumulates outside
Without the pump, Na⁺ accumulates inside, not outside.
It slowly depolarizes as the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients run down
Correct: leak continues without the pump, so the K⁺ gradient and EK gradually collapse.
It stays exactly the same because leak channels set Vm
Leak channels need gradients, which the pump maintains.
questions.note: The pump's main role is keeping gradients, not directly setting Vm.
questions.x: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump contributes only a few millivolts directly; its main role is maintaining ion gradients. When it is blocked, Na⁺ and K⁺ keep leaking down their gradients, so intracellular K⁺ falls and Na⁺ rises. EK becomes less negative and the cell slowly depolarizes. The resting potential does not collapse instantly because the existing gradients take time to dissipate.

questions.q: According to the Goldman equation, what happens to membrane potential if Na⁺ permeability suddenly rises far above K⁺ permeability?
o: Vm moves toward ENa (about +60 mV)
Correct: Vm approaches the equilibrium potential of the most permeable ion.
Vm moves toward EK (about −90 mV)
That would happen if K⁺ permeability dominated.
Vm moves toward 0 mV regardless of ions
Vm is set by weighted permeabilities, not fixed at zero.
Vm does not change because concentrations stay the same
Permeability changes alone can shift Vm.
questions.x: The Goldman equation sets Vm as a permeability-weighted average of the ions' equilibrium potentials. If Na⁺ permeability greatly exceeds K⁺ permeability, as during the rising phase of an action potential, Vm moves toward ENa, about +60 mV. Concentrations need not change at all; a change in permeability alone can shift Vm dramatically.

questions.q: A monovalent cation is 10 times more concentrated outside a cell than inside. Using 61 mV per tenfold gradient at body temperature, its equilibrium potential is about:
o: −61 mV
Sign error: a cation higher outside needs a positive interior to balance it.
The log of 10 is 1, not 10.
0 mV
0 mV would require equal concentrations.
+61 mV
Correct: E = 61 log(10/1) = +61 mV; the inside must be positive to oppose inward diffusion.
questions.x: The Nernst equation at body temperature is E ≈ (61 mV/z) × log([out]/[in]). For a monovalent cation with a 10-fold higher outside concentration, E = 61 × log 10 = +61 mV. The sign is positive because a positive interior is needed to oppose the inward diffusion of a cation; a negative answer would apply if the cation were more concentrated inside.

questions.q: Chloride is about 10 times more concentrated outside a neuron than inside. Using the Nernst equation (61 mV per decade), what is ECl?
o: About +61 mV
This forgets that Cl⁻ is negatively charged.
About −61 mV
Correct: for an anion, z = −1 flips the sign, so E = −61 log(10) = −61 mV.
About −6 mV
The log of 10 is 1, so the value is 61 mV, not 6.1 mV.
About +122 mV
This doubles the magnitude and ignores the negative charge; a 10-fold ratio of a monovalent ion gives 61 mV.
questions.note: Anion higher outside → negative equilibrium potential.
questions.x: In the Nernst equation E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]), the valence z carries a sign. For Cl⁻, z = −1, so a 10-fold higher outside concentration gives E = −61 × log 10 = −61 mV. Intuitively, a negative interior is what repels further Cl⁻ entry and balances its inward diffusion. Forgetting the charge sign gives +61 mV.

questions.q: Extracellular Ca²⁺ is roughly 10,000 times higher than cytosolic Ca²⁺. Using 61 mV per decade for a monovalent ion, ECa is approximately:
o: This forgets to divide by z = 2.
Sign error: a cation higher outside gives a positive equilibrium potential.
+30 mV
This uses log = 1 instead of log(10⁴) = 4.
questions.note: Divide by the charge: z = 2 halves the slope.
questions.x: Use E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]). For Ca²⁺, z = 2, so the slope is 30.5 mV per decade, and a 10,000-fold gradient is 4 decades: 30.5 × 4 ≈ +122 mV. The sign is positive because the cation is more concentrated outside. The most common error is forgetting to divide by the valence, which gives about +244 mV.

questions.q: A channel opens when Vm equals the equilibrium potential of the only ion it passes. What net current flows through it?
o: A maximal inward current
Maximal inward current requires Vm far from E in the right direction.
A maximal outward current
There is no net driving force at equilibrium.
A current that depends only on the ion's concentration
At equilibrium, concentration and voltage effects cancel.
None, because the electrical and chemical forces on the ion are balanced
Correct: driving force (Vm − E) is zero.
questions.x: The driving force on an ion is Vm − E. When Vm equals the ion's equilibrium potential, the electrical force exactly balances the concentration gradient, so there is no net flux even though the channel is open. Ions still cross in both directions, but the inward and outward movements are equal, so net current is zero.

questions.q: In a voltage-clamp experiment, a depolarizing step produces an early inward current followed by a sustained outward current. Adding tetraethylammonium (TEA) abolishes only the outward current. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The outward current is carried by K⁺ through voltage-gated channels
Correct: TEA is a K⁺ channel blocker, so the late outward current is K⁺ efflux.
The inward current is carried by K⁺
The early inward current survived TEA; in neurons it is carried by Na⁺ entering, not K⁺.
TEA blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
The early inward Na⁺ current was unaffected.
The outward current is caused by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Pump currents are tiny and not blocked by TEA.
questions.x: In a classic voltage clamp, depolarization first opens Na⁺ channels (early inward current) and then delayed K⁺ channels (late outward current). TEA blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels, so losing only the outward current identifies it as K⁺ efflux. The inward current survived TEA; it is blocked by tetrodotoxin, which identifies it as Na⁺ current.

questions.q: Myelin increases conduction velocity partly because it changes the electrical properties of the internodal membrane. Which change is correct?
o: Membrane resistance decreases and capacitance increases
That would make the internode leakier and slower to charge.
Both resistance and capacitance increase
Thicker insulation lowers capacitance, like moving capacitor plates apart.
Membrane resistance increases and capacitance decreases
Correct: less current leaks out and less charge is needed to change voltage, so current spreads farther.
Internal axial resistance increases
Myelin does not change axoplasm resistance; that depends on diameter.
questions.x: Myelin adds many layers of membrane, which raises transmembrane resistance (less current leaks out) and lowers capacitance (thicker insulation stores less charge per volt, like widening a capacitor gap). Both effects let local current travel farther and charge the next node faster. Axial resistance depends on axon diameter, not on myelin.

questions.q: An action potential started at the axon hillock normally travels only toward the axon terminal. Why does it not reverse direction?
o: The axon membrane only conducts current in one direction
Current spreads both ways; refractoriness prevents back-propagation of the spike.
Myelin blocks backward current flow
Unmyelinated axons also conduct one way.
Na⁺ can only diffuse toward the terminal
Ion diffusion is not directional along the axon this way.
Membrane just behind the active region is refractory
Correct: inactivated Na⁺ channels behind the spike cannot fire again immediately.
questions.x: Local current from an active patch spreads both forward and backward. Forward membrane is at rest and excitable, so it reaches threshold, but membrane just behind the spike has inactivated Na⁺ channels and is refractory. This keeps the action potential moving one way from the hillock. Unmyelinated axons conduct one way too, so myelin is not the reason.

questions.q: How do graded potentials in a dendrite differ from action potentials?
o: Graded potentials are all-or-none
All-or-none behavior belongs to action potentials.
Graded potentials have a refractory period
Graded potentials can summate without refractoriness.
Graded potentials vary in size and decay with distance
Correct: they spread passively and shrink as they travel.
Graded potentials are always depolarizing
They can be depolarizing or hyperpolarizing.
questions.x: Graded potentials are local changes whose size depends on stimulus strength; they can be depolarizing or hyperpolarizing, they sum, and they decay with distance because they spread passively. Action potentials are all-or-none, propagate without decrement and have refractory periods. Summation is possible precisely because graded potentials lack refractoriness.

questions.q: For norepinephrine released at a sympathetic synapse, what is the main way its action is terminated?
o: Hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft
Acetylcholinesterase is specific for acetylcholine.
Reuptake into the presynaptic terminal
Correct: transporters recycle most released norepinephrine.
Conversion to dopamine in the cleft
Dopamine is a precursor, not a breakdown product.
Permanent binding to the postsynaptic receptor
Binding is reversible; signal ends when transmitter is cleared.
questions.x: Most released norepinephrine is cleared by the norepinephrine transporter (NET) back into the presynaptic terminal, where it is repackaged or degraded by MAO. Enzymatic breakdown by COMT and diffusion play smaller roles. Acetylcholinesterase is specific for ACh, the one major transmitter cleared mainly by enzymatic hydrolysis in the cleft.

questions.q: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) have which effect on neurotransmission?
o: They raise levels of monoamines such as serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine
Correct: MAO normally degrades these transmitters inside neurons.
They lower acetylcholine by blocking its synthesis
MAO does not act on acetylcholine.
They block GABA receptors
MAO is an enzyme, not a GABA receptor.
They lower monoamine levels by speeding degradation
Inhibiting MAO slows degradation.
questions.x: Monoamine oxidase, on the outer membrane of mitochondria inside neurons, degrades serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine. Blocking MAO lets more monoamine accumulate and be packaged into vesicles, increasing monoamine signaling. MAO does not act on acetylcholine, which is broken down by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft.

questions.q: Compared with the internode, what is distinctive about the axon membrane at a node of Ranvier?
o: It is covered by the thickest myelin
Nodes are the unmyelinated gaps.
It has a very high density of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Correct: this lets each node regenerate the action potential.
It lacks any ion channels
Nodes are rich in channels.
It releases neurotransmitter
Release occurs at axon terminals.
questions.x: Nodes of Ranvier are short unmyelinated gaps between myelin segments where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are packed at very high density. That concentration lets each node regenerate the action potential from the passive current arriving from the previous node. Internodal membrane under myelin has few Na⁺ channels, which is why demyelination can block conduction.

questions.q: During intense exercise, runners may feel less pain. Which molecules contribute by binding opioid receptors in the CNS?
o: Endorphins
Correct: these endogenous opioid peptides reduce pain transmission.
Substance P
Substance P transmits pain signals rather than suppressing them.
Glutamate
Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in pain pathways.
Histamine
Histamine promotes inflammation and itch, not analgesia.
questions.x: Endorphins are endogenous opioid peptides that bind μ-opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord, reducing pain signaling by inhibiting transmitter release and hyperpolarizing neurons. Substance P is tempting because it is also a neuropeptide in pain pathways, but it transmits pain from nociceptors rather than suppressing it.

questions.q: Afferent neurons carry information in which direction?
o: From the CNS to skeletal muscles
That describes efferent motor neurons.
From the CNS to glands
That is also efferent output.
Between two neurons within the spinal cord only
That describes interneurons.
From sensory receptors toward the central nervous system
Correct: afferent means arriving at the CNS.
questions.note: Afferent arrives; efferent exits.
questions.x: Afferent neurons carry signals toward the CNS, usually from sensory receptors; efferent neurons carry commands away from the CNS to muscles and glands. Interneurons connect neurons within the CNS. A memory aid: afferent arrives, efferent exits. Glands and muscles are both efferent targets, which rules out the first two choices.

questions.q: Where are the cell bodies of the sensory neurons that innervate the skin of the leg located?
o: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord
The ventral horn contains motor neuron cell bodies.
In the primary motor cortex
The motor cortex holds upper motor neurons.
In the dorsal root ganglia
Correct: sensory neuron somata sit in ganglia on the dorsal roots.
In sympathetic chain ganglia
These hold postganglionic autonomic neurons.
questions.x: Primary sensory neurons from the body have their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia, just outside the spinal cord. Their central branches enter through the dorsal root. The ventral horn is a tempting answer because it is part of the same spinal segment, but it holds the cell bodies of lower motor neurons, not sensory neurons.

questions.q: The ventral root of one lumbar spinal nerve is cut in an experimental animal. What deficit is expected in the muscles supplied by that root?
o: Loss of sensation, with movement preserved
That would follow cutting the dorsal root.
Loss of both sensation and movement
Only one root is cut; sensory fibers travel in the dorsal root.
No deficit, because the ventral root carries only autonomic fibers
Ventral roots carry somatic motor axons too.
Loss of motor output, with sensation from the area preserved
Correct: ventral roots carry efferent fibers; dorsal roots carry sensory fibers.
questions.x: Dorsal roots carry sensory (afferent) axons into the cord, and ventral roots carry motor (efferent) axons out. Cutting a ventral root therefore paralyzes the muscle fibers it supplies while leaving sensation from the region intact, since sensory signals still enter through the dorsal root. Loss of sensation with intact movement would be the result of cutting a dorsal root instead.

questions.q: Tapping the patellar tendon causes the quadriceps to contract. Which receptor detects the stretch that starts this reflex?
o: Golgi tendon organ
Tendon organs sense tension and inhibit the muscle.
Muscle spindle
Correct: spindles sense muscle stretch and excite alpha motor neurons monosynaptically.
Pacinian corpuscle
Pacinian corpuscles in skin detect vibration and deep pressure.
Free nerve ending
Free nerve endings mainly detect pain and temperature.
questions.x: The patellar tap briefly stretches the quadriceps, which stretches the muscle spindles inside it. Spindle (Ia) afferents fire and excite alpha motor neurons to the same muscle, producing the kick. Golgi tendon organs are tempting because they are also proprioceptors, but they sense tension in the tendon and inhibit the muscle rather than exciting it.

questions.q: Why is the knee-jerk reflex described as monosynaptic?
o: Only one muscle fiber contracts
Many fibers contract; "monosynaptic" refers to neural wiring.
It requires the brain to process the signal once
The reflex arc is spinal and does not require the brain.
The sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron
Correct: one synapse links afferent to efferent in the spinal cord.
Only one neurotransmitter is involved in the body
Monosynaptic refers to the number of synapses in the arc.
questions.x: The knee-jerk arc contains just one synapse in the spinal cord: the spindle afferent releases glutamate directly onto the alpha motor neuron of the same muscle. This minimal wiring makes the reflex fast and stereotyped. The reflex does not require the brain, which is why it persists after spinal cord injury and is useful in neurological exams.

questions.q: A person steps on a tack, lifts the injured foot and stiffens the opposite leg. What explains the stiffening of the opposite leg?
o: Crossed extensor reflex via interneurons that cross the spinal cord
Correct: interneurons excite extensors on the opposite side to support body weight.
Monosynaptic stretch reflex in the opposite leg
Stretch reflexes are not triggered by pain on the other side.
Voluntary command from the motor cortex
The response happens before conscious perception.
Golgi tendon organ activation in the injured leg
Tendon organs inhibit muscles; they do not cross to the other leg.
questions.x: Stepping on a tack triggers a withdrawal reflex that flexes the injured leg. Simultaneously, interneurons cross the midline of the spinal cord and excite extensor motor neurons in the opposite leg, so it can bear the body's weight: the crossed extensor reflex. It is polysynaptic and spinal, and it occurs faster than a voluntary decision could.

questions.q: During a very heavy lift, a weightlifter's arm muscles suddenly relax. Which receptor's reflex most likely caused this?
o: Muscle spindle, sensing stretch and exciting the motor neurons
Spindle activation would increase contraction.
Nociceptor in the skin
Skin pain receptors trigger withdrawal, not tension-limited relaxation.
Golgi tendon organ, sensing high tension and inhibiting the motor neurons
Correct: this protective reflex prevents tendon damage.
Baroreceptor in the carotid sinus
Baroreceptors sense blood pressure.
questions.x: Golgi tendon organs sit at the muscle–tendon junction and fire in proportion to tension. Through inhibitory interneurons they reduce firing of motor neurons to the same muscle, which can make it suddenly give way under extreme loads (autogenic inhibition). Muscle spindles, by contrast, sense stretch and excite the muscle, so they would increase contraction.

questions.q: In the stretch reflex, the quadriceps contracts while the hamstrings relax. How does the hamstring motor neuron become inhibited?
o: The spindle afferent releases GABA directly onto the hamstring motor neuron
Primary afferents are excitatory (glutamate); an interneuron provides inhibition.
The quadriceps motor neuron releases glycine onto the hamstrings
Motor neurons release ACh onto muscle.
The brain sends a voluntary relaxation command
Reciprocal inhibition is a spinal reflex.
The spindle afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron that synapses on the hamstring motor neuron
Correct: reciprocal inhibition uses one inhibitory interneuron.
questions.note: An afferent can't inhibit directly; it needs an inhibitory interneuron.
questions.x: Sensory afferents are excitatory, releasing glutamate. To inhibit the antagonist muscle, the spindle afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron in the spinal cord, which releases glycine onto the hamstring motor neuron. This reciprocal inhibition lets the quadriceps contract without opposition. A direct afferent-to-motor neuron synapse can only excite.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the somatic and autonomic nervous systems?
o: Somatic efferents control skeletal muscle; autonomic efferents control smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands
Correct: this is the basic target distinction.
Somatic efferents use two-neuron chains; autonomic use one neuron
It is the reverse: autonomic pathways use two neurons.
Somatic efferents control the heart; autonomic control skeletal muscle
The targets are swapped.
Both use norepinephrine at their effector synapses
Somatic motor neurons release ACh.
questions.x: Somatic efferents are single motor neurons that release ACh onto nicotinic receptors on skeletal muscle and are largely voluntary. Autonomic efferents use a two-neuron chain (preganglionic and postganglionic) to control smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands involuntarily. The chain lengths are often swapped by mistake: it is the autonomic system that uses two neurons.

questions.q: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons originate in which region of the spinal cord?
o: Cervical segments only
Cervical segments do not give rise to sympathetic preganglionic outflow.
Thoracic and upper lumbar segments
Correct: the sympathetic division is thoracolumbar.
Sacral segments only
Sacral outflow is parasympathetic.
The brainstem cranial nerve nuclei
Brainstem outflow is parasympathetic.
questions.note: Sympathetic = thoracolumbar; parasympathetic = craniosacral.
questions.x: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons sit in the lateral horn of spinal segments T1 to about L2, giving the sympathetic division its thoracolumbar outflow. Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons are in brainstem nuclei (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X) and sacral segments S2–S4, giving craniosacral outflow. Sacral and brainstem choices therefore describe the parasympathetic division.

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries most of the parasympathetic outflow to the heart, lungs and digestive tract?
o: Vagus nerve (CN X)
Correct: the vagus supplies most thoracic and abdominal viscera.
Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
CN III carries parasympathetic fibers to the eye.
Facial nerve (CN VII)
CN VII supplies salivary and lacrimal glands.
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
CN V is mainly sensory to the face and motor to chewing muscles.
questions.x: The vagus nerve (CN X) carries roughly three quarters of all parasympathetic fibers, supplying the heart, lungs and gut down to about the proximal colon. Other cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibers to more limited targets: CN III to the eye, CN VII to lacrimal and some salivary glands, and CN IX to the parotid. Pelvic organs receive sacral parasympathetic fibers.

questions.q: What neurotransmitter and receptor are used at the ganglionic synapse in BOTH sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways?
o: Norepinephrine acting on α receptors
NE is released by most sympathetic postganglionic, not preganglionic, neurons.
Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors
Muscarinic receptors are on parasympathetic target organs.
Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors
Correct: all autonomic preganglionic neurons are cholinergic onto nicotinic receptors.
Epinephrine acting on β receptors
Epinephrine is a hormone from the adrenal medulla.
questions.x: In both autonomic divisions, preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors on postganglionic neurons in the ganglion. The divisions differ at the target: parasympathetic postganglionic fibers release ACh onto muscarinic receptors, and most sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors. Muscarinic receptors belong at targets, not ganglia.

questions.q: Why is the adrenal medulla often described as a modified sympathetic ganglion?
o: It is innervated by the vagus nerve
The adrenal medulla receives sympathetic, not parasympathetic, input.
Its chromaffin cells are innervated by preganglionic sympathetic fibers and release catecholamines into blood
Correct: they act like postganglionic neurons without axons.
It releases acetylcholine into the blood
It releases mainly epinephrine, with some norepinephrine.
It produces cortisol in response to nerve signals
Cortisol comes from the adrenal cortex under ACTH control.
questions.x: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla develop from neural crest, like postganglionic sympathetic neurons. They receive preganglionic sympathetic fibers that release ACh onto nicotinic receptors, and respond by secreting epinephrine (mostly) and norepinephrine into the blood rather than onto a nearby target. Cortisol is from the adrenal cortex, a separate, ACTH-controlled tissue.

questions.q: Which response is caused by sympathetic activation?
o: Pupil constriction
Constriction is parasympathetic.
Increased gastrointestinal motility
Sympathetic activity decreases GI motility.
Increased salivary secretion of watery saliva
Watery salivation is parasympathetic.
Bronchodilation
Correct: β2 stimulation relaxes airway smooth muscle.
questions.x: Sympathetic activation prepares the body for exertion: heart rate rises, bronchioles dilate via β2 receptors, pupils dilate, and blood glucose rises, while digestion slows. Parasympathetic activity does the opposite (rest and digest), constricting pupils, increasing GI motility and producing watery saliva. Bronchodilation is the only listed effect that fits fight-or-flight.

questions.q: Sympathetic fibers to eccrine sweat glands are an exception to the usual autonomic pattern. What is unusual about them?
o: Their postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors
Correct: they are sympathetic in origin but cholinergic at the target.
They have no preganglionic neuron
They still use a two-neuron chain.
They release epinephrine directly into sweat
Glands are activated by transmitter, not hormone secretion into sweat.
They originate from the sacral spinal cord
They arise from thoracolumbar segments like other sympathetic fibers.
questions.x: Most sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine, but those to eccrine sweat glands release ACh onto muscarinic receptors. They are still sympathetic anatomically, arising from thoracolumbar outflow through a two-neuron chain. This is why anticholinergic drugs such as atropine reduce sweating and can cause overheating.

questions.q: A patient receives atropine, a muscarinic antagonist. Which set of effects is expected?
o: Decreased heart rate, salivation and constricted pupils
Those are muscarinic agonist effects.
Increased heart rate, dry mouth and dilated pupils
Correct: blocking parasympathetic muscarinic effects unmasks sympathetic tone.
Skeletal muscle paralysis
Skeletal muscle uses nicotinic receptors, which atropine does not block.
Increased GI motility and urination
Muscarinic blockade reduces GI motility and causes urinary retention.
questions.x: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, removing parasympathetic effects at target organs. Without vagal slowing, heart rate rises; without parasympathetic secretory and sphincter drive, salivation falls and pupils dilate; GI motility decreases and urine may be retained. Skeletal muscle is unaffected because the NMJ uses nicotinic receptors, which atropine does not block.

questions.q: A patient takes a β1-selective blocker. What is the expected effect on the heart at rest?
o: Increased heart rate
Blocking β1 removes a stimulatory input.
Bronchodilation
β2, not β1, mediates bronchodilation; and blockade would not dilate airways.
Decreased heart rate and contractility
Correct: β1 receptors mediate sympathetic stimulation of the heart.
Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles
Skin vasoconstriction is α1-mediated.
questions.x: β1-adrenergic receptors on the heart are Gs-coupled; norepinephrine and epinephrine acting on them raise heart rate, conduction speed and contractility. A β1-selective blocker removes this sympathetic drive, lowering heart rate and contractility, which reduces cardiac oxygen demand. Bronchodilation is mediated by β2 receptors, and skin vasoconstriction by α1 receptors.

questions.q: Albuterol is inhaled during an asthma attack. Which receptor does it activate, and what is the result?
o: Muscarinic receptors, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
Muscarinic stimulation constricts airways.
α1-adrenergic receptors, constricting bronchioles
α1 does not mediate bronchodilation.
Nicotinic receptors, relaxing the diaphragm
The diaphragm is skeletal muscle and not the target.
β2-adrenergic receptors, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
Correct: β2 agonists cause bronchodilation.
questions.x: Albuterol is a β2-adrenergic agonist. β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle couple to Gs, raising cAMP and causing relaxation, which opens the airways during an asthma attack. Muscarinic stimulation (parasympathetic) does the opposite and constricts bronchioles, which is why antimuscarinic inhalers are also used in some lung diseases.

questions.q: Which pairing of male sexual response and autonomic division is correct?
o: Erection is sympathetic; ejaculation is parasympathetic
The divisions are reversed.
Both are controlled only by somatic motor neurons
Both depend mainly on autonomic input.
Erection is parasympathetic; ejaculation is sympathetic
Correct: remember "point and shoot."
Both are purely parasympathetic
Emission and ejaculation require sympathetic activity.
questions.note: Point (parasympathetic) and shoot (sympathetic).
questions.x: Erection depends on parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) fibers that cause vasodilation of the erectile tissue, partly through nitric oxide. Emission and ejaculation depend on sympathetic contraction of the vas deferens, seminal glands and internal urethral sphincter, with somatic help from pelvic floor muscles. The mnemonic is point (parasympathetic) and shoot (sympathetic).

questions.q: Damage to which brain region most directly causes unsteady gait and poorly coordinated movements, with normal strength?
o: Cerebellum
Correct: the cerebellum fine-tunes coordination and balance.
Medulla oblongata
Medulla damage threatens breathing and heart control.
Occipital lobe
The occipital lobe processes vision.
Pituitary gland
The pituitary is endocrine and not a motor coordinator.
questions.x: The cerebellum compares intended movement with actual movement and corrects errors, controlling coordination, balance and timing.
