Damage produces ataxia, an unsteady wide-based gait, and intention tremor, while muscle strength is preserved because the motor cortex and lower motor neurons are intact. The medulla controls vital functions, not movement coordination.

questions.q: Which brain region contains centers that regulate breathing rhythm, heart rate and blood pressure?
o: Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
Hippocampus
The hippocampus is involved in memory.
Thalamus
The thalamus relays sensory information.
Medulla oblongata
Correct: medullary centers control vital autonomic functions.
questions.x: The medulla oblongata contains the cardiovascular and respiratory centers that set breathing rhythm, heart rate and vascular tone. This is why medullary injury is quickly life-threatening. The pons modulates breathing as well, but the listed alternatives handle coordination (cerebellum), memory (hippocampus) and sensory relay (thalamus).

questions.q: Body temperature, thirst and hunger are regulated mainly by which structure?
o: Thalamus
The thalamus is a sensory relay.
Hypothalamus
Correct: hypothalamic nuclei integrate homeostatic signals and drive responses.
Pons
The pons helps regulate breathing and relays signals to the cerebellum.
Basal ganglia
The basal ganglia regulate movement initiation.
questions.x: The hypothalamus is the brain's homeostatic center: it contains thermoregulatory, thirst (osmoreceptor) and hunger/satiety nuclei, and it controls the pituitary and autonomic nervous system to carry out responses. The thalamus is often confused with it because of the similar name, but the thalamus mainly relays sensory information to the cortex.

questions.q: Which sensory modality reaches the cerebral cortex WITHOUT first relaying through the thalamus?
o: Vision
Vision relays through the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
Olfaction
Correct: smell signals travel from the olfactory bulb directly to olfactory cortex.
Hearing
Hearing relays through the medial geniculate nucleus.
Touch
Touch relays through the ventral posterior thalamus.
questions.x: Nearly all sensory pathways synapse in a thalamic nucleus before reaching the cortex: vision in the lateral geniculate, hearing in the medial geniculate, touch in the ventral posterior nuclei. Olfaction is the exception; olfactory bulb output goes directly to the olfactory (piriform) cortex and limbic structures. This direct route helps explain smell's strong links to emotion and memory.

questions.q: How does the arrangement of gray and white matter in the spinal cord differ from that in the cerebral cortex?
o: Both have white matter inside and gray matter outside
The spinal cord's outer layer is white matter.
The spinal cord has no white matter
The spinal cord has extensive white matter tracts.
The cortex has no gray matter
The cortex is the brain's outer gray layer.
The spinal cord has gray matter inside and white matter outside, the reverse of the cortex
Correct: spinal tracts run in outer white columns around a central gray core.
questions.x: In the cerebrum, gray matter (cell bodies and synapses) forms the outer cortex, with white matter (myelinated axons) beneath. In the spinal cord the arrangement is reversed: a butterfly-shaped core of gray matter with dorsal and ventral horns, surrounded by white-matter columns of ascending and descending tracts. Myelin's lipid content gives white matter its pale color.

questions.q: Which sensory receptors detect changes in plasma osmolarity to regulate thirst and ADH release?
o: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus
Correct: they shrink or swell with osmolarity and signal the hypothalamus.
Baroreceptors in the aortic arch
Baroreceptors sense stretch from blood pressure.
Chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies
Carotid bodies sense mainly blood O₂.
Nociceptors in the kidney
Nociceptors sense tissue damage.
questions.x: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus (around the anterior hypothalamus and nearby circumventricular organs) shrink when plasma osmolarity rises. This triggers thirst and ADH release from the posterior pituitary, increasing water intake and renal water reabsorption. Baroreceptors also influence ADH, but they sense pressure and volume, not osmolarity.

questions.q: A constant pressure on the skin is felt at first but soon goes unnoticed, even though the pressure continues. What explains this?
o: The mechanoreceptors die after activation
Receptors recover and respond again to changes.
The action potentials become smaller
Amplitude is fixed; firing rate falls.
Rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors reduce their firing during a sustained stimulus
Correct: sensory adaptation lowers the response to an unchanging stimulus.
The stimulus is rerouted to the motor cortex
Sensory signals are not rerouted to motor areas.
questions.x: Sensory adaptation is the decline in receptor firing during a constant stimulus. Rapidly adapting receptors such as Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles respond mainly to changes, so continuous pressure quickly fades from awareness, while slowly adapting receptors keep signaling. The action potentials themselves do not shrink; the firing rate falls.

questions.q: What is sensory transduction?
o: Transport of neurotransmitter back into the presynaptic cell
That is reuptake.
Conversion of an action potential into muscle contraction
That is excitation–contraction coupling.
Passage of a signal across the corpus callosum
That is interhemispheric communication.
Conversion of a stimulus's energy into a change in receptor membrane potential
Correct: e.g., light or pressure becomes a receptor potential.
questions.x: Transduction is the conversion of a stimulus's energy (light, pressure, chemicals, heat) into an electrical change in a receptor cell, the receptor potential. If large enough, this leads to action potentials or transmitter release that carry the signal to the CNS. Excitation–contraction coupling is a different conversion, from muscle action potential to contraction.

questions.q: How does a receptor potential in a sensory receptor cell differ from an action potential?
o: It is all-or-none
That is a property of action potentials.
It always hyperpolarizes the cell
Many receptor potentials are depolarizing.
It is graded, varying in size with stimulus strength
Correct: larger stimuli produce larger receptor potentials.
It travels without decrement along long axons
Receptor potentials spread passively and decay.
questions.x: Receptor potentials are graded: their amplitude scales with stimulus intensity and they spread passively, decaying with distance. They are converted into action potentials, whose amplitude is fixed, so intensity is then coded as frequency. Some receptor potentials hyperpolarize (as in photoreceptors), so 'always hyperpolarizing' and 'all-or-none' are both wrong.

questions.q: Receptors that monitor joint position and muscle length, allowing you to know where your limbs are with your eyes closed, are called:
o: Nociceptors
Nociceptors detect harmful stimuli.
Proprioceptors
Correct: muscle spindles, tendon organs and joint receptors provide position sense.
Photoreceptors
Photoreceptors detect light.
Thermoreceptors
Thermoreceptors detect temperature.
questions.x: Proprioceptors provide the sense of body position and movement. They include muscle spindles (muscle length), Golgi tendon organs (tension) and joint receptors, and their input goes to the cerebellum and somatosensory cortex. Nociceptors, photoreceptors and thermoreceptors detect damage, light and temperature, respectively, not limb position.

questions.q: Pressing on a closed eye can make a person "see" flashes of light even though no light enters. What principle does this illustrate?
o: The perceived modality depends on which pathway is activated, not on the stimulus type
Correct: labeled-line coding interprets any optic signal as light.
Photoreceptors respond only to pressure
Photoreceptors respond best to light; pressure is an atypical stimulus.
Sensory adaptation
Adaptation is reduced response to a sustained stimulus.
Mechanoreceptors in the eye convert pressure to light
No receptor produces light; perception is interpreted by the brain.
questions.x: Labeled-line coding means the brain interprets activity in a particular pathway as a particular sensation, regardless of what activated it. Mechanical pressure that excites retinal cells is perceived as light (phosphenes) because the signal arrives via the optic pathway. No receptor generates light; the experience is created by the brain's interpretation of the active line.

questions.q: A person stands up quickly and blood pressure briefly drops. How do arterial baroreceptors respond, and what follows?
o: They fire more, which increases parasympathetic output
Lower pressure reduces stretch, so firing falls.
They fire less, which increases sympathetic and decreases parasympathetic output
Correct: less stretch reduces firing, raising heart rate and vasoconstriction.
They fire less, which decreases sympathetic output
Reduced sympathetic output would lower pressure further.
They stop sensing pressure until it returns to normal
They continuously signal, firing at a lower rate.
questions.x: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire in proportion to arterial wall stretch. When pressure falls on standing, stretch and firing drop, and the medulla responds by increasing sympathetic output (faster heart, vasoconstriction) and decreasing vagal output. Decreasing sympathetic activity would lower pressure further, the opposite of what is needed.

questions.q: Which stimulus most strongly activates the peripheral chemoreceptors of the carotid bodies?
o: A large fall in arterial O₂ partial pressure
Correct: carotid bodies are the main sensors of hypoxemia.
A rise in blood glucose
Glucose is sensed by pancreatic and hypothalamic cells.
A rise in blood pressure
Pressure is sensed by baroreceptors in the carotid sinus.
A fall in plasma osmolarity
Osmolarity is sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors.
questions.x: The carotid bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors that respond most strongly to low arterial PO₂, especially below about 60 mmHg, and also to high PCO₂ and low pH. They signal via the glossopharyngeal nerve to increase ventilation. The carotid sinus, located nearby, contains baroreceptors that sense pressure, a common mix-up.

questions.q: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond mainly to changes in arterial CO₂, even though H⁺ crosses the blood–brain barrier poorly. How?
o: The receptors bind CO₂ directly in the blood
They sit on the brain side and sense CSF H⁺.
Bicarbonate crosses the barrier freely and activates them
Bicarbonate crosses slowly and is not the rapid signal.
They respond only to low O₂
Low O₂ is sensed mainly by peripheral chemoreceptors.
CO₂ diffuses into the CSF and forms H⁺ there, which the receptors detect
Correct: CO₂ crosses the barrier and is hydrated to H₂CO₃, releasing H⁺.
questions.x: The blood–brain barrier blocks H⁺ and HCO₃⁻, but CO₂ is small and lipid-soluble and diffuses freely into the CSF. There, carbonic anhydrase helps hydrate CO₂ to H₂CO₃, which releases H⁺; central chemoreceptors detect this fall in CSF pH and increase ventilation. Low O₂ is sensed mainly by peripheral chemoreceptors, not central ones.

questions.q: Which drug property most helps a drug cross the blood–brain barrier?
o: High charge at physiological pH
Charged molecules cross membranes poorly.
Large molecular weight with many hydrogen-bond donors
Large polar molecules are excluded.
High lipid solubility and small size
Correct: tight junctions force most molecules to cross cell membranes.
Binding to plasma albumin
Bound drug cannot cross; only free drug diffuses.
questions.x: Brain capillaries have tight junctions and few transport vesicles, so most substances must diffuse through endothelial cell membranes to enter the brain. Small, lipid-soluble, uncharged molecules cross best, which is why drugs like anesthetics act quickly. Charged, large or highly polar molecules are excluded unless a specific transporter carries them, and protein-bound drug cannot cross.

questions.q: A cluster of neuron cell bodies located outside the brain and spinal cord is called a:
o: Nucleus
A nucleus is a cluster of cell bodies within the CNS.
Tract
A tract is a bundle of axons in the CNS.
Nerve
A nerve is a bundle of axons in the PNS.
Ganglion
Correct: PNS clusters of somata are ganglia.
questions.note: CNS: nuclei and tracts. PNS: ganglia and nerves.
questions.x: Neuroanatomy uses different terms by location. In the CNS, a cluster of cell bodies is a nucleus and a bundle of axons is a tract; in the PNS, a cluster of cell bodies is a ganglion and a bundle of axons is a nerve. The dorsal root ganglia and autonomic ganglia are examples of PNS cell body clusters.

questions.q: Sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia have one process that splits into a peripheral and central branch. What type of neuron is this?
o: Multipolar
Multipolar neurons have many dendrites and one axon, like motor neurons.
Pseudounipolar
Correct: a single stem divides into two branches that act as one axon.
Bipolar
Bipolar neurons have two separate processes, as in the retina.
Anaxonic
Anaxonic neurons lack a distinct axon and are found in the CNS.
questions.x: Dorsal root ganglion neurons are pseudounipolar: one short process leaves the cell body and splits into a peripheral branch to the receptor and a central branch to the spinal cord, which together act as one continuous axon. Bipolar neurons, by contrast, have two separate processes from opposite ends of the soma and are found in the retina and olfactory epithelium.

questions.q: Which type of neuron makes up the large majority of neurons in the CNS and links sensory input to motor output?
o: Motor neurons
Motor neurons are a minority and carry output to effectors.
Sensory neurons
Sensory neurons are afferents, mostly outside the CNS.
Interneurons
Correct: interneurons process and relay signals within the CNS.
Schwann cells
Schwann cells are glia, not neurons.
questions.x: Interneurons lie entirely within the CNS and make up the vast majority of neurons. They connect sensory input to motor output and form the circuits for reflexes, integration and higher functions. Motor and sensory neurons are fewer and serve as the output and input lines; Schwann cells are glia, not neurons.

questions.q: After a complete spinal cord transection at the mid-thoracic level and recovery from spinal shock, what is expected for the legs?
o: Voluntary movement and sensation are lost, but spinal stretch reflexes still occur
Correct: reflex arcs below the lesion remain intact without brain input.
Voluntary movement returns but reflexes are lost
Descending motor tracts are severed, so voluntary control is lost.
Both reflexes and voluntary movement remain normal
Voluntary movement requires the severed tracts.
Arm movement is lost but leg movement is preserved
A thoracic lesion spares the arms.
questions.x: A complete thoracic transection cuts ascending sensory tracts and descending motor tracts, so the legs lose sensation and voluntary control. The spinal reflex arcs below the lesion are intact, so after spinal shock resolves, stretch reflexes return and are often exaggerated because descending inhibition is lost. Arm function is spared because its segments are above the lesion.

questions.q: A patient has weakness, muscle atrophy and absent reflexes in one arm. Damage to which structure best explains this pattern?
o: Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex
Upper motor neuron lesions typically produce spasticity and hyperreflexia.
The cerebellum
Cerebellar damage causes incoordination, not atrophy and areflexia.
Lower motor neurons in the ventral horn or their axons
Correct: losing the final motor pathway causes flaccid weakness, atrophy and areflexia.
Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons only
Loss of sensation alone would not cause weakness and atrophy.
questions.x: Lower motor neurons in the ventral horn are the final pathway to skeletal muscle. Their loss causes flaccid weakness, atrophy from denervation, fasciculations and absent reflexes because the reflex arc's efferent limb is broken. Upper motor neuron lesions instead cause spasticity and hyperreflexia, because the lower motor neurons survive without descending inhibition.

questions.q: During a sympathetic "fight-or-flight" response, epinephrine raises blood glucose. Which liver process is stimulated directly?
o: Glycogen synthesis
That stores glucose and is promoted by insulin.
Glucose uptake by GLUT4
GLUT4 is in muscle and fat, and is stimulated by insulin.
Fatty acid synthesis
That is an anabolic, insulin-favored process.
Glycogenolysis
Correct: epinephrine signaling via cAMP activates glycogen phosphorylase.
questions.x: Epinephrine binds hepatic adrenergic receptors (largely β2 via Gs-cAMP), activating protein kinase A, which activates glycogen phosphorylase kinase and glycogen phosphorylase. Glycogenolysis releases glucose quickly into the blood for fuel. Glycogen synthesis and GLUT4-mediated uptake are insulin-driven storage processes and are suppressed during fight-or-flight.

questions.q: Which part of the nervous system can control gut motility and secretion even when disconnected from the brain and spinal cord?
o: Enteric nervous system
Correct: its plexuses in the gut wall run local reflexes independently.
Somatic nervous system
Somatic nerves control skeletal muscle.
Central nervous system
The CNS modulates but is not required for local gut reflexes.
Sympathetic chain only
Sympathetic input modulates but does not run gut reflexes on its own.
questions.x: The enteric nervous system contains the myenteric and submucosal plexuses in the gut wall, with more neurons than the spinal cord. It can run local peristaltic and secretory reflexes even when extrinsic nerves are cut. Sympathetic and parasympathetic input modulates its activity but is not required for basic gut reflexes.

questions.q: At the neuromuscular junction, where are the acetylcholine receptors concentrated?
o: On the presynaptic terminal of the motor neuron
Receptors for ACh at the NMJ are postsynaptic.
On the motor end plate of the muscle fiber
Correct: nicotinic receptors cluster in the folded end plate membrane.
On Schwann cells covering the terminal
Schwann cells do not mediate contraction.
On the T-tubule membrane deep in the fiber
T-tubules carry the muscle action potential but are not the ACh receptor site.
questions.x: At the neuromuscular junction, nicotinic ACh receptors are densely clustered on the motor end plate, especially at the crests of the junctional folds. ACh released from the motor terminal binds them, causing an end-plate potential that triggers a muscle action potential. T-tubules carry that action potential inward but do not contain the ACh receptors.

questions.q: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce the number of functional nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Why do acetylcholinesterase inhibitors improve strength?
o: They let acetylcholine persist longer, increasing binding to the remaining receptors
Correct: more ACh per receptor compensates for fewer receptors.
They create new nicotinic receptors
They do not change receptor number.
They remove the antibodies from the end plate
They act on the enzyme, not the immune response.
They block muscarinic receptors on skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle uses nicotinic receptors.
questions.x: In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies block and remove nicotinic receptors, so the end-plate potential may fail to reach threshold, especially with repeated use. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine slow ACh breakdown, so each ACh molecule can bind receptors repeatedly, strengthening the end-plate potential. They treat symptoms but do not change receptor number or the immune attack.

questions.q: The vagus nerves to an animal's heart are cut. Resting heart rate rises from 70 to about 100 beats/min. What does this indicate?
o: At rest, sympathetic tone is dominant
Cutting the vagus removes parasympathetic, not sympathetic, input.
The vagus normally speeds the heart
Then cutting it would slow the heart.
At rest, parasympathetic tone normally slows the SA node below its intrinsic rate
Correct: removing vagal input unmasks the faster intrinsic pacemaker rate.
The SA node has no intrinsic rhythm
The rise shows the node fires on its own.
questions.x: The SA node has an intrinsic firing rate of roughly 100 beats/min. At rest, continuous vagal (parasympathetic) tone slows it to about 70. Cutting the vagus removes this braking input, so the heart rises toward its intrinsic rate. If sympathetic tone were dominant at rest, removing vagal input would not unmask a faster rate in this way.

questions.q: Most organs receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic input. Which target is controlled mainly by the sympathetic division alone?
o: The heart
The heart receives both vagal and sympathetic fibers.
Most systemic blood vessels
Correct: vascular tone is set by varying sympathetic firing, with little parasympathetic input.
The iris of the eye
The iris has both dilator (sympathetic) and sphincter (parasympathetic) muscles.
The salivary glands
Salivary glands receive both divisions.
questions.x: Most systemic arterioles and veins receive sympathetic but little or no parasympathetic innervation. Vascular tone is adjusted by raising or lowering sympathetic firing onto α1 receptors: more firing constricts, less firing allows dilation. The heart, iris and salivary glands all receive dual innervation from both divisions.

questions.q: Focusing on a nearby object requires contraction of the ciliary muscle. Which autonomic division drives this?
o: Sympathetic, via the superior cervical ganglion
Sympathetic input dilates the pupil; it does not drive near accommodation.
Somatic, via the facial nerve
The facial nerve does not control the ciliary muscle.
Enteric, via local reflexes
The enteric system controls the gut.
Parasympathetic, via the oculomotor nerve
Correct: ciliary contraction lets the lens round up for near vision.
questions.x: For near vision, parasympathetic fibers in the oculomotor nerve (via the ciliary ganglion) contract the ciliary muscle. This relaxes tension on the zonular fibers, so the elastic lens rounds up and increases its refractive power. The same parasympathetic pathway constricts the pupil. Sympathetic input dilates the pupil and does not drive accommodation.

questions.q: Which receptor type responds to tissue-damaging stimuli and starts pain signals?
o: Nociceptors (free nerve endings)
Correct: they respond to strong mechanical, thermal or chemical injury.
Meissner corpuscles
These are light-touch mechanoreceptors.
Rods
Rods are photoreceptors.
Muscle spindles
Spindles detect muscle stretch.
questions.x: Nociceptors are free nerve endings that respond to intense mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli that threaten tissue damage. Their signals travel on thin Aδ (sharp pain) and C (dull, burning pain) fibers to the spinal cord. Meissner corpuscles and muscle spindles are encapsulated mechanoreceptors for light touch and stretch, not pain.

questions.q: How do the locations of autonomic ganglia typically differ between the two divisions?
o: Sympathetic ganglia lie in the target organ; parasympathetic ganglia lie near the spinal cord
The locations are reversed.
Sympathetic ganglia lie near the spinal cord; parasympathetic ganglia lie near or in the target organ
Correct: sympathetic preganglionic fibers are short, parasympathetic ones long.
Both divisions have ganglia inside the brainstem
Autonomic ganglia are in the PNS.
Neither division uses ganglia
Both use a two-neuron chain with a ganglion between.
questions.x: Sympathetic ganglia lie close to the spinal cord, in the paravertebral chain or prevertebral ganglia, so preganglionic fibers are short and postganglionic fibers long. Parasympathetic ganglia lie near or within target organs, so preganglionic fibers are long and postganglionic fibers short. This arrangement lets sympathetic signals spread widely and parasympathetic effects stay localized.

questions.q: A typical spinal nerve, just after the dorsal and ventral roots join, contains:
o: Only sensory axons
Sensory-only fibers are found in the dorsal root.
Only motor axons
Motor-only fibers are found in the ventral root.
Both sensory and motor axons
Correct: spinal nerves are mixed nerves.
Only autonomic axons
Somatic sensory and motor axons are also present.
questions.x: Sensory axons enter through the dorsal root and motor axons leave through the ventral root, but just beyond the dorsal root ganglion these join to form the spinal nerve. The spinal nerve is therefore a mixed nerve with both sensory and motor fibers (plus autonomic fibers). Sensory-only and motor-only fibers are found only in the separate roots.

questions.q: In a nerve conduction study, a motor nerve is stimulated at two points 20 cm apart. The muscle response from the farther point arrives 4 ms later. What is the conduction velocity?
o: 5 m/s
This misplaces a factor of 10 in the unit conversion (e.g., using 0.02 m).
This treats 4 ms as 0.4 ms.
This treats 4 ms as 0.4 s: 0.2 m ÷ 0.4 s = 0.5 m/s.
50 m/s
Correct: 0.20 m ÷ 0.004 s = 50 m/s.
questions.note: Velocity = distance ÷ time; convert to meters and seconds first.
questions.x: Conduction velocity is distance divided by the difference in latency between the two stimulation points. Convert to SI units first: 20 cm = 0.20 m and 4 ms = 0.004 s, so velocity = 0.20 ÷ 0.004 = 50 m/s, typical of a large myelinated motor axon. Most errors come from unit conversion, such as treating 4 ms as 0.4 ms (giving 500 m/s).

questions.q: Why do peptide hormones such as glucagon bind receptors on the cell surface rather than inside the cell?
o: They are too small to be noticed by intracellular receptors
Size is not the reason; polarity prevents membrane crossing.
They are destroyed by the cytoplasm's acidic pH
The cytosol is near neutral pH.
They are hydrophilic and cannot cross the lipid bilayer
Correct: polar, charged peptides stay outside and use membrane receptors.
They are carried on plasma proteins that keep them outside
Most peptides circulate free; polarity is the key factor.
questions.x: Peptide hormones are chains of amino acids with many polar and charged groups, so they cannot diffuse through the hydrophobic core of the plasma membrane. They therefore act on cell-surface receptors (GPCRs or receptor tyrosine kinases) that relay the signal inward through second messengers or kinase cascades. Polarity, not size or pH, is the deciding factor.

questions.q: How do steroid hormones such as estrogen typically change target-cell function?
o: They bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors
Correct: hormone–receptor complexes bind DNA response elements to alter gene expression.
They bind GPCRs and raise cAMP
That is typical of many peptide and amine hormones.
They open ligand-gated ion channels in the membrane
That describes ionotropic neurotransmitter receptors.
They phosphorylate the insulin receptor
Steroids do not act through receptor tyrosine kinases.
questions.x: Steroid hormones are lipophilic, so they diffuse across the plasma membrane and bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus. The hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, binding hormone response elements on DNA to turn genes on or off. Raising cAMP through GPCRs is the typical strategy of water-soluble peptide and catecholamine hormones instead.

questions.q: From what precursor are steroid hormones synthesized, and in which organelle does much of this occur?
o: Tyrosine, in the rough ER
Tyrosine gives rise to catecholamines and thyroid hormones.
Amino acids, in the rough ER
That describes peptide hormone synthesis.
Tryptophan, in the Golgi
Tryptophan gives rise to serotonin and melatonin.
Cholesterol, largely in the smooth ER (and mitochondria)
Correct: steroidogenic enzymes are concentrated in smooth ER and mitochondria.
questions.x: All steroid hormones, from cortisol and aldosterone to estrogen and testosterone, are made from cholesterol. The first step (side-chain cleavage to pregnenolone) occurs in mitochondria, and many later steps occur in the smooth ER, which is abundant in steroid-producing cells. Rough ER is where peptide hormones are made, and tyrosine is the precursor of catecholamines and thyroid hormones.

questions.q: Endocrine cells that secrete peptide hormones typically store large amounts of hormone, but steroid-secreting cells do not. Why?
o: Steroids are degraded inside the cell within seconds
Steroids are not stored because they are lipid-soluble, not because they are unstable.
Peptides can be packaged in secretory vesicles, while steroids diffuse out through membranes as soon as they are made
Correct: steroid secretion is controlled by synthesis rate.
Peptides are lipid-soluble and steroids are not
It is the reverse.
Steroids are made only in the nucleus
Steroids are made in the smooth ER and mitochondria.
questions.x: Peptide hormones are made on the rough ER, packaged by the Golgi into secretory vesicles, and stored until a stimulus triggers exocytosis. Steroids are lipid-soluble, so they would simply diffuse out of any vesicle or membrane; they are released as soon as they are synthesized. Steroid secretion is therefore regulated by controlling the rate of synthesis, not release.

questions.q: Thyroid hormone (T₃) is derived from an amino acid, yet its mechanism resembles that of steroid hormones. Why?
o: It binds surface GPCRs like epinephrine
Catecholamines use GPCRs; thyroid hormone does not mainly do so.
It is lipophilic, enters cells and binds nuclear receptors that regulate transcription
Correct: T₃ acts mainly through nuclear thyroid hormone receptors.
It is a peptide stored in vesicles
T₃ is an iodinated tyrosine derivative, not a peptide.
It is made from cholesterol
T₃ comes from tyrosine and iodine.
questions.note: Amine hormones split: catecholamines act like peptides; thyroid hormones act like steroids.
questions.x: Amine hormones derived from tyrosine split into two groups. Catecholamines are water-soluble and act on surface GPCRs, like peptides. Thyroid hormones are iodinated and lipophilic, travel bound to carrier proteins, enter cells (aided by transporters), and bind nuclear receptors to change gene transcription, like steroids. Chemical behavior, not precursor, determines mechanism.

questions.q: Epinephrine is derived from tyrosine. How does it reach and act on its target cells?
o: It requires carrier proteins and binds nuclear receptors
That pattern fits steroid and thyroid hormones.
It diffuses into cells and binds DNA
Epinephrine is too polar to cross membranes easily.
It acts only on cells next to the adrenal gland
It is a hormone that circulates throughout the body.
It travels mostly dissolved in plasma and binds cell-surface adrenergic receptors
Correct: catecholamines are water-soluble and act via GPCRs.
questions.x: Epinephrine is a catecholamine: polar and water-soluble, so it circulates largely dissolved in plasma and has a short half-life. It cannot readily cross membranes, so it binds cell-surface α- and β-adrenergic receptors, which are GPCRs. Carrier proteins and nuclear receptors are features of lipophilic steroid and thyroid hormones.

questions.q: Glucagon binds a GPCR on hepatocytes. What is the correct order of the signaling steps?
o: Gs activation → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A
Correct: this is the classic cAMP second-messenger cascade.
Gq activation → phospholipase C → cAMP → protein kinase C
Gq produces IP₃ and DAG, not cAMP.
Receptor tyrosine kinase → Ras → cAMP → PKA
Glucagon does not use a receptor tyrosine kinase.
Gs activation → phosphodiesterase → cAMP → PKA
Phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP rather than making it.
questions.x: Glucagon receptors couple to Gs. Activated Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to cAMP; cAMP then activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates enzymes to promote glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Phosphodiesterase is the enzyme that ends the signal by degrading cAMP to AMP, so placing it in the activation pathway is backward.

questions.q: A drug inhibits phosphodiesterase in liver cells. How does this change the response to glucagon?
o: The response is abolished because cAMP cannot be produced
Adenylyl cyclase still makes cAMP.
The response is unchanged because glucagon uses IP₃
Glucagon uses cAMP.
The response is stronger and longer because cAMP is degraded more slowly
Correct: phosphodiesterase converts cAMP to AMP, ending the signal.
The response is weaker because receptors are blocked
The drug acts downstream of the receptor.
questions.x: Phosphodiesterase terminates cAMP signaling by hydrolyzing cAMP to AMP. Inhibiting it lets cAMP made after glucagon binding accumulate and persist, so PKA stays active longer and the glycogenolytic response is stronger and more prolonged. cAMP production by adenylyl cyclase is unaffected, which rules out the idea that the response is abolished.

questions.q: A hormone acts through a Gq-coupled receptor. Which event follows receptor activation?
o: Adenylyl cyclase is inhibited, lowering cAMP
That is Gi signaling.
The receptor autophosphorylates on tyrosine
That is a receptor tyrosine kinase.
The hormone–receptor complex enters the nucleus
That is the steroid receptor mechanism.
Phospholipase C makes IP₃, which releases Ca²⁺ from the ER
Correct: IP₃ opens ER Ca²⁺ channels, and DAG activates protein kinase C.
questions.x: Gq-coupled receptors activate phospholipase C, which cleaves the membrane lipid PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ opens Ca²⁺ channels in the ER, raising cytosolic Ca²⁺, while DAG and Ca²⁺ activate protein kinase C. Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase is Gi signaling, a common mix-up between G-protein subtypes.

questions.q: The insulin receptor belongs to which receptor class?
o: G-protein-coupled receptor
Glucagon and epinephrine use GPCRs.
Nuclear receptor
Nuclear receptors bind lipophilic hormones.
Receptor tyrosine kinase
Correct: insulin binding activates intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity and autophosphorylation.
Ligand-gated ion channel
Insulin does not directly open an ion channel.
questions.x: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase built as a pre-formed α₂β₂ dimer. Insulin binding activates the intrinsic kinase of the β subunits, which autophosphorylate and then phosphorylate insulin receptor substrates, triggering pathways such as PI3K–Akt that move GLUT4 to the membrane. Glucagon and epinephrine use GPCRs instead.

questions.q: A tiny amount of hormone binding a few surface receptors can change the activity of millions of enzyme molecules. Which feature of second-messenger signaling explains this?
o: Desensitization of the receptor
Desensitization reduces signaling.
Amplification, because each step activates many molecules of the next
Correct: one receptor activates many G proteins, and each enzyme makes many messengers.
Negative feedback on hormone secretion
That controls hormone levels, not intracellular amplification.
Direct entry of the hormone into the nucleus
Surface-acting hormones do not enter the nucleus.
questions.x: Second-messenger cascades amplify signals at each step: one activated receptor activates many G proteins, each adenylyl cyclase produces many cAMP molecules, and each protein kinase phosphorylates many targets. A few hormone molecules can therefore change the activity of millions of enzymes. Desensitization and negative feedback limit signaling rather than amplify it.

questions.q: Why do steroid hormones usually have longer plasma half-lives than peptide hormones?
o: They circulate bound to carrier proteins, which protect them from breakdown and excretion
Correct: protein binding forms a reservoir and slows clearance.
They are larger than most peptide hormones
Steroids are smaller than most peptides.
They are stored in vesicles within the blood
Hormones are not stored in vesicles within plasma.
They are never metabolized by the liver
The liver does metabolize steroids, just more slowly.
questions.x: Steroid and thyroid hormones are lipophilic, so most of each circulates bound to plasma proteins such as albumin or specific binding globulins. Bound hormone is protected from hepatic metabolism and renal filtration, creating a reservoir that prolongs half-life to hours or days. Free, water-soluble peptides are cleared within minutes. Only the free fraction is biologically active.

questions.q: A hormone is injected, and its target-cell effect appears only after several hours and requires new protein synthesis. Which hormone class is it most likely to belong to?
o: Catecholamine
Catecholamine effects begin within seconds.
Steroid
Correct: changing gene expression takes hours.
Peptide acting via cAMP
cAMP-mediated effects often begin within seconds to minutes.
Neurotransmitter acting on ionotropic receptors
Ionotropic effects take milliseconds.
questions.x: A delay of hours that requires new protein synthesis points to changes in gene transcription, the hallmark of steroid (and thyroid) hormones acting on intracellular receptors. Transcription, translation and protein processing take time. Catecholamines and cAMP-acting peptides modify existing proteins within seconds to minutes, and ionotropic receptors act in milliseconds.

questions.q: A cell releases a signal that acts on neighboring cells in the same tissue without entering the bloodstream. This type of signaling is called:
o: Paracrine
Correct: paracrine signals act locally on nearby cells.
Endocrine
Endocrine signals travel through blood to distant targets.
Autocrine
Autocrine signals act on the cell that released them.
Exocrine
Exocrine secretions are released into ducts.
questions.x: Paracrine signals diffuse through extracellular fluid to act on nearby cells, as with histamine or somatostatin in the islets. Endocrine signals travel in blood to distant targets, autocrine signals act on the secreting cell itself, and exocrine secretions are released into ducts, such as sweat or digestive enzymes. The clue is local action on neighboring cells.

questions.q: After a meal, insulin stimulates glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. How?
o: By opening Na⁺-glucose cotransporters in muscle
SGLT transporters are found in intestine and kidney.
By converting glucose to fat in the blood
Lipogenesis occurs inside cells, not in plasma.
By increasing glucose excretion in urine
Insulin lowers glucose by uptake, not urinary excretion.
By moving GLUT4 transporters to the plasma membrane
Correct: insulin signaling triggers insertion of GLUT4 from intracellular vesicles.
questions.x: In skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, GLUT4 transporters are stored in intracellular vesicles. Insulin binding to its receptor tyrosine kinase activates the PI3K–Akt pathway, which moves these vesicles to the plasma membrane, increasing facilitated diffusion of glucose into the cells. SGLT cotransporters, by contrast, are found in intestinal and renal epithelium.

questions.q: During fasting, glucagon from pancreatic α cells raises blood glucose mainly by acting on which organ?
o: Skeletal muscle
Muscle lacks glucagon receptors and cannot release free glucose.
Brain
The brain uses glucose but does not supply it.
Liver
Correct: glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Adipose tissue only
Adipose releases fatty acids, not glucose.
questions.x: Glucagon acts mainly on the liver, where it stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and releases glucose into the blood. The liver can export free glucose because it has glucose-6-phosphatase. Skeletal muscle lacks both glucagon receptors and glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen fuels only the muscle itself.

questions.q: Which pancreatic hormone, from δ cells, inhibits the secretion of both insulin and glucagon?
o: Amylin
Amylin is co-secreted with insulin from β cells.
Pancreatic polypeptide
It is secreted by PP cells and mainly affects pancreatic exocrine function.
Secretin
Secretin comes from the duodenum.
Somatostatin
Correct: somatostatin acts as a paracrine brake on islet hormones.
questions.x: Somatostatin from pancreatic δ cells acts as a local paracrine inhibitor, suppressing secretion of both insulin and glucagon; it also inhibits GH release when secreted by the hypothalamus. Amylin is co-secreted with insulin by β cells, and secretin comes from duodenal S cells. Somatostatin's broad inhibitory role is the key idea to remember.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes type 1 from type 2 diabetes mellitus?
o: Type 1 involves insulin resistance; type 2 involves loss of β cells
The two types are reversed.
Type 1 involves autoimmune loss of β cells; type 2 involves insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency
Correct: this is the core difference.
Type 1 is caused by excess glucagon; type 2 by excess insulin
Neither is the primary cause.
Both result from lack of ADH
Lack of ADH causes diabetes insipidus.
questions.x: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency; patients require insulin. Type 2 diabetes is insulin resistance in muscle, fat and liver, with β cells that eventually cannot secrete enough to compensate. Both cause hyperglycemia. Diabetes insipidus is an unrelated disorder of ADH that causes dilute urine without high glucose.

questions.q: In untreated type 1 diabetes, ketone bodies accumulate in the blood. What is the reason?
o: High insulin drives fat synthesis into ketones
Insulin is absent, and it suppresses ketogenesis.
Glucose is converted directly into ketones
Ketones come from fatty acid breakdown.
Without insulin, lipolysis and hepatic fatty-acid oxidation increase, producing excess acetyl-CoA that becomes ketones
Correct: low insulin with high glucagon drives ketogenesis.
The kidney stops excreting ketones
Ketones are excreted; overproduction is the problem.
questions.x: Insulin normally suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis. Without insulin, and with glucagon high, adipose tissue releases large amounts of fatty acids, which the liver oxidizes to acetyl-CoA faster than the citric acid cycle can use it. The excess acetyl-CoA is converted to acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate, causing ketoacidosis. Glucose itself is not converted into ketones.

questions.q: Unlike skeletal muscle, most neurons take up glucose regardless of insulin levels. What is the best explanation?
o: Neurons rely mainly on insulin-independent transporters such as GLUT3
Correct: neurons do not need insulin-triggered GLUT4 insertion.
Neurons make their own glucose from fatty acids
Fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose in humans.
Neurons lack plasma membranes
All cells have plasma membranes.
Insulin cannot reach neurons, so they store glucose as glycogen
The brain has little glycogen.
questions.x: Neurons take up glucose mainly through GLUT3, a high-affinity transporter that is always present in the membrane and does not depend on insulin. This keeps glucose supply to the brain steady even when insulin falls during fasting. Muscle and fat depend on insulin-triggered GLUT4 insertion. Humans cannot make glucose from fatty acids, which rules out choice two.

questions.q: What directly stimulates the adrenal medulla to release epinephrine during stress?
o: ACTH from the anterior pituitary
ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex.
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Cortisol supports, but does not directly trigger, catecholamine release.
Acetylcholine from preganglionic sympathetic neurons
Correct: chromaffin cells have nicotinic receptors activated by ACh.
Aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa
Aldosterone regulates Na⁺ and K⁺ handling in the kidney.
questions.x: The adrenal medulla is controlled neurally, not by pituitary hormones. Preganglionic sympathetic fibers release ACh onto nicotinic receptors on chromaffin cells, causing Ca²⁺ entry and exocytosis of epinephrine and norepinephrine. ACTH is a tempting answer because it stimulates the adrenal gland, but it targets the cortex to produce cortisol.

questions.q: Which pairing of adrenal cortex zone and main hormone is correct?
o: Zona fasciculata — aldosterone
The fasciculata makes mainly cortisol.
Zona reticularis — epinephrine
Epinephrine comes from the medulla.
Zona glomerulosa — cortisol
Cortisol comes mainly from the fasciculata.
Zona glomerulosa — aldosterone
Correct: the outer zone makes mineralocorticoids.
questions.note: Salt (glomerulosa), sugar (fasciculata), sex (reticularis).
questions.x: The adrenal cortex has three zones from outside in: glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone), fasciculata (glucocorticoids such as cortisol) and reticularis (adrenal androgens). The mnemonic salt, sugar, sex matches the order. Epinephrine is made in the medulla, the inner neural-crest-derived core, not in any cortical zone.

questions.q: What effect does aldosterone have on the principal cells of the collecting duct?
o: Increased Na⁺ reabsorption and increased K⁺ secretion
Correct: aldosterone upregulates ENaC channels and Na⁺/K⁺ pumps.
Increased Na⁺ secretion and K⁺ reabsorption
The directions are reversed.
Insertion of aquaporin-2 channels
That is ADH's main action.
Increased Ca²⁺ reabsorption
Ca²⁺ reabsorption is mainly regulated by PTH.
questions.x: Aldosterone binds intracellular mineralocorticoid receptors in principal cells and increases the number of luminal ENaC Na⁺ channels, ROMK K⁺ channels and basolateral Na⁺/K⁺ pumps. The result is more Na⁺ reabsorption (with water following) and more K⁺ secretion into urine. Inserting aquaporin-2 is ADH's action, a frequent confusion between the two hormones.

questions.q: Which stimulus causes juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney to release renin?
o: Increased blood pressure
High pressure suppresses renin.
Decreased renal perfusion pressure
Correct: low pressure in the afferent arteriole triggers renin release.
High plasma ANP
ANP inhibits renin release.
High plasma glucose
Glucose is not the main regulator of renin.
questions.x: Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole act as baroreceptors: when renal perfusion pressure falls, they release renin. Renin release is also triggered by sympathetic β1 stimulation and by low NaCl delivery sensed by the macula densa. High pressure and ANP both suppress renin, consistent with renin's role in restoring blood pressure and volume.

questions.q: A patient takes an ACE inhibitor. Which change in plasma levels is expected?
o: Lower angiotensin II and aldosterone, with a tendency toward higher K⁺
Correct: less aldosterone reduces K⁺ secretion.
Higher angiotensin II and lower renin
Blocking ACE lowers angiotensin II; renin rises from lost feedback.
Higher aldosterone and lower K⁺
Aldosterone falls, not rises.
No change in aldosterone because ACTH controls it fully
Angiotensin II is a main driver of aldosterone secretion.
questions.x: ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone release. An ACE inhibitor lowers angiotensin II and aldosterone; with less aldosterone, the collecting duct secretes less K⁺, so plasma K⁺ tends to rise. Renin rises because angiotensin II normally inhibits renin release, so loss of that feedback raises renin.

questions.q: ADH (vasopressin) increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct. From where is it released into the blood?
o: Anterior pituitary
The anterior pituitary releases tropic hormones such as ACTH and TSH.
Adrenal cortex
The adrenal cortex releases steroid hormones.
Posterior pituitary
Correct: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from posterior pituitary terminals.
Kidney
The kidney is ADH's target, not its source.
questions.x: ADH and oxytocin are synthesized by neurons in the hypothalamus (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei), transported down their axons, and released from terminals in the posterior pituitary. The posterior pituitary is neural tissue, unlike the anterior pituitary, which is glandular and releases tropic hormones under control of hypothalamic releasing hormones carried in portal blood.

questions.q: A patient makes large volumes of dilute urine. After injection of desmopressin (an ADH analog), urine becomes concentrated. Where is the defect most likely?
o: In kidney ADH receptors
Nephrogenic DI would not respond to desmopressin.
In ADH production or release from the hypothalamus–posterior pituitary
Correct: this is central diabetes insipidus.
In pancreatic β cells
β-cell failure causes diabetes mellitus with glucose in urine.
In the adrenal cortex
Adrenal defects do not produce desmopressin-responsive dilute urine.
questions.note: Response to ADH analog = central DI; no response = nephrogenic DI.
questions.x: Diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine. If the kidney concentrates urine after a synthetic ADH analog, its receptors and aquaporin machinery work, so the problem is lack of ADH from the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary: central DI. In nephrogenic DI, the kidney fails to respond to ADH, so desmopressin would have little effect.

questions.q: When the atria are stretched by high blood volume, they secrete ANP. What is its effect?
o: Increased aldosterone release
ANP inhibits aldosterone release.
Increased ADH release
ANP opposes ADH effects.
Vasoconstriction of systemic arterioles
ANP is a vasodilator.
Increased Na⁺ and water excretion by the kidney
Correct: ANP promotes natriuresis and lowers blood volume.
questions.x: ANP is released by atrial myocytes when stretched by high blood volume. It increases GFR, inhibits Na⁺ reabsorption, suppresses renin and aldosterone, and dilates vessels, producing natriuresis and diuresis that lower blood volume and pressure. It counters the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, so it reduces rather than increases aldosterone.

questions.q: Which set of actions is produced by parathyroid hormone?
o: Increased renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, increased phosphate excretion and activation of vitamin D
Correct: these actions raise blood Ca²⁺.
Decreased renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption and increased phosphate reabsorption
These effects would lower Ca²⁺ and raise phosphate.
Inhibition of osteoclasts
PTH indirectly activates osteoclasts.
Inactivation of vitamin D in the kidney
PTH stimulates 1α-hydroxylase activity.
questions.x: PTH raises plasma Ca²⁺ in three ways: it increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the distal tubule, it stimulates renal 1α-hydroxylase to make calcitriol (which increases intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption), and it indirectly activates osteoclasts via osteoblast signaling to release bone Ca²⁺. It also increases phosphate excretion, which keeps released phosphate from binding Ca²⁺.

questions.q: Calcitonin, which tends to lower blood Ca²⁺, is secreted by which cells?
o: Chief cells of the parathyroid
Chief cells secrete PTH.
Parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid
Correct: C cells sit between thyroid follicles.
Follicular cells of the thyroid
Follicular cells make T₃ and T₄.
Osteoblasts in bone
Osteoblasts form bone; they do not secrete calcitonin.
questions.x: Calcitonin is made by parafollicular (C) cells located between the thyroid follicles. It lowers blood Ca²⁺ mainly by inhibiting osteoclast activity, though its role in adult humans is minor. Follicular cells of the same gland make T₃ and T₄, and chief cells of the parathyroid secrete PTH, which raises Ca²⁺.

questions.q: What is the main action of calcitriol (active vitamin D)?
o: It lowers blood Ca²⁺ by inhibiting bone resorption
Calcitriol raises blood Ca²⁺.
It increases renal phosphate excretion
That is mainly PTH's action.
It increases Ca²⁺ absorption from the intestine
Correct: calcitriol induces intestinal Ca²⁺ transport proteins.
It is produced first in the pancreas
Activation occurs in the liver and kidney.
questions.x: Vitamin D is hydroxylated first in the liver (to 25-OH vitamin D) and then in the kidney (to 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D, calcitriol), a step stimulated by PTH. Calcitriol acts on nuclear receptors in intestinal cells to induce Ca²⁺ transport proteins, increasing Ca²⁺ and phosphate absorption. Raising renal phosphate excretion is PTH's action, not calcitriol's.

questions.q: Which change best summarizes the overall effect of thyroid hormones on metabolism?
o: Decreased oxygen consumption
That occurs in hypothyroidism.
Lower heart rate and cold tolerance
Thyroid hormone increases heart rate and heat production.
Storage of iodine in muscle
Iodine is concentrated in the thyroid.
Increased basal metabolic rate and heat production
Correct: T₃ increases Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase expression and oxygen use.
questions.x: Thyroid hormones raise basal metabolic rate in most tissues: they increase Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase expression, mitochondrial activity, oxygen consumption and heat production. They also increase β-adrenergic responsiveness, which raises heart rate. Low oxygen consumption, bradycardia and cold intolerance are therefore signs of too little, not too much, thyroid hormone.

questions.q: Which set of symptoms best fits hyperthyroidism?
o: Cold intolerance, weight gain and bradycardia
These suggest hypothyroidism.
Hypoglycemia and low blood pressure only
These are not the typical hyperthyroid picture.
Heat intolerance, weight loss and tachycardia
Correct: these reflect increased metabolism and sympathetic sensitivity.
Dehydration with very dilute urine
That suggests diabetes insipidus.
questions.x: Excess thyroid hormone raises metabolism, so heat production increases (heat intolerance, sweating), stores are burned (weight loss despite good appetite) and heart rate rises from increased β-adrenergic sensitivity. Hypothyroidism produces the mirror image: cold intolerance, weight gain and bradycardia. Dilute urine with dehydration points to diabetes insipidus instead.

questions.q: In Graves disease, antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor. What hormone pattern is expected?
o: High T₃ and T₄ with low TSH
Correct: antibodies drive the thyroid, and excess T₃/T₄ suppresses pituitary TSH.
High T₃ and T₄ with high TSH
That would suggest a TSH-secreting pituitary tumor.
Low T₃ and T₄ with high TSH
That is primary hypothyroidism.
Low T₃ and T₄ with low TSH
That is secondary (central) hypothyroidism.
questions.x: In Graves disease, stimulating antibodies mimic TSH and drive the thyroid to make excess T₃ and T₄ independently of the pituitary. High T₃ and T₄ exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so TSH falls very low. High hormone with high TSH would instead point to a TSH-secreting pituitary tumor.

questions.q: Why does dietary iodine deficiency cause an enlarged thyroid (goiter)?
o: Iodine directly inhibits thyroid cell growth
The enlargement is driven by TSH.
High T₃ and T₄ cause the thyroid to swell
T₃ and T₄ are low in iodine deficiency.
TSH falls and the thyroid swells with stored iodine
TSH rises and stored iodine is scarce.
Low T₃ and T₄ reduce negative feedback, so TSH rises and stimulates thyroid growth
Correct: chronic TSH stimulation enlarges the gland.
questions.x: Iodine is required to make T₃ and T₄. With iodine deficiency, hormone levels fall, removing negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so TRH and TSH rise. TSH is trophic for the thyroid, so chronic stimulation causes follicular cell growth and an enlarged gland (goiter). The enlargement reflects high TSH, not stored iodine or excess hormone.

questions.q: Which gland secretes melatonin, a hormone involved in sleep–wake rhythms?
o: Pituitary gland
The pituitary secretes tropic hormones, ADH and oxytocin.
Pineal gland
Correct: the pineal secretes melatonin, mostly at night.
Thymus
The thymus supports T-cell maturation.
Adrenal medulla
The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines.
questions.x: The pineal gland, in the epithalamus, secretes melatonin mainly in darkness. Light detected by the retina signals the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which inhibits melatonin release via a sympathetic pathway, linking melatonin to the light–dark cycle. Melatonin is synthesized from tryptophan via serotonin.

questions.q: Which gland is the site of T-lymphocyte maturation and is most active in childhood?
o: Thyroid
The thyroid makes T₃, T₄ and calcitonin.
Thymus
Correct: thymic hormones and environment support T-cell development.
Pineal gland
The pineal makes melatonin.
Adrenal cortex
The adrenal cortex makes steroid hormones.
questions.x: The thymus, in the upper chest, is where T-cell precursors from the bone marrow mature and undergo positive and negative selection. It also secretes hormones such as thymosin that support this process. It is largest and most active in childhood and gradually involutes and is replaced by fat in adults. The thyroid, despite the similar name, makes metabolic hormones.

questions.q: A person moves to high altitude. Which hormone increases to stimulate red blood cell production?
o: Erythropoietin from the liver in adults
In adults, EPO comes mainly from the kidney.
Thyroxine from the thyroid
Thyroxine does not directly drive red cell production in this response.
Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex
Aldosterone regulates Na⁺ and K⁺, not erythropoiesis.
Erythropoietin from the kidney
Correct: renal cells sense low O₂ and release EPO.
questions.x: At high altitude, lower arterial O₂ is sensed by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney, which increase erythropoietin (EPO) via the HIF pathway. EPO stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow, raising O₂-carrying capacity over weeks. The liver is the main EPO source only in the fetus, which makes the liver choice a tempting but wrong option for adults.

questions.q: Which pairing of appetite-related hormone and effect is correct?
o: Leptin from adipose tissue decreases appetite
Correct: leptin signals energy stores to the hypothalamus.
Ghrelin from adipose tissue decreases appetite
Ghrelin comes from the stomach and increases appetite.
Leptin from the stomach increases appetite
Leptin comes from fat cells and suppresses hunger.
Insulin from the liver increases appetite
Insulin comes from β cells.
questions.x: Leptin is secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass; it acts on the hypothalamus to reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure. Ghrelin is secreted by the stomach, mainly before meals, and increases hunger. Swapping their sources or effects is the classic trap: leptin signals 'stored energy is sufficient,' ghrelin signals 'time to eat.'

questions.q: Which cells produce testosterone in the testes, and which pituitary hormone stimulates them?
o: Sertoli cells, stimulated by LH
Sertoli cells respond to FSH and support sperm development.
Leydig cells, stimulated by prolactin
Prolactin is not the main regulator of testosterone.
Leydig cells, stimulated by LH
Correct: LH drives testosterone synthesis in interstitial Leydig cells.
Sertoli cells, stimulated by ACTH
ACTH targets the adrenal cortex.
questions.x: In the testes, LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates interstitial Leydig cells to synthesize testosterone from cholesterol. FSH acts on Sertoli cells inside the seminiferous tubules, which support spermatogenesis and secrete inhibin and androgen-binding protein. A memory aid: LH goes to Leydig cells, FSH goes to Sertoli cells.

questions.q: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin. What is its feedback target?
o: It selectively suppresses LH secretion
Testosterone mainly suppresses LH.
It stimulates GnRH release
Inhibin is inhibitory, not stimulatory.
It blocks testosterone receptors in the testis
It acts on the pituitary.
It selectively suppresses FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary
Correct: inhibin provides FSH-specific negative feedback.
questions.x: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin in proportion to spermatogenic activity, and inhibin selectively suppresses FSH release from the anterior pituitary. This lets the testis regulate FSH separately from LH, which is controlled mainly by testosterone negative feedback. In females, granulosa cells also secrete inhibin with the same FSH-specific effect.

questions.q: Just before ovulation, high estrogen levels trigger a surge of LH. What type of control is this?
o: Negative feedback
Negative feedback would lower LH.
Paracrine inhibition
The surge is a systemic hormonal feedback.
Positive feedback
Correct: sustained high estrogen switches feedback from negative to positive.
Feedforward from progesterone alone
Estrogen is the key trigger of the LH surge.
questions.x: For most of the menstrual cycle, estrogen exerts negative feedback on LH and FSH. When estrogen from the dominant follicle stays high for a couple of days, the feedback switches to positive, producing a large LH surge that triggers ovulation. Positive feedback means the output amplifies its own stimulus, the opposite of the usual stabilizing negative feedback.

questions.q: After ovulation, which structure secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrium?
o: Anterior pituitary
The pituitary secretes LH and FSH, not progesterone.
Corpus luteum
Correct: the corpus luteum forms from the ruptured follicle.
Hypothalamus
The hypothalamus secretes GnRH.
Primordial follicle
Primordial follicles are inactive structures.
questions.x: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (and estrogen) under LH stimulation. Progesterone transforms the endometrium into a secretory lining suitable for implantation and suppresses LH and FSH. Without pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates after about 14 days, progesterone falls, and menstruation begins.

questions.q: In early pregnancy, the corpus luteum does not degenerate as it would in a non-pregnant cycle. Why?
o: hCG from the trophoblast acts like LH to maintain it
Correct: hCG sustains progesterone production until the placenta takes over.
FSH rises and maintains it
FSH is suppressed during pregnancy.
Prolactin from the corpus luteum keeps it active
Prolactin comes from the anterior pituitary.
Oxytocin maintains it by contracting the uterus
Oxytocin does not maintain the corpus luteum.
questions.x: The corpus luteum normally depends on LH and degenerates as LH falls. In pregnancy, the trophoblast of the implanting embryo secretes hCG, which binds LH receptors and keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone. By the end of the first trimester the placenta produces enough progesterone itself. hCG is also the hormone detected by pregnancy tests.

questions.q: During labor, uterine contractions stretch the cervix, which increases oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions. This is an example of:
o: Negative feedback
Negative feedback would reduce contractions.
Positive feedback
Correct: the response amplifies the original stimulus until delivery.
Antagonistic hormone action
Only one hormone pathway is amplifying itself here.
Permissive hormone action
Permissive action means one hormone enables another's effect.
questions.x: In positive feedback, the response reinforces the stimulus. Cervical stretch triggers oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions, and stronger contractions stretch the cervix more, until delivery ends the loop. Negative feedback would instead dampen the contractions. Permissive action describes one hormone enabling another's effect, which is not occurring here.

questions.q: A pituitary tumor compresses the stalk and blocks hypothalamic signals to the anterior pituitary. Which hormone level is most likely to RISE?
o: Prolactin
Correct: dopamine from the hypothalamus normally inhibits prolactin, so blocking it raises prolactin.
ACTH
ACTH depends on stimulatory CRH, so it falls.
TSH
TSH depends on stimulatory TRH, so it falls.
GH
GH depends mainly on stimulatory GHRH, so it falls.
questions.note: Prolactin is the one anterior pituitary hormone under tonic inhibition.
questions.x: Most anterior pituitary hormones depend on stimulatory hypothalamic hormones (CRH, TRH, GHRH, GnRH) carried in portal blood, so cutting the stalk lowers them. Prolactin is different: it is under tonic inhibition by hypothalamic dopamine. Interrupting dopamine delivery removes this brake, so prolactin rises even as the other anterior pituitary hormones fall.

questions.q: Growth hormone stimulates bone and cartilage growth largely through which mediator?
o: Thyroxine from the thyroid
Thyroxine supports growth but is not GH's mediator.
Calcitonin from the thyroid
Calcitonin lowers blood Ca²⁺.
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Excess cortisol actually inhibits growth.
IGF-1 from the liver
Correct: GH induces hepatic IGF-1, which drives growth.
questions.x: Growth hormone has direct metabolic effects, but its growth-promoting effects on bone and cartilage are mostly mediated by insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), produced mainly by the liver in response to GH. IGF-1 stimulates chondrocyte proliferation at growth plates. IGF-1 also feeds back to inhibit GH release. Excess cortisol inhibits growth rather than mediating it.

questions.q: An adult develops enlarged hands, jaw and feet due to excess growth hormone. Why does height not increase?
o: GH cannot act on adult bone at all
GH still acts on bone, thickening it and enlarging the hands and jaw.
IGF-1 is not produced in adults
Adults still make IGF-1.
The epiphyseal growth plates have already fused
Correct: excess GH after plate closure causes acromegaly rather than gigantism.
Adult bone lacks osteoblasts
Adult bone has active osteoblasts.
questions.x: Longitudinal bone growth occurs at epiphyseal growth plates, which fuse after puberty. Excess GH before fusion causes gigantism (increased height); after fusion, bones can only grow in thickness and in certain areas, enlarging the hands, feet and jaw (acromegaly). GH and IGF-1 still act in adults, which is why these tissues enlarge.

questions.q: Which effect of cortisol helps maintain blood glucose during prolonged stress?
o: Stimulation of glucose uptake in muscle
Cortisol reduces peripheral glucose uptake.
Increased glycogen breakdown in muscle to release free glucose
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and cannot release free glucose.
Increased insulin sensitivity
Cortisol reduces insulin sensitivity.
Stimulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis
Correct: cortisol supplies amino acids and induces gluconeogenic enzymes.
questions.x: Cortisol maintains blood glucose during prolonged stress by stimulating hepatic gluconeogenesis: it induces gluconeogenic enzymes and breaks down muscle protein to supply amino acid substrates. It also reduces glucose uptake by muscle and fat, sparing glucose for the brain. Muscle glycogen cannot release free glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.

questions.q: After months of high-dose prednisone (a glucocorticoid), a patient stops the drug suddenly and develops low cortisol. Why?
o: Prednisone permanently destroyed cortisol receptors
Receptor loss would not explain low cortisol levels.
Prolonged negative feedback suppressed ACTH, causing the adrenal cortex to atrophy
Correct: the gland cannot quickly resume cortisol output.
The adrenal medulla stopped producing cortisol
Cortisol comes from the cortex, not the medulla.
ACTH levels became too high and exhausted the gland
ACTH was suppressed, not raised.
questions.note: Taper glucocorticoids: the HPA axis needs time to recover.
questions.x: Exogenous glucocorticoids exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, suppressing CRH and ACTH. Without ACTH, the cortisol-producing zones of the adrenal cortex atrophy over months. If the drug is stopped abruptly, the suppressed axis cannot restore cortisol output quickly, causing adrenal insufficiency. This is why long-term steroids are tapered.

questions.q: How do releasing hormones from the hypothalamus reach the anterior pituitary?
o: Along axons that end in the anterior pituitary
Axonal delivery describes the posterior pituitary.
Through the cerebrospinal fluid
CSF is not the delivery route.
Through the hypophyseal portal blood vessels
Correct: a portal system carries them directly to the anterior pituitary.
Through the general systemic circulation only
The portal system delivers them before dilution in systemic blood.
questions.x: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones (CRH, TRH, GnRH, GHRH, dopamine) are secreted into capillaries of the median eminence and carried by the hypophyseal portal veins straight to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary. This delivers them in high concentration before dilution in systemic blood. Axonal delivery is how the posterior pituitary works.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the posterior pituitary?
o: It stores and releases hormones made by hypothalamic neurons whose axons end there
Correct: oxytocin and ADH are neurohormones made in hypothalamic nuclei.
It synthesizes ADH and oxytocin in its own glandular cells
Synthesis occurs in hypothalamic cell bodies.
It secretes ACTH and TSH
Those are anterior pituitary hormones.
It is connected to the hypothalamus only by portal blood vessels
The posterior lobe is linked by axons.
questions.x: The posterior pituitary is neural tissue: it contains axon terminals of neurons whose cell bodies lie in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. These neurons make ADH and oxytocin, transport them down their axons, and release them into the blood when they fire. The anterior pituitary, by contrast, is a true gland linked to the hypothalamus by portal vessels.

questions.q: Which anterior pituitary hormone is a tropic hormone that stimulates another endocrine gland?
o: Prolactin
Prolactin acts directly on the mammary gland, not on another endocrine gland.
Oxytocin
Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone.
ACTH
Correct: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex.
ADH
ADH is a posterior pituitary hormone acting on the kidney.
questions.x: Tropic hormones regulate other endocrine glands. The anterior pituitary's tropic hormones are ACTH (adrenal cortex), TSH (thyroid), and LH and FSH (gonads). Prolactin is an anterior pituitary hormone, which makes it tempting, but it acts directly on the mammary gland rather than on another endocrine gland. ADH and oxytocin come from the posterior pituitary.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the stress hormone axis?
o: ACTH → CRH → cortisol
CRH comes before ACTH.
TRH → ACTH → aldosterone
TRH controls TSH; aldosterone is mainly controlled by angiotensin II.
Cortisol → ACTH → CRH
Cortisol is the end product and feeds back negatively.
CRH → ACTH → cortisol
Correct: hypothalamic CRH drives pituitary ACTH, which drives adrenal cortisol.
questions.x: The HPA axis runs top-down: the hypothalamus releases CRH into portal blood, CRH stimulates corticotrophs in the anterior pituitary to release ACTH, and ACTH stimulates the zona fasciculata to secrete cortisol. Cortisol then feeds back negatively on both the hypothalamus and pituitary. Aldosterone is controlled mainly by angiotensin II and K⁺, not by this axis.

questions.q: A patient has low cortisol, very high ACTH and darkened skin. Which diagnosis best fits?
o: Primary adrenal insufficiency
Correct: the adrenal fails, so lost feedback raises ACTH; POMC-derived MSH darkens skin.
Secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary failure
Pituitary failure would cause low ACTH.
Cushing disease from a pituitary adenoma
Cushing disease causes high cortisol.
Exogenous steroid use
Exogenous steroids suppress ACTH.
questions.x: In primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), the adrenal cortex itself fails, so cortisol is low and negative feedback is lost; the pituitary responds with very high ACTH. ACTH comes from the precursor POMC, which also yields MSH, so high production darkens the skin. In secondary insufficiency, the pituitary is the problem, so ACTH is low and skin is not darkened.

questions.q: A patient with high cortisol and high ACTH is given high-dose dexamethasone. Cortisol falls substantially. What is the most likely source of excess ACTH?
o: An ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor in the lung
Ectopic sources usually do not suppress with dexamethasone.
A pituitary adenoma
Correct: pituitary adenomas usually retain partial feedback sensitivity to high-dose dexamethasone.
An adrenal tumor secreting cortisol
Adrenal tumors cause low ACTH.
Primary adrenal insufficiency
That causes low cortisol.
questions.x: Dexamethasone is a potent synthetic glucocorticoid that suppresses ACTH through negative feedback. Pituitary adenomas are only partly resistant to feedback, so a high dose still lowers their ACTH and therefore cortisol. Ectopic ACTH tumors usually ignore glucocorticoid feedback, and adrenal tumors already have suppressed ACTH, so neither shows this suppression.

questions.q: A patient has fatigue, cold intolerance, low T₄ and high TSH. Where is the defect most likely?
o: In the thyroid gland
Correct: primary hypothyroidism; the pituitary responds to low T₄ by raising TSH.
In the anterior pituitary
Pituitary failure would cause low TSH.
In the hypothalamus
Hypothalamic failure would cause low TRH and low TSH.
In the adrenal cortex
Adrenal problems do not produce this thyroid pattern.
questions.x: When the thyroid fails (primary hypothyroidism, often Hashimoto thyroiditis), T₄ falls and negative feedback weakens, so the normal pituitary raises TSH. Low hormone with high TSH points to the gland itself. If the pituitary or hypothalamus were the problem, TSH would be low or inappropriately normal along with the low T₄.

questions.q: A patient has low T₄ and low TSH. Injection of TRH produces no rise in TSH. Where is the defect?
o: Hypothalamus
A hypothalamic defect would show a rise in TSH after TRH is given.
Thyroid gland
A thyroid defect would raise TSH.
Anterior pituitary
Correct: the pituitary cannot respond to TRH, so the problem is secondary.
Peripheral tissues lacking T₃ receptors
Resistance would raise both T₄ and TSH.
questions.note: A stimulation test locates the defect at the level that fails to respond.
questions.x: Low T₄ with low TSH means the problem is above the thyroid. Giving TRH tests the pituitary: if TSH rises, the pituitary works and the hypothalamus is failing to make TRH; if TSH does not rise, the pituitary itself is defective. Here there is no response, so the defect is in the anterior pituitary (secondary hypothyroidism).

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of negative feedback?
o: Oxytocin release during labor strengthens contractions, which release more oxytocin
That is positive feedback.
Rising blood glucose triggers insulin release, which lowers blood glucose
Correct: the response opposes the original change.
Clotting factors activate more clotting factors
That is positive feedback.
High estrogen before ovulation increases LH secretion
That is positive feedback.
questions.x: In negative feedback, the response counteracts the original change, returning a variable toward its set point. A rise in glucose triggers insulin release, which lowers glucose and so reduces the stimulus for more insulin. The other examples, oxytocin in labor, clotting cascades and the estrogen-driven LH surge, all amplify the stimulus and are positive feedback.

questions.q: Why are most hormonal control systems based on negative rather than positive feedback?
o: Positive feedback is impossible in the endocrine system
Positive feedback does occur, e.g., the LH surge.
Negative feedback always increases hormone secretion
Negative feedback reduces secretion when levels rise.
Positive feedback is used only by the nervous system
Positive feedback occurs in endocrine examples too.
Negative feedback keeps variables near a set point, whereas positive feedback drives them further from it
Correct: homeostasis requires opposing deviations.
questions.x: Homeostasis requires keeping variables such as glucose, Ca²⁺ and cortisol within narrow limits, and negative feedback does this by opposing any deviation. Positive feedback amplifies deviations, so it is used only for processes that must run to completion, like ovulation, childbirth and clotting. Positive feedback does exist in the endocrine system, so it is not impossible.

questions.q: A male athlete uses high doses of anabolic steroids for a year. What changes in his testes are expected?
o: Shrinkage and reduced sperm production due to suppressed LH and FSH
Correct: exogenous androgens feed back to lower GnRH, LH and FSH.
Enlargement due to increased LH
LH falls, not rises.
Increased sperm production due to more testosterone
Intratesticular testosterone falls when LH is suppressed.
No change because the testes ignore feedback
The testes depend on gonadotropins.
questions.x: Exogenous androgens are sensed by the hypothalamus and pituitary as high testosterone, so GnRH, LH and FSH fall. Without LH, Leydig cells stop making testosterone, so testosterone inside the testes drops even though blood androgen is high. Without FSH and local testosterone, spermatogenesis falls and the testes shrink. High blood testosterone does not substitute for intratesticular androgen.

questions.q: GnRH is normally released in pulses. If a long-acting GnRH analog is given continuously, LH and FSH eventually fall. Why?
o: GnRH is converted into testosterone
GnRH is a peptide and is not converted to steroids.
Continuous stimulation downregulates and desensitizes pituitary GnRH receptors
Correct: the pituitary needs pulsatile signals to keep responding.
Continuous GnRH stimulates inhibin release from the pituitary
Inhibin comes from the gonads.
The analog blocks LH synthesis genes in the gonads
LH is made in the pituitary.
questions.note: Pulses stimulate; constant exposure suppresses.
questions.x: Pituitary gonadotrophs respond to GnRH only when it arrives in pulses. Continuous exposure to a long-acting analog first causes a brief flare of LH and FSH, then desensitizes and downregulates GnRH receptors, so gonadotropin secretion falls. This is used clinically to suppress sex steroids, for example in prostate cancer. Inhibin comes from the gonads, not the pituitary.

questions.q: What hormone pattern is expected after an overnight fast?
o: High insulin and low glucagon
That follows a carbohydrate meal.
High insulin and high glucagon
These usually change in opposite directions with glucose.
Low insulin and high glucagon
Correct: this pattern mobilizes stored fuels.
Low insulin and low glucagon
Glucagon rises during fasting.
questions.x: During an overnight fast, blood glucose drifts down, so β cells secrete less insulin and α cells secrete more glucagon. The low insulin to glucagon ratio drives glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and lipolysis to supply fuel. High insulin and low glucagon is the fed-state pattern, the opposite of what fasting produces.

questions.q: Thirty minutes after a carbohydrate-rich meal, which response is expected?
o: Glucagon rises, promoting glycogenolysis
Glucagon falls after a carbohydrate meal.
Cortisol rises sharply to store glucose
Cortisol raises, not stores, glucose.
Epinephrine rises to promote fat storage
Epinephrine mobilizes fuel.
Insulin rises, promoting glycogen synthesis in liver and muscle
Correct: insulin promotes glucose storage.
questions.x: After a carbohydrate meal, rising blood glucose stimulates β cells to release insulin and suppresses glucagon. Insulin promotes glucose uptake into muscle and fat via GLUT4 and activates glycogen synthase in liver and muscle, storing the excess. Glucagon, epinephrine and cortisol are counter-regulatory hormones that raise glucose, so they do not rise in the fed state.

questions.q: After losing 1 liter of blood, which combined response helps restore blood pressure?
o: Decreased sympathetic activity and increased ANP
ANP lowers volume, and less sympathetic output lowers pressure.
Decreased renin and decreased ADH
