Both would worsen the loss of pressure.
Increased sympathetic activity, ADH and aldosterone
Correct: these constrict vessels and increase water and Na⁺ retention.
Increased parasympathetic activity and lower heart rate
This would decrease cardiac output.
questions.x: Hemorrhage lowers blood pressure, which reduces baroreceptor firing and triggers increased sympathetic activity (faster heart, stronger contraction, vasoconstriction). Reduced renal perfusion raises renin, leading to angiotensin II and aldosterone, which retain Na⁺ and water, and ADH is released to retain water and constrict vessels. ANP falls because the atria are less stretched.

questions.q: A hiker becomes dehydrated, and plasma osmolarity rises. Which sequence follows?
o: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors stimulate ADH release, and the kidney retains water
Correct: ADH increases collecting-duct water reabsorption.
Atrial cells release ANP, and the kidney excretes more Na⁺
ANP responds to stretch, not high osmolarity.
The adrenal medulla releases aldosterone
Aldosterone comes from the cortex and does not primarily respond to osmolarity.
The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin, and urine becomes dilute
Oxytocin does not regulate water reabsorption here.
questions.x: Dehydration raises plasma osmolarity, which shrinks hypothalamic osmoreceptors. They stimulate thirst and ADH release from the posterior pituitary. ADH causes aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct cells, so more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated, lowering plasma osmolarity. Aldosterone responds mainly to angiotensin II and K⁺ and comes from the adrenal cortex, not the medulla.

questions.q: In a cold environment, which combination of responses helps raise body temperature?
o: Skin vasodilation and sweating
These are heat-loss responses.
Decreased sympathetic activity and lower metabolic rate
These would reduce heat production.
Increased ADH and reduced thyroid hormone
ADH does not regulate heat production.
Skin vasoconstriction, shivering and increased TRH–TSH–thyroid hormone output
Correct: these conserve heat and increase heat production.
questions.x: In the cold, the hypothalamus triggers heat conservation and heat production. Sympathetic vasoconstriction in the skin reduces heat loss, shivering generates heat through muscle activity, and the TRH–TSH–thyroid hormone axis and catecholamines raise metabolic rate over time. Sweating and vasodilation are heat-loss responses used in warm conditions.

questions.q: During sudden stress, the sympathetic system acts within seconds, while the HPA axis raises cortisol over minutes. What best explains the difference?
o: Cortisol is released by neurons that conduct slowly
Cortisol is released by adrenal cortex cells.
Neural signals use fast action potentials, while hormones depend on synthesis, secretion and transport
Correct: endocrine responses are slower but longer lasting.
The sympathetic system uses steroid hormones
Sympathetic neurons use ACh and norepinephrine.
The HPA axis works only during sleep
It works at all times, with a daily rhythm.
questions.x: The nervous system transmits signals by action potentials and synaptic release, which take milliseconds, and sympathetic nerves and adrenal epinephrine act within seconds. The HPA axis needs CRH release, ACTH secretion, transport in blood, and synthesis of cortisol, which is not stored, so cortisol rises over minutes. Endocrine responses are slower but last longer.

questions.q: Compared with endocrine signaling, nervous signaling is generally:
o: Slower, longer-lasting and widely distributed
That describes endocrine signaling.
Faster, shorter-lasting and more precisely targeted
Correct: neurons send signals to specific cells within milliseconds.
Carried only by blood
Neurons signal through synapses.
Limited to steroid messengers
Neurons use many transmitter types.
questions.x: Neurons deliver signals via action potentials to specific target cells at synapses, so nervous signaling is fast (milliseconds), brief and precisely targeted. Hormones travel through the blood to every tissue with matching receptors, so endocrine signaling is slower, longer-lasting and more widespread. The first choice describes endocrine, not nervous, signaling.

questions.q: Which cells best exemplify neuroendocrine integration?
o: Pancreatic acinar cells secreting enzymes into ducts
Those are exocrine cells.
Skeletal muscle fibers releasing lactate
Lactate is a metabolite, not a neurohormone.
Red blood cells carrying O₂
Red cells do not secrete hormones.
Hypothalamic neurons that release ADH into the blood
Correct: these neurons fire action potentials and secrete hormone.
questions.x: Neuroendocrine cells are neurons that release hormones into the blood instead of, or in addition to, transmitters at synapses. Hypothalamic neurons that make ADH fire action potentials and release the hormone from posterior pituitary terminals into the circulation, linking the nervous and endocrine systems. Pancreatic acinar cells secrete into ducts, which makes them exocrine.

questions.q: A researcher removes the pancreas from a dog, and blood glucose rises sharply. Which control would best show that the rise is due to loss of a pancreatic hormone, not to surgical stress?
o: A sham operation with the same surgery but without removing the pancreas
Correct: it isolates the effect of removing the organ.
Removing the pancreas from a second dog
Repeating the treatment does not control for surgery.
Measuring glucose in the same dog a week later
This does not separate surgery from pancreas loss.
Giving the dog extra glucose
That adds a new variable.
questions.x: A good control differs from the experimental group in only the variable being tested. A sham operation exposes an animal to the same anesthesia, incision and stress but leaves the pancreas in place, so any difference in glucose can be attributed to the missing organ. Repeating the removal in another dog adds replication but does not control for surgical stress.

questions.q: A hormone's effect is blocked by an antibody that cannot cross membranes but binds the hormone's receptor. What does this suggest?
o: The receptor is in the nucleus
An impermeant antibody could not reach nuclear receptors.
The hormone is a steroid that acts on DNA
Steroid receptors are typically intracellular.
The receptor is on the cell surface
Correct: an impermeant antibody can reach only extracellular receptor sites.
The hormone acts without any receptor
Blocking with a receptor antibody shows a receptor is needed.
questions.x: An antibody is a large protein that cannot cross the plasma membrane, so it can bind only molecules exposed on the cell surface. If an impermeant antibody against the receptor blocks the hormone's effect, the receptor must be on the cell surface, as for peptide and catecholamine hormones. Steroid and thyroid hormone receptors are intracellular and would be out of reach.

questions.q: In cultured cells, a hormone increases enzyme levels after 6 hours. Pretreatment with actinomycin D, a transcription inhibitor, blocks this increase. What is the most likely conclusion?
o: The hormone acts only by activating existing enzymes
That would not require transcription.
Actinomycin D destroys the hormone in the medium
The drug inhibits RNA polymerase activity, not the hormone.
The hormone must be a catecholamine
Catecholamines act quickly through surface receptors.
The hormone acts by changing gene transcription
Correct: blocking mRNA synthesis prevented the response.
questions.x: Actinomycin D blocks transcription by binding DNA and preventing RNA polymerase from making mRNA. If it prevents a hormone-induced increase in enzyme levels, the hormone must work by increasing transcription of the enzyme's gene, as steroid and thyroid hormones do. A hormone that only activated existing enzymes would act even when transcription is blocked.

questions.q: A patient has high blood Ca²⁺, low phosphate and high PTH. Which diagnosis fits best?
o: Hypoparathyroidism
That would cause low Ca²⁺ and low PTH.
Vitamin D deficiency
That would cause low or normal Ca²⁺.
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Correct: excess PTH raises Ca²⁺ and increases phosphate excretion.
Excess calcitonin
Calcitonin would tend to lower Ca²⁺.
questions.x: In primary hyperparathyroidism, usually a parathyroid adenoma, PTH is secreted without regard to blood Ca²⁺. Excess PTH raises Ca²⁺ by increasing bone resorption, renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption and calcitriol synthesis, while also increasing renal phosphate excretion, so phosphate falls. High Ca²⁺ together with high PTH is the giveaway, since normal glands would suppress PTH.

questions.q: A patient has high blood Ca²⁺ and low PTH. What does the low PTH indicate?
o: The parathyroid glands are the cause of the high Ca²⁺
PTH would then be high.
The parathyroids are responding normally, so the excess Ca²⁺ comes from another source
Correct: high Ca²⁺ suppresses PTH; consider excess vitamin D or tumor-related causes.
The kidney is failing to activate vitamin D
That would cause low Ca²⁺.
The thyroid is secreting too much calcitonin
Calcitonin lowers Ca²⁺.
questions.x: Normal parathyroid glands sense high blood Ca²⁺ through Ca²⁺-sensing receptors and reduce PTH secretion. Low PTH with hypercalcemia means the glands are behaving appropriately and the Ca²⁺ comes from elsewhere, such as excess vitamin D or a tumor secreting PTH-related peptide. If the parathyroids were the cause, PTH would be high despite high Ca²⁺.

questions.q: In chronic kidney disease, PTH levels often rise. What is the main cause?
o: Reduced calcitriol production and phosphate retention lower blood Ca²⁺, which stimulates PTH
Correct: this is secondary hyperparathyroidism.
A parathyroid tumor develops in all patients
This is a feedback response, not a tumor.
The kidney secretes PTH when damaged
The kidney does not secrete PTH.
High blood Ca²⁺ stimulates PTH
High Ca²⁺ suppresses PTH.
questions.x: Failing kidneys make less calcitriol and excrete less phosphate. Less calcitriol reduces intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption, and retained phosphate binds Ca²⁺, so blood Ca²⁺ falls. Low Ca²⁺ appropriately stimulates the parathyroids to secrete more PTH, a compensatory state called secondary hyperparathyroidism. High Ca²⁺ would instead suppress PTH.

questions.q: A day after thyroid surgery, a patient has tingling around the mouth and muscle spasms. What is the most likely cause?
o: Loss of calcitonin, causing hypercalcemia
Loss of calcitonin has little effect on blood Ca²⁺.
Accidental removal of the parathyroid glands, causing hypocalcemia
Correct: low Ca²⁺ increases neuronal excitability.
Excess T₄ released during surgery
This would not explain tetany.
Damage to the adrenal cortex
The adrenals are not near the thyroid.
questions.x: The parathyroid glands sit on the back of the thyroid and can be removed or damaged during thyroid surgery. Loss of PTH causes hypocalcemia, and low extracellular Ca²⁺ makes nerve and muscle membranes more excitable, causing perioral tingling and tetany. Losing calcitonin has little effect on blood Ca²⁺ in adults, which rules out the hypercalcemia choice.

questions.q: A patient with diabetes injects too much insulin and becomes hypoglycemic. Which counter-regulatory responses are expected first?
o: Increased glucagon and epinephrine
Correct: these quickly raise blood glucose.
Increased insulin and somatostatin
These would worsen hypoglycemia.
Decreased glucagon and cortisol
These hormones increase.
Increased ADH and ANP
These are fluid-balance hormones.
questions.x: When blood glucose falls, α cells rapidly increase glucagon, and the sympathetic system and adrenal medulla release epinephrine; both raise glucose within minutes via hepatic glycogenolysis. Cortisol and GH help over hours. Insulin secretion falls. Epinephrine also causes warning signs such as sweating, tremor and a racing heart, which help people recognize hypoglycemia.

questions.q: An adrenal tumor secretes excess aldosterone. Which pattern is expected?
o: Hypotension, high K⁺ and high renin
That fits aldosterone deficiency.
Hypertension, high K⁺ and high renin
K⁺ falls and renin is suppressed.
Normal pressure, low Na⁺ and high renin
Aldosterone retains Na⁺ and suppresses renin.
Hypertension, low K⁺ and low renin
Correct: Na⁺ retention raises pressure, suppressing renin, while K⁺ loss increases.
questions.x: Excess aldosterone (primary hyperaldosteronism) increases Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion in the collecting duct. Na⁺ and water retention raise blood volume and pressure, which suppresses renin through renal baroreceptors and negative feedback. K⁺ loss causes hypokalemia. High renin would point to a secondary cause, such as renal artery narrowing, rather than an adrenal tumor.

questions.q: A patient has a tumor that secretes ADH regardless of plasma osmolarity. Which finding is expected?
o: High plasma Na⁺ with dilute urine
That fits diabetes insipidus.
Low plasma Na⁺ with very dilute urine
Excess ADH makes urine concentrated.
Low plasma Na⁺ with inappropriately concentrated urine
Correct: excess water retention dilutes plasma Na⁺.
High plasma K⁺ and low blood pressure
Those fit aldosterone deficiency.
questions.x: In SIADH, ADH is secreted regardless of osmolarity, so the collecting duct keeps reabsorbing water even when plasma is already dilute. Retained free water dilutes plasma Na⁺ (hyponatremia), while urine stays inappropriately concentrated. Total body Na⁺ is not the problem; excess water is. High Na⁺ with dilute urine is the opposite pattern, seen in diabetes insipidus.

questions.q: Why does drinking alcohol increase urine output?
o: Alcohol stimulates ADH release
That would reduce urine output.
Alcohol increases aldosterone secretion
Aldosterone increases Na⁺ and water retention.
Alcohol blocks ANP
Blocking ANP would reduce Na⁺ and water excretion.
Alcohol inhibits ADH release from the posterior pituitary
Correct: less ADH means fewer aquaporins and more dilute urine.
questions.x: Ethanol suppresses ADH release from the posterior pituitary. With less ADH, collecting-duct cells remove aquaporin-2 channels from their luminal membrane, so less water is reabsorbed and large volumes of dilute urine are produced. This diuresis contributes to dehydration after drinking. If alcohol stimulated ADH instead, urine output would fall.

questions.q: A radiolabeled hormone has a plasma half-life of 10 minutes. About what fraction remains in the blood 30 minutes after a single injection?
o: Elimination is exponential, not linear.
Correct: three half-lives give (1/2)³ = 1/8.
That is two half-lives, or 20 minutes.
Exponential decay never instantly reaches zero.
questions.x: Hormone clearance usually follows first-order kinetics: a constant fraction is removed per unit time, so the amount halves every half-life. Thirty minutes is three 10-minute half-lives: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5%. A linear decline would give the wrong answer, since the absolute amount removed shrinks as the concentration falls.

questions.q: Increasing doses of a hormone increase a target-cell response until the response plateaus. Further doses produce no additional effect. What is the best explanation?
o: The hormone is degraded only at high doses
Faster degradation would not create a sharp ceiling; a fixed number of receptors does.
The hormone becomes inhibitory at low doses
The response increases at low doses.
The hormone's receptors are saturated
Correct: once receptors are fully occupied, more hormone cannot increase signaling.
The response is not receptor-mediated
Saturation suggests a limited number of receptors.
questions.x: Hormone responses depend on binding to a finite number of receptors. At low doses, more hormone occupies more receptors and the response rises, but once nearly all receptors are bound, extra hormone has nothing to bind and the response plateaus. This saturation is evidence for a limited number of specific receptors, not against receptor mediation.

questions.q: Chronically high insulin levels can reduce the number of insulin receptors on target cells. What is this process called?
o: Downregulation
Correct: cells decrease receptor number after prolonged stimulation.
Upregulation
Upregulation increases receptor number.
Positive feedback
Positive feedback amplifies a signal.
Permissiveness
Permissiveness means one hormone enables another's action.
questions.x: Downregulation is a decrease in receptor number or responsiveness after prolonged high exposure to a hormone, often by internalizing and degrading receptors. It protects cells from overstimulation and helps explain reduced insulin responsiveness in hyperinsulinemic states. Upregulation is the opposite, an increase in receptors when hormone levels are low.

questions.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose, and glucagon raises it. Their relationship is best described as:
o: Synergistic
Synergistic hormones enhance each other's effects.
Permissive
Permissive action allows another hormone to act.
Antagonistic
Correct: they produce opposite effects on the same variable.
Tropic
Tropic hormones stimulate another endocrine gland.
questions.x: Antagonistic hormones have opposite effects on the same variable. Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage, while glucagon raises it by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, and their balance sets glucose. Synergistic hormones instead produce a combined effect greater than either alone, and permissive hormones enable another hormone's action.

questions.q: Light entering the eyes at night lowers melatonin secretion. Which pathway explains this?
o: Retina → occipital cortex → adrenal medulla
The adrenal medulla does not secrete melatonin.
Retina → posterior pituitary → pineal gland
The posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin.
Skin → spinal cord → thymus
The thymus is not the melatonin source.
Retina → suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus → pineal gland
Correct: light signals reduce pineal melatonin output.
questions.x: Light activates melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells that project via the retinohypothalamic tract to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the master circadian clock. The SCN, via a multisynaptic sympathetic route, controls the pineal gland, so light at night suppresses melatonin. The occipital cortex processes visual images but does not mediate this circadian pathway.

questions.q: Puberty begins when a hypothalamic signal increases. Which hormone rises first?
o: GnRH
Correct: increased pulsatile GnRH drives LH and FSH, then sex steroids.
Testosterone or estrogen
These rise after the pituitary is stimulated.
LH and FSH
These rise after GnRH increases.
Prolactin
Prolactin is not the main trigger of puberty.
questions.x: Puberty starts when the hypothalamus increases pulsatile GnRH secretion. GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH, which then stimulate the gonads to produce testosterone or estrogen and gametes. Because of this cascade, sex steroids and gonadotropins rise only after GnRH increases. Following the hierarchy from top to bottom identifies the first signal.

questions.q: After menopause, FSH and LH levels rise markedly. Why?
o: The pituitary develops tumors in all women
This is a normal feedback change.
The ovaries produce little estrogen and inhibin, removing negative feedback on the pituitary
Correct: loss of feedback raises gonadotropins.
Estrogen levels become very high
Estrogen falls after menopause.
GnRH secretion stops completely
GnRH continues and is less inhibited.
questions.x: After menopause, the ovaries run out of follicles, so estrogen and inhibin production falls sharply. Without their negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, GnRH pulses are less inhibited and LH and FSH rise markedly, with FSH rising most. Elevated FSH is a laboratory sign of menopause. Estrogen falls, so high estrogen cannot explain the change.

questions.q: Why do only certain tissues respond to a circulating hormone?
o: Only those tissues express the specific receptor
Correct: receptor expression determines target cells.
The hormone reaches only those tissues
Circulating hormones reach nearly all tissues.
Non-target tissues destroy the hormone instantly
Non-target tissues lack receptors.
Only target tissues have blood vessels
Most tissues are vascularized.
questions.x: Hormones in the blood reach essentially every tissue, but only cells that express the specific receptor can respond. Receptor expression, controlled by each cell's gene expression program, therefore defines a hormone's target tissues. For example, TSH reaches all cells, but only thyroid follicular cells have TSH receptors. Delivery is not the limiting factor.

questions.q: Destroying the ventromedial hypothalamus in rats causes overeating, while destroying the lateral hypothalamus causes refusal to eat. What do these results suggest?
o: Both regions promote hunger
Then both lesions would reduce eating.
The lateral region promotes satiety
Then destroying it would increase eating.
The ventromedial region promotes satiety and the lateral region promotes hunger
Correct: losing each center removes its function.
The hypothalamus has no role in feeding
Both lesions changed feeding.
questions.x: Lesion studies infer a region's function from what is lost. Destroying the ventromedial hypothalamus produces overeating, so it normally promotes satiety; destroying the lateral hypothalamus abolishes eating, so it normally promotes hunger. If both regions promoted hunger, both lesions would reduce eating, which contradicts the ventromedial result.

questions.q: During exercise, sympathetic activity inhibits insulin secretion. What advantage does this provide?
o: It causes glucose to be stored in fat
That would reduce available fuel.
It helps keep blood glucose available as fuel
Correct: lower insulin favors glucose release and limits storage.
It increases glucose uptake by the brain
Brain uptake is mostly insulin-independent.
It stimulates protein synthesis in muscle
This is not the main advantage during exercise.
questions.x: During exercise, muscle contraction itself increases glucose uptake through insulin-independent GLUT4 translocation, so insulin is not needed for working muscle. Sympathetic α2 inhibition of β cells lowers insulin, which allows the liver to release glucose and adipose tissue to release fatty acids, keeping fuel available in the blood. High insulin would push glucose into storage instead.

questions.q: An industrial chemical enters cells and binds estrogen receptors, causing estrogen-like effects. Where does it most likely act?
o: On adrenergic receptors in the plasma membrane
These bind catecholamines.
On insulin receptor tyrosine kinases
These bind insulin.
On voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
These generate action potentials.
On intracellular estrogen receptors that alter gene expression
Correct: classic estrogen receptors are intracellular transcription factors.
questions.x: Estrogen is a steroid whose classic receptors are intracellular; once bound, they act as transcription factors that bind estrogen response elements and change gene expression. A lipophilic chemical that enters cells and binds these receptors can mimic estrogen as an endocrine disruptor. Adrenergic receptors and insulin receptor tyrosine kinases bind entirely different ligands.

questions.q: Epinephrine stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase in fat cells, while insulin inhibits it. What is the effect of epinephrine?
o: Increased breakdown of triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol
Correct: activating the lipase releases fatty acids for fuel.
Increased fat storage
Insulin promotes fat storage.
Increased glycogen synthesis in fat cells
This does not describe lipase activation.
Increased ketone excretion by the kidney
Ketones are made by hepatic fatty-acid oxidation; the lipase acts in fat cells to release fatty acids.
questions.x: Hormone-sensitive lipase hydrolyzes stored triglycerides in adipocytes into free fatty acids and glycerol. Epinephrine activates it through β-adrenergic receptors, cAMP and protein kinase A, releasing fatty acids for fuel during stress or exercise. Insulin inhibits the lipase and promotes fat storage, so increased storage is the opposite of epinephrine's effect.

questions.q: A newborn with untreated congenital hypothyroidism is at risk for intellectual disability. Why?
o: Thyroid hormone is a neurotransmitter
Thyroid hormone is not a classic neurotransmitter.
Thyroid hormone is required for normal brain development
Correct: early deficiency impairs neural growth and myelination.
Low thyroid hormone causes too much myelin
Deficiency impairs myelination.
Thyroid hormone controls blood–brain barrier formation only
Thyroid hormone affects neuronal growth, migration and myelination broadly, not just the barrier.
questions.x: Thyroid hormone is essential for brain development during fetal life and early infancy, promoting neuronal growth, synapse formation and myelination. Deficiency during this window causes irreversible intellectual disability (congenital hypothyroidism), which is why newborns are screened and treated early. Thyroid hormone is not a classic neurotransmitter, and deficiency reduces rather than increases myelin.

questions.q: How do the immediate effects of ADH and aldosterone on body fluids differ?
o: ADH mainly retains Na⁺; aldosterone mainly retains water
The roles are reversed.
Both mainly increase water excretion
Both reduce urine output.
ADH mainly retains water and lowers osmolarity; aldosterone retains Na⁺ and water, increasing volume with little osmolarity change
Correct: aldosterone drives isotonic volume expansion.
Aldosterone lowers blood volume; ADH raises osmolarity
Aldosterone raises volume, and ADH lowers osmolarity.
questions.x: ADH increases collecting-duct permeability to water only, so it adds free water to the blood, lowering plasma osmolarity and Na⁺ concentration. Aldosterone increases Na⁺ reabsorption, and water follows osmotically, so it expands blood volume with little change in osmolarity. Thus ADH mainly controls osmolarity and aldosterone mainly controls volume.

questions.q: In a person with a normal daytime sleep–wake schedule, when is cortisol usually highest?
o: Late evening
Cortisol is usually low late in the evening.
Midnight
Cortisol is usually near its lowest early in sleep.
It is constant throughout the day
Cortisol follows a circadian rhythm.
Early morning
Correct: cortisol peaks around waking.
questions.x: Cortisol follows a circadian rhythm driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus through the HPA axis. ACTH and cortisol rise in the last hours of sleep and peak around waking, which helps mobilize fuel for the day; levels fall through the day and are lowest around midnight. Loss of this rhythm, such as high late-night cortisol, is a clue to Cushing syndrome.

questions.q: An XY individual has female external genitalia and high testosterone because androgen receptors do not work. What does this demonstrate?
o: High testosterone directly causes female development
Female external development occurs because androgen signaling is absent.
The individual lacks testes
Testes are present and make testosterone.
Hormone effects require functional receptors, even when hormone levels are high
Correct: target cells cannot respond without receptors.
Estrogen cannot be made in XY individuals
Some testosterone can be converted to estrogen.
questions.x: In androgen insensitivity syndrome, an XY individual has testes that produce testosterone (and anti-Müllerian hormone), but nonfunctional androgen receptors prevent tissues from responding. External genitalia therefore develop along the female pattern despite high testosterone. The key principle is that a hormone acts only through functional receptors, regardless of its concentration.

questions.q: When an infant suckles, sensory nerves signal the hypothalamus, causing oxytocin release and milk ejection. What does this illustrate?
o: A neuroendocrine reflex
Correct: a neural signal triggers hormone release.
A purely spinal reflex
The hypothalamus and pituitary are required.
Paracrine signaling
Oxytocin travels in blood to the breast.
Negative feedback
Milk ejection does not reduce the suckling stimulus.
questions.x: In the milk-ejection reflex, suckling stimulates nipple mechanoreceptors, whose sensory signals travel to the hypothalamus. Hypothalamic neurons then release oxytocin from the posterior pituitary into the blood, and oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells around the alveoli to eject milk. A neural input causing hormone secretion is a neuroendocrine reflex, not a purely spinal reflex.

questions.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number of β-adrenergic receptors on heart cells, so the same epinephrine level produces a larger response. This is an example of:
o: An antagonistic effect
Antagonism means opposite effects on the same variable.
Negative feedback
Negative feedback reduces hormone secretion.
A tropic effect
Tropic hormones stimulate secretion by another endocrine gland.
A permissive effect
Correct: one hormone enables or enhances the target response to another.
questions.x: A permissive effect occurs when one hormone enables or increases a tissue's response to another, often by increasing its receptors or signaling machinery. Thyroid hormone upregulates β-adrenergic receptors in the heart, so catecholamines produce a larger response, which is why hyperthyroid patients have tachycardia. Tropic hormones stimulate secretion by another gland, which is not occurring here.

questions.q: A healthy person takes a daily T₄ supplement in excess of need for several weeks. What happens to their TSH level?
o: It increases to stimulate the thyroid further
Higher thyroid hormone suppresses, not raises, TSH.
It decreases because T₄ and T₃ inhibit TRH and TSH secretion
Correct: negative feedback suppresses the axis.
It stays unchanged because supplements bypass feedback
Feedback senses circulating hormone from any source.
It rises because the thyroid gland shrinks
Gland shrinkage follows low TSH, not the reverse.
questions.x: The hypothalamus and pituitary sense circulating thyroid hormone regardless of its source. Excess T₄ (converted to T₃ in the pituitary) suppresses TRH and TSH secretion through negative feedback, so TSH falls. With prolonged TSH suppression, the person's own thyroid becomes less active and may shrink. Feedback is not bypassed just because the hormone is a supplement.

questions.q: In the lungs, where does gas exchange between air and blood actually take place?
o: Alveoli
Correct: thin alveolar walls lined by capillaries are the respiratory zone where O₂ and CO₂ diffuse.
Trachea
The trachea only conducts air; its thick wall and cartilage rings prevent exchange.
Primary bronchi
Bronchi are part of the conducting zone, which moves air but does not exchange gas.
Terminal bronchioles
Terminal bronchioles are the last conducting airways, just before the respiratory zone.
questions.note: Conducting zone moves air; respiratory zone (alveoli) exchanges it.
questions.x: Gas exchange needs a very thin barrier, a huge surface area and close contact with capillaries, which only the alveoli of the respiratory zone provide. Everything from the trachea down to the terminal bronchioles is the conducting zone: it warms, filters and moves air but its walls are too thick for diffusion. The terminal bronchiole is tempting because it is deep in the lung, but it is the last conducting airway.

questions.q: A premature infant produces too little pulmonary surfactant. Which consequence is most expected?
o: Lung compliance increases
Low surfactant makes lungs stiffer, so compliance decreases.
Alveoli tend to collapse at the end of expiration
Correct: without surfactant, high surface tension pulls small alveoli shut, causing atelectasis.
Arterial PO₂ rises
Collapsed alveoli cannot exchange gas, so PO₂ falls.
Airway smooth muscle relaxes
Surfactant acts on alveolar surface tension, not bronchial smooth muscle.
questions.note: Surfactant comes from type II pneumocytes and lowers surface tension.
questions.x: Surfactant from type II pneumocytes lowers alveolar surface tension. By the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r), small alveoli with high surface tension need high pressure to stay open, so without surfactant they collapse at end-expiration. The result is stiff lungs with lower, not higher, compliance and falling arterial PO₂, which is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.q: During a quiet inspiration, which pressure change draws air into the lungs?
o: Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure
Higher alveolar pressure would push air out; that happens during expiration.
Intrapleural pressure becomes positive
Positive intrapleural pressure occurs only in forced expiration and would compress the lungs.
Intrapleural pressure becomes more negative as the diaphragm contracts
Correct: thoracic volume rises, intrapleural and then alveolar pressure fall, so air flows in.
The internal intercostals contract to raise the ribs
Internal intercostals aid forced expiration; external intercostals raise the ribs.
questions.note: Air moves from high to low pressure; volume up means pressure down (Boyle).
questions.x: Inspiration is a negative-pressure process: the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarge the thorax, intrapleural pressure becomes more negative, the lungs expand and alveolar pressure drops below atmospheric (Boyle's law), so air flows in. Air always moves from high to low pressure, so alveolar pressure rising above atmospheric would push air out, which is expiration.

questions.q: What mainly drives quiet, resting expiration?
o: Active contraction of the diaphragm
Diaphragm contraction drives inspiration, not expiration.
Contraction of the abdominal muscles
Abdominal muscles are recruited only for forced expiration.
Active contraction of the external intercostals
External intercostals expand the chest during inspiration.
Passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall
Correct: the diaphragm relaxes and stretched elastic tissue recoils, raising alveolar pressure.
questions.note: Quiet expiration is passive; forced expiration is active.
questions.x: At rest, expiration needs no muscle work: the diaphragm simply relaxes and the stretched elastic tissue of the lungs and chest wall recoils, shrinking thoracic volume and raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric. Abdominal muscles and internal intercostals are recruited only for forced expiration, such as exercise or coughing, which is the trap in choice B.

questions.q: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond most directly to which change?
o: A fall in arterial PO₂
Low PO₂ is sensed mainly by peripheral carotid and aortic bodies.
A rise in plasma HCO₃⁻ crossing into the brain
HCO₃⁻ and H⁺ cross the blood-brain barrier poorly; CO₂ crosses freely.
A fall in cerebrospinal fluid pH caused by rising arterial CO₂
Correct: CO₂ crosses the blood-brain barrier and forms H⁺ in CSF, which these receptors sense.
A fall in hemoglobin concentration
Anemia does not change PO₂ or CO₂, so chemoreceptors are not stimulated.
questions.note: Minute-to-minute breathing is driven mostly by CO₂, not O₂.
questions.x: Central chemoreceptors sit behind the blood-brain barrier and sense H⁺ in cerebrospinal fluid. CO₂ crosses the barrier freely and is hydrated to H₂CO₃, releasing H⁺, so arterial PCO₂ is the main minute-to-minute driver of breathing. Low arterial PO₂ is tempting but is detected by the peripheral carotid and aortic bodies, not the medulla.

questions.q: A climber who reaches 5,000 m begins breathing faster within minutes. Which receptors start this response?
o: Carotid and aortic bodies sensing low arterial PO₂
Correct: peripheral chemoreceptors fire strongly once arterial PO₂ falls toward about 60 mmHg.
Central chemoreceptors sensing high CSF CO₂
At altitude CO₂ is not elevated; hyperventilation actually lowers it.
Baroreceptors sensing high blood pressure
Baroreceptors regulate blood pressure, not ventilation in hypoxia.
Pulmonary stretch receptors sensing lung inflation
Stretch receptors limit inflation (Hering-Breuer); they do not detect hypoxia.
questions.note: Hypoxic drive comes from peripheral chemoreceptors.
questions.x: At altitude the inspired PO₂ falls, so arterial PO₂ falls; once it drops toward about 60 mmHg, the carotid and aortic bodies fire strongly and drive ventilation within minutes. Central chemoreceptors cannot start this response because CO₂ is not elevated; the extra breathing actually blows CO₂ off, which tends to restrain the central drive.

questions.q: After several days at high altitude, a climber's persistent hyperventilation is partly compensated by the kidneys. What do they do?
o: Retain more HCO₃⁻ to raise blood pH
Retaining base would worsen the alkalosis.
Secrete more H⁺ into the urine
More H⁺ excretion would make the blood even more alkaline.
Increase NH₄⁺ excretion
Ammonium excretion is the compensation for acidosis, not alkalosis.
Excrete more HCO₃⁻ to lower blood pH toward normal
Correct: hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, so kidneys dump bicarbonate.
questions.note: Respiratory problem → renal compensation, which takes days.
questions.x: Hyperventilation lowers PCO₂ and causes respiratory alkalosis. Over several days the kidneys compensate by excreting more HCO₃⁻ and secreting less H⁺, which brings pH back toward normal. Retaining bicarbonate or excreting more H⁺ or NH₄⁺ are responses to acidosis and would make the alkalosis worse.

questions.q: In what form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
o: Dissolved as CO₂ gas in plasma
Only about 7 to 10% travels dissolved.
As bicarbonate ion in the plasma
Correct: about 70% of CO₂ is converted by carbonic anhydrase to HCO₃⁻ carried in plasma.
Bound to the heme iron of hemoglobin
CO₂ binds globin amino groups (carbamino), not heme iron, and that is only about 20%.
As carbonic acid in red blood cells
H₂CO₃ dissociates almost immediately; little exists as carbonic acid.
questions.x: In red cells carbonic anhydrase converts CO₂ + H₂O to H₂CO₃, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; the bicarbonate then moves into plasma, carrying about 70% of total CO₂. About 20% rides as carbamino groups on globin and only 7 to 10% is dissolved. Hemoglobin binding is tempting, but CO₂ binds amino groups on the protein, not the heme iron.

questions.q: As blood passes through systemic capillaries, HCO₃⁻ leaves red blood cells. Which ion moves in the opposite direction to keep the cells electrically neutral?
o: Na⁺ leaves the red blood cell
The exchanger swaps anions; Na⁺ is handled by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.
Cl⁻ enters the red blood cell
Correct: the chloride shift uses an anion exchanger, swapping HCO₃⁻ out for Cl⁻ in.
K⁺ enters the red blood cell
K⁺ movement is not coupled to bicarbonate transport.
H⁺ leaves the red blood cell
H⁺ stays inside, where deoxyhemoglobin buffers it.
questions.note: Chloride shift: HCO₃⁻ out, Cl⁻ in (reversed in the lungs).
questions.x: Bicarbonate made in red cells is exported to plasma through band 3, an anion exchanger that brings Cl⁻ in for every HCO₃⁻ out, preserving electrical neutrality: the chloride shift. In the lungs the exchange reverses. H⁺ leaving is tempting, but H⁺ stays inside and is buffered by deoxyhemoglobin, which is why the exchange must involve another anion.

questions.q: A patient has carbon monoxide poisoning. Which combination of findings is expected?
o: Low arterial PO₂ and low O₂ content
Lung gas exchange is intact, so PO₂ stays normal.
Normal O₂ content with a right-shifted curve
CO lowers content and shifts the curve left, holding remaining O₂ more tightly.
High arterial PO₂ and high O₂ content
CO does not raise PO₂, and it decreases content.
Normal arterial PO₂ but reduced arterial O₂ content
Correct: CO occupies heme sites, so less O₂ is bound even though dissolved O₂ (PO₂) is normal.
questions.note: PO₂ reflects dissolved O₂, not how much is bound to hemoglobin.
questions.x: PO₂ measures only dissolved O₂, which depends on alveolar gas and lung function, both normal in CO poisoning. CO binds heme with far higher affinity than O₂, occupying sites so O₂ content falls, and it shifts the remaining curve left so O₂ unloads poorly. Low PO₂ is the tempting trap, but that pattern points to lung disease or hypoventilation, not CO.

questions.q: Fetal hemoglobin binds O₂ with higher affinity than adult hemoglobin. Why is this useful?
o: It lets O₂ move from maternal to fetal blood in the placenta
Correct: at the same PO₂ fetal Hb is more saturated, so O₂ unloads from maternal Hb to fetal Hb.
It helps the fetus unload more O₂ to its own tissues
Higher affinity makes unloading harder, not easier.
It lets fetal blood carry more CO₂
CO₂ transport is unrelated to the higher O₂ affinity.
It allows the fetal lungs to absorb O₂ from amniotic fluid
Fetal lungs do not exchange gas; the placenta does.
questions.note: HbF curve is left-shifted (binds less 2,3-BPG).
questions.x: In the placenta, maternal and fetal blood face the same local PO₂. Because HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly, its dissociation curve is left-shifted, so at that PO₂ it is more saturated than maternal HbA and O₂ moves from mother to fetus. Higher affinity actually makes unloading to fetal tissues harder, not easier, which rules out choice B.

questions.q: A person has a tidal volume of 500 mL, anatomic dead space of 150 mL and a breathing rate of 12 breaths/min. What is the alveolar ventilation?
o: 1.8 L/min
That is dead-space ventilation (150 × 12), not alveolar ventilation.
4.2 L/min
Correct: (500 − 150) mL × 12/min = 4,200 mL/min.
6.0 L/min
That is total minute ventilation (500 × 12); dead space must be subtracted.
7.8 L/min
Dead space was added instead of subtracted.
questions.note: Alveolar ventilation = (VT − VD) × RR.
questions.x: The first part of each breath fills conducting airways that never exchange gas. Alveolar ventilation counts only air reaching alveoli: (VT − VD) × rate = (500 − 150) × 12 = 4,200 mL/min. Minute ventilation (6.0 L/min) is the tempting answer but ignores dead space, which is why slow deep breathing ventilates alveoli more efficiently than fast shallow breathing.

questions.q: Which lung volume cannot be measured by simple spirometry?
o: Tidal volume
Tidal breaths move air in and out of the spirometer, so VT is measurable.
Vital capacity
VC is the maximal exhaled volume after a maximal breath, which a spirometer records.
Inspiratory reserve volume
IRV is air inhaled beyond a normal breath, which passes through the spirometer.
Residual volume
Correct: air left after maximal exhalation never leaves the lungs, so a spirometer cannot record it.
questions.note: Any capacity containing RV (FRC, TLC) also needs other methods.
questions.x: A spirometer only records air that moves in and out of the mouth. Residual volume stays in the lungs even after maximal exhalation, so it, and any capacity that includes it (FRC and TLC), must be measured by helium dilution, nitrogen washout or body plethysmography. Tidal volume, IRV and vital capacity all pass through the spirometer.

questions.q: Emphysema destroys elastic fibers in alveolar walls. Which change most directly results?
o: Lower lung compliance with stiff, hard-to-inflate lungs
That describes fibrosis, a restrictive disease.
Decreased residual volume
Air trapping increases residual volume.
Higher lung compliance with difficulty exhaling fully
Correct: lungs inflate easily but lose recoil, so air is trapped and residual volume rises.
Increased surface area for gas exchange
Wall destruction merges alveoli and reduces exchange surface area.
questions.note: Obstructive (emphysema) vs restrictive (fibrosis): opposite compliance.
questions.x: Elastic fibers provide the recoil that drives passive expiration. Emphysema destroys them, so the lungs become easy to inflate (high compliance) but empty poorly, trapping air and raising residual volume and total lung capacity. Low compliance with stiff lungs is the tempting opposite, but that describes restrictive disease such as fibrosis.

questions.q: Cigarette smoke paralyzes the cilia lining the bronchi. Which defense is most directly impaired?
o: Production of surfactant by type II pneumocytes
Surfactant comes from alveolar cells, not ciliated airway cells.
Moving mucus and trapped particles up toward the pharynx
Correct: the mucociliary escalator depends on coordinated ciliary beating.
Diffusion of O₂ across the alveolar membrane
Cilia line conducting airways, not alveoli.
Secretion of mucus by goblet cells
Goblet cells still secrete mucus; it just is not cleared.
questions.x: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps inhaled particles, and ciliated epithelium beats it upward toward the pharynx to be swallowed or coughed out: the mucociliary escalator. When cilia are paralyzed, mucus is still made but not cleared, which is why smokers cough. Surfactant is tempting but comes from type II alveolar cells, which are not ciliated.

questions.q: Where is the basic rhythm of breathing generated?
o: Medulla oblongata
Correct: medullary respiratory centers generate the rhythm; the pons fine-tunes it.
Cerebral cortex
The cortex allows voluntary override but does not set the automatic rhythm.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement, not breathing rhythm.
Hypothalamus
The hypothalamus can influence breathing (e.g., fever) but does not generate the rhythm.
questions.x: Automatic breathing is generated by neuron groups in the medulla oblongata, with the pons modulating rate and pattern. The cerebral cortex can override breathing voluntarily, as when you hold your breath, but this control is limited; rising CO₂ eventually forces the medullary rhythm to resume.

questions.q: The nasal cavity has a rich capillary bed under a moist mucous membrane. What respiratory function does this mainly serve?
o: Warming and humidifying inspired air
Correct: warm blood and moist mucosa condition air before it reaches the delicate alveoli.
Absorbing O₂ into the blood
Gas exchange does not occur in the nasal cavity.
Producing surfactant
Surfactant is made in the alveoli.
Generating the breathing rhythm
Rhythm is set by the brainstem.
questions.x: The upper airway conditions air before it reaches alveoli: nasal hairs and mucus filter particles, while a dense capillary bed and moist mucosa warm inspired air to body temperature and saturate it with water vapor. This protects the alveolar surface from drying and cooling. No gas exchange happens in the nose because its epithelium is far too thick.

questions.q: Pulmonary fibrosis doubles the thickness of the alveolar-capillary membrane. According to Fick's law, the rate of O₂ diffusion will most nearly:
o: Double, because more tissue holds more O₂
Thicker barriers slow diffusion; they do not store O₂ usefully.
Halve, because diffusion is inversely proportional to thickness
Correct: rate ∝ area × ΔP / thickness, so doubling thickness halves the rate.
Stay the same, because the partial pressure gradient is unchanged
Thickness is a separate term in Fick's law.
Fall to one quarter, because diffusion depends on thickness squared
Rate depends on thickness to the first power in Fick's law.
questions.note: Fick: rate ∝ A·ΔP/T.
questions.x: Fick's law states that diffusion rate is proportional to surface area times partial pressure difference divided by membrane thickness. Thickness appears to the first power, so doubling it halves the diffusion rate, all else equal. The thickness-squared idea is tempting because diffusion time scales with distance squared, but Fick's rate expression uses thickness linearly.

questions.q: Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds more CO₂ and H⁺ than oxygenated hemoglobin. What is this phenomenon called?
o: The Bohr effect
The Bohr effect is the reverse: CO₂ and H⁺ lowering O₂ affinity.
The chloride shift
The chloride shift is Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange across the RBC membrane.
The Haldane effect
Correct: the Haldane effect describes O₂ status changing CO₂/H⁺ binding.
Cooperative binding
Cooperativity describes O₂ binding enhancing further O₂ binding.
questions.note: Bohr: CO₂/H⁺ affect O₂. Haldane: O₂ affects CO₂/H⁺.
questions.x: The Haldane effect runs from O₂ to CO₂: deoxyhemoglobin binds more CO₂ (as carbamino) and buffers more H⁺, helping blood load CO₂ in tissues and release it in the lungs. The Bohr effect is the mirror image: CO₂ and H⁺ lower hemoglobin's O₂ affinity, helping O₂ unload in active tissues. Bohr is about O₂ affinity; Haldane is about CO₂ carriage.

questions.q: A stab wound lets air into the pleural space on one side. What happens to that lung?
o: It overinflates because air pushes into the alveoli
Air in the pleural space surrounds the lung; it does not inflate alveoli.
It stays inflated because the airways are still open
Open airways cannot hold the lung out without negative intrapleural pressure.
It fills with fluid because capillary pressure rises
Pneumothorax is air, not fluid, in the pleural space.
It collapses because intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric
Correct: the negative pressure holding the lung open is lost, so elastic recoil collapses it.
questions.x: The lungs stay inflated only because intrapleural pressure is below atmospheric, opposing their elastic recoil. A chest wound lets air into the pleural space until its pressure equals atmospheric; the transpulmonary pressure gradient disappears and the lung recoils and collapses (pneumothorax). Open airways alone cannot hold the lung open without that negative pleural pressure.

questions.q: Each gram of hemoglobin can bind about 1.34 mL of O₂. If blood has 15 g of Hb per dL and is 100% saturated, about how much O₂ is bound per dL?
o: 5 mL
Too low; this would correspond to about 4 g of Hb.
10 mL
This halves the true value.
20 mL
Correct: 1.34 × 15 ≈ 20 mL O₂ per dL.
45 mL
Hematocrit (45%) was confused with O₂ content.
questions.note: Dissolved O₂ adds only about 0.3 mL/dL.
questions.x: Nearly all blood O₂ is bound to hemoglobin: capacity ≈ 1.34 mL O₂ per gram × 15 g/dL ≈ 20 mL O₂/dL at full saturation. Dissolved O₂ adds only about 0.3 mL/dL at a PO₂ of 100 mmHg. The 45 mL choice comes from confusing hematocrit with O₂ content, which are unrelated numbers.

questions.q: At the end of a quiet inspiration, when air has stopped flowing, alveolar pressure equals:
o: Atmospheric pressure
Correct: no flow means no pressure gradient between alveoli and the atmosphere.
Intrapleural pressure
Intrapleural pressure stays below alveolar pressure, keeping the lungs inflated.
A value well below atmospheric
Pressure is below atmospheric only while air is still flowing in.
A value well above atmospheric
Pressure exceeds atmospheric only during expiration.
questions.note: Flow requires a pressure gradient.
questions.x: Airflow requires a pressure gradient. During inspiration alveolar pressure is below atmospheric; when inspiration ends and flow stops, alveolar pressure has equalized with atmospheric. Intrapleural pressure stays negative throughout quiet breathing, which is what keeps the lungs expanded, so it is never equal to alveolar pressure.

questions.q: Which heart chamber pumps oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation?
o: Right ventricle
The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
Left atrium
The left atrium receives blood from the lungs and passes it to the left ventricle.
Right atrium
The right atrium receives deoxygenated systemic venous blood.
Left ventricle
Correct: the left ventricle ejects into the aorta.
questions.x: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then flows into the left ventricle, which ejects it through the aortic valve into the aorta and systemic circulation. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Atria are mainly receiving and priming chambers, not the main pumps.

questions.q: Which vessels carry oxygenated blood toward the heart?
o: Pulmonary arteries
Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the heart.
Pulmonary veins
Correct: pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
Venae cavae
The venae cavae return deoxygenated systemic blood.
Coronary arteries
Coronary arteries carry blood away from the aorta to heart muscle, not toward the heart chambers.
questions.note: Arteries go away from the heart, whatever their O₂ content.
questions.x: Vessels are named by direction relative to the heart, not by O₂ content: arteries carry blood away and veins carry blood toward it. The pulmonary veins are therefore the veins carrying oxygenated blood back to the left atrium, while the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The venae cavae also return blood to the heart, but it is deoxygenated.

questions.q: Conduction slows markedly at the AV node. What is the main benefit of this delay?
o: The ventricles can repolarize before the atria depolarize
Ventricular repolarization is not what the AV delay protects.
The atria finish contracting before the ventricles contract
Correct: the delay lets atrial systole top off ventricular filling.
It sets the resting heart rate
The SA node sets the rate.
It allows the semilunar valves to open first
Semilunar valves open during ventricular ejection, well after the AV delay.
questions.x: Nodal cells conduct slowly because they rely on Ca²⁺ upstrokes and have few gap junctions. The roughly 0.1 s AV delay lets the atria contract and add the final portion of ventricular filling before the ventricles contract. The heart rate itself is set by the SA node, the fastest pacemaker, not by the AV node.

questions.q: The rapid upstroke of an SA nodal pacemaker action potential is mainly due to:
o: Fast Na⁺ influx through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
That drives the upstroke in ventricular myocytes, not nodal cells.
K⁺ efflux through delayed rectifier channels
K⁺ efflux repolarizes the cell.
Cl⁻ influx through ligand-gated channels
Cl⁻ influx would hyperpolarize, not depolarize.
Ca²⁺ influx through voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
Correct: nodal cells lack a fast Na⁺ upstroke; L-type Ca²⁺ channels depolarize them.
questions.note: Nodal: funny Na⁺ current drifts up, Ca²⁺ fires the upstroke.
questions.x: SA nodal cells have no stable resting potential: a funny Na⁺ current and T-type Ca²⁺ channels slowly depolarize them to threshold, then L-type Ca²⁺ channels produce a slow upstroke, and K⁺ efflux repolarizes. Fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels drive the upstroke of ventricular myocytes and Purkinje fibers, which is the common trap.

questions.q: The ventricular muscle action potential has a long plateau. What is its main functional significance?
o: It creates a long refractory period that prevents tetanic contraction
Correct: the heart must relax and refill between beats, so it cannot be tetanized.
It speeds conduction through the Purkinje fibers
Conduction speed depends on the upstroke and cell coupling, not the plateau.
It allows the ventricles to beat faster than the SA node
The plateau limits, rather than raises, maximal rate.
It lets the ventricles contract without Ca²⁺
The plateau is caused by Ca²⁺ entry that triggers contraction.
questions.note: Plateau = L-type Ca²⁺ in balanced by K⁺ out.
questions.x: During the plateau, L-type Ca²⁺ influx balances K⁺ efflux, holding the membrane depolarized for about 200 ms. Because Na⁺ channels stay inactivated, the refractory period lasts nearly as long as the contraction itself, so contractions cannot summate and the heart cannot be tetanized. This guarantees relaxation and refilling between beats.

questions.q: A person's heart rate is 80 beats/min and stroke volume is 75 mL. What is the cardiac output?
o: 0.94 L/min
The two values were divided instead of multiplied.
1.55 L/min
The two values were added instead of multiplied.
6.0 L/min
Correct: CO = HR × SV = 80 × 75 mL = 6,000 mL/min.
60 L/min
Decimal error; 6,000 mL is 6 L.
questions.note: CO = HR × SV.
questions.x: Cardiac output is the volume pumped per minute: heart rate times stroke volume. 80 beats/min × 75 mL/beat = 6,000 mL/min = 6.0 L/min, a typical resting value. Watch units: 6,000 mL is 6 L, not 60 L.

questions.q: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 140 mL and an end-systolic volume of 70 mL. What is the ejection fraction?
o: Stroke volume was divided by EDV + ESV (70/210); EF uses EDV alone as the denominator.
70 is the stroke volume in mL, not a percentage.
EDV was divided by ESV.
questions.note: EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV.
questions.x: Ejection fraction is the fraction of end-diastolic volume ejected in one beat: EF = (EDV − ESV)/EDV. Here stroke volume is 140 − 70 = 70 mL and EF = 70/140 = 50%. The 70% choice confuses the stroke volume in mL with a percentage; a normal EF is about 55 to 70%.

questions.q: A rapid IV fluid infusion increases venous return to the heart. By the Frank-Starling mechanism, what happens?
o: Stroke volume falls because the ventricle is overfilled
Within physiologic range, more filling increases output.
Heart rate falls to keep cardiac output constant
Frank-Starling is about stroke volume, not a heart rate reflex.
Greater end-diastolic stretch increases stroke volume
Correct: more preload stretches sarcomeres toward optimal overlap, so the heart ejects more.
Contractility falls because of Ca²⁺ depletion
Preload changes force by stretch, not by depleting Ca²⁺.
questions.note: Frank-Starling: output matches input.
questions.x: The Frank-Starling law says the ventricle ejects more when filled more: increased venous return raises end-diastolic volume, stretching sarcomeres toward optimal actin-myosin overlap, so stroke volume rises. This intrinsic mechanism keeps the outputs of the two ventricles matched. It is not a heart rate reflex, and within the physiologic range more filling does not reduce output.

questions.q: The first heart sound (S1) is produced mainly by:
o: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Semilunar valve closure produces S2.
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Correct: S1 marks AV valve closure as ventricular systole begins.
Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Normal valve opening is silent.
Blood rushing into the atria
Atrial filling is not the source of S1.
questions.note: S1 = AV valves close (systole starts); S2 = semilunar valves close.
questions.x: Heart sounds come from valves closing, not opening. S1 occurs when ventricular systole starts and ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, slamming the mitral and tricuspid valves shut. S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of ejection, so swapping the two is the common trap.

questions.q: During isovolumetric contraction of the left ventricle, which statement is true?
o: Ventricular pressure rises while the mitral and aortic valves are both closed
Correct: the mitral valve has shut and the aortic valve has not yet opened, so volume is constant.
Blood is ejected into the aorta at a constant volume
No blood leaves during this phase; ejection begins after the aortic valve opens.
The mitral valve is open and the ventricle is filling
That is diastolic filling.
Ventricular pressure falls with both valves closed
That is isovolumetric relaxation.
questions.x: Isovolumetric contraction begins when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and closes the mitral valve, and lasts until pressure exceeds aortic pressure and opens the aortic valve. With both valves shut, the ventricle contracts without changing volume, so pressure climbs steeply. Isovolumetric relaxation is the reverse phase, with both valves closed and pressure falling.

questions.q: Which vessels contribute the most resistance to systemic blood flow and do most of the work of directing it to specific organs?
o: Arterioles
Correct: arterioles have small radii and thick smooth muscle that constricts or dilates.
Large elastic arteries
Large arteries have wide lumens and low resistance.
Capillaries
Individual capillaries are narrow, but so many run in parallel that their total resistance is lower.
Veins
Veins are low-resistance, high-capacitance vessels.
questions.note: Biggest pressure drop happens across arterioles.
questions.x: Resistance rises steeply as radius falls (R ∝ 1/r⁴), and arterioles combine small radii with thick, adjustable smooth muscle, so they produce the largest pressure drop and control flow to each organ. A single capillary is narrower, but billions in parallel give the capillary bed a lower total resistance, which is the tempting trap.

questions.q: Liver failure lowers plasma albumin. Why does edema develop?
o: Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls
Lower hydrostatic pressure would reduce filtration and edema.
Plasma oncotic pressure falls, so less fluid returns to capillaries
Correct: oncotic pressure normally draws fluid back in; less albumin means net filtration rises.
Interstitial oncotic pressure falls
That would pull fluid out of the tissues, not into them.
Lymphatic vessels become blocked by albumin
Low albumin does not block lymphatics.
questions.note: Starling forces: hydrostatic pushes out, oncotic pulls in.
questions.x: Starling forces govern capillary fluid exchange: hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, and plasma oncotic pressure, made mostly by albumin, pulls it back in. When the liver cannot make albumin, oncotic pressure falls, net filtration rises and fluid accumulates in tissues faster than lymphatics can remove it. Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure would reduce, not cause, edema.

questions.q: At rest, where is the largest fraction of the total blood volume found?
o: Systemic arteries
Arteries hold a smaller fraction at higher pressure.
Capillaries
Capillaries hold only about 5% of blood at any moment.
Systemic veins and venules
Correct: veins are compliant capacitance vessels holding roughly 60 to 70% of blood.
The heart chambers
The heart holds a small fraction of total volume.
questions.x: Veins have thin, compliant walls, so they hold large volumes at low pressure and act as the body's blood reservoir, containing roughly 60 to 70% of blood volume. Sympathetic venoconstriction can shift this reserve toward the heart to boost venous return. Arteries are tempting because they are high pressure, but their stiffness means they hold much less volume.

questions.q: An arteriole's radius is cut in half while the pressure difference across it stays constant. By Poiseuille's law, flow through it becomes:
o: 1/2 of the original
Flow depends on r⁴, not r.
1/4 of the original
That would be the r² dependence of cross-sectional area.
1/8 of the original
Uses r³; Poiseuille's law uses r⁴.
1/16 of the original
Correct: flow ∝ r⁴, and (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.
questions.note: Small radius changes make huge resistance changes.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law gives flow ∝ ΔP·r⁴/(ηL), so resistance depends on 1/r⁴. Halving the radius makes resistance 2⁴ = 16 times higher, and at constant pressure difference flow falls to 1/16. The 1/4 choice reflects cross-sectional area (r²), which is not what governs viscous flow.

questions.q: A person stands up quickly and blood pools in the legs. Which baroreceptor reflex response follows?
o: Increased vagal output slowing the heart
Vagal output rises when pressure is high, not low.
Increased baroreceptor firing
Baroreceptors fire less when stretched less by low pressure.
Increased sympathetic output raising heart rate and causing vasoconstriction
Correct: lower pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, so sympathetic tone rises.
Widespread arteriolar vasodilation
Vasodilation would drop pressure further.
questions.x: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire in proportion to stretch. Standing drops blood pressure in the upper body, reducing their firing; the medulla responds by withdrawing vagal tone and increasing sympathetic output, raising heart rate, contractility and vascular constriction. Increased baroreceptor firing is the trap, since less stretch means less firing.

questions.q: Stimulating the vagus nerve slows the heart. Which mechanism is responsible?
o: ACh acting on muscarinic receptors at the SA node
Correct: ACh increases K⁺ conductance and slows pacemaker depolarization.
Norepinephrine acting on β₁ receptors at the SA node
β₁ activation speeds the heart; it is sympathetic.
ACh acting on nicotinic receptors on ventricular muscle
The heart's vagal receptors are muscarinic.
Epinephrine released from the adrenal medulla
Adrenal epinephrine increases heart rate.
questions.x: The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine onto M₂ muscarinic receptors at the SA node. This opens K⁺ channels and reduces the funny current and Ca²⁺ current, hyperpolarizing the cells and slowing the pacemaker drift to threshold. Nicotinic receptors are found at autonomic ganglia and skeletal muscle, not on cardiac muscle.

questions.q: Blood flows most slowly in the capillaries. Why?
o: Capillaries have the highest resistance of any vessel type
Arterioles have the highest total resistance.
Capillary walls absorb kinetic energy from the blood
The thin wall is not why velocity drops.
Capillaries are farthest from the heart
Veins are farther downstream, yet blood speeds up again there.
Capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional area
Correct: by continuity (Q = Av), velocity is lowest where total area is greatest.
questions.note: Slow flow gives time for exchange.
questions.x: By the continuity equation, flow Q = A × v is the same at every level of the circulation. Each capillary is tiny, but so many lie in parallel that their total cross-sectional area is the largest of any vessel class, so velocity there is lowest, giving time for exchange. High resistance is tempting, but arterioles, not capillaries, have the highest total resistance.

questions.q: In the fetus, the ductus arteriosus carries blood from the:
o: Right atrium to the left atrium
That is the foramen ovale.
Pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the lungs
Correct: high fetal pulmonary resistance diverts blood through this shunt.
Umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava
That is the ductus venosus, which bypasses the liver.
Aorta to the umbilical vein
The umbilical arteries, not veins, carry blood toward the placenta.
questions.x: Fetal lungs are fluid-filled with high vascular resistance, so most right ventricular output bypasses them. The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta; the foramen ovale shunts right atrium to left atrium; the ductus venosus lets umbilical venous blood bypass the liver. Matching each shunt to the organ it bypasses keeps them straight.

questions.q: At birth, the foramen ovale closes functionally soon after the first breaths. What pressure change causes this?
o: Right atrial pressure rises above left atrial pressure
That gradient would keep the foramen open, as in the fetus.
Left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure
Correct: lung expansion lowers pulmonary resistance, more blood returns to the left atrium, and the flap is pushed shut.
Pulmonary vascular resistance increases
Ventilation lowers pulmonary resistance.
Systemic vascular resistance falls when the placenta is removed
Clamping the cord raises systemic resistance.
questions.x: With the first breaths, lung expansion drops pulmonary vascular resistance, so much more blood flows through the lungs and returns to the left atrium, raising its pressure. Cord clamping also removes the low-resistance placenta, raising systemic resistance. Left atrial pressure then exceeds right atrial pressure and pushes the foramen ovale flap shut.

questions.q: A person's blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. What is the approximate mean arterial pressure?
o: 80 mmHg
That is the diastolic pressure alone.
93 mmHg
Correct: MAP ≈ diastolic + 1/3 pulse pressure = 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg.
100 mmHg
A simple average overweights systole; more time is spent in diastole.
120 mmHg
That is the systolic pressure alone.
questions.note: MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3.
questions.x: The heart spends about two thirds of each cycle in diastole, so mean arterial pressure is weighted toward diastolic pressure: MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3 = 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg. The simple average of 100 mmHg is tempting but overweights systole.

questions.q: Endothelial cells release nitric oxide in response to shear stress. What effect follows?
o: Vascular smooth muscle relaxes via increased cGMP
Correct: NO activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP and causing vasodilation.
Vascular smooth muscle contracts via increased Ca²⁺
NO lowers smooth muscle Ca²⁺ and relaxes it.
Platelets aggregate at the vessel wall
NO inhibits platelet aggregation.
Heart rate increases via β₁ receptors
NO acts locally on vessels, not on cardiac β₁ receptors.
questions.x: Shear stress and agonists such as acetylcholine activate endothelial NO synthase. NO diffuses into vascular smooth muscle, activates soluble guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP, which lowers intracellular Ca²⁺ and relaxes the muscle, causing vasodilation. NO also inhibits platelet aggregation, so it does not promote clotting.

questions.q: Unlike systemic arterioles, pulmonary arterioles respond to low alveolar O₂ by:
o: Dilating, which increases flow to poorly ventilated alveoli
That is the systemic response; in the lung it would waste blood flow.
Not changing, because pulmonary vessels lack smooth muscle
Pulmonary arterioles do have smooth muscle.
Constricting, which diverts blood to better-ventilated alveoli
Correct: hypoxic vasoconstriction matches perfusion to ventilation.
Dilating, which lowers pulmonary artery pressure
Widespread hypoxia actually raises pulmonary artery pressure.
questions.note: Lung: hypoxia constricts. Body: hypoxia dilates.
questions.x: In systemic tissues, low O₂ dilates arterioles to increase delivery. In the lung, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction does the opposite, steering blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward well-ventilated ones and keeping ventilation and perfusion matched. When hypoxia is widespread, as at altitude, this constriction raises pulmonary artery pressure.

questions.q: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released when the atria are stretched by high blood volume. What does it do?
o: Increases renin release
ANP opposes the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
Increases Na⁺ reabsorption in the collecting duct
ANP decreases Na⁺ reabsorption.
Constricts systemic arterioles
ANP is a vasodilator.
Increases Na⁺ and water excretion by the kidneys
Correct: ANP promotes natriuresis, which lowers blood volume and pressure.
questions.x: ANP is released by atrial myocytes when they are stretched by excess volume. It increases glomerular filtration, reduces Na⁺ reabsorption, inhibits renin and aldosterone and dilates vessels, so the kidneys excrete more Na⁺ and water and blood pressure falls. It is a counterweight to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, not part of it.

questions.q: The left ventricular wall is much thicker than the right. Why?
o: It pumps a larger volume of blood each beat
Both ventricles eject the same stroke volume on average.
It must pump blood a shorter distance
A shorter distance would need less force, not more.
It must generate higher pressure against systemic resistance
Correct: systemic resistance is far higher than pulmonary resistance.
It receives deoxygenated blood that is more viscous
The left ventricle receives oxygenated blood; viscosity is not the reason.
questions.note: Same output, different pressures.
questions.x: The two ventricles are in series, so over time they must eject the same stroke volume. What differs is pressure: systemic resistance is several times higher than pulmonary resistance, so the left ventricle must generate about 120 mmHg versus about 25 mmHg on the right. Higher wall stress builds a thicker muscular wall, not a larger volume pumped.

questions.q: Atrial repolarization usually does not appear as a separate wave on an ECG. Why?
o: The atria never repolarize
All excitable cells must repolarize to fire again.
It occurs during the QRS complex and is masked by it
Correct: the much larger ventricular depolarization hides it.
It is the same event as the T wave
The T wave is ventricular repolarization.
It happens before the P wave
Repolarization follows depolarization, which is the P wave.
questions.note: P = atrial depol, QRS = ventricular depol, T = ventricular repol.
questions.x: On an ECG, the P wave is atrial depolarization, QRS is ventricular depolarization and T is ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization happens at the same time as ventricular depolarization, and its small signal is buried in the much larger QRS complex. Confusing it with the T wave is the common trap.

questions.q: Which plasma protein is most abundant and chiefly responsible for plasma oncotic pressure?
o: Albumin
Correct: albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and the main source of oncotic pressure.
Fibrinogen
Fibrinogen is a clotting protein present at lower levels.
Immunoglobulin G
Antibodies contribute less oncotic pressure than albumin.
Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is inside red cells, not free in plasma.
questions.x: Oncotic pressure depends on the number of protein molecules that cannot cross the capillary wall. Albumin, made by the liver, is the most abundant plasma protein and small enough to be numerous, so it supplies most plasma oncotic pressure and also carries hormones, drugs and fatty acids. Hemoglobin is tempting but stays inside red blood cells.

questions.q: Which organ produces most of the body's erythropoietin (EPO)?
o: Kidney
Correct: peritubular cells in the renal cortex release EPO when they sense low O₂ delivery.
Liver
The fetal liver makes EPO, but in adults the kidney is the main source.
Red bone marrow
Marrow responds to EPO by making red cells; it does not secrete the hormone.
Spleen
The spleen removes old red cells; it does not make EPO.
questions.x: Peritubular interstitial cells in the renal cortex sense reduced O₂ delivery through HIF and release erythropoietin, which stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow. This is why chronic kidney disease causes anemia. The fetal liver is the main source before birth, but in adults the liver contributes only a minor share.

questions.q: Mature human red blood cells lack mitochondria. How do they make ATP?
o: Oxidative phosphorylation using the O₂ they carry
That needs mitochondria, which mature RBCs lack.
Anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactate
Correct: without mitochondria, RBCs rely on glycolysis and regenerate NAD⁺ by making lactate.
β-oxidation of fatty acids
β-oxidation also occurs in mitochondria.
Breaking down hemoglobin for energy
Hemoglobin is not used as an energy source by the cell.
questions.note: RBCs do not consume the O₂ they deliver.
questions.x: Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus and mitochondria during development, so they cannot run the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation or β-oxidation. They depend on anaerobic glycolysis, converting pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺. As a result they do not consume the O₂ they carry, leaving all of it for the tissues.

questions.q: A patient has type A blood. Which antibodies are normally present in the plasma?
o: Anti-A antibodies
Anti-A would attack the patient's own red cells.
Both anti-A and anti-B
That is the pattern of type O blood.
Anti-B antibodies
Correct: people make antibodies against the ABO antigen they lack.
Neither anti-A nor anti-B
That is the pattern of type AB blood.
questions.note: Type O = universal RBC donor; AB = universal recipient.
questions.x: ABO antibodies are made against carbohydrate antigens a person lacks, largely after exposure to similar gut bacteria early in life. Type A red cells carry A antigen, so the plasma holds anti-B. Having anti-A would mean attacking one's own cells, which tolerance prevents. Type O has both antibodies and type AB has neither, which is why AB individuals can receive any ABO type of red cells.

questions.q: Hemolytic disease of the newborn from Rh incompatibility usually affects a second Rh⁺ pregnancy of an Rh⁻ mother, not the first. Why?
o: The first fetus makes antibodies that harm the second fetus
The antibodies come from the mother, not from a previous fetus.
IgM made in the first pregnancy crosses the placenta only in the second
IgM is too large to cross the placenta at all.
Rh antigens are not expressed until the second pregnancy
Rh⁺ fetuses express D antigen in every pregnancy.
The mother is first sensitized at delivery, and memory produces IgG that crosses the placenta later
Correct: fetal blood enters her circulation at birth; in the next pregnancy anti-D IgG crosses the placenta.
questions.note: Only IgG crosses the placenta.
questions.x: In the first Rh⁺ pregnancy, fetal red cells mainly enter the Rh⁻ mother's blood at delivery, so she is sensitized too late to harm that baby, and her first antibodies are IgM, which cannot cross the placenta. In a later Rh⁺ pregnancy, memory B cells quickly make anti-D IgG, which crosses the placenta and lyses fetal red cells. Giving anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) prevents the initial sensitization.

questions.q: Platelets are essential for primary hemostasis. Where do they come from?
o: Division of mature red blood cells
Mature RBCs cannot divide.
Lymphocytes in the lymph nodes
Lymph nodes produce lymphocytes, not platelets.
Fragments of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow
Correct: platelets are anucleate pieces of cytoplasm shed by megakaryocytes.
Endothelial cells lining damaged vessels
Endothelium releases factors like von Willebrand factor but does not make platelets.
questions.x: Platelets are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments pinched off from huge polyploid megakaryocytes in red bone marrow, a process stimulated by thrombopoietin from the liver. At an injury they adhere to exposed collagen via von Willebrand factor and aggregate into a plug. Endothelium supplies von Willebrand factor, which is why it is a tempting distractor, but it does not make platelets.

questions.q: In the final step of the coagulation cascade, which conversion forms the mesh of a clot?
o: Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin
Correct: fibrin strands polymerize and are cross-linked to stabilize the platelet plug.
Plasmin cleaves fibrin to fibrinogen
Plasmin breaks clots down into fragments; it does not form them.
Fibrin converts prothrombin to thrombin
Prothrombin is activated by factor Xa, not by fibrin.
Heparin converts fibrinogen to fibrin
Heparin is an anticoagulant.
questions.x: Both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge on factor X, which with factor V converts prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin then cleaves soluble fibrinogen into fibrin monomers that polymerize, and factor XIII cross-links them into a stable mesh around the platelet plug. Plasmin works in the opposite direction, dissolving fibrin during fibrinolysis.

questions.q: Warfarin interferes with vitamin K recycling. Why does this reduce clotting?
o: It directly inhibits platelet aggregation
That describes aspirin.
It speeds the breakdown of fibrin
That describes thrombolytic drugs like tPA.
It binds and removes Ca²⁺ from the blood
That describes citrate or EDTA in blood tubes.
The liver makes fewer functional factors II, VII, IX and X
Correct: these factors need vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation to bind Ca²⁺ and work.
questions.x: Factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S) need γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues, a vitamin K-dependent step, to bind Ca²⁺ and assemble on phospholipid surfaces. Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, so active vitamin K is not regenerated and the liver releases nonfunctional factors. It has no effect on platelets, which is aspirin's target.

questions.q: After a tube of blood is centrifuged, a thin whitish layer sits between the plasma and the packed red cells. What does it contain?
o: Albumin and other plasma proteins
