Plasma proteins stay dissolved in the plasma layer.
White blood cells and platelets
Correct: this buffy coat holds leukocytes and platelets, which are less dense than RBCs.
Mature red blood cells
Red cells are densest and settle at the bottom.
Fibrin from clotting
An anticoagulated tube does not form fibrin.
questions.note: Hematocrit (≈ 45%) is the red cell fraction.
questions.x: Centrifugation separates blood by density. Red cells are densest and pack at the bottom (hematocrit about 45%), plasma stays on top (about 55%), and a thin buffy coat of leukocytes and platelets, under 1% of volume, sits between them. Plasma proteins like albumin remain dissolved in the plasma rather than forming a separate layer.

questions.q: Iron-deficiency anemia lowers hemoglobin concentration. Which set of findings is expected?
o: Low PaO₂ and low SaO₂
Gas exchange in the lungs is unaffected by anemia.
Normal PaO₂ and SaO₂, but reduced arterial O₂ content
Correct: lungs work normally, so PO₂ and saturation are normal; less Hb means less total O₂.
Normal O₂ content because each Hb carries more O₂
Saturation cannot exceed 100%, so content falls.
High PaO₂ to compensate for low Hb
PaO₂ is set by alveolar gas and lung function, not Hb.
questions.note: Saturation is a percentage; content depends on how much Hb there is.
questions.x: PaO₂ reflects dissolved O₂ and SaO₂ is the percent of available heme sites bound, both set by lung function, which is normal in anemia. O₂ content, however, is mostly 1.34 × [Hb] × SaO₂, so less hemoglobin means less total O₂ per deciliter. The trap is assuming low content must mean low PO₂ or saturation; each Hb cannot carry more than full saturation allows.

questions.q: Massive hemolysis would most directly raise the blood level of:
o: Conjugated bilirubin
Conjugated bilirubin rises mainly with bile duct obstruction.
Urea
Urea comes from amino acid nitrogen in the liver, not heme breakdown.
Albumin
Hemolysis does not increase albumin synthesis.
Unconjugated bilirubin
Correct: heme from lysed red cells becomes bilirubin faster than the liver can conjugate it.
questions.x: Macrophages break down heme from old or lysed red cells into biliverdin and then unconjugated bilirubin, which travels on albumin to the liver for glucuronide conjugation. Massive hemolysis overwhelms conjugation capacity, so unconjugated bilirubin rises and causes jaundice. Conjugated bilirubin rises instead when bile flow is obstructed after the liver has done its work.

questions.q: Lymphatic vessels return excess interstitial fluid to the blood. Where does the thoracic duct empty?
o: Into the left subclavian vein
Correct: the thoracic duct joins the venous system near the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
Into the right atrium
Lymph enters veins before reaching the heart, not the atrium directly.
Into the hepatic portal vein
The portal vein carries absorbed blood from the gut, not lymph.
Into the pulmonary artery
Lymph is returned to systemic veins.
questions.x: Lymph from most of the body, including the legs, abdomen and left upper body, collects in the thoracic duct, which empties into the venous system near the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper body into the corresponding right-side veins. Lymph rejoins blood in veins before it ever reaches the heart.

questions.q: Dietary fats packaged as chylomicrons leave intestinal cells and first enter which vessels?
o: Villus blood capillaries
Capillaries take up sugars and amino acids; chylomicrons are too large.
The hepatic portal vein directly
Fat absorption mostly bypasses the portal vein.
Lacteals
Correct: chylomicrons are too large for blood capillaries, so they enter lymphatic lacteals in the villi.
The bile duct
Bile flows into the intestine, not out of it.
questions.note: Fats skip first-pass liver metabolism via lymph.
questions.x: Inside enterocytes, absorbed fatty acids and monoglycerides are reassembled into triglycerides and packaged with cholesterol and apolipoproteins into chylomicrons. These particles are too large to enter the tight blood capillaries, so they enter the lacteals, lymphatic capillaries in each villus, and reach the blood via the thoracic duct. Sugars and amino acids, by contrast, go to the liver through the portal vein.

questions.q: What is a main function of lymph nodes?
o: Producing red blood cells
Adult RBCs are made in red bone marrow.
Pumping lymph toward the heart
Nodes have no pumping function.
Secreting bile
Bile comes from the liver.
Filtering lymph and providing a site where lymphocytes meet antigen
Correct: dendritic cells bring antigen to nodes, where B and T cells are activated.
questions.x: Lymph nodes sit along lymphatic vessels and filter lymph through a meshwork rich in macrophages, which trap debris and microbes. They are also meeting points: dendritic cells carry antigen from tissues to nodes, where naive B and T cells are activated, which is why nodes swell during infection. Nodes do not pump lymph; that is done by muscle compression and valves.

questions.q: The lymphatic system has no central pump. What mainly moves lymph toward the veins?
o: Contraction of the left ventricle
Ventricular pressure is lost by the time fluid enters the interstitium.
High hydrostatic pressure in lymph capillaries
Lymph pressure is very low.
Skeletal muscle contraction and breathing movements, with one-way valves
Correct: squeezing of vessels plus valves pushes lymph in one direction.
Gravity alone
Lymph from the legs must flow upward against gravity.
questions.x: Lymphatic vessels have thin walls and one-way valves. Compression by contracting skeletal muscles, pressure changes from breathing, arterial pulsations and rhythmic contraction of lymphatic smooth muscle squeeze lymph forward, while valves prevent backflow. Lymph pressure is very low, so hydrostatic pressure from the heart does not push it.

questions.q: After surgical removal of axillary lymph nodes, a patient's arm swells chronically. Why?
o: Capillary hydrostatic pressure in the arm has risen
Node removal does not change arterial or capillary pressure.
Filtered fluid and protein in the arm can no longer be returned to the blood
Correct: lymphatic drainage normally removes excess filtrate and leaked protein.
Plasma albumin has fallen throughout the body
The swelling is limited to one arm, so the cause is local.
Arm veins have become permanently constricted
Venous tone is not the problem; lymph drainage is.
questions.note: Lymphedema fluid is protein-rich.
questions.x: Capillaries filter slightly more fluid than they reabsorb and leak small amounts of protein; lymphatics normally return both to the blood. After axillary nodes and vessels are removed, this drainage fails in the arm, so protein-rich fluid accumulates and raises interstitial oncotic pressure, causing lymphedema. Because only one arm swells, a systemic cause such as low albumin is ruled out.

questions.q: In which organ do T lymphocytes complete their maturation?
o: Thymus
Correct: T cells undergo positive and negative selection in the thymus.
Spleen
The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where mature lymphocytes meet antigen.
Lymph nodes
Lymph nodes host mature lymphocytes; they are not where T cells mature.
Liver
The liver is not a site of T cell maturation.
questions.note: Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow (B) and thymus (T).
questions.x: T cell precursors leave the bone marrow and mature in the thymus, where positive selection keeps cells that recognize self-MHC and negative selection deletes those that bind self-antigen too strongly. B cells mature in the bone marrow. The spleen and lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where already mature lymphocytes encounter antigen.

questions.q: Which defense belongs to innate rather than adaptive immunity?
o: Complement activation on bacterial surfaces
Correct: complement is a nonspecific defense that acts within hours, without prior exposure.
Antibody production by plasma cells
Antibodies are part of adaptive humoral immunity.
Killing by clonally expanded CD8⁺ T cells
Cytotoxic T cells are adaptive.
Rapid response by memory B cells
Memory is a hallmark of adaptive immunity.
questions.x: Innate immunity uses germline-encoded, nonspecific defenses that act within minutes to hours and do not improve with repeated exposure: barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, complement and inflammation. Adaptive immunity relies on clonally selected B and T cells, takes days for a first response and forms memory. Complement can be triggered by antibodies, but the system itself is innate.

questions.q: Within hours of a bacterial skin infection, which white blood cells are typically the first to arrive in large numbers?
o: B lymphocytes
B cells act later, in adaptive immunity.
Neutrophils
Correct: neutrophils are the most abundant WBC and first to migrate into acute bacterial infection.
Eosinophils
Eosinophils mainly target parasites and act in allergy.
Plasma cells
Plasma cells appear days later, after B cell activation.
questions.note: Pus is mostly dead neutrophils.
questions.x: Neutrophils are the most numerous circulating white cells and respond to chemokines from the site of acute bacterial infection within hours, squeezing out of vessels to phagocytose bacteria. Their dead remains form pus. Lymphocytes and plasma cells belong to the adaptive response and take days to become significant, while eosinophils target parasites.

questions.q: How do macrophages recognize bacteria they have never encountered before?
o: T cell receptors bind specific peptide antigens
TCRs are on T cells and need MHC presentation.
They rearrange antibody genes for each microbe
Gene rearrangement occurs in lymphocytes, not macrophages.
Toll-like receptors bind conserved microbial patterns like LPS
Correct: pattern recognition receptors detect PAMPs shared by many microbes.
They recognize MHC class II on the bacteria
Bacteria do not have MHC molecules.
questions.x: Innate cells like macrophages use germline-encoded pattern recognition receptors, such as Toll-like receptors, that bind molecular patterns shared by whole classes of microbes: LPS, flagellin, peptidoglycan or viral nucleic acids. No prior exposure is needed. Gene rearrangement to create unique receptors is a feature of B and T lymphocytes only.

questions.q: A virus causes infected cells to stop displaying MHC class I, hiding them from CD8⁺ T cells. Which cell is best suited to kill them?
o: Helper T cells
CD4⁺ T cells coordinate immunity; they do not directly kill infected cells.
B cells
B cells make antibodies and do not directly kill cells.
Mast cells
Mast cells release histamine; they are not cytotoxic.
Natural killer cells
Correct: NK cells kill cells that lack normal MHC I (the missing-self signal).
questions.x: Cytotoxic T cells need MHC class I to see infected cells, so viruses that suppress MHC I escape them. NK cells are innate lymphocytes that are restrained by inhibitory receptors recognizing normal MHC I; when MHC I is missing, inhibition is lost and they kill the cell with perforin and granzymes. Helper T cells coordinate responses but do not directly kill.

questions.q: What is the main role of the complement fragment C3b?
o: Forming pores directly in bacterial membranes
Pores are formed by the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9).
Presenting antigen to T cells
Antigen presentation uses MHC molecules on APCs.
Coating pathogens so phagocytes ingest them more easily
Correct: C3b is an opsonin recognized by receptors on phagocytes.
Neutralizing viruses by blocking receptor binding
Neutralization is an antibody function.
questions.x: Complement activation cleaves C3; the C3b fragment binds microbial surfaces and is recognized by complement receptors on phagocytes, greatly enhancing phagocytosis (opsonization). C3b also helps assemble the C5 convertase that starts the membrane attack complex, but the pore itself is formed by C5b to C9, which is the tempting confusion.

questions.q: A person allergic to pollen sneezes, with itchy eyes and swollen nasal tissue. Which cell releases the histamine responsible?
o: Mast cells with IgE bound to their surface
Correct: allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, triggering degranulation.
Neutrophils with IgM bound to their surface
Neutrophils are not the main histamine source, and IgM is not involved.
Plasma cells secreting IgA
IgA protects mucosa and does not trigger histamine release.
Cytotoxic T cells
Type I allergy is antibody and mast cell mediated, not T cell mediated.
questions.x: Type I hypersensitivity begins with sensitization, when IgE against the allergen binds Fc receptors on mast cells. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links that IgE and triggers degranulation, releasing histamine that causes vasodilation, increased permeability, itching and sneezing. Neutrophils and cytotoxic T cells play no central role in this immediate reaction.

questions.q: Virus-infected cells release type I interferons. What do these signals mainly do?
o: Directly lyse virus particles in the blood
Interferons act on host cells, not on virions.
Act as antibodies that bind the virus
Interferons are cytokines, not antibodies.
Suppress MHC class I expression
Interferons increase MHC I expression.
Induce an antiviral state in nearby uninfected cells
Correct: interferons trigger expression of proteins that block viral replication.
questions.x: Type I interferons (α and β) are cytokines released by virus-infected cells that bind receptors on neighboring cells and induce proteins that degrade viral RNA and block translation, creating an antiviral state. They also increase MHC I expression and activate NK cells. They do not bind or destroy virus particles directly, which is the job of antibodies.

questions.q: Lysozyme in tears and saliva protects against bacteria by:
o: Binding bacterial antigens with high specificity
Specific binding describes antibodies.
Hydrolyzing peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls
Correct: lysozyme breaks the glycosidic bonds of peptidoglycan.
Inserting pores into bacterial plasma membranes
That is the complement membrane attack complex.
Blocking bacterial ribosomes
That is how some antibiotics work.
questions.x: Lysozyme is an innate antimicrobial enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that hydrolyzes the β-1,4 glycosidic bonds of peptidoglycan, weakening the bacterial cell wall so the cell lyses osmotically. It is most effective on Gram-positive bacteria with exposed thick peptidoglycan. Its action is enzymatic and nonspecific, unlike antigen-specific antibody binding.

questions.q: A patient with an intestinal worm infection would most likely show elevated levels of which white blood cell?
o: Neutrophils
Neutrophils mainly rise in acute bacterial infection.
Eosinophils
Correct: eosinophils attack helminths that are too large to phagocytose.
Monocytes
Monocytes rise in chronic infections but are not the hallmark of worms.
Basophils only
Basophils may rise slightly, but eosinophilia is the classic finding.
questions.x: Helminths are far too large for phagocytes to engulf. Eosinophils, recruited by Th2 cytokines like IL-5, bind antibody-coated worms and release toxic granule proteins onto their surface. Eosinophilia is therefore the hallmark of parasitic worm infection and also allergy, whereas neutrophilia points to acute bacterial infection.

questions.q: At the onset of a fever, a person shivers and feels cold even though body temperature is normal. Why?
o: Skin vasodilation is losing heat too quickly
At fever onset, skin vessels constrict to save heat.
The hypothalamic set point has dropped below normal
A lowered set point would trigger sweating.
Muscles shiver because bacteria damage motor neurons
Shivering is a regulated hypothalamic response.
Pyrogens have raised the hypothalamic set point above the current temperature
Correct: the body now reads 37 °C as too cold and makes heat to reach the new set point.
questions.note: When the fever breaks, the set point falls and sweating starts.
questions.x: Pyrogens such as IL-1 and prostaglandin E₂ raise the hypothalamic temperature set point. The body temperature, still at 37 °C, is now below that set point, so the hypothalamus triggers heat-conserving and heat-producing responses: skin vasoconstriction, shivering and a feeling of cold. When the set point drops back, the body is too warm relative to it, so sweating and vasodilation follow.

questions.q: Which cell is most effective at activating naive T cells in a lymph node?
o: Dendritic cell
Correct: dendritic cells capture antigen in tissues, migrate to nodes and present it with costimulation.
Neutrophil
Neutrophils phagocytose but do not travel to nodes to activate naive T cells.
Red blood cell
RBCs lack MHC molecules.
Plasma cell
Plasma cells secrete antibody; they are not antigen presenters.
questions.x: Dendritic cells capture antigen in peripheral tissues, mature, migrate through lymphatics to lymph nodes and present peptide on MHC along with costimulatory molecules such as B7. Naive T cells need both signals to activate, and dendritic cells provide them most effectively. Neutrophils are phagocytic but do not travel to nodes to prime T cells.

questions.q: During inflammation, what causes the local swelling (edema)?
o: Vasoconstriction traps blood in the tissue
Inflammation causes vasodilation.
Lymphatic vessels pump fluid into the tissue
Lymphatics drain tissue fluid; they do not add to it.
Increased capillary permeability lets fluid and protein leak into tissue
Correct: histamine and other mediators open endothelial gaps.
Plasma albumin rises
Higher plasma albumin would pull fluid back into vessels.
questions.note: Redness and heat come from vasodilation; swelling from permeability.
questions.x: Inflammatory mediators such as histamine, bradykinin and leukotrienes cause vasodilation (redness and heat) and contraction of endothelial cells, opening gaps so plasma fluid and protein leak into the tissue. The leaked protein raises interstitial oncotic pressure, adding to the swelling. Vasoconstriction is tempting but inflammation causes the opposite.

questions.q: Which statement correctly pairs a branch of adaptive immunity with its main cells?
o: Cell-mediated immunity is mediated by antibodies
Cell-mediated immunity relies on T cells.
Humoral immunity is mediated by cytotoxic T cells
Cytotoxic T cells are cell-mediated immunity.
Cell-mediated immunity is mediated by neutrophils
Neutrophils are innate cells.
Humoral immunity is mediated by B cells and antibodies
Correct: humoral immunity acts through antibodies in body fluids.
questions.x: Adaptive immunity has two arms. Humoral immunity uses B cells, which become plasma cells secreting antibodies into blood and other body fluids, effective against extracellular pathogens and toxins. Cell-mediated immunity uses T cells, including cytotoxic T cells that kill infected cells. Neutrophils are innate and belong to neither arm.

questions.q: A cell infected by a virus displays viral peptides to cytotoxic T cells. Which molecule presents these peptides?
o: MHC class II
MHC II presents ingested antigens to CD4⁺ T cells on APCs.
CD4
CD4 is a coreceptor on helper T cells, not a presenting molecule.
MHC class I
Correct: MHC I presents peptides made inside the cell to CD8⁺ T cells and is on all nucleated cells.
Immunoglobulin M
IgM is an antibody, not a presenting molecule.
questions.note: Rule of 8: MHC I × CD8 = 8; MHC II × CD4 = 8.
questions.x: Nearly all nucleated cells constantly display fragments of their own cytosolic proteins on MHC class I. When a virus infects the cell, viral peptides are displayed too, and CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells recognize them and kill the cell. MHC class II is restricted to professional antigen-presenting cells and presents ingested antigens to CD4⁺ helpers.

questions.q: A macrophage engulfs a bacterium and presents its peptides to activate helper T cells. Which molecule is used?
o: MHC class I
MHC I mainly presents cytosolic peptides to CD8⁺ cells.
MHC class II
Correct: professional APCs present exogenous peptides on MHC II to CD4⁺ T cells.
CD8
CD8 is a coreceptor on cytotoxic T cells.
Toll-like receptor 4
TLR4 detects LPS but does not present peptides.
questions.x: Professional antigen-presenting cells, including macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells, break down engulfed material in endosomes and load the peptides onto MHC class II for display to CD4⁺ helper T cells. MHC class I is tempting because macrophages express it too, but it mainly shows peptides from proteins made inside the cell, to CD8⁺ cells.

questions.q: HIV depletes CD4⁺ T cells. Why does this weaken both antibody and cytotoxic T cell responses?
o: Helper T cells release cytokines needed to activate B cells and CD8⁺ T cells
Correct: helper T cells coordinate both humoral and cell-mediated responses.
CD4⁺ cells are the cells that make antibodies
Plasma cells (from B cells) make antibodies.
CD4⁺ cells directly kill all infected cells
Direct killing is done by CD8⁺ T cells and NK cells.
CD4⁺ cells produce complement proteins
Complement proteins are made mostly by the liver.
questions.x: Helper T cells are the coordinators of adaptive immunity. Their cytokines, such as IL-2 and IL-4, and their CD40L contact help drive B cell class switching and antibody production and support the proliferation of CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells. Losing CD4⁺ cells therefore cripples both arms, leaving patients open to opportunistic infections, even though CD4⁺ cells neither make antibodies nor kill cells directly.

questions.q: Which antibody class is the first to be secreted during a primary immune response?
o: IgM
Correct: IgM is secreted first as a pentamer before class switching occurs.
IgG
IgG dominates the secondary response, after class switching.
IgA
IgA is mainly found in mucosal secretions.
IgE
IgE is present at very low levels and mainly mediates allergy.
questions.x: Naive B cells express IgM and IgD on their surface, and when first activated they secrete pentameric IgM, which is good at agglutination and complement activation. With T cell help, class switching then produces IgG, IgA or IgE. IgG dominates later and in secondary responses, so a high IgM level suggests a recent, primary infection.

questions.q: Breast milk protects a nursing infant's gut. Which antibody class is most abundant in milk and other mucosal secretions?
o: IgM
IgM is the first antibody in blood, not the main secretory antibody.
IgA
Correct: secretory IgA, a dimer, is transported across epithelia into secretions.
IgE
IgE is bound to mast cells.
IgD
IgD is mostly a surface receptor on naive B cells.
questions.x: Secretory IgA is a dimer joined by a J chain that is carried across epithelial cells by the poly-Ig receptor, whose leftover piece (secretory component) protects it from proteases. It is the main antibody in milk, saliva, tears and mucus, neutralizing microbes at mucosal surfaces. IgG, not IgA, is the antibody that crosses the placenta.

questions.q: Antibody titers are measured after two exposures to the same antigen a month apart. The second response peaks sooner and higher and is mostly IgG. What best explains this?
o: Antibodies from the first exposure multiplied in the blood
Antibodies are proteins and cannot replicate.
The antigen became more immunogenic the second time
The antigen is the same; the immune system has changed.
Memory B cells that already class-switched and affinity-matured respond quickly
Correct: memory cells from the first exposure skip the slow naive activation steps.
Innate immunity learned the antigen during the first exposure
Innate immunity lacks antigen-specific memory.
questions.note: Vaccines and boosters exploit the secondary response.
questions.x: The first exposure produces memory B cells that have already undergone class switching and affinity maturation. On re-exposure, these cells are more numerous and activate faster, so the secondary response is quicker, larger, longer lasting and dominated by high-affinity IgG. The antigen has not changed; the immune system has, which is the principle behind booster shots.

questions.q: According to clonal selection, how does the body produce lymphocytes specific for a new antigen?
o: The antigen instructs lymphocytes to fold their receptors to fit it
Specificity is not shaped by antigen contact; that is the old instructive model.
Macrophages convert into lymphocytes with matching receptors
Macrophages and lymphocytes are separate lineages.
All lymphocytes proliferate equally after any infection
Only clones that bind the antigen expand.
The antigen selects pre-existing lymphocytes with matching receptors, which then proliferate
Correct: receptor diversity exists before exposure; antigen triggers expansion of matching clones.
questions.x: Through V(D)J recombination, each developing lymphocyte gets a unique receptor before it ever meets antigen, creating a vast pre-existing repertoire. When an antigen arrives, it binds and selects the rare clones with matching receptors, which proliferate and differentiate into effector and memory cells. The instructive idea that antigen shapes the receptor is the historical misconception the clonal selection theory replaced.

questions.q: Which part of an antibody molecule binds antigen?
o: The constant region of the Fc stem
Fc mediates effector functions such as binding phagocytes and complement.
The disulfide bonds joining the chains
Disulfide bonds hold the chains together structurally.
The variable regions at the tips of the Fab arms
Correct: variable regions of heavy and light chains form the antigen-binding site.
The hinge region only
The hinge provides flexibility, not binding specificity.
questions.x: An antibody is a Y-shaped molecule of two heavy and two light chains. The variable regions at the tips of the two Fab arms form the antigen-binding sites, and their hypervariable loops determine specificity. The constant Fc stem sets the antibody class and effector functions such as complement activation and binding to phagocyte receptors.

questions.q: In the thymus, developing T cells that bind self-peptide-MHC complexes very strongly are:
o: Eliminated by apoptosis through negative selection
Correct: deleting strongly self-reactive cells creates central tolerance.
Kept because they will respond best to infection
Strong self-reactivity would cause autoimmunity.
Converted into B cells
T and B cells are separate lineages.
Released immediately into the blood as memory cells
Memory cells form only after antigen exposure in the periphery.
questions.note: Positive selection: must bind MHC. Negative selection: must not bind self too strongly.
questions.x: Thymic education has two steps. Positive selection keeps thymocytes whose receptors can bind self-MHC at least weakly, while negative selection eliminates by apoptosis those that bind self-peptide-MHC strongly, preventing autoimmunity (central tolerance). Strong self-binders would be dangerous, not helpful, which rules out keeping them.

questions.q: A newborn has protective IgG that crossed the placenta from the mother. What kind of immunity is this?
o: Natural active immunity
Active immunity means the infant's own immune system made the response.
Artificial active immunity
That describes vaccination.
Artificial passive immunity
That describes injected antibodies such as antivenom.
Natural passive immunity
Correct: antibodies made by someone else were received without a deliberate procedure.
questions.note: Passive immunity fades in weeks to months; no memory forms.
questions.x: Immunity is active when the person's own immune system makes the response and passive when ready-made antibodies come from someone else. It is natural when it happens without medical intervention and artificial when it comes from a vaccine or injection. Maternal IgG crossing the placenta is therefore natural passive immunity, which gives immediate protection but no memory and fades within months.

questions.q: How do cytotoxic T cells kill virus-infected cells?
o: Secreting antibodies against viral proteins
Antibodies come from plasma cells.
Releasing perforin and granzymes that trigger apoptosis
Correct: perforin opens pores and granzymes activate caspases in the target cell.
Phagocytosing the whole infected cell
Phagocytosis is done by macrophages and neutrophils.
Activating the complement cascade with IgM
Complement activation is not how CD8⁺ T cells kill.
questions.x: CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells recognize viral peptide on MHC I and release granules containing perforin, which forms pores in the target membrane, and granzymes, proteases that enter and activate caspases. They can also kill through Fas ligand. Either way the infected cell dies by apoptosis, which avoids spilling viral particles. Phagocytosis of whole cells is a macrophage function.

questions.q: When a B cell class-switches from making IgM to making IgG, what stays the same?
o: The heavy-chain constant region
This is exactly what changes in class switching.
The antigen specificity of the antibody
Correct: switching swaps the heavy-chain constant region but keeps the same variable region.
The antibody's effector functions
Effector functions depend on the constant region, which changes.
Its pentameric structure
Secreted IgG is a monomer, unlike pentameric IgM.
questions.x: Class switching uses DNA recombination to replace the heavy-chain constant region, for example Cμ with Cγ, while keeping the same rearranged VDJ variable exon. The antibody therefore binds the same antigen but gains new effector functions, such as crossing the placenta for IgG. Effector functions are tempting but they live in the constant region, which is exactly what changes.

questions.q: In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies block and destroy acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. What symptom results?
o: Sustained, uncontrollable muscle contraction
Blocking receptors reduces stimulation; it does not cause spasms.
Loss of skin sensation
Sensory neurons do not rely on these nicotinic muscle receptors.
Increased muscle strength
Fewer functional receptors weaken contraction.
Muscle weakness that worsens with repeated use
Correct: fewer receptors make end-plate potentials fail more often as ACh release runs down.
questions.x: Normally each nerve impulse releases far more ACh than needed, giving a safety margin. In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce the number of nicotinic ACh receptors, so end-plate potentials barely reach threshold. With repeated stimulation ACh release per impulse declines, more fibers fail to fire and weakness worsens with use, improving with rest or acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

questions.q: Why can a transplant recipient's T cells attack a donor kidney?
o: Donor cells display MHC molecules that the recipient recognizes as foreign
Correct: mismatched MHC (HLA) is the main trigger of rejection.
Donor cells lack all MHC molecules
Donor cells do express MHC, just a different set.
The kidney releases toxins that activate T cells
Rejection is driven by antigen recognition, not toxins.
The recipient's B cells convert into cytotoxic T cells
B cells cannot become T cells.
questions.note: Closer HLA matching means less rejection.
questions.x: MHC molecules (HLA in humans) are extremely polymorphic, so donor and recipient usually differ. Recipient T cells recognize foreign donor MHC, directly or as peptides presented by their own APCs, and attack the graft. This is why transplant teams match HLA closely and use immunosuppressive drugs. Donor cells are not missing MHC; they express a different set.

questions.q: Chemical digestion of starch begins in which part of the digestive tract?
o: Stomach, through pepsin
Pepsin digests protein, not starch.
Duodenum, through bile
Bile emulsifies fat and has no enzymes.
Mouth, through salivary amylase
Correct: salivary amylase starts hydrolyzing starch before food is swallowed.
Large intestine, through bacterial fermentation
Fermentation acts only on carbohydrate that escaped earlier digestion.
questions.x: Salivary α-amylase begins hydrolyzing starch into maltose and short dextrins while food is in the mouth; it is inactivated by stomach acid. Pancreatic amylase continues the work in the duodenum, and brush border enzymes finish it. Pepsin in the stomach is a protease, so carbohydrate digestion pauses there.

questions.q: An autoimmune disease destroys gastric parietal cells. Which deficiency is most likely to follow?
o: Pepsinogen, because parietal cells make it
Chief cells make pepsinogen.
Bile salts, because parietal cells produce them
Bile salts are made by the liver.
Vitamin K, because parietal cells synthesize it
Vitamin K comes from diet and gut bacteria.
Vitamin B₁₂, because intrinsic factor is no longer made
Correct: parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, needed for B₁₂ absorption in the ileum.
questions.note: Parietal cells: HCl + intrinsic factor. Chief cells: pepsinogen.
questions.x: Parietal cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B₁₂ and is required for its absorption in the terminal ileum, so autoimmune destruction of parietal cells causes B₁₂ deficiency and pernicious (megaloblastic) anemia. Pepsinogen is the tempting answer, but it comes from chief cells.

questions.q: Pepsinogen secreted by chief cells becomes active pepsin mainly because of:
o: Enteropeptidase from the duodenal brush border
Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen in the small intestine.
Bile salts from the gallbladder
Bile does not activate gastric enzymes.
The low pH created by HCl in the stomach lumen
Correct: acid triggers autocatalytic cleavage of pepsinogen, and pepsin then activates more.
Bicarbonate from the pancreas
Bicarbonate raises pH and inactivates pepsin.
questions.note: Zymogens protect the cells that secrete them.
questions.x: Chief cells release inactive pepsinogen so they do not digest themselves. Below about pH 2 to 3, HCl from parietal cells unfolds pepsinogen and triggers its autocatalytic cleavage to pepsin, and pepsin then activates more pepsinogen. Enteropeptidase is the tempting answer, but it activates trypsinogen in the duodenum.

questions.q: Peptides and stomach distension after a meal stimulate G cells. Which hormone do they release, and what does it do?
o: Secretin, which stimulates HCl secretion
Secretin comes from the duodenum and reduces gastric acid.
Gastrin, which stimulates HCl secretion
Correct: gastrin acts on parietal cells (directly and via histamine) to raise acid output.
Cholecystokinin, which stimulates HCl secretion
CCK comes from the duodenum and slows gastric activity.
Gastrin, which inhibits gastric motility
Gastrin increases gastric motility and acid.
questions.x: G cells in the stomach antrum release gastrin when they detect peptides and amino acids, stomach distension or vagal stimulation. Gastrin travels in blood to parietal cells, increasing HCl secretion directly and via histamine from ECL cells, and it increases gastric motility. Secretin and CCK come from the duodenum and generally slow the stomach.

questions.q: Acidic chyme enters the duodenum. Which hormone is released, and what does it do?
o: Secretin, which stimulates bicarbonate release from the pancreas
Correct: secretin triggers HCO₃⁻-rich pancreatic juice to neutralize acid.
Gastrin, which stimulates bicarbonate release from the stomach
Gastrin increases acid; it is not released by duodenal acid.
Insulin, which stimulates bile release
Insulin regulates blood glucose, not bile.
Secretin, which stimulates gallbladder contraction
Gallbladder contraction is mainly a CCK action.
questions.x: When acidic chyme lowers duodenal pH, S cells release secretin, which tells the pancreas and bile ducts to secrete HCO₃⁻-rich fluid that neutralizes the acid and protects the mucosa and enzymes. Secretin also reduces gastric acid secretion. Gallbladder contraction is the job of CCK, the other duodenal hormone, which is the common mix-up.

questions.q: A fatty meal reaches the duodenum. Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released. Which effect does CCK produce?
o: Gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion
Correct: CCK delivers bile and digestive enzymes to digest fat and protein.
Faster gastric emptying
CCK slows gastric emptying to give the duodenum time.
Increased gastric acid secretion
Duodenal hormones like CCK tend to inhibit the stomach.
Relaxation of the gallbladder
CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.
questions.x: Fats and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate I cells to release CCK. CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to deliver bile, stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, and slows gastric emptying so the small intestine can process the meal. It also promotes satiety. Faster gastric emptying is the tempting reverse.

questions.q: How do bile salts aid fat digestion?
o: They hydrolyze triglycerides into fatty acids
Bile contains no digestive enzymes; lipase does the hydrolysis.
They emulsify fat droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
Correct: amphipathic bile salts break large droplets into small ones.
They activate pancreatic lipase by cleaving it
Lipase is secreted active; colipase helps it, not bile cleavage.
They transport fats across the enterocyte membrane by active transport
Fatty acids diffuse into enterocytes after micelles deliver them.
questions.x: Bile salts are amphipathic: their hydrophobic face binds fat and their hydrophilic face faces water, breaking large fat globules into small droplets (emulsification) and greatly increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase. They then form micelles that ferry fatty acids and monoglycerides to the enterocyte surface. Bile contains no digestive enzymes itself.

questions.q: A patient has surgery that removes the terminal ileum. Which combination of problems is most likely?
o: Iron deficiency and calcium excess
Iron is absorbed mostly in the duodenum.
Loss of gastric acid and pepsin
Acid and pepsin come from the stomach.
Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency and fat malabsorption
Correct: the ileum absorbs B₁₂-intrinsic factor and recycles bile salts; losing bile salts impairs fat digestion.
Inability to digest starch in the mouth
Salivary amylase is unaffected by ileal surgery.
questions.note: Enterohepatic circulation returns bile salts from the ileum to the liver.
questions.x: The terminal ileum has two special jobs: absorbing the vitamin B₁₂-intrinsic factor complex and reabsorbing bile salts for enterohepatic recycling. Without it, B₁₂ deficiency develops and the bile salt pool shrinks, so fat is poorly emulsified and absorbed, causing steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin loss. Iron is mostly absorbed in the duodenum, so iron deficiency is the less likely problem.

questions.q: A person with lactase deficiency drinks milk. Why do bloating and diarrhea follow?
o: Lactose is absorbed and becomes toxic in the blood
Without lactase, lactose is not absorbed.
Milk protein triggers IgE-mediated allergy
That is milk allergy, a different condition.
Lactose blocks bile secretion
Lactose does not affect bile.
Undigested lactose draws water into the gut and is fermented by colon bacteria
Correct: lactose stays in the lumen, causing osmotic diarrhea and gas.
questions.x: Lactase on the brush border splits lactose into glucose and galactose for absorption. Without it, lactose stays in the gut lumen, osmotically drawing water and causing diarrhea, and colonic bacteria ferment it into gas and short-chain acids, causing bloating. It is an enzyme deficiency, not an immune reaction, unlike true milk protein allergy.

questions.q: Glucose is absorbed from the intestinal lumen into enterocytes against its gradient. What powers this?
o: Direct ATP hydrolysis by a glucose pump
No primary active pump moves glucose.
Simple diffusion through the membrane
Polar glucose cannot cross lipid bilayers efficiently and cannot move uphill by diffusion.
The Na⁺ gradient, through Na⁺-glucose cotransport
Correct: SGLT1 uses Na⁺ moving down its gradient, which the Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains (secondary active transport).
Endocytosis of glucose molecules
Glucose is too small to need vesicle transport.
questions.x: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the basolateral membrane keeps enterocyte Na⁺ low. On the apical side, SGLT1 couples glucose entry to Na⁺ flowing down its gradient, letting glucose accumulate inside against its own gradient; glucose then leaves by facilitated diffusion through GLUT2. This is secondary active transport: ATP is spent indirectly, by the pump, not by a glucose-specific pump.

questions.q: What is the main role of micelles in the small intestine?
o: Carrying fatty acids and monoglycerides to the brush border for absorption
Correct: micelles ferry hydrophobic lipid products through the watery layer next to enterocytes.
Carrying triglycerides through the lymph to the blood
That is the role of chylomicrons.
Digesting proteins into amino acids
Proteases, not micelles, digest proteins.
Absorbing water in the colon
Micelles form in the small intestine and handle lipids.
questions.note: Micelles in the lumen; chylomicrons leave the cell.
questions.x: Lipase products (fatty acids and monoglycerides) are hydrophobic and cannot cross the watery layer lining the brush border on their own. Bile salts form micelles that dissolve these products in their core and ferry them to the enterocyte surface, where they diffuse in. Inside the cell they are rebuilt into triglycerides and exported in chylomicrons, which is the tempting mix-up in choice B.

questions.q: What is the main absorptive function of the large intestine?
o: Absorbing most amino acids
Amino acids are absorbed mainly in the small intestine.
Digesting fats with bile
Fat digestion happens in the small intestine.
Secreting intrinsic factor
Intrinsic factor is secreted by the stomach.
Absorbing water and electrolytes
Correct: the colon concentrates the remaining contents into feces.
questions.note: Colon bacteria also make vitamin K and some B vitamins.
questions.x: By the time chyme reaches the colon, nearly all nutrients have been absorbed in the small intestine. The colon's job is to absorb most of the remaining water and electrolytes such as Na⁺, compacting contents into feces; its bacteria also ferment fiber and make vitamin K and some B vitamins. Faster transit through the colon leaves too much water behind, causing diarrhea.

questions.q: A section of intestine removed from the body still shows peristalsis when stretched. What best explains this?
o: The vagus nerve is still sending signals
The vagus was cut when the segment was removed.
The enteric nervous system in the gut wall coordinates motility on its own
Correct: the myenteric plexus can drive peristalsis without CNS input.
Skeletal muscle in the wall contracts voluntarily
The intestinal wall has smooth muscle.
Hormones from the brain are still circulating in the tissue
Isolated tissue receives no brain hormones.
questions.x: The gut wall contains its own enteric nervous system: the myenteric plexus between muscle layers controls motility and the submucosal plexus controls secretion and local blood flow. Stretch activates local sensory neurons that trigger contraction behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it, so peristalsis continues without the brain. Autonomic nerves only modulate this intrinsic activity.

questions.q: During a stressful sprint, sympathetic activity rises. What happens to digestive activity?
o: It increases, as gut motility and secretion rise
That is the parasympathetic (rest and digest) effect.
It decreases, as gut motility and secretion are inhibited
Correct: sympathetic output diverts blood away from the gut and slows digestion.
Only salivary secretion increases greatly
Sympathetic input makes a small amount of thick saliva, not a large increase.
It does not change, because the gut has no autonomic input
The gut receives both sympathetic and parasympathetic input.
questions.x: The sympathetic fight-or-flight response shifts resources to muscles, heart and lungs: it constricts gut arterioles, reduces motility and secretion, and tightens sphincters. Parasympathetic (vagal) activity does the opposite, promoting rest-and-digest functions. Expecting increased digestion confuses the two divisions.

questions.q: Which enzyme, secreted by the pancreas, digests triglycerides?
o: Amylase
Amylase digests starch.
Trypsin
Trypsin digests proteins.
Lactase
Lactase is a brush-border enzyme for lactose.
Lipase
Correct: pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides.
questions.x: Pancreatic juice contains enzymes for every major macronutrient: lipase for triglycerides, amylase for starch, and proteases such as trypsin for protein. Lipase, aided by colipase and bile-salt emulsification, cleaves triglycerides into two fatty acids and a monoglyceride. Lactase is a brush-border enzyme, not a pancreatic secretion.

questions.q: Severe liver disease raises blood ammonia. Which normal liver function has failed?
o: Converting ammonia to urea
Correct: the urea cycle in hepatocytes detoxifies ammonia.
Storing bile
The gallbladder stores bile.
Producing pancreatic enzymes
The pancreas makes its own enzymes.
Absorbing amino acids from the gut
Absorption occurs in the small intestine.
questions.x: Amino acid breakdown releases ammonia, which is toxic to the brain. Hepatocytes convert ammonia and CO₂ into urea through the urea cycle, and the kidneys excrete it. When the liver fails, ammonia accumulates and causes confusion and coma (hepatic encephalopathy). Bile storage is a gallbladder function and would not affect ammonia.

questions.q: An oral dose of a drug reaches lower blood levels than the same IV dose. Why?
o: Absorbed drug goes straight to the kidneys first
Gut blood drains to the liver, not directly to the kidneys.
Oral drugs enter the blood through the lungs
Oral drugs are absorbed in the GI tract.
Absorbed drug travels in the hepatic portal vein to the liver before reaching the systemic circulation
Correct: first-pass metabolism in the liver removes some drug.
The lymphatic system destroys absorbed drugs
Lymph does not metabolize drugs.
questions.x: Blood from the stomach and intestines drains into the hepatic portal vein, so an oral drug passes through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation. Liver enzymes metabolize part of it (first-pass metabolism), lowering bioavailability. An IV dose enters systemic veins directly and skips this step. Gut blood does not go straight to the kidneys.

questions.q: Villi and microvilli line the small intestine. What is their main function?
o: Moving chyme forward by beating like cilia
Microvilli do not beat; smooth muscle moves chyme.
Secreting hydrochloric acid
HCl comes from gastric parietal cells.
Storing bile between meals
The gallbladder stores bile.
Increasing surface area for absorption
Correct: these folds expand the absorptive area hundreds of times.
questions.x: Absorption rate depends on surface area. The small intestine multiplies its area with circular folds, finger-like villi and microvilli forming the brush border, together expanding the absorptive surface hundreds of times. Microvilli are rigid actin-supported projections that do not beat; chyme is moved by smooth muscle contraction.

questions.q: Long-term use of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause gastric ulcers. What is the main reason?
o: Increased pepsinogen activation by bile
NSAIDs do not work through bile.
Direct stimulation of gastrin release
NSAIDs do not raise gastrin.
Reduced prostaglandin-driven secretion of protective mucus and bicarbonate
Correct: NSAIDs block COX, lowering prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining.
Destruction of chief cells
Chief cell loss is not the mechanism.
questions.x: Prostaglandins, made by COX enzymes, protect the stomach by increasing mucus and bicarbonate secretion, maintaining mucosal blood flow and reducing acid secretion. NSAIDs block COX, removing this protection so acid and pepsin injure the mucosa. The problem is weakened defense, not increased gastrin.

questions.q: Weak tone in the lower esophageal sphincter most directly leads to:
o: Bile backing up into the liver
The LES has nothing to do with bile flow.
Reflux of acidic stomach contents into the esophagus
Correct: the LES normally blocks backflow; weakness causes heartburn.
Food moving too fast into the small intestine
That relates to the pyloric sphincter.
Impaired swallowing reflex in the pharynx
Swallowing is initiated above the LES.
questions.x: The lower esophageal sphincter stays contracted between swallows to keep acidic stomach contents out of the esophagus, whose lining lacks the stomach's protective mucus. When it is weak, acid refluxes, causing heartburn (GERD). The pyloric sphincter, at the other end of the stomach, regulates emptying into the duodenum.

questions.q: A proton pump inhibitor blocks the parietal cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Which effect is expected?
o: Less conversion of pepsinogen to pepsin
Correct: higher gastric pH slows pepsinogen activation.
More intrinsic factor secretion
PPIs do not increase intrinsic factor.
Lower gastrin release
Higher gastric pH removes acid feedback, so gastrin rises.
Faster fat digestion in the stomach
Fat is digested mainly in the small intestine; PPIs do not speed it.
questions.x: The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the final step of acid secretion, so blocking it raises gastric pH. Pepsinogen needs low pH to be cleaved into pepsin, so protein digestion in the stomach slows. Gastrin release is normally inhibited by acid, so a PPI removes this negative feedback and gastrin rises, which is why lower gastrin is the trap.

questions.q: In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus blocks the pancreatic ducts. Which stool finding is most likely?
o: Fatty, bulky stools from poor lipid digestion
Correct: little lipase reaches the duodenum, so fat passes undigested (steatorrhea).
Black, tarry stools from upper GI bleeding
Duct blockage does not cause bleeding.
Small, hard stools from too much water absorption
Malabsorbed fat causes loose, bulky stool.
Normal stools, because the liver replaces pancreatic enzymes
The liver does not make digestive enzymes.
questions.x: Thick secretions in cystic fibrosis block pancreatic ducts, so lipase, amylase, proteases and bicarbonate cannot reach the duodenum. Fat digestion depends almost entirely on pancreatic lipase, so undigested fat passes into stool, producing bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea) and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins. The liver makes bile but no digestive enzymes.

questions.q: In what form are dietary proteins mainly absorbed by enterocytes?
o: Intact proteins
Adults absorb almost no intact protein.
Amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides
Correct: brush-border peptidases and cotransporters handle these small products.
Polypeptides of 50 or more residues
These are too large for the transporters.
Nucleotides
Nucleotides come from nucleic acids, not protein.
questions.x: Pepsin and pancreatic proteases break proteins into peptides, which brush-border peptidases cut further. Enterocytes absorb free amino acids via Na⁺-coupled transporters and dipeptides and tripeptides via the H⁺-coupled PEPT1 transporter, then finish digestion inside. Adults absorb almost no intact protein, which is why oral insulin does not work.

questions.q: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct. Which effect is most expected?
o: Increased absorption of vitamin K
Without bile, vitamin K absorption falls.
Lower blood bilirubin
Blocked bile flow raises blood bilirubin, causing jaundice.
Pale stools and reduced absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
Correct: no bile reaches the gut, so fats and vitamins A, D, E and K are poorly absorbed.
Increased gastric acid secretion
The blockage does not affect parietal cells.
questions.x: A stone in the common bile duct stops bile from reaching the duodenum. Without bile salts, fats and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are poorly absorbed, and without bilirubin-derived pigments the stools turn pale. Conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood, so blood bilirubin rises, causing jaundice and dark urine.

questions.q: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
o: Glomerulus
The glomerulus is only the filtering part of the nephron.
Renal pelvis
The renal pelvis collects urine; it does not form it.
Ureter
The ureter carries urine to the bladder.
Nephron
Correct: each nephron filters blood and processes filtrate into urine.
questions.x: Each kidney has about a million nephrons, and each one performs every step of urine formation: filtration at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule, reabsorption and secretion along the tubule, and concentration in the collecting duct. The glomerulus is only the filtering part, so it is not the full functional unit.

questions.q: Where does filtration of blood plasma occur in the nephron?
o: In the loop of Henle
The loop reabsorbs water and salt.
In the collecting duct
The collecting duct adjusts water reabsorption.
From the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule
Correct: high glomerular pressure pushes fluid across the filtration barrier.
In the distal convoluted tubule
The DCT reabsorbs and secretes ions.
questions.x: Glomerular capillaries have unusually high hydrostatic pressure because they lie between two arterioles. This pressure forces water and small solutes through fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane and podocyte slits into Bowman's capsule. Every later segment modifies the filtrate by reabsorption or secretion rather than filtering blood.

questions.q: Which substance is normally almost absent from glomerular filtrate?
o: Albumin
Correct: plasma proteins are too large and too negatively charged to pass the filter.
Glucose
Glucose is freely filtered, then reabsorbed.
Urea
Urea is small and freely filtered.
Na⁺
Na⁺ is freely filtered.
questions.note: Protein in urine signals glomerular damage.
questions.x: The glomerular barrier filters by size and charge. Small solutes such as glucose, urea and Na⁺ pass freely, but albumin is large and negatively charged, so it is repelled by the negatively charged basement membrane. Glucose is freely filtered but then reabsorbed, so its absence from urine reflects reabsorption, not filtration.

questions.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered Na⁺ and water, as well as nearly all filtered glucose?
o: Loop of Henle
The loop reabsorbs about 25% of Na⁺ and builds the medullary gradient.
Distal convoluted tubule
The DCT reabsorbs only a small fraction.
Collecting duct
The collecting duct fine-tunes the last few percent.
Proximal convoluted tubule
Correct: the PCT reabsorbs about 65% of filtered Na⁺ and water and nearly all glucose and amino acids.
questions.x: The proximal convoluted tubule is the bulk reabsorber: its brush border and many mitochondria let it reclaim about 65% of filtered Na⁺ and water and nearly all glucose and amino acids, mostly via Na⁺-coupled transport. Later segments handle smaller fractions; the loop takes about 25% of Na⁺ and the DCT and collecting duct fine-tune the rest under hormonal control.

questions.q: In uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, glucose appears in the urine. Why?
o: The glomerulus stops filtering glucose
Glucose is filtered more, not less, when plasma levels rise.
The filtered glucose load exceeds the maximum rate of the proximal tubule transporters
Correct: once transporters saturate (transport maximum), extra filtered glucose is excreted.
The collecting duct secretes glucose into the urine
Glucose is not secreted by the collecting duct.
Insulin is needed for glucose to be filtered
Filtration does not require insulin.
questions.note: Glucosuria also causes osmotic diuresis.
questions.x: Glucose is freely filtered, and Na⁺-glucose cotransporters in the proximal tubule normally reclaim all of it. These carriers have a transport maximum, so when blood glucose rises above about 180 mg/dL the filtered load exceeds it and the excess is excreted. The glucose then draws water osmotically, causing polyuria; filtration itself is increased, not stopped.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the loop of Henle?
o: The ascending limb is permeable to water; the descending limb is not
The permeabilities are reversed.
The descending limb is permeable to water; the ascending limb is not
Correct: water leaves the descending limb while the ascending limb pumps out salt.
Both limbs are freely permeable to water
Then no medullary gradient could be built.
The descending limb actively pumps NaCl out
Active NaCl transport occurs in the thick ascending limb.
questions.x: The loop's two limbs have opposite properties. The thin descending limb is permeable to water but not salt, so water leaves into the salty medulla and filtrate becomes concentrated. The ascending limb is impermeable to water and removes NaCl, actively in the thick segment, which builds the medullary gradient and dilutes the filtrate. Reversing these permeabilities is the common trap.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the countercurrent multiplier in the loop of Henle?
o: Filtering proteins out of the blood
Filtration happens at the glomerulus.
Secreting H⁺ ions
Acid secretion is not the multiplier's job.
Producing renin
Renin is made by juxtaglomerular cells.
Creating a high solute concentration in the medulla so concentrated urine can form
Correct: the gradient lets water leave the collecting duct when ADH is present.
questions.x: The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl into the interstitium without water, and the countercurrent flow in the two limbs multiplies this small effect into a gradient from about 300 mOsm/L in the cortex to about 1,200 mOsm/L deep in the medulla. When ADH opens aquaporins, water leaves the collecting duct into this hypertonic medulla, producing concentrated urine.

questions.q: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) reduces urine volume by:
o: Inserting aquaporin channels into collecting duct cell membranes
Correct: aquaporin-2 lets water leave the duct into the hypertonic medulla.
Increasing Na⁺ reabsorption in the proximal tubule
ADH acts on the collecting duct, mainly on water.
Decreasing glomerular filtration
ADH does not mainly work by lowering GFR.
Pumping water actively out of the tubule
Water always moves passively by osmosis.
questions.x: ADH binds V₂ receptors on collecting duct cells, raising cAMP and causing vesicles with aquaporin-2 to fuse with the apical membrane. Water then moves passively by osmosis from the tubule into the hypertonic medulla, so urine becomes concentrated and smaller in volume. Water is never actively pumped; it always follows osmotic gradients.

questions.q: A patient produces 10 L/day of very dilute urine. Injecting ADH quickly concentrates the urine. What is the most likely cause?
o: The kidneys do not respond to ADH
In kidney-unresponsive DI, injected ADH would not help.
Too much aldosterone
Excess aldosterone retains Na⁺ and water; it does not cause large dilute urine output.
Too little ADH is released by the posterior pituitary
Correct: central diabetes insipidus responds to replacement ADH.
Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus causes glucose-rich urine, and ADH would not fix it.
questions.x: Large volumes of dilute urine suggest diabetes insipidus, in which collecting ducts cannot reabsorb water. If injected ADH (desmopressin) concentrates the urine, the kidneys respond normally, so the problem is too little ADH from the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary: central DI. In nephrogenic DI, the kidneys ignore ADH and injected hormone would not help.

questions.q: Loop diuretics block the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb. Why do they produce a large diuresis?
o: They increase glomerular filtration of proteins
They do not affect protein filtration.
They block aquaporins in the descending limb
They target an ion cotransporter, not aquaporins.
They stimulate ADH release
More ADH would decrease urine volume.
They weaken the medullary gradient, so less water is reabsorbed
Correct: without salt pumping, the medulla is less concentrated and ADH cannot pull out as much water.
questions.x: Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ transport in the thick ascending limb both reabsorbs a large share of filtered Na⁺ and builds the hypertonic medullary gradient. Loop diuretics like furosemide block it, so more salt stays in the tubule and the medulla becomes less concentrated; even with ADH, the collecting duct cannot pull water out. The result is a powerful diuresis that does not involve aquaporins directly.

questions.q: Which stimulus triggers renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells?
o: A rise in blood pressure
High pressure suppresses renin release.
A rise in NaCl delivered to the macula densa
High NaCl delivery suppresses renin.
A fall in renal perfusion pressure
Correct: low afferent arteriole pressure (and low NaCl at the macula densa) triggers renin.
A rise in ANP
ANP inhibits renin.
questions.x: Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole release renin when they sense low perfusion pressure, when the macula densa detects low NaCl delivery, or when sympathetic β₁ stimulation increases. All three signal low blood volume or pressure. High pressure, high NaCl delivery and ANP all suppress renin, so they are the opposite of what is needed.

questions.q: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure most directly by:
o: Dilating systemic arterioles
Dilation would lower blood pressure.
Constricting systemic arterioles
Correct: angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that raises total resistance.
Inhibiting aldosterone release
Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone release.
Inhibiting thirst
Angiotensin II increases thirst.
questions.x: Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, and ACE in the lung converts it to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II raises blood pressure most directly by constricting arterioles, which increases total peripheral resistance; it also stimulates aldosterone and ADH release and thirst, which raise blood volume more slowly. Vasodilation would lower pressure, not raise it.

questions.q: If only the efferent arteriole of a glomerulus constricts, what happens to the glomerular filtration rate in the short term?
o: It increases, because glomerular capillary pressure rises
Correct: constriction downstream backs up pressure in the glomerulus.
It decreases, because less blood enters the glomerulus
That describes afferent arteriole constriction.
It is unchanged, because filtration depends only on oncotic pressure
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure is a major driver of filtration.
It drops to zero, because blood can no longer leave the glomerulus
Partial constriction still lets blood leave.
questions.note: Afferent constriction lowers GFR; efferent constriction raises it.
questions.x: Glomerular capillary pressure depends on resistance on both sides. Constricting the efferent arteriole, downstream of the glomerulus, backs blood up and raises glomerular hydrostatic pressure, so GFR increases, though renal plasma flow falls. Constricting the afferent arteriole, upstream, lowers glomerular pressure and GFR, which is the tempting reversal.

questions.q: Inulin is used to measure the glomerular filtration rate. Which property makes it suitable?
o: It is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted
Correct: all inulin in the urine got there by filtration, so its clearance equals GFR.
It is fully reabsorbed after filtration
Then none would appear in urine, giving a clearance of zero.
It is actively secreted by the proximal tubule
Secretion would make clearance exceed GFR.
It binds tightly to plasma proteins
Protein-bound substances are not filtered.
questions.x: Clearance equals GFR only for a substance whose entire urinary amount arrived by filtration. Inulin is freely filtered, not protein bound, and neither reabsorbed, secreted nor metabolized, so its clearance equals GFR. A secreted substance would have clearance above GFR, and a reabsorbed one would have clearance below GFR.

questions.q: A freely filtered marker that is neither reabsorbed nor secreted has a urine concentration of 50 mg/mL and a plasma concentration of 0.5 mg/mL. Urine flow is 1 mL/min. What is the GFR?
o: 25 mL/min
The concentrations were multiplied instead of divided.
50 mL/min
Plasma concentration was left out of the formula.
100 mL/min
Correct: clearance = (U × V)/P = (50 × 1)/0.5 = 100 mL/min.
200 mL/min
Arithmetic error; 50 divided by 0.5 is 100.
questions.note: C = UV/P.
questions.x: Clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute: C = (U × V)/P. For a marker that is only filtered, clearance equals GFR: (50 mg/mL × 1 mL/min)/0.5 mg/mL = 100 mL/min. The common error is multiplying by plasma concentration instead of dividing, which gives 25 mL/min.

questions.q: A drug has a renal clearance of 300 mL/min, while the GFR is 120 mL/min. What can you conclude?
o: The drug undergoes net tubular reabsorption
Net reabsorption would make clearance less than GFR.
The drug is not filtered
An unfiltered, unsecreted drug would have near zero clearance.
The drug undergoes net tubular secretion
Correct: clearance above GFR means more leaves in urine than filtration alone delivers.
The drug is bound to albumin
Protein binding would lower clearance.
questions.note: Clearance > GFR: secreted. Clearance < GFR: reabsorbed.
questions.x: GFR sets the clearance a substance would have from filtration alone. A clearance of 300 mL/min, far above a GFR of 120 mL/min, means more drug reaches the urine than filtration delivers, so the tubules must be secreting it (net secretion). Net reabsorption, or protein binding that reduces filtration, would push clearance below GFR.

questions.q: In chronic metabolic acidosis, how do the kidneys compensate?
o: They excrete more HCO₃⁻
Losing base would worsen acidosis.
They reduce ammonia production
Ammonia production rises to carry away acid.
They lower the breathing rate
Breathing is controlled by the brainstem; the kidneys do not set it.
They secrete more H⁺ and generate new HCO₃⁻
Correct: more acid is excreted (much of it as NH₄⁺) and new bicarbonate returns to the blood.
questions.x: In metabolic acidosis the lungs compensate within minutes by hyperventilating, and over days the kidneys add their own correction. Tubule cells secrete more H⁺, buffered in urine by phosphate and especially by NH₄⁺ produced from glutamine, and each H⁺ excreted this way generates a new HCO₃⁻ returned to the blood. Excreting HCO₃⁻ would worsen the acidosis.

questions.q: After leaving the loop of Henle, filtrate flows next into the:
o: Proximal convoluted tubule
The PCT comes before the loop.
Bowman's capsule
Bowman's capsule is at the start of the nephron.
Distal convoluted tubule
Correct: the thick ascending limb leads into the DCT.
Ureter
Urine reaches the ureter only after the collecting duct and renal pelvis.
questions.note: Bowman's → PCT → loop → DCT → collecting duct.
questions.x: Filtrate follows a fixed path: Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, then the collecting duct, which several nephrons share. From there urine drains to the renal pelvis, ureter and bladder. The PCT comes before the loop, not after.

questions.q: Which sphincter of the urinary bladder is under voluntary control?
o: The external urethral sphincter, made of skeletal muscle
Correct: skeletal muscle under somatic control lets us delay urination.
The internal urethral sphincter, made of smooth muscle
Smooth muscle at the bladder neck is involuntary.
The detrusor muscle
The detrusor is smooth muscle that contracts under parasympathetic control.
The ureteral valves
These prevent backflow and are not voluntary.
questions.x: Two sphincters control the urethra. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle at the bladder neck under autonomic control, while the external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle of the pelvic floor under somatic, voluntary control, which lets us delay urination. The detrusor is the bladder wall's smooth muscle that contracts parasympathetically to empty the bladder.

questions.q: Patients with chronic kidney disease often develop low blood Ca²⁺. Which lost kidney function contributes most?
o: Secreting parathyroid hormone
PTH comes from the parathyroid glands.
Storing calcium in the medulla
The kidney does not store calcium.
Producing calcitonin
Calcitonin comes from the thyroid.
Converting vitamin D to its active form, calcitriol
Correct: renal 1α-hydroxylase makes calcitriol, which drives intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption.
questions.x: Vitamin D from skin or diet is hydroxylated first in the liver and then by 1α-hydroxylase in the proximal tubule, producing active calcitriol, which drives Ca²⁺ absorption in the intestine. Damaged kidneys make little calcitriol, so blood Ca²⁺ falls and PTH rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism). PTH and calcitonin come from other glands, so they are distractors.

questions.q: Urea helps the kidney concentrate urine. How?
o: It is actively pumped into the cortex
Urea's role is in the medulla, and it moves passively.
It is reabsorbed from the inner medullary collecting duct, adding to medullary osmolarity
Correct: urea recycling contributes about half of inner medullary solute.
It blocks aquaporins in the collecting duct
Urea does not block aquaporins.
It is secreted into the proximal tubule to dilute the filtrate
Urea concentrates the medulla; it does not dilute filtrate.
questions.x: With ADH present, water leaves the cortical and outer medullary collecting duct, concentrating urea in the tubule. The inner medullary collecting duct has urea transporters, so urea diffuses into the inner medulla, contributing about half of its osmolarity and strengthening the gradient for water reabsorption. Urea moves passively here, not by active pumping.

questions.q: What is the osmolarity of fluid leaving the thick ascending limb, compared with plasma?
o: Isotonic, because water follows solute everywhere
Water cannot follow NaCl out of the ascending limb.
Hypotonic, because NaCl is pumped out without water
Correct: the water-impermeable ascending limb is the diluting segment (about 100 mOsm/L).
Hypertonic, because water is reabsorbed
The ascending limb does not reabsorb water.
Hypertonic, because urea is added
The fluid becomes dilute here despite any urea.
questions.x: The thick ascending limb removes NaCl through Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporters but is impermeable to water. Solute leaves while water stays, so fluid leaving it is hypotonic, about 100 mOsm/L versus 300 in plasma, which is why it is called the diluting segment. Assuming water always follows solute is the trap; that holds only where the epithelium is water-permeable.

questions.q: What is the osmolarity of tubular fluid at the end of the proximal convoluted tubule, compared with plasma?
o: Much lower than plasma
Dilution happens in the thick ascending limb.
Much higher than plasma
Concentration happens deeper in the medulla.
Close to zero
Filtrate always contains solute.
About the same as plasma (isotonic)
Correct: water follows solute closely in the PCT, so osmolarity stays near 300 mOsm/L.
questions.x: The proximal tubule is highly permeable to water through aquaporin-1, so water follows reabsorbed solute almost exactly. Although about two thirds of filtrate volume is reabsorbed, the fluid leaving the PCT stays isotonic at about 300 mOsm/L. Changes in osmolarity begin in the loop of Henle, not the proximal tubule.

questions.q: After heavy sweating with little fluid intake, which kidney response is expected?
o: More ADH release, producing a small volume of concentrated urine
Correct: rising plasma osmolarity triggers hypothalamic osmoreceptors and ADH release.
Less ADH release, producing a large volume of dilute urine
That would worsen dehydration.
More ANP release, increasing Na⁺ excretion
ANP rises with high, not low, blood volume.
Less renin release
Low blood volume increases renin.
questions.x: Sweating loses more water than salt, so plasma osmolarity rises and blood volume falls. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger thirst and ADH release, inserting aquaporins so the kidney returns a small volume of concentrated urine. Falling volume also stimulates renin, while ANP falls, because the atria are less stretched.

questions.q: In a glomerulus, capillary hydrostatic pressure is 55 mmHg, Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure is 15 mmHg, and capillary oncotic pressure is 30 mmHg. What is the net filtration pressure?
o: 40 mmHg favoring filtration
The oncotic pressure, which opposes filtration, was ignored.
70 mmHg favoring filtration
Bowman's pressure was added instead of subtracted.
10 mmHg favoring filtration
Correct: 55 − 15 − 30 = 10 mmHg outward.
10 mmHg favoring reabsorption
The sign is reversed; outward forces exceed inward forces.
questions.note: Bowman's space oncotic pressure is about zero.
questions.x: Net filtration pressure is the sum of Starling forces: glomerular hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, while Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure and glomerular oncotic pressure push it back. NFP = 55 − 15 − 30 = 10 mmHg favoring filtration, since Bowman's oncotic pressure is about zero. Forgetting the oncotic pressure gives 40 mmHg.

questions.q: Where in the male reproductive system does spermatogenesis occur?
o: Epididymis
The epididymis stores sperm and lets them mature; it does not make them.
Prostate gland
The prostate adds fluid to semen.
Vas deferens
The vas deferens transports sperm during ejaculation.
Seminiferous tubules of the testes
Correct: germ cells develop into sperm along the walls of the seminiferous tubules.
questions.x: Spermatogenesis takes place along the walls of the seminiferous tubules, where spermatogonia divide and pass through meiosis while being nourished by Sertoli cells. The resulting sperm then move to the epididymis to mature and gain motility, and the vas deferens carries them during ejaculation. The prostate only adds fluid to semen.

questions.q: In the testes, LH and FSH act on different cells. Which pairing is correct?
o: LH stimulates Sertoli cells to make testosterone; FSH acts on Leydig cells
The targets are reversed.
Both hormones act only on sperm cells directly
Sperm lack these receptors; somatic support cells respond.
LH stimulates Leydig cells to make testosterone; FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis
Correct: Leydig cells are interstitial; Sertoli cells nurse developing sperm.
FSH stimulates Leydig cells to make estrogen only
Leydig cells mainly make testosterone in response to LH.
questions.x: The two gonadotropins act on different testicular cells. LH stimulates interstitial Leydig cells to make testosterone, while FSH acts on Sertoli cells, which nurse developing sperm, make androgen-binding protein and secrete inhibin that feeds back to suppress FSH. Swapping the targets is the classic trap; Sertoli cells support sperm and do not make testosterone.

questions.q: Sperm leaving the seminiferous tubules cannot yet swim effectively. Where do they mature and gain motility?
o: Urethra
Sperm pass through the urethra only during ejaculation.
Epididymis
Correct: sperm spend days to weeks in the epididymis acquiring motility.
Seminal vesicles
Seminal vesicles add fluid but do not store maturing sperm.
Bladder
Sperm do not pass through the bladder.
questions.note: Path: seminiferous tubules → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
questions.x: Sperm leaving the seminiferous tubules are not yet motile or fully able to fertilize. During one to two weeks in the epididymis they mature and gain motility, and they are stored there until ejaculation propels them through the vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra. Final capacitation happens later, in the female reproductive tract.

questions.q: Semen contains fructose that fuels sperm. Which gland supplies most of it?
o: Seminal vesicles
Correct: seminal vesicles secrete fructose-rich fluid that forms most of semen's volume.
Prostate gland
The prostate adds a milky, slightly alkaline fluid with enzymes.
Bulbourethral glands
These secrete a small amount of clear mucus before ejaculation.
Sertoli cells
Sertoli cells support sperm in the tubules but do not supply semen fructose.
questions.x: Three accessory glands make seminal fluid. The seminal vesicles contribute most of the volume, a fructose-rich fluid that fuels sperm motility; the prostate adds a milky, slightly alkaline fluid with enzymes; and the bulbourethral glands release a small amount of mucus that neutralizes residual urine. Sertoli cells nourish sperm in the tubules but do not contribute to semen.

questions.q: Why are the testes located in the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity?
o: Spermatogenesis needs a temperature about 2 °C below core body temperature
Correct: undescended testes at core temperature produce few sperm.
Testosterone production needs direct sunlight
Testosterone synthesis does not depend on light.
The scrotum lets sperm be delivered directly into the blood
Sperm are never released into the blood.
There is no room in the abdomen for the testes
Location reflects temperature needs, not lack of space.
questions.x: Spermatogenesis works best at about 2 to 3 °C below core temperature, so the testes sit in the scrotum, where muscle contraction and a countercurrent heat exchanger in the spermatic cord keep them cool. Testes that remain in the abdomen (cryptorchidism) produce few sperm, although Leydig cells may still make testosterone. The position reflects temperature needs, not space.

questions.q: At what stage is the human oocyte arrested when it is released at ovulation?
o: Prophase I, completed only at fertilization
Prophase I arrest ends just before ovulation, when meiosis I is completed.
Metaphase II, completed only if fertilization occurs
Correct: the secondary oocyte finishes meiosis II after sperm entry.
Anaphase I, completed at implantation
Oocytes do not pause in anaphase I.
Meiosis already completed, so it is haploid and mature
Meiosis II is not finished until fertilization.
questions.x: Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I from fetal life until puberty. Just before ovulation the LH surge lets one complete meiosis I, forming a secondary oocyte and the first polar body, which then arrests again at metaphase II. Meiosis II finishes only if a sperm fertilizes it, producing the second polar body. The ovulated egg is therefore not yet a completed haploid ovum.

questions.q: What triggers ovulation in the middle of the menstrual cycle?
o: A sharp fall in estrogen
Estrogen peaks just before the LH surge.
A rise in progesterone from the corpus luteum
The corpus luteum forms after ovulation.
An LH surge caused by positive feedback from high estrogen
Correct: sustained high estradiol switches the hypothalamus and pituitary to positive feedback.
A drop in FSH to zero
FSH actually rises a little along with the LH surge.
questions.note: Mid-cycle is the classic example of positive feedback.
questions.x: Through most of the cycle, estrogen exerts negative feedback on GnRH, LH and FSH. When a dominant follicle sustains high estradiol for about two days, feedback switches to positive, causing a sharp LH surge (with a smaller FSH rise) that triggers ovulation about a day later. Progesterone rises only after ovulation, when the corpus luteum forms.

questions.q: After ovulation, what is the main role of the corpus luteum?
o: Releasing a second oocyte
Only one oocyte is normally released per cycle.
Secreting LH to trigger ovulation
LH comes from the anterior pituitary.
Producing FSH to recruit new follicles
FSH is a pituitary hormone.
Secreting progesterone that maintains the endometrium
Correct: progesterone keeps the uterine lining ready for implantation.
