questions.x: After ovulation, the remaining follicle cells become the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone and some estrogen. Progesterone turns the endometrium secretory and ready for implantation, and suppresses new LH and FSH surges. Without hCG from an embryo, the corpus luteum degenerates in about two weeks, progesterone falls and menstruation begins.

questions.q: Home pregnancy tests detect hCG. What is hCG's main role in early pregnancy?
o: Triggering ovulation of another oocyte
Ovulation is suppressed during pregnancy.
Stimulating milk ejection
Milk ejection is triggered by oxytocin.
Maintaining the corpus luteum so it keeps secreting progesterone
Correct: hCG from the trophoblast acts like LH and prevents corpus luteum regression.
Breaking down the endometrium
hCG helps preserve the endometrium.
questions.note: The placenta takes over progesterone production later.
questions.x: The corpus luteum normally degenerates about 14 days after ovulation. If an embryo implants, its trophoblast secretes hCG, which acts on LH receptors to rescue the corpus luteum so it keeps making progesterone and maintaining the endometrium. By the end of the first trimester the placenta makes enough progesterone itself, and hCG falls.

questions.q: Where does fertilization usually take place?
o: The ampulla of the uterine (fallopian) tube
Correct: sperm usually meet the oocyte in the widest part of the tube.
The uterine cavity
The embryo implants in the uterus several days after fertilization.
The ovary
The oocyte is released from the ovary before fertilization.
The cervix
The cervix is a passage for sperm, not the usual fertilization site.
questions.x: After ovulation, the oocyte is swept by the fimbriae into the uterine tube, and fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, its widest section. The zygote then divides as cilia and smooth muscle move it toward the uterus, where the blastocyst implants about a week after fertilization. Implantation in the tube instead causes an ectopic pregnancy.

questions.q: During the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, which change occurs in the uterus?
o: Progesterone drives secretory changes in the endometrium
Secretory changes occur in the luteal phase.
The endometrium is shed
Shedding is menstruation, at the start of the cycle.
hCG maintains the endometrium
hCG appears only if a pregnancy occurs.
Estrogen drives proliferation of the endometrium
Correct: rising estradiol from growing follicles thickens the lining.
questions.x: The ovarian and uterine cycles are linked by hormones. In the follicular phase, growing follicles secrete rising estradiol, which drives the proliferative phase: the endometrium thickens and its glands and spiral arteries grow. Only after ovulation does progesterone from the corpus luteum make the lining secretory, so attributing secretory changes to this phase is the common trap.

questions.q: Hormone levels across a 28-day cycle show progesterone peaking near day 21 and falling sharply by day 28, when menstruation starts. What best explains the onset of menstruation?
o: An LH surge causes the endometrium to shed
The LH surge triggers ovulation at mid-cycle.
The corpus luteum regresses, so progesterone and estrogen fall
Correct: without hormone support, spiral arteries constrict and the functional layer sheds.
Rising progesterone causes the lining to break down
Progesterone maintains the lining; its fall causes shedding.
hCG from the embryo dissolves the endometrium
hCG would prevent menstruation, not cause it.
questions.x: Without hCG from an embryo, the corpus luteum regresses about 10 to 12 days after ovulation, so progesterone and estrogen fall. Loss of this support makes spiral arteries constrict, the functional layer becomes ischemic and is shed as menstruation. Progesterone maintains the lining; it is its withdrawal, not its rise, that triggers shedding.

questions.q: Combined oral contraceptives contain estrogen and progestin. How do they mainly prevent pregnancy?
o: They destroy sperm in the uterus
That describes spermicides.
Negative feedback suppresses GnRH, FSH and LH, preventing ovulation
Correct: steady hormone levels block the follicle development and LH surge needed to ovulate.
They raise FSH to exhaust all follicles
They lower FSH.
They trigger an early LH surge
Ovulation requires the LH surge they prevent.
questions.x: Steady doses of estrogen and progestin exert continuous negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering GnRH, FSH and LH. Without enough FSH, no dominant follicle develops, and without a rising estrogen spike there is no positive-feedback LH surge, so ovulation does not occur. Progestin also thickens cervical mucus as a secondary effect.

questions.q: After menopause, which hormone pattern is typical?
o: High estrogen with low FSH and LH
Estrogen falls after menopause.
Low estrogen with low FSH and LH
The pituitary is still working, and without feedback it secretes more.
High progesterone with low LH
Without ovulation there is no corpus luteum making progesterone.
Low estrogen with high FSH and LH
Correct: depleted follicles make little estrogen, so negative feedback is lost and gonadotropins rise.
questions.x: At menopause the ovaries run out of responsive follicles, so estrogen and inhibin production collapse. The hypothalamus and pituitary still work, and without negative feedback they secrete much more GnRH, FSH and LH. High FSH with low estrogen is the hallmark lab pattern; low gonadotropins would point to a pituitary problem instead.

questions.q: In the placenta, how do the fetal and maternal circulations relate?
o: They exchange substances across tissue layers without their blood mixing
Correct: fetal capillaries in villi are bathed by maternal blood but stay separate.
Maternal blood flows directly through fetal vessels
The bloods do not mix normally.
Fetal blood flows directly into maternal arteries
Separation also prevents this.
They are linked only by lymphatic vessels
Exchange happens across villus capillaries, not lymphatics.
questions.x: Fetal blood stays inside capillaries within the chorionic villi, which are bathed by maternal blood pooled in intervillous spaces. O₂, nutrients, wastes and IgG cross the thin layers between them by diffusion and transport, but the two bloodstreams normally never mix. This separation is why mother and fetus can have different blood types.

questions.q: During labor, stretch of the cervix increases oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions and further stretches the cervix. This is an example of:
o: Negative feedback
Negative feedback would reduce the stimulus.
Feedforward control
Feedforward anticipates a change before it happens.
Positive feedback
Correct: the output amplifies the stimulus until delivery ends the loop.
Homeostatic set-point regulation
This loop drives change rather than maintaining a set point.
questions.x: In positive feedback the response amplifies the original stimulus rather than opposing it. Cervical stretch triggers oxytocin release, oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions, and stronger contractions stretch the cervix more, until delivery removes the stimulus and ends the loop. Negative feedback, the usual homeostatic pattern, would weaken contractions instead.

questions.q: Which branch of the autonomic nervous system mainly controls erection, and which mainly controls ejaculation?
o: Sympathetic controls erection; parasympathetic controls ejaculation
The roles are reversed.
Parasympathetic controls both
Emission and ejaculation need sympathetic input.
The somatic nervous system controls both
Erection is autonomic, not voluntary motor control.
Parasympathetic controls erection; sympathetic controls ejaculation
Correct: parasympathetic NO-mediated dilation causes erection; sympathetic output drives emission.
questions.note: Mnemonic: point (parasympathetic) and shoot (sympathetic).
questions.x: Erection results from parasympathetic pelvic nerves releasing NO, which raises cGMP and dilates penile arterioles so the erectile tissue fills with blood. Emission (moving sperm and glandular fluid into the urethra) is driven by sympathetic output, and ejaculation adds rhythmic somatic contraction of pelvic floor muscles. The mnemonic point and shoot captures parasympathetic then sympathetic.

questions.q: A bodybuilder takes high doses of synthetic testosterone. What is expected in his testes?
o: Enlargement and higher sperm counts
Exogenous androgen suppresses, rather than boosts, testicular function.
Increased LH release and Leydig cell growth
High testosterone lowers LH.
Atrophy and lower sperm counts, from suppressed LH and FSH
Correct: negative feedback shuts down gonadotropins, so the testes shrink.
No change, because synthetic hormones bypass feedback
Synthetic androgens still act on the hypothalamus and pituitary.
questions.x: Testosterone feeds back on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary to suppress GnRH, LH and FSH. Exogenous androgen therefore shuts down LH, so Leydig cells stop making testosterone within the testis, and without high local testosterone and FSH, Sertoli cells cannot support spermatogenesis. The testes shrink and sperm counts fall, even though blood androgen levels are high.

questions.q: Which description fits skeletal muscle?
o: Non-striated, single nucleus, involuntary
That describes smooth muscle.
Striated, multinucleated and under voluntary control
Correct: skeletal fibers form by fusion of myoblasts and are controlled by somatic motor neurons.
Striated, mostly single nucleus, linked by intercalated discs
That describes cardiac muscle.
Non-striated, multinucleated and voluntary
Skeletal muscle is striated.
questions.x: Skeletal muscle fibers form when many myoblasts fuse, so each fiber is long and multinucleated; regular sarcomeres make them striated, and somatic motor neurons give voluntary control. Cardiac muscle is also striated but its cells usually have one or two nuclei and are joined by intercalated discs, while smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle cells contract in a coordinated wave. Which structure makes this possible?
o: Gap junctions in intercalated discs
Correct: gap junctions let ions pass directly, so action potentials spread between cells.
Neuromuscular junctions on every cell
Cardiac cells are not individually innervated by motor neurons.
Tight junctions that block ion flow
Blocking ion flow would prevent electrical coupling.
T-tubules connecting neighboring cells
T-tubules carry signals into one cell, not between cells.
questions.x: Cardiac myocytes are joined end to end by intercalated discs. Desmosomes in the discs hold cells together mechanically, while gap junctions allow ions to flow directly between cells, so an action potential spreads rapidly and the myocardium contracts as a functional syncytium. Unlike skeletal muscle, individual cardiac cells are not each driven by a motor neuron.

questions.q: Smooth muscle has no troponin. In smooth muscle, what does Ca²⁺ bind to start contraction?
o: Calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase
Correct: Ca²⁺-calmodulin activates MLCK, which phosphorylates myosin.
Tropomyosin directly
Ca²⁺ does not bind tropomyosin.
Actin directly
Ca²⁺ does not bind actin to start contraction.
Acetylcholinesterase
That enzyme breaks down ACh at synapses.
questions.x: In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺ from the extracellular fluid and SR binds calmodulin. The Ca²⁺-calmodulin complex activates myosin light-chain kinase, which phosphorylates myosin heads so they can cycle on actin. This regulation is on the myosin side, unlike skeletal and cardiac muscle, where Ca²⁺ binds troponin to move tropomyosin off actin.

questions.q: When a skeletal muscle sarcomere shortens, which band stays the same length?
o: I band
The I band shortens as thin filaments slide inward.
A band
Correct: the A band equals the length of the thick filaments, which do not shorten.
H zone
The H zone shrinks as thin filaments overlap the thick ones.
Distance between Z lines
Z lines move closer as the sarcomere shortens.
questions.note: Filaments slide; they do not shorten.
questions.x: Contraction works by sliding filaments: thin filaments are pulled toward the center of the sarcomere, but neither filament shortens. The A band spans the full length of the thick filaments, so it stays constant, while the I band and H zone, which are regions without overlap, shrink and the Z lines move closer together.

questions.q: After death, muscles become stiff (rigor mortis). Why?
o: Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Removing Ca²⁺ relaxes muscle; it does not stiffen it.
Acetylcholine release increases
Neural activity stops at death.
Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Correct: ATP binding is required to release the myosin head from actin.
Actin and myosin filaments break down instantly
Filament breakdown later is what ends rigor.
questions.x: In the cross-bridge cycle, ATP binding is what releases myosin from actin. After death, ATP is depleted while Ca²⁺ leaks from the SR and exposes binding sites, so myosin heads bind actin and remain locked in place, stiffening the muscle. Rigor ends days later only when the proteins themselves decompose.

questions.q: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine causes depolarization of the motor end plate by:
o: Activating muscarinic G protein-coupled receptors
Muscarinic receptors are at parasympathetic targets, not skeletal muscle.
Opening Cl⁻ channels
Cl⁻ influx would hyperpolarize.
Releasing Ca²⁺ directly from the T-tubules
Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, later in the sequence.
Opening ligand-gated nicotinic receptor channels that let Na⁺ in
Correct: nicotinic receptors are cation channels; Na⁺ influx dominates.
questions.x: Acetylcholine released by a motor neuron binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate. These are ligand-gated cation channels; Na⁺ influx outweighs K⁺ efflux, producing an end-plate potential that triggers a muscle action potential. Muscarinic receptors are G protein-coupled and mediate parasympathetic effects on organs like the heart and gut, not skeletal muscle.

questions.q: How does an action potential on the skeletal muscle surface trigger Ca²⁺ release inside the fiber?
o: It causes Ca²⁺ to enter only from the extracellular fluid
Skeletal muscle relies mainly on SR stores.
It triggers ACh release inside the fiber
ACh acts only at the end plate surface.
It travels down T-tubules, where voltage sensors open ryanodine receptors on the SR
Correct: DHP receptors in T-tubules are mechanically linked to SR release channels.
It breaks down the SR membrane
The SR stays intact and releases Ca²⁺ through channels.
questions.x: The muscle action potential spreads into T-tubules, where voltage-sensing dihydropyridine receptors change shape. In skeletal muscle they are physically linked to ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so depolarization opens these release channels and Ca²⁺ floods the cytosol. Cardiac muscle differs by relying on Ca²⁺ influx to trigger SR release.

questions.q: What is required for a skeletal muscle to relax after contraction?
o: ATP-driven pumping of Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Correct: SERCA pumps lower cytosolic Ca²⁺ so troponin-tropomyosin cover binding sites again.
Release of more Ca²⁺ from the SR
More Ca²⁺ sustains contraction.
Binding of ACh to more receptors
More ACh would stimulate further contraction.
Breakdown of tropomyosin
Tropomyosin must stay intact to block binding sites.
questions.note: Relaxation, like contraction, uses ATP.
questions.x: Contraction continues as long as cytosolic Ca²⁺ keeps troponin shifted and actin binding sites exposed. Relaxation requires SERCA pumps to use ATP to move Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum; as Ca²⁺ falls, tropomyosin again blocks the sites. ATP is also needed to detach myosin heads, so both contraction and relaxation consume ATP.

questions.q: A muscle is stimulated repeatedly at a high frequency, so that each twitch begins before the last one ends. Force builds into a smooth, sustained contraction. Why?
o: Each action potential is larger than the last
Action potentials are all-or-none and do not grow.
More ATP makes each myosin head pull harder
Force per cross-bridge does not rise with ATP.
The refractory period of skeletal muscle is longer than its twitch
The short refractory period is what makes tetanus possible.
Cytosolic Ca²⁺ stays high, keeping binding sites exposed continuously
Correct: rapid stimuli outpace Ca²⁺ reuptake, giving summation and fused tetanus.
questions.x: A single twitch is brief because Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the SR quickly. When action potentials arrive faster than Ca²⁺ can be removed, cytosolic Ca²⁺ stays elevated and twitches summate, fusing into tetanus. This is possible because the skeletal muscle refractory period (a few ms) is much shorter than the twitch, which is the key contrast with cardiac muscle.

questions.q: How does the nervous system produce a stronger skeletal muscle contraction to lift a heavier load?
o: Making each action potential larger
Action potentials are all-or-none.
Recruiting more motor units, from small to large
Correct: activating more motor units (size principle) raises total force.
Making individual fibers contract with more than maximal force
Individual fibers cannot exceed their maximal tetanic force.
Adding new muscle fibers on the spot
Fiber number does not change on the spot.
questions.x: Each muscle fiber gives an all-or-none action potential, so force is graded in two ways: recruiting more motor units and increasing their firing rate. Under the size principle, small, fatigue-resistant motor units are recruited first and larger, more forceful ones are added as demand rises. Action potentials cannot be made larger, which rules out choice A.

questions.q: Which fiber type would a marathon runner's leg muscles rely on most?
o: Type IIx (fast glycolytic) fibers with few mitochondria
These fatigue quickly and suit sprints.
Type I (slow oxidative) fibers rich in mitochondria and myoglobin
Correct: these fibers resist fatigue by using aerobic metabolism.
Fibers with no myoglobin
Myoglobin stores O₂ needed for endurance.
Fibers that rely mainly on creatine phosphate
Creatine phosphate lasts only seconds.
questions.x: Type I slow oxidative fibers have many mitochondria, dense capillaries and abundant myoglobin, giving them a red color and the ability to make ATP aerobically for hours with little fatigue. Type IIx fast glycolytic fibers produce rapid, powerful contractions but tire within seconds to minutes, so they suit sprinting and lifting rather than marathons.

questions.q: During the first few seconds of a maximal sprint, what keeps muscle ATP levels nearly constant?
o: Oxidation of fatty acids
β-oxidation is too slow for an instant burst.
Breakdown of muscle protein
Protein is not a fast energy source.
Gluconeogenesis in muscle
Gluconeogenesis occurs in liver and kidney and uses ATP.
Creatine phosphate donating phosphate to ADP
Correct: creatine kinase regenerates ATP almost instantly from phosphocreatine.
questions.x: Muscle holds only a few seconds' worth of ATP. Phosphocreatine is a high-energy buffer: creatine kinase transfers its phosphate to ADP almost instantly, keeping ATP nearly constant during the first several seconds of maximal effort. Anaerobic glycolysis then takes over, and oxidative pathways like β-oxidation are too slow for this initial burst.

questions.q: A skeletal muscle is stretched far beyond its resting length before being stimulated. Compared with optimal length, its active force will be:
o: Lower, because thick and thin filaments overlap less
Correct: fewer myosin heads can reach actin.
Higher, because stretch stores more energy in the filaments
Active force depends on overlap; passive tension is different.
Unchanged, because force depends only on Ca²⁺
Ca²⁺ is required, but overlap limits force too.
Higher, because more Ca²⁺ is released
Stretching does not substantially increase Ca²⁺ release.
questions.note: Length-tension curve peaks at optimal overlap.
questions.x: Active force depends on how many myosin heads can bind actin, which depends on filament overlap. At optimal length overlap is maximal; when stretched far beyond it, thin filaments are pulled away from thick filaments, so fewer cross-bridges form and active force falls. Passive tension from elastic tissue rises with stretch, but that is not contractile force.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release from motor neurons. What effect results?
o: Sustained spastic contraction
Spasms come from too much ACh or blocked breakdown.
Increased muscle tone
Less ACh lowers tone.
Flaccid paralysis
Correct: no ACh means no end-plate depolarization and no contraction.
Faster muscle twitches
Without ACh release there are no twitches.
questions.x: Botulinum toxin is a protease that cleaves SNARE proteins needed for synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, so motor neurons cannot release ACh. Without ACh, the end plate is not depolarized and the muscle cannot contract, causing flaccid paralysis. Spastic contraction is the opposite pattern, produced by excess ACh or blocked inhibitory signaling.

questions.q: Organophosphate pesticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase. What happens at the neuromuscular junction?
o: ACh release stops, causing immediate flaccid paralysis
Release is unaffected; breakdown is blocked.
ACh receptors are destroyed by antibodies
That is myasthenia gravis.
Ca²⁺ can no longer bind troponin
The toxin acts at the synapse, not on troponin.
ACh builds up, causing twitching followed by paralysis from persistent depolarization
Correct: lasting depolarization inactivates Na⁺ channels near the end plate.
questions.x: Acetylcholinesterase normally ends the signal by hydrolyzing ACh in the synaptic cleft. When it is inhibited, ACh accumulates and keeps nicotinic receptors open, first causing twitching, then persistent depolarization that inactivates nearby voltage-gated Na⁺ channels so new action potentials cannot fire, producing paralysis. ACh release itself is not affected.

questions.q: In the knee-jerk reflex, which receptor detects the sudden stretch of the quadriceps?
o: Golgi tendon organ
Golgi tendon organs sense tension and inhibit contraction.
Pacinian corpuscle in the skin
Pacinian corpuscles detect vibration and deep pressure.
Muscle spindle
Correct: intrafusal spindle fibers sense muscle stretch and trigger reflex contraction.
Nociceptor
Nociceptors detect harmful stimuli.
questions.x: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors made of intrafusal fibers lying parallel to the main muscle fibers. A tap on the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps and its spindles, whose Ia afferents synapse directly on α motor neurons in the spinal cord, causing reflex contraction. Golgi tendon organs sit in series with the tendon and sense tension, not stretch.

questions.q: Shivering helps restore body temperature in the cold. How?
o: Shivering constricts skin blood vessels
Vasoconstriction is a separate response.
Rapid muscle contraction hydrolyzes ATP, releasing heat
Correct: muscle metabolism is inefficient, and much energy becomes heat.
Shivering produces sweat that insulates the skin
Sweat cools the body.
Shivering reduces the metabolic rate
Shivering raises metabolic heat production.
questions.x: Shivering is rapid, involuntary contraction of skeletal muscle that does little external work. Most of the energy from ATP hydrolysis is released as heat, raising heat production several-fold. It works with heat-conserving responses such as skin vasoconstriction, which reduces heat loss but does not itself generate heat.

questions.q: The smooth muscle of the intestinal wall can contract as a coordinated sheet. What allows this?
o: Gap junctions link single-unit smooth muscle cells electrically
Correct: single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle behaves like one unit.
Each cell has its own motor neuron
That describes multi-unit smooth muscle.
The cells are fused into multinucleated fibers
Multinucleated fibers are skeletal muscle.
Sarcomeres line up across all cells
Smooth muscle lacks sarcomeres.
questions.x: Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle, found in the gut, uterus and small blood vessels, has many gap junctions that let depolarization spread from cell to cell, so a whole sheet contracts together, often driven by pacemaker cells. Multi-unit smooth muscle, as in the iris and large airways, has cells innervated individually for fine control.

questions.q: Which cells break down bone matrix and release Ca²⁺ into the blood?
o: Osteoclasts
Correct: osteoclasts secrete acid and enzymes that resorb bone.
Osteoblasts
Osteoblasts build new bone matrix.
Osteocytes
Osteocytes maintain matrix and sense strain but do not do most resorption.
Chondrocytes
Chondrocytes make cartilage.
questions.note: Osteoclasts Carve; osteoblasts Build.
questions.x: Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells derived from monocytes. They seal onto bone and secrete H⁺ to dissolve hydroxyapatite and proteases such as cathepsin K to digest collagen, releasing Ca²⁺ and phosphate into the blood. Osteoblasts do the opposite, laying down new matrix, and become osteocytes once they are embedded in it.

questions.q: Blood Ca²⁺ falls. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is released. Which effect on bone helps restore Ca²⁺?
o: Increased deposition of Ca²⁺ into bone
That would lower blood Ca²⁺ further.
Increased bone resorption
Correct: PTH indirectly activates osteoclasts to release Ca²⁺ from bone.
Decreased osteoclast activity
That is the effect of calcitonin.
Conversion of bone to cartilage
PTH does not convert bone to cartilage.
questions.x: When blood Ca²⁺ falls, PTH raises it in three ways: it stimulates bone resorption, increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the distal tubule and stimulates calcitriol synthesis to boost intestinal absorption. In bone, osteoblasts respond to PTH by expressing RANKL, which activates osteoclasts indirectly. Decreasing osteoclast activity is what calcitonin does, the opposite hormone.

questions.q: Bone matrix contains hydroxyapatite and type I collagen. What does collagen mainly contribute?
o: Hardness and resistance to compression
That is mainly the mineral, hydroxyapatite.
Storage of fat
Fat is stored in yellow marrow.
Flexibility and tensile strength
Correct: collagen fibers resist pulling and keep bone from being brittle.
Production of blood cells
Blood cells are made in red marrow.
questions.x: Bone is a composite. Hydroxyapatite crystals give hardness and resistance to compression, while type I collagen fibers give flexibility and tensile strength, preventing brittle fracture. Removing the mineral leaves a rubbery bone, while defective collagen, as in osteogenesis imperfecta, makes bones brittle and fracture-prone.

questions.q: Where does a long bone grow in length during childhood?
o: At the outer periosteum only
The periosteum adds width, not length.
In the medullary cavity
The medullary cavity holds marrow.
At the articular cartilage
Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces.
At the epiphyseal (growth) plate
Correct: chondrocytes proliferate at the plate and are replaced by bone.
questions.note: Plates close after puberty.
questions.x: Long bones lengthen by endochondral growth at the epiphyseal plate: chondrocytes divide and enlarge on the epiphyseal side, while older cartilage on the diaphyseal side calcifies and is replaced by bone. After puberty, sex steroids close the plates, so length stops increasing. The periosteum adds bone to the outer surface, increasing width, not length.

questions.q: In adults, where does most hematopoiesis occur?
o: Yellow marrow in long bone shafts
Yellow marrow is mostly fat.
Compact bone osteons
Osteons are structural units of compact bone.
Red marrow in flat bones and the ends of long bones
Correct: red marrow in the pelvis, sternum, vertebrae and proximal long bones makes blood cells.
Articular cartilage
Cartilage does not make blood cells.
questions.x: At birth almost all marrow is red and active in blood cell production. With age, marrow in the shafts of long bones becomes fat-filled yellow marrow, so in adults hematopoiesis is concentrated in red marrow of flat bones, such as the pelvis, sternum, ribs and vertebrae, and in the proximal ends of the femur and humerus.

questions.q: In compact bone, how do osteocytes deep in the matrix receive nutrients?
o: Through canaliculi linking them to the central (Haversian) canal
Correct: tiny channels connect lacunae to vessels in the central canal.
By diffusion straight through mineralized matrix
Mineralized matrix blocks diffusion.
From synovial fluid
Synovial fluid nourishes articular cartilage.
Through lymph capillaries within each lacuna
Lacunae do not contain lymph capillaries.
questions.x: Compact bone is built of osteons: concentric lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal containing blood vessels. Osteocytes sit in lacunae between lamellae and extend cytoplasmic processes through tiny canaliculi, which link lacunae to each other and to the central canal, carrying nutrients and wastes. The mineralized matrix itself is too dense for diffusion.

questions.q: Damaged articular cartilage heals very slowly. What is the main reason?
o: Cartilage is heavily mineralized
Hyaline cartilage is not mineralized like bone.
Cartilage cells divide too rapidly
Adult chondrocytes divide slowly.
Cartilage is full of osteoclasts
Osteoclasts resorb bone, not cartilage.
Cartilage is avascular, so nutrients reach it only by diffusion
Correct: no blood supply means few repair cells and slow delivery.
questions.x: Hyaline articular cartilage has no blood vessels, nerves or lymphatics. Its chondrocytes, sparse and trapped in lacunae, get nutrients only by diffusion from synovial fluid, and there is no blood supply to deliver repair cells. Damage therefore heals slowly and incompletely, unlike bone, which is richly vascular.

questions.q: Which structure connects a muscle to a bone?
o: Ligament
Ligaments connect bone to bone.
Tendon
Correct: tendons transmit muscle force to bone.
Cartilage
Cartilage cushions joints.
Bursa
A bursa is a fluid sac that reduces friction.
questions.x: Dense regular connective tissue forms both tendons and ligaments, but they connect different things. Tendons attach muscle to bone and transmit contractile force to move the skeleton, while ligaments connect bone to bone and stabilize joints. A bursa is a fluid-filled sac that reduces friction where tendons glide over bone.

questions.q: After menopause, women lose bone mass faster. Which mechanism best explains this?
o: Higher estrogen stimulates osteoblasts too much
Estrogen falls after menopause.
Lower estrogen allows osteoclast activity to increase
Correct: estrogen normally restrains osteoclasts, so its loss favors resorption.
Calcitonin secretion rises sharply
Calcitonin would reduce resorption, and it does not rise sharply.
Bone stops absorbing Ca²⁺ from the diet
Bone does not absorb dietary Ca²⁺; the intestine does.
questions.x: Estrogen restrains bone resorption by limiting osteoclast formation and promoting osteoclast apoptosis, partly by reducing RANKL signaling and increasing osteoprotegerin. After menopause estrogen falls, osteoclast activity outpaces osteoblast formation, and bone mass drops, leading to osteoporosis. Calcitonin plays only a minor role in adult humans and does not rise at menopause.

questions.q: The biceps inserts on the forearm close to the elbow, far from the hand. What is the consequence of this lever arrangement?
o: The muscle needs less force than the load
The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so more force is needed.
The hand moves a shorter distance than the insertion point
The hand moves farther than the insertion.
The joint acts as a second-class lever
Effort between fulcrum and load makes it third-class.
The muscle must exert more force than the load, but the hand moves farther and faster
Correct: a short effort arm trades force for range and speed.
questions.note: Torque balance: F × short arm = load × long arm.
questions.x: The elbow is a third-class lever: the fulcrum is the joint, the biceps applies effort between the fulcrum and the load in the hand. Torque balance (force × lever arm) means a short effort arm must produce much more force than the load. The payoff is that a small shortening of the muscle moves the hand through a large arc quickly, trading force for speed and range.

questions.q: In the epidermis, which layer contains the dividing stem cells that replace lost skin cells?
o: Stratum basale
Correct: basal keratinocytes divide and push new cells upward.
Stratum corneum
The corneum is made of dead, flattened cells.
Stratum lucidum
The lucidum is a clear layer of dead cells in thick skin.
Stratum granulosum
Cells here are already differentiating and dying.
questions.x: The stratum basale, the deepest epidermal layer, contains keratinocyte stem cells that divide continuously; their daughters are pushed upward through the spinosum, granulosum and (in thick skin) lucidum, filling with keratin and dying. They end as the dead, flattened stratum corneum, which is shed. The basale also contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.

questions.q: Differences in human skin color are mainly due to differences in:
o: The number of melanocytes per area of skin
Melanocyte density is fairly constant across skin tones.
The thickness of the dermis
Dermal thickness does not set skin color.
The amount and type of melanin made by melanocytes
Correct: melanocyte numbers are similar; their melanin output differs.
The amount of keratin in the stratum corneum
Keratin does not set pigment.
questions.note: Melanin shields keratinocyte DNA from UV.
questions.x: People of all skin tones have roughly the same number of melanocytes per area. Differences in color come from how much melanin those cells make, the ratio of dark eumelanin to reddish pheomelanin, and how melanosomes are packaged and transferred to keratinocytes. Assuming darker skin has more melanocytes is the common misconception.

questions.q: On a hot day, which skin responses help cool the body?
o: Constriction of dermal arterioles and piloerection
These conserve heat in the cold.
Shivering and sweating together
Shivering produces heat.
Reduced blood flow to the skin
Less skin flow would trap heat in the core.
Dilation of dermal arterioles and sweating
Correct: more blood near the surface loses heat, and sweat evaporation removes heat.
questions.x: To cool the body, the hypothalamus dilates dermal arterioles, carrying warm core blood to the surface where heat radiates away, and activates eccrine sweat glands, whose sweat removes heat as it evaporates. Constriction of skin vessels and piloerection are heat-conserving responses to cold, so they are the opposite of what is needed.

questions.q: In cold conditions, what does constriction of dermal arterioles accomplish?
o: It produces heat by muscle contraction
Heat production is the role of shivering.
It increases sweating to insulate the skin
Sweating cools the body.
It reduces heat loss by keeping warm blood in the body core
Correct: less warm blood near the surface means less heat radiated away.
It increases blood flow to the skin to warm it
Constriction decreases skin blood flow.
questions.x: Skin is the main site of heat loss to the environment. When it is cold, sympathetic nerves constrict dermal arterioles, shunting warm blood away from the surface and keeping it in the core, so less heat is lost by radiation and conduction. This conserves heat but does not produce it; heat production comes from shivering and increased metabolism.

questions.q: How does the skin contribute to vitamin D production?
o: Melanocytes secrete active vitamin D
Melanocytes make melanin.
UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into a vitamin D precursor
Correct: the precursor is then hydroxylated in the liver and kidney.
Sweat glands release vitamin D onto the skin
Sweat does not contain meaningful vitamin D.
The skin fully activates vitamin D without the kidney
The final activating step occurs in the kidney.
questions.x: In the skin, UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into previtamin D₃, which becomes cholecalciferol. This is inactive: the liver adds a hydroxyl to form 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and kidney 1α-hydroxylase forms active calcitriol. So the skin starts synthesis but cannot activate vitamin D by itself.

questions.q: A patient has burns that destroy the epidermis over a large area. Which threats are most immediate?
o: Loss of body fluid and infection
Correct: the stratum corneum normally blocks water loss and microbes.
Inability to absorb nutrients
Absorption is a gut function.
Loss of bone marrow function
Marrow is not part of the skin.
Excess vitamin D production
Burned skin makes less vitamin D, not more.
questions.x: The epidermis, especially the keratinized stratum corneum with its lipid layer, is the body's main barrier against water loss and microbial invasion. Losing it over a large area lets plasma fluid leak out, risking hypovolemic shock, and lets bacteria enter, risking infection and sepsis. These are the most urgent threats after major burns.

questions.q: Langerhans cells are scattered in the epidermis. What is their main role?
o: Capturing antigens and presenting them to T cells in lymph nodes
Correct: they are dendritic cells of the skin.
Producing melanin
That is the role of melanocytes.
Sensing light touch
Merkel cells and Meissner corpuscles sense touch.
Secreting sweat
Sweat glands secrete sweat.
questions.x: Langerhans cells are the dendritic cells of the epidermis. They extend processes between keratinocytes to capture antigens that cross the skin, then migrate through lymphatics to lymph nodes, where they present peptides on MHC to activate naive T cells. Pigment comes from melanocytes and touch sensing from Merkel cells and corpuscles.

questions.q: Two runners exercise at the same intensity, one in dry air and one in very humid air. The humid-air runner's core temperature rises faster. Why?
o: Humid air stops the sweat glands from secreting
Sweat glands still secrete; the sweat just does not evaporate well.
Sweat evaporates poorly in humid air, so less heat is removed
Correct: cooling comes from evaporation, which slows when the air is saturated.
Humid air causes dermal arterioles to constrict
Heat stress dilates skin vessels.
Humid air increases muscle heat production
Heat production is the same at equal intensity.
questions.x: Sweat cools the body only when it evaporates, because evaporation absorbs heat of vaporization from the skin. In very humid air the vapor pressure gradient between skin and air is small, so sweat drips off without evaporating and little heat is removed. Sweat glands keep secreting, which is why humid heat causes heavy sweating yet poor cooling.

questions.q: During vigorous exercise, which combination of changes occurs?
o: Arterioles constrict in active muscle and dilate in the gut
Blood flow is redirected toward working muscle.
Heart rate falls while stroke volume rises
Both heart rate and stroke volume rise.
Arterioles dilate in active muscle and constrict in the gut
Correct: local metabolites dilate muscle vessels while sympathetic tone diverts flow from the gut.
Breathing slows to conserve O₂
Ventilation rises to clear CO₂ and take in O₂.
questions.x: During exercise, local metabolites in working muscle (CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine, low O₂) dilate its arterioles, while sympathetic output constricts arterioles in the gut and kidneys, redirecting cardiac output to muscle. Heart rate and stroke volume both rise to increase cardiac output, and ventilation increases to supply O₂ and remove CO₂.

questions.q: A person loses 1 L of blood quickly. Which set of compensations is expected?
o: Slower heart rate, vasodilation, less renin, more urine
These would lower pressure further.
More ANP and greater Na⁺ excretion
ANP is released when volume is high, not low.
Less EPO, to reduce blood viscosity
Blood loss lowers O₂ delivery, which increases EPO.
Faster heart rate, vasoconstriction, more renin and ADH, less urine
Correct: baroreflex and hormones work together to restore pressure and volume.
questions.x: Rapid blood loss lowers pressure, reducing baroreceptor firing. The sympathetic response raises heart rate and contractility and constricts arterioles and veins, while reduced renal perfusion triggers renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone, and ADH rises, so urine output falls and volume is conserved. ANP falls because the atria are less stretched, and EPO rises later to replace red cells.

questions.q: An opioid overdose depresses breathing. Which immediate change in arterial blood is expected?
o: Lower PaCO₂ and higher pH
That is respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation.
Higher HCO₃⁻ with normal pH right away
Renal compensation takes days.
Higher PaCO₂ and lower pH
Correct: hypoventilation retains CO₂, causing respiratory acidosis.
Lower PaCO₂ and lower pH
Retained, not blown-off, CO₂ is what lowers pH here.
questions.note: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻
questions.x: Opioids depress the medullary respiratory centers, so ventilation falls and CO₂ is not removed. Rising PaCO₂ shifts CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ to the right, lowering pH: acute respiratory acidosis. HCO₃⁻ rises only slightly at first; meaningful renal compensation takes days. Low PaCO₂ would indicate hyperventilation, the opposite condition.

questions.q: Over weeks at high altitude, which adaptation increases the blood's O₂-carrying capacity?
o: More EPO release, raising red cell mass and hematocrit
Correct: chronic hypoxia drives the kidneys to release EPO.
Lower 2,3-BPG in red cells
2,3-BPG actually rises at altitude, aiding unloading.
Less ventilation to save energy
Ventilation stays elevated.
Smaller lung capacity
Lung capacity does not shrink.
questions.x: Chronic hypoxia at altitude stabilizes HIF in kidney cells, increasing EPO release, which stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red cells. Over weeks the hematocrit and hemoglobin concentration rise, increasing O₂-carrying capacity. Higher 2,3-BPG also helps, but by easing O₂ unloading to tissues rather than by raising carrying capacity.

questions.q: Which process is an example of negative feedback in homeostasis?
o: Platelets at a wound release signals that recruit more platelets
This amplifies the change, which is positive feedback.
Rising estrogen before ovulation triggers an LH surge
This mid-cycle loop is positive feedback.
Suckling increases oxytocin, which increases milk ejection and suckling
This loop amplifies the stimulus.
Rising body temperature triggers sweating, which lowers temperature
Correct: the response opposes the original change.
questions.x: Negative feedback counteracts a change and returns a variable toward its set point, as when rising body temperature triggers sweating and vasodilation that cool the body. Positive feedback amplifies a change until some outside event ends it, as in platelet plug formation, the mid-cycle LH surge and the milk-ejection reflex. Most homeostatic control is negative feedback.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how two organ systems cooperate to maintain homeostasis?
o: The kidneys remove CO₂, while the lungs remove urea
These roles are reversed and wrong; lungs exhale CO₂, kidneys excrete urea.
The respiratory system removes CO₂, helping the kidneys keep blood pH stable
Correct: lungs adjust CO₂ in minutes; kidneys adjust HCO₃⁻ and H⁺ over days.
The skin absorbs O₂ for the body, so the lungs handle only CO₂
Human skin gas exchange is negligible.
The digestive system excretes most urea, sparing the kidneys
Urea is excreted mostly by the kidneys.
questions.x: Blood pH depends on the ratio of HCO₃⁻ to dissolved CO₂. The lungs control CO₂, adjusting ventilation within minutes, while the kidneys control HCO₃⁻ and H⁺ excretion over hours to days. Together they keep pH near 7.4, and each can partly compensate when the other is disturbed. Lungs exhale CO₂ and kidneys excrete urea, so reversing these roles is wrong.
